News.title: AI could be nationalised and taken away from tech chiefs to ‘serve communities’, says Greens’ deputy leader
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TAKING BACK TECH AI could be nationalised and taken away from tech chiefs to ‘serve communities’, says Greens’ deputy leader







Next

ARTIFICIAL intelligence tech could be nationalised, according to the Greens’ deputy leader.

Rachel Millward said that AI should “serve communities” rather than “being owned by Silicon Valley proto-fascists”.



She also said a Green government would bring water firms into public ownership by Christmas.

Ms Millward told the party’s conference in Brighton: “Forget compensation for shareholders and creditors, these are insolvent companies.



“It’s time to take them back. What else could we take back?

“Imagine that instead of new technology being owned by Silicon Valley proto-fascists, it was owned by us.



“AI that serves communities instead of billionaires who buy our democracy.”

In his first Labour Party conference speech earlier this week, Mr Burnham said new legislation would repeal “Margaret Thatcher’s ideological ban on public ownership of water companies”.

He said it would start a decade-long process to strengthen public control, with mayors getting “new powers to hold water companies to account, with tougher consequences for those which repeatedly fail”.

The Greens warned that Burnham‘s 10-year plan was not urgent enough.

News.title: Andy Burnham accused of being ‘in hock to trade unions’ after caving in to their demands after first conference
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham was accused of being “in hock” to trade unions after caving in to their demands.

The PM made several bungs to the unions at his first conference as Labour leader this week.



It comes despite him saying that previous Governments had run the country for “vested interests”.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43million from unions.



Shadow Business Secretary Julia Lopez said: “If anyone needed proof that Labour are in hock to the unions, they need look no further. Labour know who pay their wages.

“Labour simply do not get business, because too many of their frontbench have never worked in one and have spent most of their careers pushing union demands.”

Announcements included £15million of taxpayers’ cash to bring back the Union Learning Fund.

And he announced a public ownership blitz of everything from water to housing.

Avanti West Coast train services will also be nationalised from March next year.

Chancellor John Healey promised a new age of industrialisation including a massive “buy British” push.



Controversially, the Home Secretary paved the way for a major climbdown on her flagship immigration curbs.

Shabana Mahmood signalled that tens of thousands of foreign workers would be protected from tougher settlement rules.

It came after a backlash led by Housing Secretary Angela Rayner and heavy union pressure.

Meanwhile Labour peer Lord Richard Walker fears the Government will raid business like “a piggybank” at the October 28 Budget.

He said firms are being lumbered with an “avalanche of costs” and called for an end to tax raids on them.

News.title: Green councillor sparks fury after telling campaigners to dress modestly & use Arabic phrases to win over Muslim voters
News.content:
Next

A GREEN councillor told campaigners to dress modestly and speak Arabic to win Muslim votes.

Asma Alam suggested door knockers could wear a keffiyeh, a scarf associated with Palestinians.



And they could greet voters by saying “As-salamu alaykum”, meaning “Peace be upon you”.

Manchester City councillor Ms Alam made the comments at a fringe event during the Green Party conference in Brighton.



She said there were “etiquettes” to take when approaching residents and voters in mosques.

Ms Alam, who described using bilingual speakers to target voters during the Gorton and Denton by-election, won by Green MP Hannah Spencer, added: “Saying as-salamu alaykum when you see a voter is instant brownie points from me.”

However, critics rounded on the policy, which Zack Polanski’s Greens insisted was “called treating people with respect”.

Fiyaz Mughal, a Muslim counter-extremism expert from charity Faith Matters, said: “It plays to the bigotry of low expectations by lumping all Muslims together as though we are religious zealots.”

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “The Green Party’s virtue-signalling is unprecedented.

“This is sectarian politics creeping into British elections.”



And Lord Ian Austin, a former Labour minister, added: “It is yet another pathetic example of how far Zack Polanski is willing to bend the knee to radical Islamists in pursuit of power.”

News.title: Labour finally ditch David Lammy’s plan to abolish most jury trials over fears it could erode people’s rights
News.content:
Next

LABOUR has finally scrapped its plan to ditch most jury trials.

The idea, set out by former Justice Secretary David Lammy, was condemned as an attempt to erode people’s rights in the court system.



It has been abandoned over the backlash, although more cases will still be heard in lower courts.

The Criminal Bar Association warned the revised plans would still shift 25,000 cases, including more complex assault, sexual assault and child abuse offences, on to magistrates every year.



BA chairman Andrew Thomas KC said: “They do not have enough magistrates, enough qualified legal advisers or enough resources to take on thousands of more sensitive cases.

“It would be a car crash if they tried to do it, especially at this time.”



It comes as the magistrates’ court backlog has risen by 40 per cent in some areas.

The Government is running a magistrates recruitment drive, but a Justice Committee report warned proposed targets are ambitious.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy described the latest proposals as “restricting juries by the back door”.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said strength of feeling on judge-only trials led to the change but he was still set on reforming the system — and said: “Justice delayed is justice denied.”

News.title: Baffled ‘dogger’ caught by Top Gear legend went ‘you’re Jeremy Clarkson!’ after being confronted in woods by farm
News.content:
Next

JEREMY Clarkson has revealed how he confronted a suspected dogger in the woods by his farm – and the surprising response the teen gave when caught.

The star of Clarkson’s Farm, 66, had previously told that the beautiful Cotswolds countryside was popular with doggers.



According to the former Top Gear host, his pub car park was a favourite spot to get frisky.

At first Jeremy suspected they were fly-tippers getting up to no good in the dead of night.



But no there was another reason why vehicles would be parked up in a lane, in what he calls the “black labrador and warm pint countryside”.

Writing for The Times, he said: “We like to think this is mostly the preserve of suburban housewives in home country pampas places like Beaconsfield but in the not too distant past, the car park at my remote Cotswolds pub was a hot spot as well.



“It’s even happened, on a smaller scale, on my farm.”

He was driving back one evening from his local pub when he spotted a “suspicious-looking” car parked up by one of the woods.

Unsure of what was going on he pulled up quietly to the passenger window.

What he saw caught him by surprise.



Clarkson said that he saw a young man, around the age of 17, who was smoking a “doobie” with one hand and was “frantically” performing a sex act with the other.

Eventually, the young man realised he was being watched and wound down his window, saying: “Oh my God, you’re Jeremy Clarkson.”

Then he added: “I rather wish we had met in different circumstances.”

Which Jeremy thought was the best line he’d ever heard.

When he officially opened his pub, The Farmer’s Dog, in 2024, Clarkson quickly found nothing was smooth sailing with the boozer.



And it turned out, the pub had always been popular but for very different reasons.

He was left flabbergasted when he discovered his new establishment was a popular haunt for doggers.

They would strip off their clothes and host romps in the bushes – he even found a G-string in the undergrowth.

He admitted at the time: “It was a very famous dogging site.

“It was gentleman usually, who stopped off there once it had gone dark to do whatever it is gentlemen in woods do at night.

“So I was a bit surprised to find a G-string there, because it suggested it had become more inclusive.

“Alan the Builder, who features in the show, he’s very local to there he was very aware, although he is keen to point out he never visited himself.”

News.title: Nigel Farage was ignored when he voiced his fears over death threats, says Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice
News.content:
Next

NIGEL Farage was ignored when he told of death threats, his party’s deputy leader claims.

The Reform UK boss had voiced his fears on many occasions over many years, according to Richard Tice.



But despite getting up to 300 death threats a month his claims were not believed, he said.

Mr Tice, speaking as the man accused of killing colleague Ann Widdecombe was charged with a terror offence against Mr Farage.



He said: “When actually things occur that are very close to home, so to speak, it’s pretty shocking.

“And I think what’s particularly upsetting for those of us in and around him is sometimes he’s not being believed, not being listened to, and, you know, we have just got in a sense deep regret over everything that’s happened over a long period of time.”

Mr Tice also warned the area around Parliament could be threatening for MPs, who often faced a cauldron of abuse.

He told BBC Radio 4: “I’ve had a pretty grim experience which resulted in armed police having to attend at very great speed at very short notice.”

Mr Farage faced criticism over a £5million gift from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne in April 2024. He insisted it was for security.

Joshua Kerry, 28, will face court next week over an alleged firebomb attack on Mr Farage’s London home last year.

News.title: Kemi has a chance to draw a clear line between her party and Labour by delivering the honest truth on our economy
News.content:
KEMI CAN OUTSCORE BLINKERED BURNHAM







Next

ANDY Burnham’s big speech has left the Tories an open goal on the economy.

This week Kemi Badenoch must make sure she doesn’t miss it.



The PM’s blinkered “back to the future” vision, which sets Britain on course for a 1970s recipe for chaos, is bad enough.

But Burnham was so dazzled by his dream of a state-run socialist paradise he failed to address any of the mounting problems throttling our finances today.



As Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith points out, our £330billion welfare bill is spiralling out of control, Labour tax raids are driving business chiefs abroad and there is a £5billion hole in our defence plan.

Rather than tackle this, the PM’s big ideas involve scrapping the triple lock, ripping up our voting system and rejoining the EU.

The Tory leader has the chance to draw a clear line between her party and Labour on all three fronts.

But what will really cut through to voters is a politician who understands that the answers to our problems are less government, less spending and less taxation.

Labour is supposed to be the workers’ party. So why does it not try to lift the crushing tax burden off their backs?

Andy Burnham claims he wants to bring honesty to our politics. But when he talks about Britain being run by “vested interests”, he is never honest about the bungs for his own vested interests: the unions who finance his party.



At Labour’s party conference in Liverpool, a new £15million trade union training fund was announced.

At the same time, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood backtracked on her immigration curbs under heavy union pressure.

And when the PM launches yet another attack on Margaret Thatcher, he should remember one thing.

Under Thatcher’s three terms the Tories created one million jobs, while under Labour there are a million young people alone out of work.

This week in Birmingham, Mrs Badenoch must deliver the honest truth: that unless we slash spending now, our economy may never recover.



GREEN-EYED MONSTERS

GREEN Party fanatics are voting today on a motion to declare Zionism as racism.

Zack Polanski’s infantile rabble are blinded by their hatred of Israel. But they also want to be the world’s wokest party.

So why don’t they direct their moral outrage towards a brutal regime that uses lethal force against women, secretly murders 30,000 innocent protesters and threatens anyone in a same-sex relationship with the death penalty?

It’s a country called Iran.

News.title: Chilling tales of US executions from killer bursting into flames to odd final meals after Christa Pike’s botched death
News.content:
Next

KILLER Christa Pike’s failed execution is the latest grim chapter in America’s death row history.

Pike — who tortured and ­murdered 19-year-old Colleen ­Slemmer in 1995 — refused her last meal, said her goodbyes and was strapped to a bed at a Tennessee prison.



“I’m ready to be free. This is a happy day,” she revealed, braced for lethal drugs to pulse through her veins on Wednesday. Instead, two ­pentobarbital jabs failed to kill her.

She was taken to hospital, where she remains in a critical condition, unconscious and on a ventilator.



It was announced yesterday that the head of prisons in Tennessee would be resigning.

The history of US executions is littered with similar chilling tales, from killers bursting into flames in the electric chair to bizarre final meals, last words and inmates ­surviving the bid to end their life.

Ted Bundy, who kidnapped, raped and murdered at least 30 women in the Seventies, died in the electric chair in 1989.

He refused a final meal, so Florida State Prison served the default menu of steak, eggs, hash browns and toast, which he did not touch.

His final words were: “Give my love to my family and friends.”

Minutes later, 2,000 volts surged through the electric chair, known as Old Sparky, while a crowd outside celebrated with fireworks and signs reading, “Fry Ted”.



Meanwhile, John Wayne Gacy — who murdered at least 33 men and boys — tucked into fried chicken, prawns, chips and strawberries as a final dish before his 1994 lethal injection.

And Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, who killed 168 with a 1995 truck blast, chose two pints of mint chocolate-chip ice cream before his 2001 execution.

But for a remarkable few, their “final day” was not to be final.



Romell Broom, who had been convicted of ­kidnap, rape and murder, dodged execution in Ohio in 2009 after ­officials spent two hours trying unsuccessfully to find a usable vein, puncturing his limbs 18 times.

After protracted legal wranglings and delays, a new date to end Broom’s life was set for 2022. But he died in 2020 after getting Covid.

Christa Pike was not Tennessee’s first failed execution this year.

In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers, who murdered three people in 1994, was called off.

Governor Bill Lee granted him a year’s reprieve as intravenous lines could not be found.



But botched bids are nothing new. Before lethal injection, condemned prisoners went to the electric chair, meant to be a humane alternative to hanging.

However, in 1946, Willie Francis, 17 — convicted of a 1944 murder — survived ­Louisiana’s electric chair as the equipment was not properly set up. He was successfully executed the following year.

Florida’s Old Sparky became infamous in 1990 during the execution of cop-killer Jesse Tafero, when flames erupted from his head as electricity surged through him.



Seven years on, teacher-killer Pedro Medina suffered a similar fate. And in 1999, when murderer Allen Lee Davis was executed in the same chair, blood poured from his nose and he suffered severe burns.

By then, America was shifting towards lethal injections. In 1982, killer Charles Brooks Jr was the first to die by this method in Texas.

Since 1976, most of the US’s 1,600 executions have been by injection, with just 163 by electrocution.

Yet nine states still authorise the electric chair, though alternatives in the US now include lethal injection, nitrogen gas and firing squad.

Michelle Lyons, who saw almost 300 executions between 2000 and 2012 while working for the Texas prison system, says: “There’s a strange smell in the execution chamber.



A weird, chemical odour I was told is due to the type of filter used in the air-conditioning system.”

Not all inmates use their dying breath for a profound farewell. Double murderer Thomas Grasso’s parting shot in 1995 was: “I did not get my Spaghettios.”

And in 2007, Texas murderer Vincent Gutierrez joked: “Where’s my stunt double?”



Killer Gary Gilmore declared, “Let’s do it” as he was executed by firing squad in Utah in 1977, apparently inspiring Nike’s Just Do It slogan.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And Jimmy Glass, who died in Louisiana in 1987, quipped at the end: “I’d rather be fishing.”

But serial killer Aileen Wuornos, ­executed in Florida in 2002, perhaps made the strangest statement. Like Arnold Scharwzenegger’s Terminator, she declared: “I’ll be back.”

News.title: Friends of FlyDubai pilot stabbed in cockpit left 'broken' and in 'disbelief'
News.content:
Friends of FlyDubai pilot stabbed in cockpit left 'broken' and in 'disbelief'

FlyDubai Captain Machchhar received blows to the back of his head, "one after the other" in what has been described as a 'terrorist attack' - his freinds have now shared their shock when they heard the news

View 5 Images Capt. Smit Machchhar was brutally attacked with an axe (Image: Israel's Foreign Ministry via AP)

Friends of the pilot who was attacked with an axe as he flew 182 people to Tel Aviv have described being 'broken' and in 'disbelief' when they heard the news.

A FlyDubai co-pilot, Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, is alleged to have attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with an axe before attempting to seize control of the plane. The flight, carrying 182 people, was nearly crashed before passengers and others intervened.

Captain Machchhar described how he received blows to the back of his head, "one after the other". The captain, who was badly injured, has said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarmingly unusual sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilise the plane.

Two passengers reportedly helped take control of the Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and land it. Passenger Almog Itali said one of them was a British pilot and that they "entered (the cockpit) and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia". Fighter jets were scrambled to escort the aircraft during its emergency landing.

View 5 Images Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, left, visits injured Indian Flydubai Capt. Smit Machchhar (Image: Government of Dubai Media Office)

FlyDubai pilot's chilling mayday call as passengers scream amid hijacking fears READ MORE :

Yaniv Hayoun was one of the passengers labelled a "hero" by Israeli Prime Minister after he overpowered the knifeman who allegedly stabbed the pilot of the plane.

He revealed that he had learned how to land the jet after watching a TV show, Air Crash Investigation.

Yaniv told Benjamin Netanyahu: “We pinned him down to keep him secure and then I jumped into it (the cockpit) and pulled the controls.” Netanyahu asked how he knew to pull in a backwards motion, to which Yaniv said: “I watch Air Crash Investigations Mr Prime Minister.”

Captain Machchhar was praised as a "true hero" by the Israeli prime minister, who said he was "amazed" by Captain Machchhar's "courage and coolness of judgement under impossible conditions". Mr Netanyahu said the pilot had "saved so many souls" during the incident.

View 5 Images Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi speaking with FlyDubai pilot Capt. Smit Machchhar on YouTube (Image: Narendra Modi YouTube Channel vi)

“When it happens to the person you know, the person you love, it breaks you”

Captain Dhaval Patel, a fellow pilot who trained alongside Machchhar in New Zealand, told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) that he and Machchhar have known each other for “close to two decades” accoriding to PEOPLE.

“I saw the first glimpse, and I was just not ready to believe it was Captain Smit,” he said of the moment he learned of the attack. “When it happens to the person you know, the person you love, it breaks you.”

“I vividly remember him helping colleagues and peers, educating them on the concepts of aviation with so much clarity and knowledge,” he continued. “And I had the privilege of getting my fourth stripe on becoming a captain by his hand.”

View 5 Images A sculpture made by India's sand artist Sudarsan Pattnaik depicts India's pilot Smit Machchhar (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Mr Netanyahu claimed the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radicalisation", but provided no evidence.

In a phone call with Mr Netanyahu, Captain Machchhar described the terrifying attack in more detail. He said: "It was a normal flight. The co-pilot wanted to pray, which a lot of locals do. It's not out of the ordinary.

"While he was praying, out of respect, I was looking at the front and not at the back [of the cockpit]. After about four or five minutes, there was a big blow to the back of my head. My first thought was that there was catastrophic damage to the aircraft and something is not right.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 5 Images Hamam Al Hammami allegedly attacked the pilot (Image: LINKEDIN)

‌



"But after that, the blows kept coming, one after the other. That's when I realised it wasn't the aicraft. It was the other guy who was in the cockpit with me. I did try to stop him but because of his initial blows, my vision was almost like nothing. I was completely blurred out and, at that point, the next feeling that I had was that the aircraft was sharply going down.

"My memory is still in bits and pieces but this is what I remember. I did manage to open the door once but I think he shut it back. I was lying down on the cockpit floor and I felt the aircraft and the whooshing sound and people screaming. I had one last fight left in me.

"Call it personal or for the people, but I knew that if I didn't [open the door], I was going to die. That's when I pushed against everything I had and opened the door. Thankfully, people were waiting to pounce back and take over control. The rest is what you know, sir."

UAE officials have described the incident as "terrorist" in a statement that cited the UAE attorney general.

News.title: Andy Burnham praised for axing controversial plan to curb jury trials
News.content:
Andy Burnham praised for axing controversial plan to curb jury trials

The proposals had been pushed by former PM Keir Starmer to tackle the court backlog, but met furious opposition, including from Labour MPs and legal professionals

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has scrapped the controversial plan to curb jury trials (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Andy Burnham has scrapped the controversial plan to curb jury trials in a move praised as “common-sense” by legal groups.

‌



‌



The proposals had been pushed by former PM Keir Starmer to tackle the court backlog, but met furious opposition, from both Labour MPs and legal professionals.

‌



Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he decided to “change course” after hearing the “strength of feeling on the proposals”.

‌



He said: “This Government inherited criminal courts on the brink of collapse, with victims waiting years for their day in court. I remain committed to bringing down the backlog and delivering swifter justice for those who so desperately need it.

Powerful moment as Labour MP describes 'agony' of wait for justice after rape READ MORE :

Jury trials scrapped for thousands of cases: The four things you need to know READ MORE :

View 2 Images David Lammy had insisted scrapping jury trials would help reduce the court backlog (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Wire)

“But I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the crown court and have made the decision to change course.

‌



“Justice delayed is justice denied, and I am committed to maximising efficiencies in our system alongside record investment. I remain committed to structural reform which is crucial if we are to bring down the backlog.”

Only some fraud and financial offences will now be allowed to be heard before a judge alone without a jury.

Welcoming the decision, Mark Evans, president of the Law Society of England and Wales said: “Too much time has been wasted to reach this common-sense position while the backlogs in the Crown and magistrates’ courts have remained unacceptably high.

‌



“We remain concerned that putting more cases into the magistrates’ court, which also faces record backlogs, without increasing capacity places even greater strain on an already overburdened system and risks serious cases facing summary justice.”

Bar Council Chair Kirsty Brimelow KC said: “This is a significant and welcome move away from reducing the only part of the criminal justice system that actually works, namely jury trials.

“We welcome the government’s swift action in retaining juries and particularly thank the new Lord Chancellor for listening to the Bar and wider legal profession.”

Article continues below

Former justice secretary David Lammy, who championed the move, had claimed the reforms were “desperately needed” to prevent victims facing “agonising delays”.

Mr Lammy wanted to reserve jury trials for “indictable-only” offences such as murder and rape, and lesser “either-way” offences with a likely sentence of more than three years in prison.

Barrister Karl Turner, who had the Labour whip suspended after he criticised the plan, welcomed the decision, and thanked the Prime Minister “for his support”

News.title: Air ambulance heading to Boston with six people onboard vanishes after plunging 10,000ft
News.content:
Air ambulance heading to Boston with six people onboard vanishes after plunging 10,000ft

The aircraft, which was carrying six people, had taken off from Bermuda this morning and was heading to Boston, Massachusetts, on the east coast of the United States

View 2 Images The US Coast Guard is conducting air and surface searches (Image: Getty Images)

An air ambulance carrying six people has been reported missing.

‌



‌



The aircraft had taken off from Bermuda this morning and was heading to Boston, Massachusetts, on the east coast of the United States. Six people were on board but the aircraft is said to have aircraft plunged more than 10,000 feet, losing contact with air traffic control.

‌



Search and rescue operations are now conducted by the US Coast Guard off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts. The Bermuda government said officials have been in touch with the families of those on board.

‌



View 2 Images Search and rescue operations are now conducted by the US coast guard off the coat of Nantucket, Massachusetts (Image: Boston Globe via Getty Images)

A statement from the government reads: "The Government of Bermuda confirms that an air ambulance which departed Bermuda for Boston early this morning, carrying six people, has been reported missing after contact was lost with air traffic control.

‌



"The United States Coast Guard is conducting search and rescue operations off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts. The Government has been in contact with the families of those on board and remains in contact with the overseas authorities coordinating the search."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Of the six people on board, four are understood to have been crew members, with the other two passengers. Two of the people on board are from Bermuda, while the other four are Canadian.

Article continues below

The air ambulance belongs to Latitude Air Ambulance, who said in a statement that "we're praying for a safe outcome". The US Coast Guard said air and surface crews were searching for the aircraft.

Bermuda premier David Burt said: "My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time. We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts."

News.title: Mega-rich HSBC banker banned from the City for almost £6,000 thousands in train fares
News.content:
Mega-rich HSBC banker banned from the City for almost £6,000 thousands in train fares

Joseph Molloy, 53, saved almost £6,000 over a number of years by buying tickets covering only the beginning and end of his journeys from his home in south London to Canary Wharf

View 2 Images Joseph Molloy was sentenced to 10 months imprisonment, suspended for 18 months (Image: Handout)

A successful banker has been banned from the City after dodging almost £6,000 in train fares on the commute from his plush £2million mansion.

‌



‌



Wealthy Joseph Molloy, 53, pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation after using a tactic known as "doughnutting" between the station near his property in Orpington, southeast London, and HSBC's HQ in Canary Wharf.

‌



His money-saving scam involved buying tickets for the start and end of a journey, but leaving out the stations in between. But his career is over after attempting to save a few pounds daily. The former head of passive equity at HSBC Asset Management would use fake names and email addresses to purchase tickets.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images He attempted to save a few pounds every day travelling to Canary Wharf (Image: Getty Images)

Molloy was sentenced to 10 months imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, at Inner London Crown Court on February 17. He was also banned from travelling on Southeastern trains for a year and forced to pay the rail company £5900 in compensation.

‌



The Financial Conduct Authority said it had banned now-retied Molloy from working in any regulated financial services role due to his conviction. In its ruling, the watchdog states: "Mr Molloy’s conviction demonstrates a clear and serious lack of honesty and integrity such that he is not fit and proper to perform regulated activities"

Molloy used two separate accounts with Southeastern under false names, addresses and email accounts to buy travel cards. He did so at for at least 740 journeys, dodging £5,911 in total between October 2023 and September 2024.

The banker had initially declined to comment when he was interviewed about the fraud, but he confessed in full after the police showed him the evidence against him, the court heard. Mirror has approached HSBC for comment.

‌



Molloy was appointed head of passive equity at HSBC Global Asset Management in 2015 before retiring last year. This is an investment strategy in which funds automatically track a stock market index, rather than paying a manager to pick stocks.

The judge described his offending as a "sophisticated and determined fraud". The court heard he was "clearly in a financial position to pay the fares" but decided to evade them, causing a "loss to the whole of society".

Molloy, the court also heard, was experiencing "difficult" personal circumstances at the time, had shown genuine remorse and stopped offending of his own volition. The FCA said Molloy had accepted he fell below the standards expected from the financial watchdog.

Article continues below

It noted: "Mr Molloy has informed the Authority that he accepts that he fell below the standards of behaviour expected by the Authority". The Express understands Molloy has not lodged an appeal.

The court heard the church-goer had been suffering from stress and grief at the loss of his mother. Will Hanson, representing Molloy, said in court: "He was going through a pretty difficult period when he did this. He cannot explain why he did this.

"It is a fraud that was discreet in nature, committed against no individual and no one from the public was made to suffer and a large private company was the victim."

News.title: Man shot dead in London street at memorial service as murder probe launched
News.content:
Man shot dead in London street at memorial service as murder probe launched

The victim was pronounced dead after multiple shots were heard at the junction of Braybrook Street and Erconwald Street in East Acton

View Image Braybrook Street, Acton (Image: Google Street View)

A man has been shot dead at a memorial service in London in front of 50 people, as a murder investigation was launched.

Met Police detectives are investigating after the 40-year-old was found at the junction of Braybrook Street and Erconwald Street in East Acton on Friday evening. Officers were called at around 7.47pm after members of the public reported hearing multiple shots.

Around 50-people - including children - had been gathered in the area for a memorial service when the incident occurred.

Police and London Ambulance Service crews attended the scene and treated the man, but despite the efforts of medical staff, he was pronounced dead.

The Metropolitan Police said that, while a post-mortem examination is yet to take place, the victim is "believed to have sustained a gunshot wound".

No arrests have been made yet. The police added that the man's family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

Detectives are now working to establish the full circumstances of the incident and a crime scene was still in place on Braybrook Street as of 5pm. Detective Chief Inspector Brian Howie, who is leading the investigation, said the incident happened as a "large number of people had gathered for a memorial service".

He said: "Our thoughts are with the family and friends of a man whose life was taken in a senseless act of violence. We understand a large number of people had gathered for a memorial service and what should have been a time to come together in remembrance has instead left a family devastated.

"We believe between 40 and 50 people, including children, were present when this incident occurred. Someone knows what happened and we need them to come forward.

Article continues below

"If you were around Erconwald Street, Braybrook Street, the surrounding roads or Wormwood Scrubs playground between 18:00hrs and 20:00hrs, please think carefully about what you saw. Did you see anyone carrying or concealing weapons, people on bicycles acting suspiciously, or vehicles being driven at speed?

"We also want to hear from anyone with photographs, video, dashcam, doorbell or mobile phone footage or who has seen anything relevant on social media. However insignificant it may seem, the smallest piece of information could prove crucial in helping us establish what happened and identify those responsible."

Anyone holding information about this incident is asked to contact the police quoting CAD 7011/2Oct.

News.title: Christa Pike's lawyers give brutally honest reaction to prison chief quitting
News.content:
Christa Pike's lawyers give brutally honest reaction to prison chief quitting

Frank Strada handed in his resignation amid intensifying scrutiny of Tennessee’s execution procedures after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections and was rushed to hospital

View 3 Images Tennessee's Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada has quit (Image: AP Photo/George Walker IV)

Lawyers representing Christa Pike have responded to the news Tennessee's head of prisons is resigning following her extraordinary botched execution.

‌



‌



The death-row prisoner survived two lethal injections and has been left fighting for her life. She was supposed to be put to death on Wednesday evening for the brutal murder of Colleen Slemmer, 19, back in 1995 but she was hospitalised after becoming the first person in the US to undergo such an execution attempt and live.

‌



It was announced today that Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada has quit, a decision he said is "in the best interests" of the state. He called the ongoing investigation into the incident "entirely appropriate and necessary".

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Christa Pike, sentenced to death for the murder of Colleen Slemmer three decades ago, survived two injections (Image: WVLT 8)

Christa Pike: Everything we know as killer left unconscious and on ventilator READ MORE :

Pike's attorneys welcomed Strada's departure, but said it "does nothing to help Christa now.”

‌



Her four-lawyer team said in a statement: “What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person. We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”

Her legal team said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital.

‌



View 3 Images The prisoner remains unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital (Image: Tennessee Department of Correction/AFP via Getty Images)

Pike was scheduled to be executed at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, where witnesses were present for the administration of the injections.

One of her lawyers, Stephen Ferrell, said Pike had "small veins that make insertion of a needle more difficult". The execution went ahead, however, and Pike was given two doses of pentobarbital. Witnesses said she was heard crying, gasping and breathing loudly as her right arm turned purple.

Article continues below

An independent review into the failed execution has been ordered by Tennessee governor Bill Lee. Mr Strada said: "I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred."

Departing Strada said in his resignation statement: “Serving as commissioner of the Tennessee department of correction has been a great honor, and I continue to believe the department carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.

"I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred.”

News.title: Man stabbed ex-girlfriend's former partner after threatening to 'kill him over and over'
News.content:
Man stabbed ex-girlfriend's former partner after threatening to 'kill him over and over'

Aaron Law Glindon, from Trafford, Greater Manchester, continued to live in his ex-girlfriend's house after they'd split up and launched a savage attack on another one of the woman's former partners

View 2 Images Aaron Law-Glindon (Image: Manchester Evening News)

A man told his ex-girlfriend's former partner he was going to "kill him over and over again" as he chased him with a knife before stabbing him - but he was sparred an immediate jail sentence.

‌



‌



Aaron Law-Glindon, 28, had split with the woman in February 2024 but they continued to live together at her home. Another of the woman's ex-boyfriends was visiting in September the same year when Law-Glindon savagely attacked the man, stabbing him in the chest.

‌



The incident happened on September 9, 2024, when the woman and her former partner were chatting in the living room as Law-Glindon arrived to the house unannounced. Manchester Crown Court heard the defendant came "straight in through the front door and came straight towards" the victim.

‌



Law-Glindon then began punching the man in the head, "telling him he was going to kill him over and over again". The victim then managed to push the attacker onto the sofa to get away.

The woman shouted at Law-Glindon to stop before he went to the front door and locked it. Afterwards, he went to the kitchen, which gave the woman and the male victim the change to escape into the front garden.

But Law-Glindon followed the pair with a knife, with the woman describing the blade as "one of the biggest" she had in the kitchen. When the woman threatened to call the police, the 28-year-old fled the scene.

‌



View 2 Images Aaron Law-Glindon was pictured holding a lottery scratch card after escaping an immediate prison sentence (Image: Manchester Evening News)

The victim, in a statement, said he has been left with lasting chest pain and paranoia. Law-Glindon initially told officers his victim was the aggressor and denied picking up a knife, Manchester Evening News reports.

Thomas Sherrington, defending, said Law-Glindon, who admitted one charge of wounding, used to do drugs, but has since stopped. He has had a "long period of reflection", the court heard.

‌



Law-Glindon's new partner is "anti-offending", Mr Sherrington added. He has a new job at a paper company, he said, telling the judge: "He has proved to the court that he can be rehabilitated.

"He has a stable job and has stayed out of trouble. His partner is keeping him on the straight and narrow."

Law-Glindon, of Hayfield Walk, was handed a 20-month term, suspended for three years. The offender, from Timperley, Trafford, was also told to abide by a two-year probation requirement and ordered to carry out 200 hours of unpaid work.

Article continues below

Recorder Imran Shafi KC told him: "Your actions that day were absolutely disgraceful. You behaved like an animal, which is doing a disservice to most animals."

Following the hearing, Law-Glindon - who has dice tattooed on his hand - was pictured holding a lottery scratch card after escaping an immediate prison sentence.

News.title: Burnham scraps controversial plans to curb jury trials
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has scrapped controversial plans to curb some jury trials.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had introduced proposals to allow judges to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-alone - and it proposes that thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he had changed course came after hearing the "strength of feeling". Criminal lawyers have welcomed the decision and the Conservatives say it is a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury.

Former Justice Secretary David Lammy first announced the plans in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases - having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during the national lockdowns. Official projections have estimated it could reach 100,000 before the next general election and, in a worst case scenario, climb to double that number by 2035.

There are, however, indications the backlog is now stabilising after the government committed unlimited funding to pay for more judges to sit in courts that were otherwise being unused.

Under the original plans, Lammy had wanted to reserve jury trials for the most serious "indictable" offences - meaning cases that are always sent to Crown Court, including murder and rape.

Less serious offences, where the sentence would be no more than three years, would be decided without a jury in the Crown Court by a judge alone. Even less serious offences would stay in magistrates' courts, abolishing defendants' right to ask for a trial by jury when they feel that is their best chance of beig cleared.

The proposals triggered an outcry across many parts of the criminal justice world, with many opponents saying that eroding the 800-year-old right to trial by jury would not solve the backlogs.

News.title: Tories pledge to remove £100,000 childcare 'cliff edge'
News.content:
The Conservatives have promised to scrap the "absurd cliff edge" that mean parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than Â£100,000 a year.

Under the current system, only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for government-funded or tax-free childcare.

"What we want to see is that people who work harder don't get punished for doing so," Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham.

The party said the move would be a "first step" in broader efforts to address issues in the tax system which damage incentives to work or invest.

This will be a theme of shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith's conference speech on Monday.

Since September 2025, working parents in England have been entitled to 30 hours of free childcare, external for children aged between nine months and four years old.

However, to qualify both parents must earn less than Â£100,000 a year.

The same Â£100,000 threshold applies to the government's tax-free childcare scheme, external.

For every Â£8 paid into an online childcare account, the government adds Â£2, up to Â£2,000 per child per year, which parents can then use to pay for childcare.

The Tories said that if they return to power they would remove the Â£100,000 threshold entirely so parents no longer lose childcare support when their income exceeds this level.

The threshold has been criticised by economists, who point out it can leave parents worse off overall even after a pay rise of tens of thousands of pounds.

Badenoch told the BBC the party didn't want "people to stop working because of that".

Speaking before the party's conference, she added: "What we want to see is more people in work and not taking the wrong decisions or the wrong choices, and it doesn't matter whether they're earning Â£10,000 or Â£100,000 - what matters is that people are out there working".

Asked if this could result in someone who earns Â£1 million a year get free childcare under a Conservative government, Badenoch responded: "It doesn't matter what you earn - we don't want you to be punished for working hard. What we're trying to do is grow our economy."

News.title: The Celebrity Traitors connections that might surprise you
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first two episodes of The Celebrity Traitors

"I know Rob very, very well. I mean, I've sat next to him as he's had a colonic."

That was Romesh Ranganathan, reminding us - in case we were in any doubt - of his close friendship with Rob Beckett in the opening episode of The Celebrity Traitors.

His words sum up the key difference between this series and the regular civilian version. In Celebrity Traitors, the players aren't just on-screen competitors - many actually know each other outside the show.

Lots have worked together, and some are even friends. And those previous connections can have a huge impact on the show's dynamics.

It's also partly why it is quite so delightful to watch - as friendships unravel, and former co-stars turn on each other.

We've been unpicking the six degrees of separation. Here are some of the connections we've found - if you spot any more, we'd love to know. Get in touch with your thoughts in the comments section below.

News.title: How to spot a psychopath at work - from a man who worried he could be one
News.content:
Most of us have had colleagues who can be tricky to work with.

They may act impulsively, be manipulative, or even outright lie to advance their careers - but how can you tell the difference between an unpleasant co-worker and someone displaying psychopathic traits?

Geraint Anderson, a former London banker-turned author, said he was assessed by a clinical psychologist who told him he may have had "situational psychopathy" in order to succeed in the cut-throat corporate world.

"I had to really become a kind of worse version of myself in order to thrive in this environment," he said.

Anderson, 53, who now lives in Monmouthshire, said some modern workplaces and social influences reward psychopathic traits.

He worked for 12 years as an analyst in London's financial district and earned millions of pounds before leaving his job ahead of the financial crash in 2008.

"The city rewards this dark triad behaviour... being uber confident, being able to control and manipulate others, not getting emotionally involved in decisions and being decisive," he said.

"I adapted myself for the city and started bringing out the kind of worst side of myself."

News.title: When parenting advice becomes too much
News.content:
Before Rosie Whitfield became a mum, she imagined herself parenting very calm children.

"Then I had two wild boys," she says with a laugh.

Following the birth of her kids, Rosie spent hours online looking for the best advice and was drawn to one particular approach to parenting: Gentle parenting, which focuses on empathy and mutual respect with little emphasis on punishment, albeit with boundaries.

But she constantly worried her choices, from sleep schedules to handling toddler tantrums, were "ruining their lives forever".

Rosie does not blame the gentle parenting philosophy itself but instead says the overall amount of parenting advice online was "overwhelming" and "made mundane parenting choices feel like the absolute end of the world."

"I felt like if I was choosing to put the TV on for 20 minutes while I did the dishes or had a coffee, I was choosing to destroy my children's brains," says Rosie, who is originally from Birmingham and now lives in Dubai.

Rosie believes her confidence and intuition were stripped away as she questioned every parenting decision. And she is not alone.

Government research suggests that around two-thirds of parents with young children feel overwhelmed by the amount of parenting information available and struggle with conflicting advice, with many turning to social media for support.

News.title: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion
News.content:
Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.

He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.

"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.

Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.

So what would it be like if it happened?

The first phase of a war could be quite short.

According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week

Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.

Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.

The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.

The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.

He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.

An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.

Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.

"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.

"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."

Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.

But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.

"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.

Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

News.title: Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to put her party back on the big stage
News.content:
The 2026 Conservative conference is big enough to justify using Birmingham's Symphony Hall as its main stage again.

So, Kemi Badenoch will tread the same stage ageing rockers Marillion took last month - and where sequinned soprano Katherine Jenkins will perform next week. She'll also avoid the humiliation of a national party leader being squashed into a side room at a corporate conference centre (with drapes portioning off the empty space). Simply, the party is able to put bums on seats again - and by that measure, things are looking up.

Badenoch goes into the conference with her own position secure in the party. One senior Tory says "she has actually defied cynics like me" who initially disapproved of her leadership. Her standing with the public has improved and she is now, again on a very simple but crucial measure, much better known. Her allies are sure she has developed a clear identity among the public, confiding: "People now know who she is and they enjoy her interventions - the thing we hear most is I don't always agree with her but I know where she stands."

News.title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford released on bail
News.content:
A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.

Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.

Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

News.title: Homemade bomb part of alleged plot on Manchester's Jewish community, court told
News.content:
Two Iranian men have appeared in court charged with terror offences over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade bomb.

Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool, were accused at Westminster Magistrates' Court of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on or before 20 September.

One of the buildings they are alleged to have carried out reconnaissance at is the Heaton Park synagogue which was attacked on 2 October 2025.

Both men, who had arrived in the UK by small boat, were arrested in Manchester's Northern Quarter on the eve of Yom Kippur - the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

Salehi and Ahmadyan were remanded in custody by District Judge Nina Tempia until 23 October, when they will appear at the Old Bailey in London.

As part of the investigation, searches were carried out at addresses in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford.

The Metropolitan Police said the men were alleged to have obtained instructions to make a chlorine bomb, acquired liquids and other components to make an improvised explosive device.

They are accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps.

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told the court: "Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device.

"The defendants were observed carrying out, what the prosecution say, is a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester's Jewish community, identifying attempted targets such as the Jewish Museum and Heaton Park Synagogue."

News.title: Wakefield beat Warrington to win Super League
News.content:
This is a final few would have predicted seven days ago, let alone at any point throughout the season.

But Warrington snuck past Leeds Rhinos, and Wakefield Trinity then stunned the whole of rugby league as they demolished Wigan on the Warriors' own patch to make it to Old Trafford.

While Warrington have been close in previous years, Wakefield have been spectacular bolters in 2026.

Only two years ago, they were winning the Championship play-off final before their place in Super League was confirmed by the IMG grading system, having been relegated in 2023.

They were sixth last year and went two places better this season before memorable play-off successes over Leigh Leopards and then the Warriors.

In the build-up during the week, Powell had challenged his players to earn legendary status, knowing that was their long-term reward if they could emerge victorious.

After scoring 33 unanswered points in a spell at Wigan, Wakefield simply brought that momentum with them to Old Trafford as they absolutely bossed the first half, stretching that streak to 52 points.

Johnstone had already had one try denied by a TV review before Lachlan Walmsley's brilliant reverse pass sent Scott over to score.

And in a period where everything they did was working, Jake Trueman's high kick on the last tackle was spectacularly caught by Johnstone above opposite wing Albert Hopoate and tapped back for the supporting Vagana to dive over.

They were overpowering their opponents, exemplified by Tevaga being unstoppable from close to the posts for their third try.

And showing the sort of game smarts his revered father Sir Kevin Sinfield had in his Leeds Rhinos days, son Jack added an extra point to keep the scoreboard ticking as the half closed to leave Warrington needing more than three converted tries.

News.title: Huge crowds turn out in support of residents over Drumcree parade dispute
News.content:
Rallies were held on both sides of the Drumcree parade dispute on Saturday as the stand-off between Garvaghy Road residents and the Portadown District Orange Lodge continues.

Addressing thousands of people at an event on the Garvaghy Road, First Minister and Sinn FÃ©in vice president Michelle O'Neill said she heard the Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant "talk about being between a rock and a hard place", adding she has "never heard such nonsense, this is between right and wrong".

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said anyone blocking the Garvaghy Road will be "treated as participating in an unnotified and therefore illegal protest and that anyone "found to have broken the law will face criminal justice consequences".

Speaking at Drumcree church, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MP Carla Lockhart repeated calls for PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher and his officers to "do their job" and facilitate the parade, describing the current impasse as "mob rule".

For most of the afternoon stewards in high visibility jackets kept people off the Garvaghy Road and those attending were told it was important to allow traffic to flow freely.

However, by 15:00 BST the crowd was so large that they were standing on the road as police closed it to traffic.

The fallout over the proposed Portadown District Orange Lodge march - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning after the Parades Commission's decision that the parade could go ahead with restrictions.

News.title: Sinfield completes final ultramarathon challenge
News.content:
Sir Kevin Sinfield has completed his latest endurance challenge raising money for motor neurone disease (MND) causes in memory of his friend and teammate Rob Burrow, who died in 2024.

Sinfield completed seven ultramarathons in seven days, crossing the finish line at Old Trafford Stadium in Manchester ahead of the Super League Grand Final.

The fundraiser and his team have raised more than Â£13m for the MND community since his first annual challenge in 2020.

Speaking to the crowd, Sinfield said: "The rugby league community has got right behind the MND community and Rob would be so proud to see how you've supported and cared, and showed your love for a community that really needs us."

Sinfield began his final ultramarathon challenge in Hull on September 27 and visited all 12 Super League clubs along the way.

The 7 in 7: The Grand Finale week ended at Old Trafford earlier where he brought out the trophy ahead of the game between Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity.

News.title: Greens would offer two-year jobs to unemployed under-24s
News.content:
Young people would be offered a guaranteed two-year job within four months of leaving education or training, under a new proposal unveiled by the Green Party.

Announcing the policy at the party's conference in Brighton, co-deputy leader Mothin Ali said there were a million "bored, desperate and lost" young people who were out of work, training or education.

Under the proposed scheme, youngsters would be offered posts in the private sector, with the government paying half their salary.

Ali said an initial pilot scheme - rolled out in areas with the fewest job openings for young people - would create 9,000 jobs, at an overall cost of Â£110m.

The pilot would start in areas such as Rotherham, Ceredigion, Newcastle-under-Lyme, Broxtowe and South Staffordshire, with an ambition to roll it out nationwide.

The party said that a person not in work, education or training would cost the state an estimated Â£240,000 in benefits over the course of their lifetime.

It argued that its policy would reduce spending on welfare and boost tax receipts from employment.

Employers would be exempt from paying National Insurance contributions, but would have to provide in-job training, the party says.

The party is seeking to pitch the plan as more ambitious than the government's own scheme, which subsidises six-month job placements for benefit claimants who have been looking for work for 18 months.

Ali also criticised ministers for previously suggesting youngsters refusing a role under that scheme could lose access to benefits, telling activists: "Threatening young people with cuts to Universal Credit if they don't accept short-term work placements - that's not a youth strategy."

Speaking to BBC News after his speech, Ali said: "If we don't take action now, we're losing a generation of young people."

The number of 16-24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training has been rising since the Covid pandemic, with figures reaching almost one million.

A long-awaited report into the problem by former Labour minister Alan Milburn is expected to be published this autumn.

News.title: Fury wants 'old pal' President Trump for Joshua ringwalk
News.content:
Former heavyweight champion Tyson Fury plans to ask US president Donald Trump to lead his ringwalk before fighting Anthony Joshua.

Fury and Joshua are set to meet in an long-awaiting all-British bout at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

Trump and Fury met at UFC Freedom 250 at the White House in June.

The Manchester-born fighter wore a cap emblazoned with the words "Donald Trump for Prime Minister" after his US travel ban was lifted by the 80-year-old.

"I'll definitely make that offer to my old buddy, old pal, and we'll see if he's available," said 38-year-old Fury.

"Probably unlikely because of the situation he's in at the moment, being the President of the United States."

News.title: Landslip leaves Skye drivers facing 40-mile diversion
News.content:
Drivers on Skye are facing a 40-mile diversion after a landslide led to a road closure.

The ground fell away from the side of the A855 north of Uig onto a local access road on Friday afternoon and an inspection later confirmed it would have to stay shut over the weekend.

The A855 road encircles the Trotternish peninsula in the north of the island and a diversion route is now in place.

No-one was injured by the landslip - which was caught on CCTV from a nearby house - but a group of visiting schoolchildren found themselves temporarily separated from their packed lunches until a local woman volunteered to retrieve them by bike.

The road could have to remain closed into next week as "detailed surveying" works continue, according to local councillor Chrissie Gillies.

A FlyDubai co-pilot who attempted to hijack a Tel Aviv-bound passenger jet with a cockpit crash axe studied at a British university.

Hamam al-Hammami, 29, earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023. The UK institution has since said that the qualification involved no practical flight training.

Earlier reporting byThe Independent confirmed that Mr al-Hammami is an Omani national born in the UAE to an Omani father and Syrian mother.

A spokesperson for the university told Press Association: “Our thoughts are with the injured pilot, crew and passengers involved in this incident.

“Hamam al Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management. He did not undertake any pilot training at the University.”

Mr al-Hammami was reportedly banned from flying by Omani authorities last year due to his radical views. Following his detention he allegedly told investigators that he intended to crash the airliner in Israel.

open image in gallery Hammam al-Hammami received higher education from a British institution ( Reuters )

The revelations come as Israeli investigators arrived in the UAE on Saturday to interrogate the suspect.

Authorities from both nations are focusing on whether Mr al-Hammami operated independently as a "lone wolf" or under the direction of an external extremist network.

According to accounts obtained by Emirati prosecutors, two hours into Wednesday’s flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Hammami seized the emergency axe and repeatedly slashed Indian captain Smit Machchhar.

The struggle sent the Boeing 737 MAX into a sudden 17,000-foot plunge toward the Gulf.

Despite sustaining severe injuries, Captain Machchhar has said he was able to unlock the flight deck door, allowing passengers to force their way inside, subdue Hammami, and stabilise the aircraft before making an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

Speaking to reporters, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed intelligence services are investigating whether Mr al-Hammami operated under external direction, warning that any accomplices would pay a "heavy price."

open image in gallery Netanyahu has since warned that accomplices will pay a "heavy price” ( Reuters )

As speculation surrounding Mr al-Hammami motives heightens, former US diplomats and regional analysts have suggested the attack carried a “dual target,” and may have been a deliberate attempt to derail the 2020 Abraham Accords, which established commercial air routes between Israel and Gulf states.

The joint investigation is currently focused on how Mr al-Hammami passed employment background checks.

Oman Air previously removed Hammami from flight duties after intelligence officials discovered extremist materials on his devices and noted visits to radical websites, according to reports by The Wall Street Journal and ABC News.

It remains unclear whether Omani officials shared these security concerns with neighbouring states or international carriers.

Mr al-Hammami was later transferred to an administrative desk job before briefly training at Royal Air Maroc, which ultimately rejected his application. FlyDubai then hired him eight months ago.

Former Israeli intelligence officials have said that allowing a national from a country with no diplomatic ties to Israel onto the Tel Aviv route represents a critical failure by Israeli and Emirati security agencies.

Following the incident, regional aviation authorities have launched urgent reviews of all aircrew screening protocols.

Andy Burnham has scrapped a controversial plan to curb jury trials in yet another reversal of one of Sir Keir Starmer’s major policies.

The move is a U-turn on radical plans, introduced by former justice secretary David Lammy under Sir Keir’s leadership, to cut thousands of jury trials across England and Wales in a bid to tackle the court backlog.

It led to an outcry from MPs, lawyers and campaigners, with the proposals condemned as “madness” and described as being against Labour values.

Justice secretary Alex Norris has now said he has decided to “change course” after hearing the “strength of feeling on the proposals”.

Only some fraud and financial offences will now be allowed to be heard before a judge alone without a jury, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said.

open image in gallery Alex Norris has changed course on the controversial proposal ( PA )

Announcing the move, Mr Norris said scrapping the proposal would allow the government to reduce the backlog faster, as it would require less structural change.

“This government inherited criminal courts on the brink of collapse, with victims waiting years for their day in court,” he said. “I remain committed to bringing down the backlog and delivering swifter justice for those who so desperately need it.

“But I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the crown court and have made the decision to change course.

“This allows us to start that work far earlier, ensuring that under this government we do not have victims waiting endlessly for justice.”

He added: “Justice delayed is justice denied, and I am committed to maximising efficiencies in our system alongside record investment. I remain committed to structural reform which is crucial if we are to bring down the backlog.”

open image in gallery David Lammy proposed curbing jury trials ( Jonathan Brady/PA Wire )

It represents the Burnham government’s latest move away from Sir Keir’s legacy. Last month, Mr Burnham intervened in the early release scheme by making it more restrictive following an “urgent review” over who would be eligible.

Last week, the prime minister also raised the prospect of a potential second Brexit referendum, indicating he would reconsider Sir Keir’s post-Brexit red lines.

In a significant shift from the position Labour fought the 2024 election on, Mr Burnham said the government could keep the current arrangements, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” in what would be full EU membership.

The move to curb jury trials had been championed by Mr Lammy, who said the reforms were needed to prevent victims facing “agonising delays”.

Mr Lammy wanted to reserve jury trials for “indictable-only” offences such as murder and rape, and lesser “either-way” offences with a likely sentence of more than three years in prison. Other cases would instead have been heard by a single crown court judge. The proposals were produced after a review by the retired judge, Sir Brian Leveson.

Ministry of Justice figures showed there were 80,829 cases still to be dealt with at the end of June, with the backlog almost doubling since 2020.

open image in gallery Karl Turner has welcomed Labour’s U-turn (PA) ( PA Archive )

Barrister Karl Turner, who had the Labour whip suspended after he criticised the plan, welcomed the decision, and thanked the prime minister “for his support during my campaign”.

Mr Turner, MP for East Hull who has yet to have the whip restored, said he had “engaged directly with the justice secretary” about the issue in recent weeks.

The decision has also been welcomed by Law Society of England and Wales president, Mark Evans, who said that backlogs remained high as time had been wasted on the proposal.

“We welcome the government’s decision to step back from some of its proposed changes to jury trials that risked fairness and public trust,” he said. “Too much time has been wasted to reach this common-sense position while the backlogs in the Crown and magistrates’ courts have remained unacceptably high.

“Investment in infrastructure and technology is encouraging but this must be new money coming into the criminal justice system, a vital public service which has been drained of resources for too long. We have been calling for a whole-system approach that combines sustained investment and long-term planning.

“We remain concerned that putting more cases into the magistrates’ court, which also faces record backlogs, without increasing capacity places even greater strain on an already overburdened system and risks serious cases facing summary justice.

open image in gallery Starmer’s proposal was condemned by a number of parties (Gareth Fuller/PA)

“It is essential to invest in legal aid. The prospect of people facing imprisonment while being denied legal representation remains a serious concern and lack of legal representation adds to delays.”

Liberal Democrat Justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller MP said the proposal should never have been introduced in the first place, and the government should look to bring down the court backlogs so victims can get the justice they deserve.

“This starts with adopting Liberal Democrat plans to double sitting time in courtrooms across the country and introducing specialist courts for victims of rape and serious sexual offences as promised in the 2024 Labour manifesto.”

Siân Berry, Green MP for Brighton Pavilion with the Home Office brief, said it was another example of Labour conceding to Green pressure.

“This is a victory for justice and fairness,” she said. “As Zack [Polanski] said at conference, 'vote Green and watch Labour move.’

“The right to choose trial by a jury of your peers is an absolute cornerstone of our justice system, and the government’s attempt to completely abolish this was profoundly disturbing and wrong.”

open image in gallery Nick Timothy issued a warning about Labour’s decision to move a number of cases through the magistrates to clear the backlogs ( UK Parliament )

Another change announced by the MoJ will see criminals accused of what they described as “relatively minor crimes” losing the right to choose a Crown Court jury trial rather than a magistrates one, with courts having the final say on where “either-way” offences are sent.

This decision has been criticised by the Criminal Bar Association (CBA), who warned the proposals will shift 25,000 cases a year, including 5,500 jury trials, on magistrates - including complex assaults, sexual assaults and child abuse which volunteer magistrates are “completely unequipped to try”.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy declared it a major victory for the Conservative party and those who had fought to defend jury trials, but condemned shifting cases onto the Magistrates’ doorstep.

“This is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour have been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the Crown Court,” he said.

“Labour are restricting juries by the back door, scrapping the right to elect one and dumping those cases on magistrates whose backlog is at a record high.

“Nearly 81,000 cases are stuck in the Crown Court, yet there is no commitment to get courts sitting more often, but Labour did find the time to write into law a review of how its reforms treat people of different backgrounds.

“Sixty-four crown courtrooms stand empty every day. A Conservative government would get every courtroom sitting so we can protect the right to a jury.”

News.title: Andy Burnham’s decision to keep the right to jury trials is welcome
News.content:
