The right to a jury trial is an essential protection against an authoritarian state. Juries may be flawed, but the ability of a jury to return even a perverse verdict is one of the guarantees of a free society. It should not be given up lightly.

So Andy Burnham’s decision to scrap Sir Keir Starmer’s plan to dramatically restrict the number of cases that could be heard by a jury is a welcome one. It is the second such change to criminal justice policy made by the new prime minister and Alex Norris, his new justice secretary.

The first adjustment to the policies inherited from Sir Keir and David Lammy was to limit the number of prisoners granted early release in order to ease overcrowding in jails. This had the effect of keeping two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper behind bars, which was the right decision – although it took Mr Burnham and Mr Norris more than one attempt to arrive at it. It is still not clear exactly how the solution, which Mr Burnham at one point described as impossible, was achieved.

Much the same applies to the U-turn on the right to jury trial. Mr Lammy insisted that the courts backlog had become so serious that there was no way to reduce it except by restricting the right to jury trial, because jury trials take so much longer than cases heard only by a judge.

Mr Norris has now decided that there is, after all, another way to tackle the backlog without taking away this essential component of the justice system. He says the change of policy allows the government to start work on “maximising efficiencies” earlier: “I remain committed to structural reform, which is crucial if we are to bring down the backlog.”

We look forward to hearing the details, because The Independent always had its doubts that the restriction of jury trials proposed by Sir Brian Leveson, the former senior judge, was the only way to make the courts more efficient. Anyone who has had any contact with the criminal justice system knows that it is chronically dysfunctional.

We are aware that part of the problem has been the lack of funds over the years, which is why we are inclined to take the credit claimed by Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, for Mr Norris’s U-turn with a pinch of salt. The Labour government has increased planned spending on the courts, but it has rightly insisted that the increase be accompanied by reform.

Equally, it is right that Mr Norris should not be applying to the taxpayer for further funding to pay for the preservation of the right to jury trial. There is plenty of scope elsewhere in the justice system for further savings.

If anyone deserves credit for the change of course, it is Karl Turner, the former Labour MP who was suspended by the party after his outspoken criticism of his own government on this issue. He should have the whip restored immediately.

But praise is also due to Mr Burnham and Mr Norris. Not because they are better at politics than Sir Keir and Mr Lammy, although they are, but because the plan to restrict the right to jury trial was wrong in principle.

The next stage, though, is the most difficult. Mr Norris implied that, because the bill to reform the courts will not now be held up in the House of Lords, he would be able to press ahead more quickly with making the courts more efficient.

Everyone repeats the phrase derived from Magna Carta that justice delayed is justice denied. The most important prize will go to the ministers, officials and lawyers who act on it and deliver the justice that the people deserve.

Nigel Farage has claimed people were “quite impressed” by his party securing a record-breaking £72 million from two cryptocurrency magnates, as he brushed off mounting scrutiny over Reform UK’s financial backing.

Speaking during a campaign visit to Doncaster, the Reform leader acknowledged that while he had initially feared public backlash over the funding would force him "into hiding," the historic sum has instead generated "grudging respect."

The donations – split equally between businessmen Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo – represent the largest single political donation in British history, shattering the previous record of £10m left to the Conservatives in 2022.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, Mr Farage said: “The fact that I managed to pull off a coup of that magnitude, I think people were quite impressed”, arguing the funds served as a vital equaliser to compete against established political parties.

open image in gallery Farage has claimed voters are ‘impressed’ by the donations his party has racked in ( Getty )

The intervention comes as Mr Farage said he was recently interviewed in the Palace of Westminster by the parliamentary commissioner for standards, Daniel Greenberg.

The 30-minute inquiry centred on whether Mr Farage breached parliamentary rules by failing to formally register a separate £5 million gift received from Mr Harborne in 2024.

Mr Farage strongly denies any wrongdoing, maintaining the funds were allocated exclusively to cover his personal security expenses. But should the commissioner rule against him, Mr Farage could face a suspension from the House of Commons, potentially triggering a by-election in his Clacton constituency.

Security concerns surrounding the Reform leader have intensified this week following confirmation that a 28-year-old suspect charged with the murder of former party figure Ann Widdecombe was also allegedly involved in a terror plot targeting Mr Farage.

open image in gallery The Reform UK leader is believed to have been another target of the man charged with murdering Ann Widdecombe ( PA Wire )

Mr Farage also addressed his party's recent slip in opinion polls, admitting Reform had entered a "trough" after losing its earlier lead over Labour and facing increased pressure from the Conservatives.

"The narrative that Reform has peaked? No, it’s troughed. It’s a very different thing, it’s troughed," Mr Farage said.

He attributed the decline to a drop in his personal visibility on the national campaign trail, months of damaging headlines surrounding internal party finances, and vote-splitting caused by Restore, a far-right political party founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

While conceding that Restore was "starting to hurt [Reform]," Mr Farage dismissed its long-term electoral threat in key working-class constituencies.

open image in gallery Farage dismissed Restore as a threat to his party’s potential electoral success ( Reuters )

Mr Farage declared that Reform’s general election campaign was now underway following a "major summer of reorganisation" at its headquarters.

To spearhead the push, the party is putting its multi-million-pound war chest has been earmarked for professionalising campaign infrastructure, overhauling field operations, and building dedicated production facilities for its online broadcast channel, Reform TV– a move the party insists is vital to competing with more established Westminster blocs.

Mr Farage has previously told the media that the multi-million-pound donations are “100 per cent compliant with the law today” and continues to insist that Reform is entirely confident it will not have to return any of the funds.

Six Flags, which owns one of the nation's oldest amusement parks — Cedar Point, in Sandusky, Ohio — is considering changing the location's name.

The company reportedly sent surveys to a group of season pass holders asking them how they would feel about a new name that incorporates the phrase "Six Flags."

Six Flags added its name to another major amusement park after buying it — Six Flags Magic Mountain in California — and reportedly hopes to do the same in northern Ohio.

Among the names pitched in the survey is reportedly 'Six Flags Over North Ohio," which would completely remove the name "Cedar Point" from the title, according to WCPO.

A Six Flags spokesperson told the broadcaster the suggestions were potential options meant to help them better develop possible new names.

open image in gallery Six Flags reportedly is considering changing the name of Cedar Point, one of America’s oldest amusement parks ( AFP/Getty )

"The survey was designed to test a variety of naming concepts and better understand what resonates with guests. The options are research concepts, not proposed or final names. Exploring a broad range of ideas helps us learn what guests value most about our parks and brands and gives us another input as we make decisions for the future," the statement said. "No decisions have been made regarding park names."

The company also owns another large Ohio amusement park, Kings Island, and is considering adding its name to that park as well.

Some suggestions for that park's rename include "Kings Island by Six Flags" and "Six Flags Over Kings Island."

Kings Island has received similar renaming in the past. When Paramount purchased the park in 1992, it was renamed "Paramount's Kings Island."

Many comments left on the Kings Island Season Pass holders Facebook page were critical of the potential name change.

"Leave it as is. Kings Island will always be what it is called," one user wrote.

Six Flags also slapped its name on another iconic Ohio amusement park, Geauga Lake, located in northeastern Ohio. Six Flags rebranded the park in 2000 as Six Flags Ohio — though locals still called it Geauga Lake — and sold it in 2004 to Cedar Fair, which previously owned Cedar Point.

Geauga Lake closed permanently in 2007.

Inside a commercial kitchen near Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns pours a blue-green substance into gridded moulds to create a flagship product for his business: high-strength THC gummies containing the main psychoactive component found in marijuana.

He could soon be forced to close the operation. The United States’ multibillion-dollar market for intoxicating hemp items — spanning THC-infused seltzers stocked by Target stores to smokable cannabis flower — faces potential shutdown after Congress voted to plug a federal loophole that permitted the trade to expand.

Industry lobbyists and several lawmakers are working to rescue the sector. A short-term federal spending bill signed by President Donald Trump last month pushed back the implementation date of the "hemp THC ban" from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, granting Congress additional time to consider regulating the products rather than an outright prohibition.

“It’s such a weird spot to be in,” said Hohns. “You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it.”

open image in gallery Nicholas Hohns shows off a tray of strawberry-lemon CBD gummies at his Deutermann Farms kitchen in Clayton, N.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Allen G. Breed) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved )

Marijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. “Rope, not dope” was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp.

To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill.

But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole. Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high.

Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country, including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana’s THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned.

The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal.

Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products.

McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history.

The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn’t take effect for a year.

open image in gallery A mixer stirs a batch of blueberry lemonade gummies in a heated pot at the Deutermann Farms kitchen in Clayton, N.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Allen G. Breed) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved )

The ban “threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion,” according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market.

The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds.

The owners of Kentucky’s Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that’s what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said.

“If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it’s gone,” Zipperle said.

They have 105 employees, sell hemp beverages in 18 states and expect to bring in $65 million this year.

The 0.4-milligram cap is so low that it would ban even some non-impairing CBD products, such as topical lotions, said Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the industry group U.S. Hemp Roundtable.

open image in gallery Hot gummy mixture drips off the table's edge as Nicholas Hohns uses a pastry knife to fill mold at his Deutermann Farms kitchen in Clayton, N.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Allen G. Breed) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved )

Hohns, who runs Deutermann Farms in Clayton, North Carolina, entered the hemp industry after losing his job as a personal trainer during the COVID-19 pandemic. North Carolina has not legalized either medical or recreational marijuana, but many of the edibles Hohns makes are more potent than what's available in states that have.

“When I started seeing THC edibles being sold … I was like, I got 18 months to two years to make money in this industry,” Hohns said. “No way is the government just going to sit here and let us do this when this was supposed to be for fiber, plastics, building materials, rope.”

That was more than four years ago. Hohns kept his capital investments minimal, fearing a shutdown. He has considered making other products, such as creatine gummies, if he has to get out of the hemp THC business.

Things have been more stressful for others. Drinkin' Buds, a cannabis beverage company in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, has mothballed production. Co-founder Matt Swanson took himself off the payroll on Thursday.

“There’s just so much uncertainty,” Swanson said. “I'm actively looking for employment.”

open image in gallery Bags of THC- and CBD-infused edibles await delivery at Deutermann Farms in Clayton, N.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Allen G. Breed) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved )

Among those who have come to the defense of the hemp industry are alcohol retailers, including Total Wine & More. Sales of cannabis seltzers have helped offset falling alcohol sales.

Opponents include people who say the products are dangerous.

“I have sympathy for people losing their jobs, but I also have sympathy for the many, many more people whose lives are affected by this,” said Kevin Sabet, CEO of Smart Approaches to Marijuana.

The regulated legal marijuana industry, which sees hemp THC as unfair competition, also supports the ban. Cory Harris, a lobbyist for state-legal cannabis operators, suggested that dire predictions about its effect on the intoxicating hemp industry are overstated.

While the ban would end interstate sales of products like THC seltzers and gummies, some could find a home in legal in-state markets, he said. It's possible THC drinks could be sold at stores in the states where they were produced. States like North Carolina could adopt legal hemp programs.

“If you go from having virtually no rules to suddenly having an awful lot of rules, that’s a buzzkill,” Harris said. “Welcome to our world. But if you establish your whole business within a legally questionable loophole, that’s just sort of the risk you take.”

Jake Hutzler spends his working days directing planes from an airport tower. Once a week, however, he travels there by attaching a propeller to his back and soaring through the Colorado skies.

To start his journey, the 28-year-old air traffic controller lays out a large wing on the street outside his apartment complex, ignites the engine and begins running. Within seconds, his feet leave the ground.

For the next 20 minutes, Hutzler cruises at a relaxed 35 mph (56 kph) over expansive fields surrounding Pueblo, a city near the Front Range mountains. Listening to his favourite music, he passes over a highway, a water tower and finally the airport.

Before taking off, Hutzler phones colleagues at the tower to announce his departure. Once airborne, he keeps them updated on his exact location and the altitude at which he is flying.

“I’m very small and I don’t show up on radar,” Hutzler said, “so they’ll want to kind of keep track of my location and get updates on my progress.”

As the airport comes into view, he waits for the OK to land on the airport’s ramp. Pulling down on toggles to slow down the paramotor, he lets his feet dangle and meets the ground with a brief jog. He packs up the wing, strips off his jacket to reveal his collared work shirt and begins his shift telling planes when it's safe to land and take off.

open image in gallery In this image taken from video provided by Jacob Hutzler shows Hutzler flies his paramotor to work as an air traffic controller in Pueblo, Colo., on Aug. 13, 2026. (Jacob Hutzler via AP) ( Jacob Hutzler )

For someone who has been fascinated with flying since childhood, it's a particularly satisfying commute. Hutzler says it's as close as you can get to flying like a bird.

“In a paramotor, you have a view that almost nobody gets to experience,” he said. “You have no cockpit, nothing in front of you. You’re just sitting there in the air and total freedom to go wherever you want.”

His grandfather used to take him up in a small four-seat aircraft. In college, Hutzler put in about 20 hours toward getting a pilot's license, but the costs were too high for him to continue.

Everything changed when he came across a viral video of a man flying a paramotor to McDonald’s and eating his hamburger on the flight home.

“After I saw that, I was like, ‘I’m sold,’” he said. “I gotta do that.”

open image in gallery Jake Hutzler, who often flies to his air traffic controller job, shakes sand from his paramotor wing outside his home in Pueblo, Colo., on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Thomas Peipert)

Hutzler started training to fly the contraption — also known as powered paragliding — in 2021 in Florida and later became an instructor.

Part of the appeal is just how accessible paramotors are. There’s no license required and the price tag is a fraction of the cost of many other forms of flying. However, they're still subject to federal rules on ultralight vehicles, including that they can only be operated during the day and fliers must avoid congested cities and towns.

The sport became a part of Hutzler's life story. He trained the woman he would go on to marry, and when he was ready to propose he used fake engine trouble on his paramotor to lure her to the contraption, where he had left a ring. On their wedding day, their paramotors were with them at the altar. Now he’s looking forward to the day their 2½-year-old daughter is old enough to go on a tandem ride.

But after Hutzler started working in air traffic control earlier this year, his job left him less time to fly.

The solution: Start flying to work.

He approached his manager about commuting by paramotor and they went through the rule book and made sure he'd have two-way communication with the tower when he entered their airspace. He made his first flight to work in June and has been doing it ever since, weather permitting.

open image in gallery Jake Hutzler, who often flies to his air traffic controller job, inspects his paramotor outside his home in Pueblo, Colo., on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Thomas Peipert)

But paramotoring is a very fair-weather sport. It only takes about 10 mph (16 kph) of wind — basically a light breeze — to keep Hutzler on the ground. It can also be problematic if the sun heats the ground and causes updrafts — making for an extremely bumpy ride.

The airborne commute isn't actually faster

With the time needed to set up the paramotor and put away all the gear, the trip takes slightly longer than driving to work. But, he said, it’s so much more fun.

“You could be having your favorite song playing in your headphones, and you just can relax and take in this awesome experience,” he said.

News.title: Rees-Zammit taunts Pollock as Bristol outplay Northampton
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Bristol Bears vs Northampton Saints from the Gallagher Prem, with both teams looking to build on winning starts following the opening weekend of action.

Last season’s champions Northampton kicked off their title defence with an emphatic 59-26 victory over a new-look Newcastle Red Bulls outfit at Franklin’s Gardens.

While Henry Pollock’s new cornrow hairstyle was the centre of attention at kick-off, the limelight was soon stolen by Tommy Freeman and James Pater, who both notched hat-tricks for Phil Dowson’s side.

Of 19-year-old full-back Pater, who starts on the bench today, Dowson said afterwards: “He doesn’t let the occasion get to him. He has an incredible skill set, great speed and ability to manoeuvre away from defenders.”

Bristol, meanwhile, began their season with an impressive 34-24 victory away at Sale Sharks, with Pat Lam’s side ensuring Courtney Lawes’s return to the English game was a disappointing one.

Louis Rees-Zammit was operating in his favoured wing position and got Bristol off to a strong start with two tries in the opening 23 minutes, offering Lam hope of a fruitful campaign from the Welshman.

“When you look at our wingers in the past, they scored a lot of tries and Louis is a world-class finisher,” the Bristol director of rugby said. “You get the ball to him in space and you create the opportunity, there’s a good chance he’ll finish it.”

Northampton will be hoping for a repeat of the meeting between the sides at Franklin Gardens in May when they thumped Bristol 94-33, but they have not won at Ashton Gate since 2021.

Both teams have made a pair of changes following their opening-weekend victories, with England international Ellis Genge among the players to drop out after spraining his wrist against Sale.

News.title: Sublime England thrash Croatia in best performance for a decade
News.content:
We came out of the World Cup wondering if Tuchel really had an idea of how he can get England over the line. After last Saturday’s defeat by world and European champions Spain, followed by Tuesday’s win over the Czech Republic we still did not know.

But here the standard was set – it was an exhilarating example of the football England are capable of. On display we saw the speed, the movement, the passes under pressure, the ambition, the control and aggression. This was the full package. Bottle it. Bag it. Believe it.

Croatia have an ageing team and are in transition, but they were left looking callow. It looked as though it was men against boys. There were plenty of boys in the stands, with 6,200 children allowed in for what was supposed to be a behind-closed-doors fixture – Croatia’s punishment for crowd trouble.

Their new head coach Slaven Bilic would doubtless have been relieved that the match was not played in front of the usual, passionate, partisan crowd. Even then some of the kids booed and left early. Bilic looked shell-shocked. As well he might.

News.title: Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying
News.content:
The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

News.title: Bath complete revenge mission on Exeter despite imperious Feyi-Waboso
News.content:
Bath held off a furious comeback from Exeter, led by the irrepressible Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, to avenge their Gallagher Prem semi-final defeat here in June.

It felt as if lightning might strike Bath twice. Once again Exeter overturned a 26-10 half-time deficit, to manufacture a second-half lead thanks to a pair of blistering finishes by Feyi-Waboso. Four months ago, Bath failed to take a drop goal in the closing stages, but this time with the reassuring presence of Finn Russell at fly-half, they kept their cool.

The Scotland playmaker twice sent penalties deep into the Exeter 22 from where Stephen Varney conceded a yellow card and penalty try before Bath replacement Ted Hill powered through a thicket of Exeter tacklers.

“Finn is one of the best 10s in the world and I thought he had a very good game,” Johann van Graan, the Bath head of rugby, said. “His decision making is above most players in the world and I thought that came through tonight.”

Despite the appearance of yet another high-scoring shoot-out, both teams defended with real bite, although Bath struggled to lay a finger on Feyi-Waboso who ended up in a scrap with a fan in the stands here when he was a spectator in May. He exacted a measure of revenge beating eight defenders and carried for 132 metres.

“Manny still needs game time,” Rob Baxter, the Exeter director of rugby, said. “When he’s on the ball, you see something incredible, but it is his ability to get on the ball again. He is just getting his game minutes and match fitness up.”

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco, which is placed between the cheek and lower gum, is particularly popular in south Asia. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

News.title: Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.

When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.

Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.

Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.

In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.

She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”

News.title: Eight tips to improve your laptop’s performance (and save your sanity)
News.content:
MacBooks and Windows laptops both have modes intended to maximise battery life. Low Power Mode (Mac) and Power Saver (Windows) should be avoided if you want peak performance.

On a Mac, you’ll find the Low Power Mode switch in Settings > Battery. For the best experience, set this to Never, but remember to change it back if you need your MacBook to last longer.

On a Windows laptop, there are two controls you need to consider. Both are found in Settings > System > Power & Battery.

Energy Saver mode uses multiple tactics to reduce battery consumption, including lowering maximum power. Switch this off, and you have access to Power Mode controls.

Your options are Best Power Efficiency, Balanced and Best Performance. While Balanced is the default, I was able to unlock up to 33 per cent more power by playing around with these settings using my own laptop.

To make matters more complicated, some laptops have their own performance modes. Many Asus laptops have MyAsus or Armory Crate, for example. Lenovo has the Vantage app, Dell has MyDell, and MSI laptops have MSI Center.

3. Stop applications from opening on start-up

If your laptop is slow when it first starts up, it may be because a whole bunch of apps have been given the green light to wake up with it.

Some applications such as antivirus software are critical, but most can be toggled off. As an example, I make sure apps such as Spotify, Steam and WhatsApp don’t open on startup; I only launch them when I need them.

On a MacBook, you can see which apps have this permission in Settings > General, under Open at Login. Select an app entry and click the “minus” button to remove it.

On a Windows laptop, you’ll find the list of start-up apps in Settings > Apps > Startup. Each entry has a little on/off slider.

Sports.title: Humphries to face Price in World Grand Prix final in 2023 repeat
Sports.content:
Gerwyn Price and Luke Humphries will look for their second World Grand Prix titles when they meet in Sunday's final of the double-start event in Leicester.

Price, the 2020 champion, beat Nathan Aspinall 5-2 in Saturday's first semi-final before 2023 winner Luke Humphries defeated James Wade 5-3 to reach his fourth straight final and set up a repeat of the showpiece game three years ago - when he saw off Price 5-2.

A major drought will end either way at the Mattioli Arena, with Humphries going over a year since his last premier title - the 2025 Premier League - and Price's previous elite silverware coming way back in 2022 at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.

The final, in which the winner will earn £150,000 and runner-up £80,000, will be first to six sets, with Humphries hoping to fare better than he did in 2024 and 2025, when he lost 6-4 to Mike De Decker and 6-1 to Luke Littler respectively.​​​

Price prevails after being frustrated by Aspinall antics

Price romped into a 3-0 lead over Aspinall, peeling off two 13-darters and then a 15-darter to sweep the opener before he broke The Asp in the deciding leg of set two.

The third set went on throw until the fourth leg, when Aspinall missed six darts to hold, including two at double one, and Price subsequently pinned D10 to move 3-0 up.

Things seemed bleak for Aspinall when Price broke in 14 darts at the start of the fourth set, only for The Asp to win back-to-back legs with well-thrown darts at D16 around failed ones before pulling back a set with a stunning 132 finish featuring two bullseyes.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Nathan Aspinall's superb 132 checkout during his defeat to Gerwyn Price as he fired in successive bullseyes before hitting D16

The 2022 runner-up won the fifth set against the throw but Price did likewise in the sixth to move one away from victory and then broke Aspinall twice in a row in the seventh set, after being broken himself, to qualify for a fourth Grand Prix final following 2020, 2021 and 2023.

Speaking afterwards, Price said he had been annoyed by Aspinall complaining about the rowdy crowd, telling Sky Sports: "I was upset with him a little bit. I said, 'they're on your side bud, I'm up against it'.

"As good as the crowd is for me, they were all for him. He's performing a little bit on stage. I'm good friends with Nathan, but sometimes you've got to let your darts go. It did [affect my game]."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Price said he had words with Aspinall on stage after becoming annoyed with his opponent's reactions to the crowd

'Controlled' Humphries into another Leicester final

Later, Humphries ended Wade's hopes of a third World Grand Prix crown, and first since 2010.

'Cool Hand' won the sixth set on throw after the first five had been taken 3-1 by the player throwing second.

Wade, who produced the checkout of the game with a 141 in the second set but largely struggled to hit the mandatory leg-opening double, took the next stanza, but Humphries was not to be denied, firing in back-to-back 137s to break 'The Machine' in the eighth set around two holds of throw.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Humphries gave Wade a nod of respect after The Machine pinned a fantastic 141 checkout during their semi-final

Humphries, who had beaten Dave Chisnall, Jermaine Wattimena and Niels Zonneveld prior to knocking out Wade, told Sky Sports: "I did say I was going to play a lot better and I did - I felt a lot more relaxed.

"That was the real me there today and I'm really proud of myself for performing like that. It's been a long time since I've felt that control and not like I was going to flounder a little bit.

"To make four Grand Prix finals on the trot is super special. It's history and I'm proud of that but unless I pick that trophy up, unfortunately that history doesn't mean anything.

"I've got to do it again [on Sunday] because there's so many major finals I've let slip. Gezzy [Price] is playing well but if I play like that again, it's going to be a cracking game."

Sports.title: Third time lucky for Pocognoli as Scotland mark Robertson's 100th cap with win
Sports.content:
Sebastien Pocognoli secured his first Scotland win at the third time of asking as captain Andy Robertson became just the second player to reach 100 caps.

The head coach insisted there was no extra pressure after drawing a blank in their opening two Nations League games, but he and the players silenced some critics with a strong performance in Skopje despite a second red card inside a week as they beat North Macedonia 2-0.

Robertson missed two brilliant chances before Kieron Bowie - hooked after Jack Hendry's early sending off against Switzerland in midweek - smashed the ball into the bottom corner to earn his first international goal and Scotland's first in over 420 minutes.

Play was stopped by a dog running onto the pitch before Scotland continued to dominate with Bowie, Robertson and Ben Gannon-Doak going close before the break.

Scotland were awarded a penalty when Gannon-Doak went down in the box after half-time, only for the referee to overturn his decision after being called to the monitor.

VAR did then award the visitors a penalty soon after. Rangers striker Bojan Miovski was judged to have stopped Bowie's rebound with his arm after Scott McKenna hit the post.

Questions had been asked about John McGinn's Scotland future but the Aston Villa skipper sent the 'keeper the wrong way to double their lead. It was his 22nd goal for his country.

Image: John McGinn celebrates making it 2-0 from the penalty spot

But with the visitors looking comfortable, it was a repeat of Hendry's red on Tuesday as McKenna was sent packing late on for his last-man challenge on Agon Elezi.

Scotland host Solvenia at Hampden Park on Tuesday night in the final Nations League match of this extended international break.

Image: Scotland's Scott McKenna (R) was sent off late on

The key moments from the Philip II Arena

5: SAVE! A clean strike from Andy Robertson, a brilliant save from Stole Dimitrievski.

7: GOAL SCOTLAND! Kieron Bowie hammers the ball into the bottom corner from outside the box.

10: CLOSE! Robertson again. The Scotland captain fires wide of the far post with Oli McBurnie screaming for the pass.

10: PITCH INVASION! Well, there's a dog on the pitch. They catch the pooch quickly and the game gets back underway.

Image: A dog ran onto the pitch during the first half in Skopje

13: OVER! Robertson is a man on a mission, with this effort going just over the bar.

28: OVER! Bowie waits for the opening and cuts the ball back to Ben Gannon-Doak, but he gives it too much and it's over.

30: HUGE CHANCE! Bowie chases down the ball and just has to take it around the 'keeper, but it's eventually blocked.

34: SAVE! Dimitrievski does well to hold onto Gannon-Doak's effort from the edge of the box.

50: CHANCE! McGinn does well to set up Gannon-Doak, but he hits it straight at the 'keeper.

51: PENALTY FOR SCOTLAND! Gannon-Doak is brought down as he bursts into the box, and the referee points to the spot.

54: NO PENALTY! The referee is called to the monitor, and after a review it is overturned.

Image: Referee Francois Letexier overturns Scotland's penalty decision

56: SAVE! Brilliant again from Gannon-Doak as he takes a touch before firing towards goal.

57: CLOSE! John McGinn is so close to Scotland's second, but the Aston Villa captain's effort is just wide.

64: PENALTY FOR SCOTLAND! Scott McKenna hits the post and Bowie's rebound looks to be stopped by Bojan Miovski.

69: GOAL SCOTLAND! John McGinn sends the 'keeper the wrong way and Scotland are two up.

83: RED CARD! It was all going so well, but Scott McKenna is sent packing for a last-man challenge on Agon Elezi.

Progress under Pocognoli

Image: Scotland's Kieron Bowie celebrates with Oliver McBurnie and John McGinn after scoring the opener against North Macedonia

"Not much to say" was Sebastien Pocognoli's verdict after their midweek defeat to Switzerland but the new boss will be far more encouraged by what he saw in Skopje.

They looked far more like the side that impressed in the second half of their goalless draw in Slovenia a week ago.

Controlled and dominant, although the level of opposition cannot be overlooked given North Macedonia's place at the bottom of the group.

Kieron Bowie looked brilliant and should have added to his first international goal. Pocognoli's new call-ups, Stephen Welsh and Luis Binks, also impressed.

Image: Brondy captain Luis Binks has started Scotland's last two games

Scotland have ended their last two games with 10 men and in Skopje that made the last few minutes more uncomfortable that it should have been.

That will be a concern, but the chances created will bring confidence. Now, they just need to finish a few more of them.

Robertson: 'It means everything'

Image: Andy Robertson applauds the Scotland fans at full time

Scotland captain Andy Robertson speaking to BBC Scotland about his 100th cap:

"It means everything to me, it means everything to my family.

"I've been away now 100 times, I've got to feel sorry for my wife! It's been an unbelievable journey, I remember my first game and it's been a process since then.

"It's emotional for me. I love this country, there's only one person before me in the men's game to do that, it's a pretty special achievement.

"I thought Kenny Dalglish was going to be worried about his goalscoring record in the first five minutes! I had about six shots.

"They did a nice presentation for me, I told them I wanted the win. The lads did so well to get the win, it'll be a special one for me and my family."

On Scott McKenna's sending off, which came from a tackle after Robertson's short pass, the captain adds: "I apologise for the pass to Scott McKenna, I'll have to go in and apologise to him for that.

"We played really well on a really difficult pitch. We made it a wee bit interesting with the sending off but we defended so well for the last 10 minutes. All of the lads were magnificent and it was a big win. You want to get it as early as possible for the new manager and thankfully we did that tonight."

Pocognoli refuses to get carried away

Image: Sebastien Pocognoli celebrated his first win with Scotland

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli speaking to BBC Scotland.

"I'm very pleased with this first win. But, we stay stable because we have a game in three days, and we want just to have another good game before the end of the first break.

"We played a very good game, we created a lot of chances, we keep two times a zero in three games, which for me means a lot also.

"We played with the right attitude, and for me it was a nice game, not everything was perfect, because we should have scored more goals, but we are in the continuity of the second half from Slovenia, and I hope we can have another good game at home."

On Kieron Bowie's first Scotland goal, he added: "He scored the most difficult one from the game. I was really pleased for him, because I know that the topic about not scoring will be on the table after 25 minutes.

"I was really pleased with his performance, and from many of the lads."

Sports.title: 'Our boys can't believe it' - Powell on Wakefield's 'phenomenal, immense' title run
Sports.content:
Wakefield Trinity head coach Daryl Powell revealed members of his playing squad were in shock following their stunning Super League Grand Final victory, two years on from playing in England's second tier.

Wakefield were crowned Super League champions for the first time in the club's history with a resounding 23-10 victory over Warrington Wolves in the Grand Final at Old Trafford, a week on from travelling to huge favourites Wigan Warriors and dispatching of them 33-6 in the semi-finals.

The success proved Wakefield's first league title for 58 years dating back to 1968, and all the more remarkable considering they were relegated from Super League in 2023, playing the 2024 season in the Championship under Powell.

"I'm just amazed really at the players and how good they've been," Powell said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Super League Grand Final between Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity

"Obviously it's pretty sweet for me as an individual but for the club, the players, the coaching staff, everything that we've built up over the last three years is phenomenal.

"We've been building for a while but the last two weeks in particular have been just incredible performances from an unbelievable group of players.

"The boys have got such confidence in each other, that if we all do our jobs then we can do anything we want. We've done that this year. It's just immense.

"It's been an amazing finish to the season, wow. I couldn't speak more highly of the boys about everything they do, really.

"I know there's quite a few boys in there who just can't believe it. That we've been able to do all that.

"But it's just a testament to how good they are. I'm so proud of everything. The club, the fans - the way that they've been - obviously the players. They are just such a pleasure to coach and be around. It makes it an easy job."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tom Johnstone's sensational finish proved the key try of the second half to snuff out Warrington's fightback

For Powell, 61, it was his first time leading a side out in a Super League Grand Final since 2017, when he was Castleford Tigers head coach and lost heavily to Leeds Rhinos.

Saturday's success was made even sweeter for Powell by the fact it came against Warrington, where he coached for two seasons before being dismissed in 2023.

"This is the best [achievement], really," he added. "It looked like maybe I'd slip through my career and not win the big game after 2017 and it's been a long time.

"I had a tough time at Warrington, and then to come back and do this with Wakefield, it's phenomenal.

"For me, it's right up there. Just being at Wakefield and feeling at home again in a place and being able to get a group of men together who can do special things, it's unbelievable.

"I've had some great times in my coaching career, but this is the best."

Sports.title: Whittaker clings on to beat Wallace despite final round fright
Sports.content:
Ben Whittaker was left clinging on as he got through a torrid final round to outpoint Conor Wallace.

An Olympic silver medallist and unbeaten professional hope, Whittaker was looking to advance to world level in this IBF title eliminator against Wallace in Birmingham.

Whittaker showed off his skills over the first half of the fight, dominating proceedings as he commanded the distance between them.

He whipped hard shots into the Irishman, now based in Australia. Wallace however withstood them but Whittaker, who sprinkled in some of his trademark showboating, was so comfortably ahead through nine rounds that he seemed to be in complete control.

Image: Whittaker dominated the first nine rounds of the fight with Wallace.

But that all suddenly changed. Wallace hurt him with a big shot in the 10th round. He punished Whittaker for holding his hands low, keeping that pressure on the Olympic star.

Wallace badly shook up Whittaker in the 12th and last round. He had Whittaker reeling and lunging in to clinch and grab Wallace. That saw Whittaker slipping and stumbling to the canvas, falling three times but the referee deemed none of them to be a knockdown.

Image: Whittaker slumps into Wallace on the ropes

Whittaker ultimately won unanimously, taking it 117-111, 116-112 and 115-113 on the cards.

Bilal Fawaz retained the British and Commonwealth super-welterweight titles with an impressive knockout finish as he took out Eithan James in their eighth round.

Sports.title: Wakefield claim historic win over Warrington to become Super League champions
Sports.content:
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Super League Grand Final between Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity Highlights of the Super League Grand Final between Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity

Wakefield Trinity were crowned Super League champions for the first time in the club's history with a 23-10 victory over Warrington Wolves in the Grand Final at Old Trafford.

It is the first time Wakefield have made the Grand Final and they achieved their greatest glory on their first attempt.

They also become the sixth winner of Super League, joining Wigan Warriors, St Helens, Leeds Rhinos, Bradford Bulls and Hull KR.

It rounds out a fairy-tale story for Wakefield who were relegated in 2023, returned to Super League in the 2025 season, and have now written themselves into the history books as champions.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Wakefield take the lead against Warrington after an incredible pass from Lachlan Walmsley sets up Cameron Scott in the corner Wakefield take the lead against Warrington after an incredible pass from Lachlan Walmsley sets up Cameron Scott in the corner

Wakefield held a dominant 19-0 half-time lead thanks to converted tries from Cameron Scott, Isaiah Vagana and Jazz Tevaga, Max Jowitt staying calm under pressure with the boot.

The extra point was then added by Jack Sinfield with just minutes left in the first half.

Early in the second half there was drama as Corey Hall was sent to the sin bin for a high shot on Arron Lindop. Lindop scored with Wakefield a player down, and added a second later on, Ewan Irwin converting the first.

However, a try from Trinity winger Tom Johnstone was enough for them to stay far enough ahead and seal immortality.

Johnstone picked up the Rob Burrow Award for his phenomenal display in both attack and defence.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Wakefield complete the fairy tale with stunning Grand Final win

In front of an electric and sold-out Old Trafford, it was a flawless first 40 from Wakefield Trinity.

They thought they had opened the scoring on the sixth minute when Johnstone went over in the corner. However, on review, it was clear he had been held up then forced into touch.

It took only six minutes longer though for the Yorkshire side to get on the board thanks to a sublime no-look, one-handed flick pass from Lachlan Walmsley which sent Scott walking in and with the Jowitt conversion, they had a 6-0 lead.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Wakefield score two quick-fire tries to take complete control in the Grand Final Wakefield score two quick-fire tries to take complete control in the Grand Final

While it was end-to-end stuff, metres were coming much more easily to Wakefield with their pack proving too strong. That meant every set ended in pressure.

In the 25th minute, a brilliant Jake Trueman pressure kick saw Johnstone jump highest and find Vagana on his shoulder to walk in. Jowitt added the extras once again.

Just over 10 minutes later, Tyson Smoothy went close and then was followed by Tevaga who threw a dummy and then used his power to barrel over. Jowitt stayed perfect with the boot to extend Wakefield's lead further.

With less than two minutes remaining of the opening half, Jack Sinfield used some big-game nous to send over a drop goal to give Wakefield a more than three-score lead, and left Warrington with a mountain to climb at 19-0 down.

There was drama immediately in the second half when Wakefield's Corey Hall was sent to the sin bin for a high shot on Arron Lindop to give Warrington their opportunity to hit back, and they did.

Irwin threw a lovely dummy and then passed to open up the space and with a player advantage, Lindop had all the room to walk over in front of the Warrington faithful. Irwin converted to bring the scoreline to 19-6.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Warrington are back in the game as they score shortly after Corey Hill is sin-binned for a high tackle Warrington are back in the game as they score shortly after Corey Hill is sin-binned for a high tackle

Warrington thought they had gone in again through Matty Ashton just minutes later, but a forward pass ruled out what would have been a score that brought the game right back in the balance

However, with numerical parity restored, it did not take long for Wakefield to get back on top once again and off the back of huge metres from Caleb Hamlin-Uele, they sent it out to Johnstone who used his step to pull off a sensational finish and with a 23-6 lead and 20 minutes to play, the Wakefield end was bouncing.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Wakefield are closing in on a Grand Final win after a fabulous try to extend their lead Wakefield are closing in on a Grand Final win after a fabulous try to extend their lead

Warrington would not give up and with eight minutes left on the clock they kept the last tackle alive; Irwin sent over a looping pass and Lindop was in for his second. However, this time Irwin could not convert and the score was 23-10.

However the clock quickly ran away, Wakefield stayed strong, and immortality was theirs as the full-time hooter went and their name was etched onto the Super League trophy.

Wakefield Trinity head coach Daryl Powell to Sky Sports:

"We just kept talking about it, and the players have gradually developed and got better. Then it becomes a reality when they see what they are capable of.

Burgess: They beat us physically - it hurts

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Warrington Wolves head coach Sam Burgess reflects on his side's Grand Final loss Warrington Wolves head coach Sam Burgess reflects on his side's Grand Final loss

"It was Wakefield's day today .The challenge is to now take that next step. It will be a long few weeks away."

Sports.title: 'Complete' England display reinvigorates faith in Tuchel project - for now
Sports.content:
"We will always have a scar, we will always feel pain and disappointment. But this is the way to move forward."

Thomas Tuchel knows England's frustrating, much-criticised semi-final defeat to Argentina at the World Cup will hang over him and his team right through until the Euros in 2028 - and even beyond.

But in Croatia on Saturday, a thumping 7-0 win was a performance and result to reinvigorate Tuchel's England project.

It was a historic scoreline: Croatia's heaviest defeat. No team had scored more than four goals away to them before.

Of course, the Nations League is not the World Cup and this ageing Croatia side, a shadow of their great teams of the past, could not provide an elite examination. But England's "complete" performance, as it was described by manager, players and pundits alike, is something to get behind again.

Last week, the positives against Spain were clouded by defensive mistakes and a clear gap in quality; the win over Czech Republic was distorted by the first-half red card. But this was emphatic.

The front four were electric and devastating. Elliot Anderson and Alex Scott, on his first start, bossed the midfield battle against their far more capped counterparts. There was a horror miss from Mateo Kovacic at 3-0 but Croatia were limited to little else, with England's full-backs far busier creating chances than having to stop them.

"When England are rampaging all over the pitch like this, winning back possession when they have no right to do so, passing forward at every opportunity and finishing ruthlessly, there is no better team in world football to watch," wrote Sky Sports News football correspondent Rob Dorsett from the press box.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rob Dorsett gives his player ratings for England's dominant 7-0 victory over Croatia.

It was the best performance of the Tuchel era, and the England boss agreed. "It was a fantastic victory. It's an outstanding result, of course, and the performance underlying this result is just on the highest level, from the first minutes to the last," he said.

"The speed and the technical quality today and the hunger off the ball was on the very highest level."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Thomas Tuchel praised England's 'dangerous' front four in their 7-0 victory over Croatia and the team's 'complete performance' across 90 minutes

When Tuchel named his squad for this international break, he used his first press conference since the World Cup to insist on the message that this summer's tournament would increase his team's chances of success in the future. The "brotherhood" they built and experiences they shared in North America would be crucial in the next chapter, he explained.

That assessment will have been difficult to swallow for many England fans at the time, with Tuchel's tactical decisions late on against Argentina and his subsequent criticism of English footballers' "DNA" still raw. But perhaps in Rijeka there were signs of that theory starting to play out.

"I just believe we have now a lot of experience together," said Tuchel, when asked why it had clicked in Croatia.

"We had a qualifying campaign together, we had a big tournament together, we have big positive emotions together, we lived through them together, we had big pain together. We just get to know each other better, know the players better and know what to demand and how to motivate.

"It was a good spirit from the start of the camp and it's nice to see that it builds up. It was a day where every puzzle piece fell into place."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Harry Kane felt is was 'as good as it gets' after England's dominant win over Croatia in the Nations League

Tuchel warned that Czech Republic will provide a different test at Wembley on Tuesday and suggested England fans shouldn't demand seven goals and floods of chances in every game. But they have reasons to expect excitement in that next Nations League game now. A 7-0 win does that.

Spain away on November 15, however, will have a far more powerful impact on the feeling about Tuchel's England and whether the idea they are on a progressive path to glory is correct.

England may well have secured their place in the Nations League quarter-finals by that final group game, with Croatia at home in the days before it. But facing the world champions in Madrid is the kind of test where England must really show how far they have come - and whether they have learned the lessons of the past.

That game will set the tone and feeling over the winter months about whether England are able to go and win on the biggest stages.

For now, this 7-0 thrashing of Croatia, in a small stadium filled with schoolchildren, will provide a welcome uplift.
