World.title: Hungry and Out of Options, More Poor Liberians Turn to Begging as Prices Outrun Income
World.content:
Members of Vamoma group seeking assistance in Monrovia. Photo: Fatu A. Kamara

Summary

As Liberia’s economy shows signs of recovery on paper, soaring food and fuel prices, worsened by a government fuel surcharge and new health care fees imposed after US aid cuts, have outpaced wage growth.

Ten Liberians interviewed in Monrovia say growing unemployment, lost livelihoods and financial hardship in the last two years have pushed them to depend on strangers and charitable support to survive.

Humanitarian organizations and government say they are seeing growing demand for assistance as families struggle with food, school fees, healthcare and other basic needs.

By Fatu Kamara with New Narratives

BROAD STREET, Monrovia – It has been a long day for Joseph. The sun is beginning to set, and the 48-year-old father of three has been trawling the streets of Monrovia since morning, asking for money.



On most days, he begs for money to feed his family. Today, he can’t even raise enough to get home to Brewerville, on the outskirts of the city.

“Since this morning, nobody has given me a dime,” he says.

Joseph lost his job in waste management in 2025 after the death of his boss. A high school graduate who earned L$10,000 (US$55) monthly, he spent about a year looking for another job without success.

He says he now has two options: begging or stealing. “It is not fair for me to be begging people in the streets, but I will not go to steal.”

Joseph is one of 10 people interviewed for this story who said they began begging within the past two years. Most said they had no jobs, had lost sources of income or lacked money to start a business. (FrontPage Africa/New Narratives is withholding the names of people in this story to protect them from stigma.) Liberia’s economy grew 5.1 percent in 2025, according to the African Development Bank, a jump from years before, but most families haven’t felt it. Growth came mostly from mining royalties to government, not job creation, and extreme poverty still rose to 35.8 percent.

The crisis deepened when the Trump administration canceled 27 of 29 USAID programs in Liberia in May 2025, cutting nearly US$360 million from health and education. Large cuts by other donors followed too. The government responded by adding a $0.25 per gallon petroleum surcharge and implementing new patient fees for healthcare. For families already struggling to afford food, the surcharge pushed up transport and food costs, and the hospital fees have deterred many from going for treatment or crippled them financially when they face emergencies. Baba Conteh, an economist, says economic recovery has not translated into meaningful jobs and stable incomes for ordinary households. Aid cuts have trickled down throughout the economy. “Job loss is one of the most common pathways into poverty,” Conteh says, particularly when the loss continues long enough for families to exhaust their savings and sell productive assets. In extreme cases, he says, people may become homeless, engage in high-risk survival activities, depend heavily on public charity or even resort to committing crimes.

That is exactly what is happening. At Vamoma house on Tubman Boulevard, in Sinkor, Esther Kamara leads a group of widows, elderly people and people with disabilities who gather to seek assistance. She says the group had about 280 members in 2024 and has since grown by 50.

People living in poverty gather at Vamoma house, on Tubman Boulevard, in Sinkor

“I have even started refusing people because the number just getting plenty and no help is coming,” Kamara says.

After more than a decade of leading the group, Kamara says the past two years have been the toughest. “Many days the women come to me when they or their children are sick and no money to take them to hospital, so we just buy drugs and they take it,” she says. The drugs are usually antibiotics, bought without a prescription and taken with no medical guidance, making the child likely to build antibiotic resistance.

Support groups under pressure from growing demand

The pressure is being felt by organizations that provide assistance. Siakeh Foundation and Kimbo Foundation, two organizations working with vulnerable Liberians, say requests for help have doubled over the last two years.

Four Hunger, a U.S.-registered nonprofit in Liberia, reports an increase in requests from families who previously managed to meet at least some of their basic needs but now struggle with food, school fees, healthcare and other essentials.

“The growing demand has put considerable pressure on our resources. One of the most difficult parts is that we often receive requests we genuinely want to respond to but cannot fully meet,” says co-founder Windell S. King.

At Rescue for Abandoned and Children in Hardship, or REACH, Ne-Suah Livingstone, founder and executive director, says she has also seen families pushed into situations they previously managed to avoid.

“One case that remains with me involved a family whose daughter’s annual school fees were about US$1,000. Her father had previously worked on a USAID-funded project but lost his job after the projects ended.”

She says the fees were far beyond the reach of the small organization.

REACH receives about twice as many requests for assistance as it did two years ago.

“This is one of the hardest tasks I face every day,” says Livingstone. “To say to a person in dire need that neither I nor my organization is able to help you; saying this can be like you have asked me to hurt someone.”

“I won’t steal” but begging comes with humiliation

At Vamoma, Hawa, a 43-year-old widow with two children, says asking for help became a last resort after she lost her husband in 2024. She says her youngest child, 14, is still in school through support from her church. Her older child is at home because she has not found the money to keep him in school.

“People were mocking me in my community because I am poor,” Hawa says. “I felt embarrassed and I could not bear the shame anymore.”

She says Vamoma offers more than the possibility of receiving money or food.

“At least when I am among my friends and we are laughing, the stress goes down,” Hawa says. “I don’t know what I was going to do if I had not joined the group.”

For some members, the hardship goes beyond asking strangers for help. Kamara says some elderly and vulnerable people face stigma in their communities.

“You know when people are like this, you will not find any family member coming around them,” she says. “They can abandon them. Sometimes they call them witches and wizards.”

Larwuo, a member of Vamoma, stands in front of her home. She says she was abandoned by her son.

Last month one elderly member of the group died here. Kamara had to ask government to collect the body.

Government response constrained by limited resources

Officials at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection have observed the growing need but have little money to help.

“The key gap in addressing the issues affecting these vulnerable groups is limited resources, preventing the ministry from reaching them,” says Alex Divine, the ministry’s assistant director of Programs, Partnership and Resource Mobilization.

The government tried to reduce the rapidly growing number of street children, which hit 366,000 according to a survey in 2023, before the cost-of-living crisis escalated. Through its “Support a Child, Save the Future” initiative, launched in 2024 to remove children from the streets through school enrollment, family reunification and support for caregivers. The government has conceded that it did not raise any of the $15 million cost of the project from donors and only budgeted a total of $1.3m itself. The ministry came under public fire this month when an official posted the names of children who were allegedly helped on Facebook. Since then, the ministry has refused to share details. There has been no independent audit of the project.

Women share cooked food donated by the Jetty company.

“While existing programs provide critical support, the support is insufficient because it reaches a limited number of the overall vulnerable population across the country,” Divine says.

At Vamoma, the group has no permanent shelter. Kamara says members once put together sticks and zinc to create a small shelter, but police later dismantled it.

“When the rain is falling, some people cover themselves with plastic,” she says. “Sometimes you see people trembling with the cold. We are disappointed in our leaders because they are sitting down and the people dying.”

The only help comes in food donations from groups like the Indian company Jeety Rubber or Yamah Brown, a dry goods seller in Red Light, who recently donated two bags of rice.

“They are our mothers. They don’t deserve it, but condition made them like this,” Brown says. “We will continue to help as long as we can afford.”

While assistance is important, Kamara says they want something reliable.

“What we really want is jobs for members, especially the widows, people who are able to work,” she says. “Many of them are strong and able to work, but we all come here and sit from morning to night because there’s nothing to do. If we had jobs, we won’t be here.”

Joseph agrees that breaking the cycle of dependency requires opportunities beyond daily charity.

“Even if I can get money to start a business, I would be grateful,” he says. “And a man is only respected when he provides for his family.”

For now, as the sun sets, Joseph gives up finding enough money to get transport home. He sets out on foot for a walk that may take hours and will end with the faces of disappointed and hungry children. He will wake up tomorrow and try again.

This report is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency which had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Landmark Rape Trial, Defendant Jallah Accuses Police of Planting His Saliva on Survivor’s Clothing
World.content:
Monrovia – Peter Bon Jallah, on trial for alleged gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping involving a 16-year-old boy, took the witness stand Thursday and accused investigators of deliberately placing his DNA on the teenager’s clothing to implicate him in the case. Jallah denied the charges, said he was elsewhere when the alleged assaults occurred, and insisted he did not know the teenager.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Jallah told Criminal Court “E” that police had obtained his saliva sample during the investigation and used it to connect him to clothing recovered from the alleged survivor.



“Why is my saliva DNA profile on the white T-shirt and boxer?” Jallah asked the court, directing attention to the Liberia National Police, which he said had custody of his DNA sample.

He went further, alleging that investigators intentionally placed his saliva on the clothing.

“They intentionally placed my saliva DNA on the white T-shirt and the boxer. Obviously, it was a means to an end,” he testified.

Jallah did not present evidence during his testimony to substantiate the allegation, and the court has made no finding that police manipulated or planted the DNA evidence.

What the Forensic Report Says

The DNA evidence is a significant component of the prosecution’s case.

Clothing recovered during the investigation was submitted to the Rwanda Forensic Institute for examination. According to the forensic report, a male DNA profile recovered from a white T-shirt, black T-shirt, shorts and boxer shorts matched Jallah’s DNA profile.

The Judiciary has confirmed that Rwandan forensic examiner Bavugirije Pascal was summoned to testify regarding the findings.

Jallah has not simply disputed the laboratory’s conclusion. His defense is that his DNA could have been placed on the clothing after investigators obtained his saliva sample.

That allegation now puts the handling and chain of custody of the DNA evidence at issue before the court.

Jallah: ‘I Was Somewhere Else’

Jallah also denied being present during any of the alleged assaults.

The teenager has testified that he was assaulted on three occasions—twice at Jallah’s residence in November and December 2025, and again in January 2026 at a building on Camp Johnson Road after he was allegedly taken from the Airfield area and held for several days.

Jallah rejected that account.

He testified that he was in the Mikey Gray Community on Du-Port Road with his partner and her family on the relevant date. He also denied being at his home on November 29 and December 24, 2025, when two of the alleged assaults were said to have occurred.

Jallah questioned the teenager’s description of his residence, telling the court that the boy could not accurately describe the bedroom where the alleged assaults were said to have occurred.

He further pointed to phone records from January 1 to 3, 2026, and around Christmas 2025, which he said could establish his whereabouts.

‘I Never Knew Him’

Jallah also rejected the prosecution’s account of his relationship with the teenager.

Prosecutors have alleged that the boy was familiar with Jallah’s residence and performed chores there, including washing his vehicle.

Jallah denied knowing the teenager.

He told the court that he has an assigned vehicle and a driver who, according to him, washes the vehicle twice daily.

He also denied giving the teenager LD$1,500 to dispose of garbage, describing the allegation as untrue.

Jallah Challenges Medical Evidence

Jallah also challenged the interpretation of the medical evidence presented in the case.

He argued that the medical findings, at most, indicated signs consistent with penetration and ejaculation but did not independently establish that rape occurred.

He similarly questioned the ability of the Rwandan forensic examiner to determine whether a sexual assault had occurred, maintaining that the expert’s role was limited to the scientific examination of evidence.

The statutory rape charge, however, is based on the alleged victim’s age and the applicable provisions of Liberian law.

Testimony Comes After Failed Acquittal Bid

Jallah’s testimony came a day after Criminal Court “E” Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr. denied his motion for a judgment of acquittal.

In his September 30 ruling, Judge Wesseh found that the prosecution had presented sufficient evidence for the trial to continue.

The defense had asked the court to dismiss the charges after the prosecution rested its case, arguing, among other things, that the teenager’s descriptions of the alleged crime scenes did not correspond with observations made during the court’s visit to the locations.

With the motion denied, Jallah took the stand to present his defense and directly challenge the evidence and testimony presented by the prosecution.

DNA Evidence Now Central to Defense

The prosecution has presented testimony from the alleged survivor, police investigators and medical personnel and has relied, in part, on the forensic findings linking Jallah’s DNA to clothing examined by the Rwanda Forensic Institute.

Jallah disputes the prosecution’s account and maintains that investigators manipulated the DNA evidence.

Whether the DNA evidence was properly collected, handled and preserved—and whether the forensic findings establish the connection alleged by the prosecution—are matters for the court to determine based on the evidence presented at trial.

Jallah faces charges of gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping. He has pleaded not guilty and remains presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Two other men allegedly linked to the January incident have not been arrested and were charged in absentia.

World.title: Coming Home to Heal: Liberian American Surgeon Bringing Global Team to Treat Patients and Train Health Workers
World.content:
Monrovia – Dr. Carolyn Baindu Moore built her career in the United States as a robotic thoracic surgeon, operating on the chest with some of medicine’s most advanced tools. In December, she is bringing a team home to Liberia, where some counties have no specialist surgeon at all.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Moore is CEO and founder of the Liberia Global Health & Surgery Consortium (LGHSC), which officially launches in the country from December 1 to 15. Over two weeks, the group plans to operate on patients, train 250 people in emergency care, screen 100 market women for cancer and hold its first fundraising dinner in Monrovia.



She says she doesn’t want this to be a one-time trip.

“Our goal is to leave a lasting impact through compassionate care, practical training, and partnership with Liberian healthcare teams,” she said.

The gap

Liberians who have had to travel to Monrovia for an operation, or wait weeks for one, know the problem well. The civil war emptied hospitals and drove doctors and nurses abroad. Ebola came a decade later and killed health workers the country could not afford to lose. Liberia has been rebuilding ever since.

The most recent nationwide count of surgical staff, published in the World Journal of Surgery, found 286 surgical providers in Liberia in 2018. Only 67 were accredited specialists. That is 1.6 specialist surgeons, anaesthetists and obstetricians for every 100,000 people. The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery says a country needs at least 20. At the time, Liberia had three specialist anaesthesiologists for the whole country.

Most of those specialists work in Montserrado. In the poorest counties, the study counted 0.7 per 100,000 people.

Women pay much of the price. A UNFPA policy brief drawn from the 2022 national census puts Liberia’s maternal mortality ratio at 854 deaths per 100,000 live births, roughly one mother lost for every 117 babies born alive. The sub-Saharan African average is 536. The global target is under 70.

Then there is cervical cancer. The ICO/IARC Information Centre on HPV and Cancer estimates that 656 Liberian women are diagnosed with it each year and 469 die, about nine women every week. Most of those deaths can be prevented, because screening can catch the disease before it turns deadly. But many women are never screened, and by the time they reach a doctor, little can be done.

Who is coming

The visiting team is made up of five surgeons, six nurses, four global health partners and two medical students. On the ground, they will join five Liberian surgeons, 15 nurse volunteers and 17 Consortium volunteers. The Consortium says it works in partnership with the Ministry of Health, and that its plans were drawn up with Liberian hospital leaders, county health teams and community representatives.

In the operating room

From December 7 to 11, visiting and Liberian surgeons will operate side by side. Where equipment and facilities allow, that will include laparoscopic surgery, sometimes called “keyhole” surgery. Instead of one long cut, the surgeon works through a few small openings with a camera. Patients generally hurt less, heal faster and go home sooner. Few Liberian hospitals offer it now, and teaching it is one of the main reasons for the mission.

The hospital where the operations will take place, and how many patients will be treated, have not yet been confirmed. Local clinical teams will screen patients.

Learning to save a life

The same week, at the Liberian Learning Center at Paynesville Town Hall, the Consortium plans to train 250 people in Basic Life Support and Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support. The courses teach CPR and what to do when a heart stops, the kind of emergency where a few minutes decide whether someone lives.

Not all the trainees are medical workers. Doctors, nurses, residents and emergency medical staff will sit alongside ordinary citizens. Some will be trained to teach the course themselves, so the skills keep spreading after the visitors leave. The team is also donating automated external defibrillators, or AEDs, the portable machines that can shock a stopped heart back into rhythm. They are still hard to find in Liberia.

For the women who feed the city

On December 14 and 15, a mobile clinic will set up in the Rock Church community in Duazon for 100 market women. They will get health education, consultations, breast and reproductive health checks, and screening for cervical cancer and high-risk HPV. The Consortium’s pathology team will process the samples, and its OB/GYN workgroup will work with local health authorities to make sure women who need further care are referred.

The choice of market women is deliberate. They keep homes running and children in school, often on what they earn in a single day. Taking a day off to sit in a clinic queue means losing that money, so many simply don’t go. This time, the clinic is coming to them.

A dinner and a longer plan

On December 12, the Consortium will host its founding fundraiser banquet at Afro Beach, Thinker Village, from 6:00 to 10:30 p.m. Dr. Deddeh E. P. Supuwood will give the keynote address, and Mr. Leo Lekpele Nupolu-Johnson will be master of ceremonies. Money raised will go to patient care, training, equipment, and community outreach.

Medical missions to Africa have a mixed reputation. Too often, a team flies in, operates, takes pictures and flies out, leaving behind patients with no follow-up and local staff no better prepared than before. LGHSC, which now counts more than 120 members in more than 16 workgroups on four continents, says it is trying to do the opposite. It wants to work through Liberian teams, keep mentoring them, and keep checking on patients long after December.

Whether that works will only be clear after the visitors fly home. It will show in the nurse in Paynesville who can now run a resuscitation, the surgeon who can do a keyhole operation without help, and the market woman in Duazon whose results come back in time.

“Our measure of success,” Moore said, “is the quality of care we provide and the knowledge, confidence, and capacity that remain long after we leave.”

Those wishing to volunteer, partner, or support the launch can contact [email protected] or visit www.libghsc.org. Donations can be made at https://givebutter.com/XYetak.

World.title: Liberia: House Honors Fallen Former Bong County Lawmaker Ranney Jackson
World.content:
Monrovia – The leadership and members of the House of Representatives on Thursday paid their final respects to the late Dr. Ranney B. Jackson Sr., a former Bong County lawmaker and veteran public servant, during a State Funeral held at the Capitol Building in Monrovia.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The ceremony brought together members of the Legislature, government officials, family members, friends, former colleagues, and well-wishers who gathered to honor Jackson’s decades of service to Liberia.



Speaker of the House Richard Nagbe Koon, speaking on behalf of the leadership and members of the House, extended condolences to the bereaved family and recognized Jackson’s contributions to the Legislature and the Liberian state.

Speaker Koon said the presence of the House leadership and members at the funeral reflected the institution’s respect for those who have served the Liberian people under its mandate.

Members of the House joined the Speaker in a moment of solemn reflection and paid their final respects to their former colleague.

Dr. Jackson’s public service career spanned local government, the Legislature, national administration and public policy.

He served as a member of the National Transitional Legislative Assembly (NTLA) from 2003 to 2005, representing Bong County during a critical period in Liberia’s post-war transition.

During his two-year tenure, Jackson chaired the NTLA’s Post and Telecommunications Committee. His work on the committee included efforts that contributed to reducing the cost of SIM cards from US$65 to US$15 in 2005.

Following his service in the transitional legislature, Jackson remained active in national politics and public administration. He made three unsuccessful bids for the Bong County senatorial seat, contesting the elections in 2005, 2011 and 2014.

He later served as Superintendent of Bong County during the first administration of former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. During Sirleaf’s second term, he was appointed Deputy Minister for Operations at the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

Jackson’s public service continued under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, who in 2024 appointed him Co-Chairman of the Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Core Team, where he served alongside Chairman Cllr. Edwin Kla Martin.

At the Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Task Force, Jackson was recognized for his experience in governance, public administration, finance and public policy as the government intensified efforts to trace, recover and safeguard public assets.

Before his death, Jackson had also recently earned a Ph.D. in Public Policy and Administration, specializing in Local Government Management and Sustainable Communities, from Walden University in the United States.

His career reflected a progression through several levels of public service—from county administration and the transitional Legislature to senior positions within the national government and public policy.

Dr. Jackson died at the John F. Kennedy Memorial Hospital in Monrovia on August 22, 2024, at age 74, following a brief illness.

According to the obituary, the body will be taken to Bong County on Friday, October 2, for a night of wake-keeping, followed by the funeral service and burial on Saturday.

World.title: Liberia: FPA Report Triggers Action as China Union Assesses Pollution, Road Damage in Mining Communities
World.content:
MARGIBI COUNTY — A FrontPage Africa investigation into alleged environmental damage and deteriorating living conditions in communities surrounding China Union’s mining concession has prompted the company and Margibi County District Four Representative Emmanuel O. Yahr to conduct a joint field assessment of affected areas.

By Yawah Y. Jaivey

Bangli, a subsidiary of China Union, which is engaged in iron ore extraction around Bong Mountain in Bong and Margibi Counties, joined Rep. Yahr’s office over the weekend to inspect communities where residents have raised concerns about water pollution, damaged farmland, deteriorating feeder roads and other impacts they associate with mining activities.



The assessment followed an FPA report published two weeks ago documenting complaints from residents of several villages bordering the China Union concession.

Residents alleged that mining activities have contributed to the pollution of waterways and farmland, deposits of mud and mining debris, excessive dust and damage to roads used to transport agricultural produce and access essential services.

Following the publication, Rep. Yahr conducted an initial assessment of the affected communities and engaged residents about their concerns before bringing the issues to the attention of Bangli management.

During the latest joint assessment, representatives of Bangli and Rep. Yahr’s office visited several communities to examine the allegations firsthand, including claims involving contaminated water sources, damaged crops and deteriorating farm-to-market roads.

At the conclusion of the assessment, Bangli management committed to addressing concerns raised by the affected communities and taking appropriate measures going forward.

Residents, meanwhile, commended Rep. Yahr for responding to their complaints and expressed hope that the company would follow through on its commitments.

The affected communities include Neitasue, Gboryourmue, Benmue and Jack Village, with residents estimating that more than 2,000 people across the communities are affected by the reported conditions.

During an earlier FPA tour of communities near the Bangli mining area, residents described what they said were worsening environmental and living conditions.

An FPA reporter observed deposits of mud and iron ore debris covering sections of vegetable gardens and rice fields. Some waterways and surrounding farmland also contained visible sediment and mining-related debris.

Residents said the situation becomes particularly severe during heavy rainfall, when muddy water and sediment reportedly flow from mining areas into creeks and other water sources used by surrounding communities.

Residents Complain of Water Pollution

Moses Kollie, Town Chief of Gboryourmue Village in Margibi County, said residents have increasingly struggled to access what they consider safe drinking water since mining activities intensified.

“In our villages, we ran out of drinking water. After the mine started, most of our backwaters have been polluted,” Kollie said.

He also alleged that pollution has affected agricultural production by reducing the amount of land residents can effectively cultivate.

“All our farming lands and waters have been polluted. Dust has covered all our plants. Productivity of the land is reduced. There’s less cultivable soil available,” Kollie told FPA.

Residents said the reported conditions are threatening household food security and their ability to generate income from farming.

Tamba Philip, a resident of Neitasue Village in Fuamah District, Bong County, said a water source once used for drinking, bathing and washing clothes has become increasingly muddy.

“This is where we get drinking water, wash our clothes, and bathe, but now it has turned murky. There are already sediments, which were not here when there were no mining operations up in the mountain,” Philip said.

He said the problem becomes more pronounced during periods of heavy rainfall.

“You visit us here when there’s rain and see our body of waters. Murky water will go to several neighboring villages,” Philip said.

Mud, Mining Debris Affect Road Access

Residents also blamed mining-related runoff and sediment for worsening the condition of a feeder road linking some of the affected villages to surrounding communities.

According to residents, large quantities of mud and iron ore debris carried downstream from the mining area have accumulated along sections of the road, making transportation difficult and, at times, nearly impossible.

They said the deteriorating road has made it harder for farmers to transport produce to markets and for residents to access health care, schools and other essential services.

Samuel K. David, a resident of Gboryourmue, said China Union resumed mining operations nearly four years ago and alleged that the renewed activities have coincided with increased pollution of creeks and farmland.

David said residents have repeatedly requested assistance, including the installation of hand pumps and rehabilitation of damaged roads, but alleged that their concerns have not received adequate attention.

Blasting Raises Health, Structural Concerns

Residents have also raised concerns about loud blasting they associate with mining operations.

Some alleged that blasting, particularly at night, has disrupted sleep and created anxiety among people living near the mining areas.

Residents further claimed that repeated blasting has caused cracks in some houses. However, determining whether mining activity caused the reported structural damage would require an independent technical assessment.

Amara Tate, a Gboryourmue resident, said the combination of water pollution and blasting has heightened anxiety among residents.

“With the blasting that’s going on, our backwaters are not just polluted, but our houses are being damaged and we, especially those with hypotension, are left to endure those loud explosions. So, we’re mostly concerned about our health,” Tate said.

Residents Question Social Development Benefits

Beyond environmental concerns, residents say they have yet to see what they consider meaningful social and economic benefits from the company’s presence in their communities.

David alleged that communities directly affected by mining activities have not benefited sufficiently from social development initiatives associated with the concession.

He cited what he described as inadequate access to basic services, including clinics, safe drinking water, schools and employment opportunities.

According to David, communities affected by mining should receive tangible development benefits, particularly where their farmland, waterways, roads and livelihoods are affected.

Activist Calls for Accountability

Social justice activist Ambassador Joseph Orland Beyan has also called for greater accountability in the management of Liberia’s mineral resources, arguing that resource development should not come at the expense of communities living in mining areas.

Beyan said the Mineral Development Agreement between the Government of Liberia and China Union should protect the lives, dignity, health and livelihoods of people living within and around the concession.

He said he finds it difficult to believe that the Liberian government would knowingly enter into an agreement that places citizens at risk.

“Yet, the reality on the ground is deeply troubling. Our brothers and sisters living around the company’s operational areas are facing serious challenges. Their farmlands, sources of water, crops, homes, roads, and overall health and well-being are being affected, while many communities continue to live in conditions that deserve urgent attention,” Beyan said.

He urged authorities and the company to treat the concerns as issues affecting real communities rather than merely administrative matters.

“These are not just statistics or issues written on paper. These are our people. These are families. These are communities whose lives and livelihoods matter,” he said.

Beyan called for affected communities to have a meaningful platform to seek redress.

“We cannot remain silent when the people who are supposed to benefit from our natural resources are instead left struggling to protect their land, homes, health, and future,” he said.

He added that his group was preparing what he described as a new advocacy approach focused on accountability and the peaceful pursuit of justice for affected communities.

“Our natural resources must not come at the cost of the lives and dignity of our people,” Beyan said.

World.title: Integrity Watch Warns Liberia Must Verify Its Mineral Wealth Before Signing Major Deals
World.content:
Monrovia – Integrity Watch Liberia Executive Director Harold Marvin Aidoo is calling on the government to move cautiously in developing Liberia’s emerging critical-mineral sector, warning that the country could repeat its long history of exporting valuable resources while mining communities remain poor and little wealth is retained domestically.

In a detailed policy commentary released Thursday titled “Liberia Must Not Miss the Critical Minerals Moment,” Aidoo said growing global demand for minerals used in batteries, electric vehicles and renewable-energy technologies presents Liberia with another opportunity to turn its natural resources into long-term economic gains.

But he cautioned that the opportunity could become another resource curse if the government fails to establish the country’s actual mineral potential, strengthen oversight and negotiate investment agreements with enforceable benefits for Liberians.



Aidoo recommended that the government publish the non-confidential findings of a China-supported mineral survey and commission an independent geological verification before making major commitments to potential investors.

The survey has reportedly identified indications of lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, rare-earth elements and other strategically important minerals.

Aidoo, however, cautioned against treating mineral indications as proof of commercially viable reserves.

“Liberia has another chance to turn mineral wealth into lasting prosperity,” he said, arguing that the first step must be establishing exactly what minerals Liberia possesses, where they are located, their commercial value and whether they can be extracted responsibly.

Learning From Iron Ore

Aidoo pointed to Liberia’s experience with iron ore as a cautionary lesson.

He traced commercial iron-ore production to Bomi Hills in 1951, noting that the industry has generated exports and government revenue but has historically had limited connections to the wider Liberian economy.

“Railways and ports moved ore abroad, while the knowledge and industrial capacity needed to transform the wider economy remained insufficient,” he said.

He warned that the global transition toward cleaner energy could reproduce that pattern if Liberia becomes primarily a supplier of raw materials for green technologies manufactured elsewhere.

“The energy transition could reproduce that pattern,” Aidoo said. “Liberia might supply minerals for cleaner technologies overseas while absorbing environmental damage and receiving only a modest share of the value.”

He added: “A green product does not guarantee a fair supply chain.”

Global Competition Creates Leverage

Aidoo said growing competition among major economies for critical minerals could give Liberia greater bargaining power, provided the country approaches potential investors from a position of knowledge and strategic planning.

He cited China’s strong position in mineral processing and efforts by the United States and its partners to diversify their supply chains.

Liberia, he said, should engage China, the United States, Europe and other potential partners, but any agreements should be transparent and aligned with the country’s development priorities.

“The question for every partnership should be practical: what will Liberia gain beyond the export of ore?” he asked.

He recommended that future mining agreements contain measurable commitments covering Liberian employment, skills development, local procurement, shared infrastructure and environmental protection.

“Political friendship cannot substitute for a sound commercial bargain,” Aidoo said.

Verify Mineral Wealth, Strengthen Institutions

Aidoo identified geological knowledge and institutional capacity as immediate priorities.

He called for publication of the non-confidential findings of the mineral survey and independent verification of the country’s mineral potential.

He also urged the government to build institutions capable of interpreting geological data and independently assessing proposals from mining companies.

“Negotiating without that capacity places the country at a disadvantage before discussions even begin,” he said.

Aidoo further recommended a national critical-minerals strategy linking the sector to Liberia’s electricity, education, industrial and trade policies.

He argued that Liberia’s existing legal and policy framework—including the 2000 Minerals and Mining Law and 2010 Mineral Policy—predates the current global competition over minerals critical to the energy transition.

Any reforms, he said, should translate policy objectives into enforceable obligations.

Transparency in Mining Deals

Aidoo called for mineral licensing to be conducted transparently and competitively, with the beneficial ownership of companies seeking mining rights disclosed.

He also urged the government to make mining contracts publicly accessible and provide lawmakers responsible for ratifying agreements with independent technical advice.

Commitments on local procurement, training and mineral processing, he said, should include clear deadlines, measurable targets and consequences for non-compliance.

“Local procurement, training and processing commitments need deadlines, measurable targets and consequences for non-performance,” Aidoo said.

He also called for stronger safeguards to protect government revenue, including the capacity to independently verify mineral quality, production volumes and export values.

Such capacity, he said, would help the government detect under-invoicing and abusive pricing arrangements involving related companies.

“Without these safeguards, apparently attractive agreements can still leave the country collecting far less than it should,” he warned.

Value Addition Without Unrealistic Promises

While advocating greater domestic value addition, Aidoo cautioned against assuming that every mineral discovery should automatically lead to a refinery or processing plant.

“Liberia cannot demand a refinery for every deposit without considering electricity costs, water availability, environmental risks and markets,” he said.

Instead, he recommended that Liberia initially focus on retaining more geological, engineering, maintenance and logistics work associated with mining while gradually developing capacity for commercially viable processing.

Reliable and affordable electricity, he said, will be critical to that effort.

Major mining investments, Aidoo argued, should also contribute to electricity and transportation infrastructure that can benefit surrounding communities and other businesses.

“Shared railways, ports and transmission infrastructure can create economic opportunities well beyond the mine,” he said.

Skills, Jobs and Communities

Aidoo placed particular emphasis on developing Liberian technical expertise.

He called for greater investment in universities and vocational institutions to train geologists, engineers, laboratory technicians and environmental specialists.

Mining agreements, he said, should finance apprenticeships and recognized qualifications while creating opportunities for women and young people from mining-affected communities.

“Counting Liberians on payrolls is insufficient if technical knowledge and managerial authority remain elsewhere,” Aidoo said.

He said mining development should therefore be measured not only by the number of Liberians employed but also by whether Liberians acquire the technical knowledge and decision-making experience necessary to assume senior positions in the sector.

Aidoo also urged the government to ensure that communities affected by mining have a meaningful voice in decisions that could affect their livelihoods and environment.

Water protection, community consultation, accessible grievance mechanisms and adequately funded mine-closure plans, he said, should be enforceable requirements.

“Development cannot be measured only by export earnings when families lose farmland, fisheries or safe drinking water,” he said.

‘What Remains After the Minerals Are Gone?’

Aidoo further encouraged Liberia to work with neighboring countries to develop regional markets and industrial capacity around critical minerals.

While Liberia may not be able to manufacture every finished product domestically, he said the country can participate in African processing and manufacturing chains instead of remaining dependent on raw-material exports.

For Aidoo, the most consequential decisions will be made before mining licenses and long-term sales agreements are signed.

He urged the government to use the current period to establish the scale and commercial viability of Liberia’s mineral potential, strengthen regulatory institutions and define the benefits investors will be required to deliver.

“The decisions taken before licences and long-term sales agreements are signed will shape what Liberia retains for decades,” Aidoo said. “We should use this period to verify our mineral potential, strengthen institutions and define the benefits investors must deliver.”

He said Liberia’s success should ultimately be measured not simply by the volume of minerals exported or government revenue generated during individual projects, but by what remains after the resources are exhausted.

“Minerals are finite. Skills, productive infrastructure and capable institutions can outlast them,” Aidoo said.

“Liberia’s goal should be to turn the resources beneath our soil into the capacity to build prosperity long after the mines close.”

World.title: Holiness Revival Movement Brings Call For Righteousness, Heaven and Biblical Truth to Liberia
World.content:
Monrovia – A Christian ministry known as the Holiness Revival Movement is calling on Liberians to return to what it describes as the Biblical teachings of righteousness, holiness and preparation for eternity.

By Anthony Gray

Speaking ahead of a four-day conference scheduled for October 1–4 in Congo Town, outside Monrovia, Pastor Paul Rika said the movement is in Liberia to “revive holiness” and encourage Christians and non-Christians to embrace what he described as the truth of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.



Pastor Rika said the non-denominational movement was established as a means of bringing Christians together around Biblical teachings, emphasizing that human beings will ultimately face judgment.

According to him, the world is not a permanent place and people must therefore prepare for what comes after life.

He said Jesus Christ came and died for humanity so that people could have access to God, urging Christians to take seriously the teachings contained in the Bible.

Pastor Rika also linked some of the social problems and corruption in society to what he described as a decline in the preaching of biblical truth and the fear of God.

He referenced the Biblical instruction to observe the things written in Scripture, arguing that stronger adherence to Christian teachings could help promote moral discipline and responsible living.

The preacher further challenged those who question the existence of heaven and hell, saying Christians should take seriously the Bible’s teachings about life after death and divine judgment.

Meanwhile, Evangelist Linda Paul Rika shared her personal testimony, recounting what she described as a dramatic transformation from a lifestyle she considered contrary to Christian teachings.

She said that before encountering Jesus Christ, she struggled with alcohol, multiple relationships, drug use, tattoos, what she described as “naked dressing,” and visits to herbalists for charms.

Evangelist Linda said her experience eventually led her to embrace Christianity and dedicate herself to spreading a message of repentance, righteousness and holiness.

She also warned that, in her view, Satan is blinding people to the seriousness of sin and the consequences associated with it.

The Holiness Revival Movement says its Liberian campaign is intended to serve as a catalyst for Christians from different denominations to come together and renew their commitment to Biblical teachings.

Pastor Rika, who is currently on a tour of Liberia, said the campaign seeks to bring what he called “the life of the truth of Jesus Christ” to the Liberian people.

The conference is scheduled to run from October 1 to 4 with morning sessions beginning at 8:00 a.m. at the Oldest Congo Town, opposite SATCOM

Organizers are expecting large numbers of people to attend and are inviting Liberians from across the country to participate in what they describe as a life-changing Christian gathering focused on repentance, holiness and faith in Jesus Christ.

World.title: Don’t Be Distracted By “Pe Lampi” Chants; Focus On Delivering!
World.content:
When there was a power outage at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium during the Zambia-Togo match in Ndola the other day, a pocket of fans erupted into “Pe Lampi!” chants as they flashed the Tonse Alliance symbol.

It is common knowledge that PF cadres who have since metamorphosed into Tonse are stubborn in their support. This is not likely to change any time soon. Just look at how Tonse supporters led by the likes of Jay Jay Banda, Binwell Mpundu, Lillian Mutambo and Emmanuel Mwamba behave on social media. Not a single day passes without them offloading cheap propaganda. How can they be spreading lies that the President is indisposed or even calling for his assassination, and yet we have Church leaders cheering them on? Hypocrites!

We would like to urge the President and his incoming administration to keep ignoring these dimwits and minions and focus on his Grow Zambia Agenda – the 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 blueprint that speaks to real issues: maize, electricity, tourism, copper, soya, wheat, sugar and beef exports.

Let the work speak for itself!

President Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda is ambitious. But for it to work, it must move like lightening from every village, city and province.

1. 10 Million Tonnes of Maize – Who Will Grow It?

Is it only the commercial farmers? How does the villager in Shangombo or on Chilubi Island participate and benefit? This is where Cooperatives come in. The whole concept of cooperatives needs to be overhauled and adapted to changing seasons. We need genuine, production-based cooperatives – not briefcase cooperatives formed just to share FISP. Let us equip them with irrigation, mechanization and guaranteed markets.

2. 10,000 MW of Electricity – Diversify Now.

With El Nino always looming around the corner, the country must speed up diversification into alternative sources of energy. We cannot continue to depend on hydro alone. Councils must prioritize using part of the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to invest in solar power plants and even waste-to-energy plants. Every district has an abandoned dump site or sewer ponds that can host a solar plant.

3. 5 Million Tourists – Clean Up Zambia First.

No tourist is going to come to a dirty country. They are afraid of contracting cholera or malaria. The Mayor-Elect of Lusaka is already doing a commendable job cleaning up Lusaka. We hope this will be replicated countrywide. We expect clean cities, paved walkways, street lights, working traffic lights and flowers blossoming everywhere! Tourism starts with order and cleanliness.

4. 3 Million Tonnes of Copper – Not Raw.

Is this copper going to be exported in its raw form as we have done for 60 years? We expect to see value addition. We want to see copper cables, electrical wiring, motor windings and EV battery components manufactured right here in Zambia. That is how we create jobs.

5. 3 Million Tonnes of Soya Beans – The Feed and Oil Link.

Soya is the new gold. It links directly to stock feed, cooking oil and exports. Let us support out-grower schemes and oil processing plants in every province.

6 & 7. 1 Million Tonnes Wheat and 1 Million Tonnes Sugar – Winter Cropping.

This calls for serious irrigation investment. We have water everywhere but we only farm in the rainy season. Wheat and sugar are winter crops that can be grown under irrigation.

8. $1 Billion Beef Exports – Bring Back Ranches.

We had great ranches in Mumbwa, Chisamba and Southern Province. They collapsed. Let us revive them with proper breeding, veterinary services and abattoirs that meet export standards.

In short, 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 is possible – but only if we decentralize it to cooperatives, councils and ordinary Zambians.

Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

Secretary General

HH Mpaka 2O31 People’s Alliance

World.title: Zambia Post‑2026: Can the Grow Zambia Agenda Coexist with Civic Space Decay?
World.content:
By Venus N Msyani

The aftermath of Zambia’s 2026 general election has ushered in a period of deep uncertainty, marked by what many observers describe as a rapid decay of civic space. President Hakainde Hichilema’s administration appears intent on pushing the nation to “move on,” yet the methods being used to enforce this political closure have raised serious concerns.

Arrests, intimidation, and punitive actions against critics have become increasingly visible, creating an atmosphere of fear rather than unity. This is occurring against the backdrop of an election whose credibility has been questioned by the European Union and several other reputable monitoring bodies, all of whom expressed dissatisfaction with the conduct and outcome of the polls.

One of the most striking developments has been the targeting of religious leadership. The Archbishop of Lusaka, Alick Banda, widely respected for his defense of human rights, democracy, and the marginalized, spent a night in jail on charges related to a previously settled stolen‑vehicle case.

For many Zambians, this incident symbolized a troubling shift: even the Church, historically a moral anchor and mediator during political crises, is no longer safe from state pressure. Archbishop Banda’s consistent advocacy for truth and justice appears to be the very reason he is now facing persecution.

Beyond the clergy, ordinary citizens and political actors have also felt the weight of state power. Passports have been confiscated from individuals who refuse to accept what they view as a compromised election victory. Others have been detained for prolonged periods without clear timelines for court appearances. These actions collectively paint a picture of shrinking civic freedoms at a moment when national cohesion is desperately needed.

It is within this tense environment that President Hichilema unveiled the Grow Zambia Agenda during his inauguration on 1 September 2026. The agenda promises job creation, wealth generation, and shared prosperity over the next five years. His first international trip of the new term, a working visit to the United Arab Emirates from 29 to 30 September, was framed as the official launch of this development program. Upon his return to Lusaka, the President confirmed to reporters that the UAE trip was indeed aligned with the Grow Zambia vision.

However, not everyone interpreted the trip as a confident stride into Zambia’s developmental future. Notably, there was no media interaction during his departure, in contrast to the engagement seen upon his arrival. This absence of transparency fueled speculation.

Days earlier, Hichilema had explained that he delegated attendance at the United Nations General Assembly to the Foreign Affairs Minister to reduce costs associated with presidential travel. Critics seized on this explanation, suggesting that the UAE trip may have been an emergency visit, possibly for medical reasons. Some even speculated about serious illness. While such claims remain unverified, their circulation reflects a broader erosion of public trust.

Returning to the central question: Can the Grow Zambia Agenda coexist with democratic decay? History suggests the answer is NO. Zambia’s most successful national initiatives have relied on collective effort, public confidence, and broad civic participation. Development is not merely a technical process; it is a social contract. When citizens feel silenced, intimidated, or excluded, they cannot meaningfully contribute to national progress.

The failure of Hichilema’s anti‑corruption campaign during his first term, widely viewed as ineffective due to lack of inclusive engagement, serves as a recent example of how initiatives falter without collective effort.

The current trajectory indicates that the Grow Zambia Agenda is being launched on a fractured foundation. Prosperity cannot be built where dissent is criminalized. Economic growth cannot flourish in an environment where civic freedoms are shrinking. A development program that requires national unity cannot succeed while key voices, clergy, activists, opposition leaders, and ordinary citizens, are suppressed.

The logical conclusion is clear: fresh elections may be necessary to restore legitimacy, rebuild trust, and create the collective environment required for Zambia’s development. Only a renewed mandate, earned through a transparent and credible process, can reconcile the Grow Zambia Agenda with the democratic principles essential for its success.

World.title: Chellah Tukuta is on point; the President is on his own!
World.content:
Presidential photographer Chellah Tukuta has lamented that some Presidential appointees – Cabinet Ministers, Permanent Secretaries and District Commissioners have neglected to rise to the occasion and defend the President whenever he has come under attack from the opposition.

“There’s no way you can be watching your President being disrespected, being called names and being insulted everyday and you are just there enjoying the fruits and the benefits of the appointments he gave you….” charges Tukuta.

The camera man has hit the bull’s eye! The conduct of most of these government officials leaves much to be desired. Most of them are reluctant to put their necks on the chopping board for the President for fear of being pursued in future for whatever wrongs they may have committed.

Such misgivings and frustrations were equally shared with us by a Chingola-based senior clergyman when we had a meeting with him in his office.

“How come senior government officials choose to remain silent when the President is being abused and attacked daily,” wondered the pastor. “Could it be because they’re eating with both hands or their hands have come dirty?”

We are left with no choice but to keep reminding the President that he’s on HIS OWN. He needs to urgently audit those he’s working with to establish their loyalty and commitment to help him realise his Grow Zambia Agenda otherwise some of them don’t mean well at all.

When we as concerned members of the public came up with a mass movement, HH Mpaka 2O31 People’s Alliance whose mission is to help defend and protect the President from unnecessary attacks, we sought appointments with most government officials to gather the necessary data so as to engage the media or the public better equipped. But lo and behold, most of them weren’t willing to interact with us let alone picking up our calls and yet we’ve going extra miles defending the President!

Clean up the system before it’s too late, Sir.

Thank you,

Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

Secretary General

HH Mpaka 2O31 People’s Alliance

Zambezi

World.title: Mbala Central MP urged to address water challenges
World.content:
Village Headmen in Maround and Overspill townships in Mbala District have called on Mbala Central Member of Parliament, Raphael Chilufya to help address the persistent water challenges affecting residents in the two areas.

One of the Village Headmen in Maround, Penza Siame says residents have been facing challenges to access clean and safe drinking water for a long time, forcing them to walk long distances to fetch the commodity from the Lucheche stream.

Mr Siame told ZANIS in Mbala that there is an urgent need for a lasting solution to the water challenges facing the two communities.

And Mbala Central Member of Parliament, Raphael Chilufya, said he had taken note of the concerns raised by residents from the respective townships.

Mr Chilufya said he will engage the council and other departments to explore ways of addressing the problem.

He urged the Village Headmen to remain united, regardless of their political affiliations, in order to contribute to the development of the constituency.

“Water is a basic need, and I have taken note of the challenges raised by the residents. I will engage the relevant authorities to see how best this problem can be addressed. I also encourage Village Headmen to remain united, regardless of their political affiliations, because unity is important for the development of Mbala Central Constituency,” he advised.

World.title: Zambia Police Deputy IG visits Northern Province
World.content:
Zambia Police Service Deputy Inspector General for Administration, Charity Munganga, has reiterated the Service’s unwavering commitment to professionalism, integrity, and accountability in the execution of their duties.

Ms Munganga says effective policing lies in upholding the Constitution, respecting human rights, and maintaining impartiality in all operations.

Speaking when she paid a courtesy call on Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary, Beauty Undi-Phiri, Ms Munganga said her visit to the province forms part of a nationwide tour aimed at strengthening operational efficiency and reinforcing discipline.

Ms Munganga emphasized that leadership within the Police Service is not a privilege for personal gain but a sacred trust that must be exercised responsibly.

“Every officer, regardless of rank, must remember that the badge we wear represents public trust. Any abuse of power or deviation from our code of conduct will not be tolerated,” she stated.

Ms Munganga further commended the Police command and officers in the province for ensuring peace and security in the August 13, 2026 general elections.

And Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary, Beauty Undi-Phiri has praised the Zambia Police Service in the region for their unwavering professionalism and dedication to duty.

Ms Undi-Phiri noted that the conduct of Police Officers in the August general elections demonstrated integrity, discipline, and respect for human rights, which has helped strengthen public confidence in law enforcement.

She highlighted that the officers’ commitment to fair and impartial service delivery has been particularly evident during community engagements, crime prevention patrols, and the handling of sensitive cases.

“Our Police Officers have shown that professionalism is not just about wearing the uniform, but about serving with honesty, fairness, and respect for the law, which has not only enhanced security but also fostered trust between the Police and communities they serve,” she said.

She further urged officers to continue maintaining high standards of professionalism as the province continues to address emerging security challenges.

Ms Undi-Phiri has also called on the public to work closely with the Police by providing timely information to help prevent crime.

World.title: Govt. targets five million tourists as engine for growth
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its ambitious target of attracting five million tourists in the coming years, with culture and tourism positioned as major drivers of inclusive economic growth and international cooperation.

Vice President, Mutale Nalumango, says Government will continue to strengthen cultural tourism through strategic investment, an enabling regulatory environment and stronger partnerships with the private sector and local communities.

ZANIS reports that the Vice President said this in a speech read on her behalf by the Ministry of Tourism Permanent Secretary, Evans Muhanga, during the official opening of the 6th Edition of the Diplomatic Funfair in Lusaka held under the theme “Zambia moves you connecting culture and inspiring the future.”

Mrs Nalumango said Government, under the leadership of President Hakainde Hichilema, recognizes the central role that culture plays in shaping national identity, strengthening unity, and building bridges of understanding among nations.

“Government recognises the central role that culture plays in shaping our national identity, strengthening unity, and building bridges of understanding among nations so we therefore see cultural exchange and engagements such as this as important platforms for advancing diplomacy, promoting trade, and deepening mutual understanding,” she said.

She said this year’s theme speaks directly to how the funfair has always represented the power of culture to move people, to move economies, and to move relationships forward.

Mrs Nalumango recalled that in line with the vision, the Ministry of Tourism officially launched the Brand Zambia Initiative on 3rd March 2026 under the inspiring theme “Zambia Moves You.”

She explained that the national brand captures the emotion, warmth and authenticity that visitors experience in Zambia from the Victoria Falls, to the richness of culture, the abundance of wildlife, the depth of heritage, and above all, the warmth of the Zambian people.

“Zambia moves you” is more than a slogan, it is an invitation to the world to come, experience, connect and be moved by Zambia. It also reaffirms our commitment to positioning Zambia as a distinctive, competitive and attractive destination on the global tourism stage,” she said.

Mrs Nalumango said as nations showcase the diversity of their culture through crafts, cuisine, music and fashion, participating countries have the opportunity to share their heritage and inspire the next generation to see the world as connected rather than divided.

She expressed delight that this year’s edition introduced a new feature, the Fashion Parade, presented under the sub-theme Connecting Cultures Through Fashion which allows diplomatic missions to showcase their traditional, cultural and contemporary attire while sharing the history and story behind each garment.

The Vice President noted that the parade was deliberately designed not as a competition, but as a celebration of diversity, with every participating mission and model recognised for their contribution.

Mrs Nalumango said as models conclude by walking together as one, they offer a powerful symbol of friendship, unity and cooperation among nations.

She added that occasions such as the Diplomatic Funfair provide a platform for countries to open their doors to one another, to share their cultures, tastes and traditions, and to encourage their people to travel, discover and appreciate one another.

Meanwhile, Dean of Diplomatic Corps in Zambia, Hawa Mohamed said the Diplomatic Funfair provides a unique opportunity for the diplomatic community and Zambians to engage and experience the rich traditions, food, music and performances of different countries, reminding everyone that despite different histories, nations share aspirations for peace, prosperity and development.

She said the Funfair is more than a cultural celebration, it is a space for dialogue, discovery and opportunity that promotes tourism, trade, investment and people-to-people connections while showcasing Zambia as a welcoming destination.

Earlier, Director of Culture, Bessie Chelemu welcomed guests to the Funfair, organised by the diplomatic community with support from Government, and expressed hope that the strategic platform will continue to grow.

World.title: Runfusa schools receive 83 boxes of cooking oil
World.content:
Rufunsa District Commissioner, (DC) Richard Mabena has reaffirmed Government’s commitment to supporting the school feeding programme in the area.

Speaking when he handed over 83 boxes of cooking oil to schools across the district, with each box containing four 5-litre containers. Mr Mabena said Government has provided cooking oil specifically to support the school feeding programme.

“We are grateful for the provision of the cooking oil by the Government to support the school feeding programme,” he said.

ZANIS reports that Mr Mabena said Government also provided 1,000 sachets of fresh milk to Early Childhood Education (ECE) learners last term.

Mr Mabena said the interventions demonstrated the Government’s commitment to improving the welfare and learning conditions of learners.

He further appealed to stakeholders to complement Government’s efforts in supporting the school feeding programme.

“Government cannot do everything alone and therefore, I appeal to organisations, companies, NGOs, churches, businesses and well-wishers to come on board and support our schools,” Mr Mabena said.

And Rufunsa District Education Board Secretary (DEBS), Damian Milimo has commended Government for its continued support towards the school feeding programme.

Mr Milimo said the provision of cooking oil was another demonstration of Government’s commitment to ensuring that learners were adequately supported.

“We understand that feeding our learners is an important part of improving education outcomes and we therefore, appreciate the efforts being made to ensure that schools receive the necessary support to implement this programme,” Mr Milimo said.

He urged head teachers and teachers to ensure that the feeding programme achieves its intended objectives.

Meanwhile, Mr Mabena has commended teachers in Rufunsa District for their role in conducting the August 13 general elections.

Mr Mabena said the teachers conducted themselves professionally, resulting in the elections being held in a free and transparent manner.

World.title: Chilanga Councillors under MMPR system sworn-in
World.content:
Chilanga Town Council has sworn- in three Councillors elected under the Mixed Member Proportional Representation (MMPR) system.

The new Councillors include Precious Mulenga for Women representation, Kampata Banda for persons with disabilities and Gift Banda representing youths.

In an interview with ZANIS shortly after the swearing-in ceremony, Mr Banda said he will champion policies that uplift persons with disabilities in the district.

“I look forward to representing persons with disabilities effectively and contributing to national development,” Mr Banda said.

And Youth Representative, Gift Banda pledged to support the Grow Zambia Agenda and foster development in Chilanga District.

The swearing-in brings the special representation of women, youths and persons with disabilities at the local authority as provided for under the MMPR electoral system.
