World.title: Nigeria: Boko Haram Fighters Gun Down Farmers in Borno
World.content:
Suspected Boko Haram insurgents have ambushed and killed 15 farmers, while abducting three others in Marte Local Government Area of Borno State.

According to local sources, the tragic incident took place across the Ala, Gumna, and Musune wards near the headquarters of the area council, on Wednesday.

While initial reports of the attack reached the community on Wednesday evening, the task of recovering the bodies could not be completed until Thursday morning.

Recounting the borrowing aftermath of the assault, an anonymous source said, "Five bodies were initially recovered from the field, while others were found later. Three persons are still missing, and sources indicate they were abducted by the insurgents."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Public Relations Officer, Borno State Police Command, DSP Kenneth Nahum Daso, confirmed that 15 people lost their lives and confirmed that authorities were actively investigating the situation.

"We are making efforts to determine the whereabouts of the three people still missing," Daso said.

A grieving relative, whose cousin was among the victims, shared details of the execution-style killings.

She explained that the victims had gone to their farms to harvest crops when they were ambushed.

"They were forced to lie down and were shot in the head at close range. It was a gory sight," she said.

According to the relative, local community members bravely mobilized to scour the fields, retrieve the bodies, and ensure they were buried according to Islamic rites.

The massacre has drawn widespread outrage, with the human rights organization Amnesty International strongly condemning the violence as a horrific violation of international humanitarian law.

In a statement released on Friday, the organization expressed deep concern over the escalating violence against vulnerable populations in Northeast Nigeria.

"Amnesty International strongly condemns the horrific killing of at least 15 people in Marte Local Government Area of Borno State," the statement read. "The victims, who were local residents venturing into the surrounding areas to earn a living or harvest their crops, were ambushed and targeted by a suspected Boko Haram group."

The rights group emphasized that the deliberate targeting of civilians by non-state armed groups constitutes a war crime.

"Amnesty International calls on the Nigerian authorities to take immediate, transparent, and human-rights-compliant measures to protect vulnerable communities living in the region," the statement concluded.

Despite ongoing military operations in Nigeria's Northeast, farming communities continue to face severe security threats as insurgents frequently target agricultural workers in remote areas

World.title: Somalia: Somaliland Detains Austrian Over Spiny-Tailed Lizard Smuggling
World.content:
Hargeisa — Somaliland police and the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change have detained an Austrian national in the port city of Berbera after he was allegedly caught attempting to purchase and collect spiny-tailed lizards, locally known as caasho-badhi.

The Ministry of Environment said the man was apprehended in a joint operation with police in the Sahil region.

"The Ministry of Environment, in cooperation with the police, arrested an Austrian national in Berbera who was collecting spiny-tailed lizards, locally known as caasho-badhi," the ministry said.

Authorities said the animals were allegedly being collected with the intention of taking them to Europe. Officials displayed containers and other equipment they said were connected to the case.

The ministry did not identify the Austrian national or specify how many lizards had been recovered. It also did not immediately say whether formal charges had been filed.

Spiny-tailed lizards, commonly known as Uromastyx, are reptiles distinguished by their thick, heavily spiked tails and are found in arid regions of Africa and the Middle East.

The case has raised concerns about the collection of Somaliland's wildlife for the international exotic-pet trade, in which reptiles and other wild animals can be captured and sold abroad.

The Somaliland government warned residents against illegally capturing, selling or trafficking wildlife and urged the public to report suspicious activities to the Environment Ministry or security authorities.

(Reporting by HornDiplomat News Desk)

World.title: Ethiopia: AU Urges Restraint As Ethiopia, Eritrea, Egypt Tensions Rise
World.content:
Addis Ababa — The African Union Commission has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise maximum restraint amid heightened tensions between the three countries, warning against actions or statements that could further destabilise the region.

In a statement issued in Addis Ababa on Oct. 1, the commission said it was closely following the situation with concern and called on the three African Union member states to avoid further escalation.

"The Commission calls on all three Member States to exercise maximum restraint and refrain from actions or statements that could further escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability," the statement said.

The AU Commission also stressed the importance of maintaining channels of communication between Addis Ababa, Asmara and Cairo as tensions have increased across the Horn of Africa.

It urged the three governments to address their differences through established diplomatic channels and peaceful dialogue, in accordance with the principles of the Constitutive Act of the African Union.

"The Commission further underscores the importance of preserving channels of communication and urges the three countries to address their differences through established diplomatic channels and peaceful dialogue," it said.

The commission said it was prepared to assist the three countries in efforts to reduce tensions and resolve their differences peacefully.

"The AU Commission stands ready, in consultation with the countries concerned, to support efforts towards de-escalation, dialogue and the peaceful resolution of differences," the statement said.

Reporting by HornDiplomat News Desk)

World.title: Uganda: Mountain Gorilla Population Rises to 1,063 Amid Calls to End Illegal Tracking
World.content:
The population of mountain gorillas in Uganda, Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo has risen to 1,063, up from about 300 in 1990, conservation officials have announced.

Of these, 459 are found in Uganda's Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, while the others live in Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park and the Democratic Republic of Congo's Virunga National Park.

The figures were revealed during Uganda's national World Gorilla Day celebrations held at Ruhija Community Playground in Rubanda District. World Gorilla Day is marked globally every September 24 to promote gorilla conservation.

This year's celebrations, hosted under the theme "Securing the Future: Restoring Indigenous Trees, Healthy Gorillas and Resilient Communities," brought together conservationists, government officials, local leaders and communities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Uganda rotates the national World Gorilla Day event among Rubanda, Kisoro and Kanungu districts.

Officials attributed the increase in the gorilla population to habitat protection, regular monitoring, law enforcement and greater involvement of communities living near protected areas.

Ruhija Town Council Mayor Geoffrey Tumuhimbise commended communities around Bwindi for embracing conservation and urged the Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA) to increase support to residents so they can benefit tangibly from protecting wildlife.

"Conservation should not only focus on protecting wildlife, but should also consider the welfare and livelihoods of communities living alongside protected areas," Tumuhimbise said.

Representing the Minister of Tourism, Wildlife and Antiquities, Commissioner John Magambo, Tom Butiime welcomed the increase but warned against illegal gorilla tracking in Kigezi, saying it undermines conservation and tourism.

"Gorillas are a key tourism asset that boosts national revenue and community incomes. Tracking must follow established guidelines. Some conservation partners use their positions to facilitate irregular tracking," Butiime noted.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerians Don't Deserve This Hardship, Atiku Tells Tinubu
World.content:
Former Vice President and Presidential Candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, says the Tinubu administration has failed one of government's most basic duties: protecting ordinary Nigerians from crushing economic hardship.

In a statement by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Atiku said President Tinubu's Independence Day address revealed how far his government has drifted from the people's daily reality.

The President spoke of prosperity while defending policies that have made fuel and basic necessities increasingly unaffordable, and dismissed subsidies as "addictive."

Atiku also challenged his claim that salaries and pensions have been paid "on time and in full," as federal workers report delays and pensioners continue to protest.



He said Germany had cut gasoline and diesel taxes by €0.17 per litre from October through December, at an estimated cost of €2.5 billion and prices at the pump have begun to fall.

"When petrol becomes more expensive, transport becomes more expensive. When transport costs rise, food and other essentials cost more. The hardship follows Nigerians from the filling station to the market and into their homes.

"Germany understands that when fuel prices put families under pressure, government must act. Nigerians deserve the same compassion and urgency.

"Our plan is to restore targeted, budgeted support for fuel refined in Nigeria, with strict auditing and a guarantee that the benefit lowers pump prices. Support will follow the barrel refined here, creating jobs here and easing costs for Nigerians. It will be funded by cutting waste, protected against diversion and price manipulation, and will not apply to imported fuel.

"To every Nigerian forced to choose between feeding a family, paying for transport or meeting another basic need, I am deeply sorry. You did not deserve this hardship. Tinubu made life unbearably expensive and called your suffering the price of reform. I will make life affordable again."

Atiku said lower fuel costs can mean a cheaper bus ride, more affordable goods at the market and more money left in a family's pocket.

"Nigeria's wealth should ease the burden on its people."

World.title: Nigeria: Drug-Resistant Bacterial Infections Kill 1m People Annually - WHO
World.content:
The World Health Organisation (WHO) says drug-resistant bacterial infections kill about one million people globally every year, calling for coordinated action across human, animal, food and environmental sectors to curb the growing threat.

Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, Acting Director of the AMR Department at WHO Headquarters, said this at a virtual media conference marking an exhibition at the European Parliament on AMR and its human impact.

The virtual conference preceded the exhibition, "AMR: The Human Stories Behind a Silent Pandemic," being held at the European Parliament from 28 September to 2 October and featuring stories of people affected by AMR across Europe.

"AMR is taking many lives. One million people die every year due to drug-resistant bacteria alone - that is, two people every minute die of bacterial AMR," Mr Nyemazi said.



He said the scale of deaths meant that AMR should no longer be treated as a "silent pandemic", stressing that "we know what works" to prevent and control the threat.

"Preventing infections is the number one priority. This can be done through better vaccination, infection prevention and control, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), and improved animal husbandry," he said.

"All of these work and can prevent AMR."

Mr Nyemazi said strengthening surveillance, responsible use of antimicrobials, access to quality medicines and diagnostics, and reduction of environmental contamination could also make a difference.

"The tools exist, and the evidence is there, but the cost of inaction is rising. The longer we delay action, the higher the cost becomes," he said.

He said the One Health approach, which recognises the links between human, animal, plant and environmental health, was essential because drug-resistant pathogens could move across sectors and borders.

According to him, parliamentarians have a critical role in ensuring that national AMR commitments are supported by legislation, financing and accountability.

"The media also plays an indispensable role. Journalists help bring AMR out of scientific circles and into public debate," he said.

"They raise awareness, combat misinformation, and ensure that AMR remains visible to decision-makers and the public alike."

He said WHO Member States approved an updated Global Action Plan on AMR at the World Health Assembly in May, providing a framework for combating AMR over the next 10 years through a One Health approach.

Mr Nyemazi said the updated plan placed stronger emphasis on prevention, governance, behavioural change and measurable targets, and that the four Quadripartite organisations developed it jointly.

He said the organisations comprised the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), WHO and World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH).

"What is new about the updated Global Action Plan on AMR for the next 10 years is that it is truly multi-sectoral - a genuine One Health plan.

"The previous plan was heavily focused on human health; this time the four Quadripartite organisations worked together and engaged all sectors," he said.

Mr Nyemazi said a 10 per cent reduction in AMR was achievable through infection prevention and control, vaccination and improved access to quality antimicrobials, with better coordination, education and surveillance capable of delivering further gains.

He also called for investment in new antibiotics, antifungals, phage therapy and other technologies, while stressing the need to preserve existing medicines.

He said there was also a major access problem, with many regions unable to obtain even existing antibiotics.

A member of the European Parliament, Martin Häusling, said excessive antibiotic use in food-producing animals was contributing to the problem, particularly through mass treatment.

"When it comes to food-producing animals, we still use far too many last-resort antibiotics, and we must get away from that," Mr Häusling said.

He said AMR was a global issue that could affect anyone, adding that it could destroy families and livelihoods.

To tackle it, the parliamentarian said it was important to create public awareness so that parliaments could address the issue properly, adding that the issue was still not taken as seriously as a future challenge should be.

Close 

Rob Purdie, an AMR survivor and member of the WHO Task Force of AMR Survivors, said his experience demonstrated the consequences of delayed diagnosis and treatment.

Mr Purdie said an infection that began with a headache eventually progressed to fungal meningitis after he received antibiotics for a condition that had not been properly diagnosed.

He said he eventually spent about $250,000 on hospital costs and had been unable to work for about five years.

"My ability to earn a living was eliminated for about five years in a single-income household where I provided for my wife and two children," he said.

Mr Purdie said his experience underscored the need to keep AMR visible in public discussions.

"That is why it is so important for those of us who have survived and can speak, to remove the word 'silent' from the 'silent pandemic'," he said.

(NAN)

World.title: Ethiopia: U.S. Lawmakers, Europe Peace Foundation Urge Dialogue As Fighting Escalates in Ethiopia
World.content:
Addis Abeba — The Europe Peace Foundation and three US lawmakers have separately called for an immediate end to hostilities in Ethiopia, urging the parties to return to negotiations as fighting intensifies in Tigray and neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions.

UN news coverage In a statement issued on 1 October, the Europe Peace Foundation said it was concerned by reports of explosions in Addis Ababa and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia, warning of risks to civilians. It called on all parties to cease hostilities, protect civilians and engage in peace talks.

The foundation's statement, issued by Sappan KC Hum, also renewed an invitation for Ethiopia to join the "Peaceful Nation" roadmap under the Global Peace 2030 initiative. It said Mr. KC was prepared to support or mediate dialogue with the agreement of the parties.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Separately, US Representatives Ilhan Omar (D-MN), chair of the U.S.-Africa Policy Working Group, John Garamendi (D-CA), co-chair of the Ethiopian American Caucus, and Jim McGovern (D-MA) expressed alarm over the escalating violence. In a statement released on 1 October, the lawmakers cited what they described as an Ethiopian military strike on an aid convoy in Tigray the previous week.

The lawmakers said the renewed fighting threatened Ethiopia and the wider region, which they said was already affected by the previous northern Ethiopia war and the conflict in Sudan. They urged all parties to recommit to peace negotiations and uphold the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, including commitments on civilian protection, humanitarian access and transitional justice.

Amharic language resources They also called on Ethiopia's neighbours and the international community to help de-escalate tensions, while urging the US State Department to engage the parties to end the violence and pursue accountability.

The renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia has drawn growing international calls for de-escalation and dialogue. Addis Standard reported yesterday that Pope Leo XIV urged all parties involved in the fighting in Tigray and neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions to abandon armed confrontation and return to dialogue.

Discover moreSocial media analysisEthiopian capital insightscourtEthiopian political insightsNews subscription serviceBrowse MagazinesRead Local NewsAddis Ababa travel guideNewsBusiness news analysis Speaking during his General Audience at the Vatican on Wednesday, Pope Leo said he was following developments "with deep concern" and called on the international community to provide timely humanitarian assistance to people affected by the renewed hostilities.

"I extend my heartfelt plea to all parties to choose the path of dialogue," the Pope said, warning that armed conflict leaves behind "death, destruction, and resentment."

Regional political updates His appeal came amid renewed clashes involving Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan forces, with fighting reportedly extending into parts of Afar.

The Pope's appeal comes days after six U.S. senators urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the State Department to engage Ethiopia's federal government, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and associated armed groups to halt renewed hostilities and return to mediation.

In a statement sent to Addis Standard by the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Monday, Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Cory Booker, Chris Coons, Jeff Merkley, Chris Van Hollen and Tim Kaine said the deteriorating security situation risked undermining the 2022 peace agreement that ended the two-year Tigray war.

"We are alarmed by the deteriorating security situation in Ethiopia," the senators said, citing escalating conflict in Tigray, Oromia and Afar and warning that the renewed violence could unravel the agreement brokered by the African Union and strongly supported by the United States.

The senators called on the international community to press the parties to the agreement to de-escalate tensions and return to mediation, warning that renewed fighting could trigger another conflict across the Horn of Africa.

The renewed fighting has also drawn growing concern from the United Nations over the protection of civilians and the humanitarian consequences of the escalation.

Ethiopian news analysis In a statement sent to Addis Standard on Wednesday, United Nations Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Ethiopia Ozonnia Ojielo said he was "closely monitoring" developments with humanitarian partners across the affected regions. He warned that the renewed conflict was exposing civilians, including people displaced during the previous war, to further protection risks while triggering new displacement.

Close 

"The situation presents serious concerns over the protection of civilians, particularly those who were displaced by the last conflict, facing further protection risks, while new displacements are emerging," Ojielo said.

His warning followed a statement by UN Secretary-General António Guterres expressing grave concern over the deteriorating situation, including the reported seizure and occupation of airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire and intensified fighting in and around Tigray and neighboring areas. Guterres called on all parties to exercise maximum restraint, protect civilians and ensure safe and unhindered humanitarian access.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk separately warned on 25 September that the renewed hostilities were already having harmful consequences for civilians and urged all parties to immediately de-escalate tensions.

World.title: Ethiopia: Alamata Fighting Leaves Trail of Civilian Casualties - Adigrat Eparch Appeals for Help
World.content:
Addis Abeba — More than 50 civilians have reportedly been killed in and around Alamata, southern Tigray, during several days of intense fighting in late September, as renewed hostilities in northern Ethiopia leave residents displaced, medical facilities overwhelmed and humanitarian access increasingly difficult.

Discover moreShop African ArtPolitical commentary subscriptionBreaking news alerts A resident who fled Alamata to North Wollo Zone in the neighboring Amhara Region told Addis Standard that the fighting erupted as residents were preparing for the Saturday market.

"We were hoping for a market day on Saturday when suddenly the town was rocked by heavy artillery. Suddenly, the town looked like a full-blown war zone," the resident said.

The resident added that hundreds had fled in search of safety and that artillery fire striking a crowded marketplace had killed "more than a dozen civilians."



Hospital sources and a doctor at Alamata General Hospital told the BBC that at least 52 civilians were killed during approximately three days of fighting, primarily between 26 and 29 September.

The victims reportedly included children, mothers and cattle herders, with some of the shelling striking residential areas. One attack on the town's marketplace reportedly killed 12 people.

Ethiopian capital insights The reported toll comes amid a sharp deterioration in the security situation across Tigray, where renewed clashes between federal forces and Tigrayan forces have displaced residents and disrupted essential services. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has also reported a significant influx of wounded people at hospitals it supports across the region.

Discover moreSocial media analysisNewsRead Daily NewsUN news coverageInternational relations analysisEthiopian import/export dataAddis Ababa travel guideEthiopian news analysisSocial affairs reportingRead Local News The fighting has been accompanied by communications disruptions, bank closures and restrictions on movement, complicating independent verification of casualty figures and limiting access to affected communities.

The humanitarian consequences are also being felt further north. The Eparch of Adigrat, Tesfaselassie Medhin, has appealed for urgent humanitarian access and dialogue, warning that the Church and local communities have been cut off from the outside world.

"We are completely isolated, communications are blocked, and we have no contact with anyone," Medhin told Fides News Agency in a message transmitted with the support of UNICEF.

Amharic language resources "All communications are blocked; our Church, our missions, religious, the local clergy, we are in our places, as usual," he said, adding that the Church would continue accompanying and assisting people through its presence.

Medhin described mounting difficulties as banking services have also been suspended and uncertainty grows over the ability of seminaries and schools to continue operating.

"We do not know for sure how our seminaries and schools will continue operating, but it is our intention to continue. We have no idea how we will manage provisions. Only God knows; we rely on Divine Providence," he said.

The Eparch stressed the urgency of facilitating humanitarian access and pursuing dialogue to prevent further deterioration.

His appeal came as Pope Leo XIV expressed deep concern over the renewed hostilities in Tigray during his General Audience on September 30, urging all parties to return to dialogue.

"Armed conflict never solves problems but only worsens them, leaving in its wake a trail of death, destruction, and resentment," the Pope said, calling for "honest engagement" as the foundation for lasting peace.

News subscription service He also urged the international community to make a timely contribution to ensuring humanitarian assistance reaches people in need.

Close 

The renewed fighting follows months of escalating tensions and mutual accusations of violations of the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the two-year war in Tigray. The latest escalation has raised fresh concerns over the durability of the peace agreement and the risk of a wider conflict in northern Ethiopia.

Pro-government forces have since recaptured Alamata, a strategically important town approximately 120 kilometers south of Mekelle, and subsequently advanced northward.

However, tensions also intensified in the areas between the Tigray Peace Force and members of the Raya Zeb, a newly organized paramilitary force established by the Amhara Regional State. The friction reportedly escalated after federal forces mobilized further toward Mehoni, amid indications of preparations for a possible advance toward Mekelle, the regional capital.

World.title: Yankees lose ALDS Game 1 to Rays as Austin Wells is thrown out at third after breaking up no-hitter
World.content:
Austin Wells turned the New York Yankees’ only hit into their most painful out.

With two outs in the eighth inning and the Yankees trailing by a run, Wells broke up Drew Rasmussen’s no-hit bid with a double down the right-field line. But the catcher tried to stretch the hit into a triple and was easily thrown out, ending New York’s best scoring opportunity in a 1-0 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the American League Division Series on Saturday night.

Rays right fielder Victor Mesa Jr. retrieved the ball and threw to shortstop Taylor Walls, whose relay reached third baseman Junior Caminero well ahead of Wells.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The out prevented Ryan McMahon from coming to the plate with the potential tying run in scoring position and allowed Rasmussen to walk off the mound having completed eight scoreless innings.

Rasmussen limited the Yankees to one hit and two walks while striking out 10 on 101 pitches. He once again tormented a New York lineup he nearly no-hit during Tampa Bay’s division-clinching victory at Yankee Stadium late in the regular season.

Bryan Baker replaced Rasmussen for the ninth and made quick work of the Yankees. Baker struck out pinch hitter Giancarlo Stanton and Ben Rice before getting Cody Bellinger to ground out, completing the combined one-hitter and giving Tampa Bay a 1-0 series lead.

Jonathan Aranda provided the game’s only run when he drove a Gerrit Cole pitch 417 feet to right-center field in the third inning.

Cole kept the Yankees within striking distance but received no offensive support. The right-hander allowed one run on five hits and one walk while striking out five over five innings and 82 pitches.

Ryan Weathers, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick combined to hold Tampa Bay hitless over the final three innings, but New York’s lineup never found an answer for Rasmussen.

The shutout represented a dramatic reversal for a Yankees offense that scored 18 runs during its two-game Wild Card Series sweep of the Boston Red Sox. New York was again without captain Aaron Judge, who was left off the ALDS roster as he continues recovering from a right calf strain.

World.title: Trump touts ‘golden age’ at Ohio rally, urges voters to deliver GOP midterm wins
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump swept into Ohio Saturday night promoting what he calls a new "golden age" for America, pointing to billions of dollars in investment and new jobs in the Buckeye State as he urged voters to help keep Republicans in power in November.

For the third time in as many nights, Trump rallied supporters outside Dayton for Republicans Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, casting the midterms as a chance to extend the economic and political gains he said the GOP has delivered since his return to the White House.

And with his own name absent from the ballot, Trump gave voters gathered a simple instruction.

TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG

"Just pretend that I’m running," Trump said. "When I run, we win."

Trump, who carried Ohio in all three of his presidential campaigns, later echoed the same message as he sought to rally his political coalition behind Republicans fighting to maintain control of Congress.

"If you don’t mind, please pretend that I’m on the ballot," Trump said. "And you need to turn out for a midterm victory."

The president used much of the rally to make an economic case for the Republican ticket, declaring Ohio is "booming" as he hailed investments he credited to both his trade and tariff policies.

Trump pointed to a $400 million Stellantis investment in Toledo and an $850 million Electra aerospace investment near Springfield.

Weaving in an anecdote about his daily aspirin habit, the president also featured Bayer’s plans for a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing campus near Columbus, which the company says will support approximately 600 permanent jobs and 1,500 construction jobs.

"Your state is booming," Trump told the gathered crowd. "Every state is booming."

FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY

Trump credited the investments to his tariff agenda, arguing the U.S. is finally leveling the playing field after years of other countries using tariffs against American products while giving companies a powerful incentive to build at home.

The president also threw his support behind Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation aimed at shielding consumers from additional electricity costs associated with data centers.

"We want them," Trump said of data centers. "There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China."

Husted brought the legislation to the Senate floor days before the rally, where it failed to advance. President Trump pledged to sign it if Congress can send it to his desk.

TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE'

"I will sign this Ratepayer Protection Act into law immediately," Trump said.

Trump broadened his victory lap from Ohio to the country as a whole, hailing stock market records, manufacturing growth, investment and employment while contrasting his own administration’s economic record with former President Joe Biden's.

"Our nation is doing better now than ever before," Trump said.

He also praised GOP-backed tax provisions, including no tax on tips and overtime, and reiterated his previously announced proposal for $5,000 payments to adult Americans if Republicans retain the House and Senate.

Trump then shifted to immigration and Springfield, Ohio, dedicating his recitation of the poem "The Snake" to the city that became a national flashpoint during the 2024 presidential campaign over an influx of Haitian nationals into the community.

"I dedicate this to Springfield, Ohio," Trump said. "They went through hell."

After finishing the poem, which the president has long admired as an immigration allegory, he told the crowd, "That’s what happened at our border," before hailing his administration’s immigration crackdown.

The president also briefly touched on Venezuela, claiming the U.S. had more than recouped the costs of its military operation against former Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro through the country's vast oil resources.

"We paid for the cost of the war many, many times over," Trump said. "We’re making a fortune with it."

Trump repeatedly weaved the election 31 days away into his remarks, urging Ohioans to support Husted, Ramaswamy and Republican congressional candidates.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

He also pitched Ohio as a potential home for the U.S. National Space Academy, citing both the state's aviation history and the Wright brothers.

"If we win the midterms, Ohio will be very, very strongly considered for this," Trump said. "I really want you to go out and vote again for John Husted and for Vivek."

World.title: France’s violent student protests raise warning for America: ‘A cautionary tale’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

France’s violent student protests are fueling fresh warnings about the consequences of open-border immigration policies, with the unrest being held up as a "cautionary tale" for the U.S.

"I would also say as we’re sitting here in beautiful New York City, this is a cautionary tale," "The Big Weekend Show" co-host Tomi Lahren said Saturday.

She continued: "This is something we’re learning from Europe, and we would be wise to learn from Europe. They decided they wanted to have open borders. They decided they wanted diversity as their strength, and of course, Joe Biden tried that for four years. We’re undoing that currently."

FRANCE'S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT

Lahren posited that "when you let so many people come into your country, leech off of your system, then the people who are from there are going to at some point get upset."

She said that anger often becomes misplaced and, "they end up lighting things on fire, which I think is stupid no matter what you’re angry with, but it’s no doubt these countries that say we’re going to be a global home for everybody, they end up paying the price, and it’s usually the native Frenchmen, or whenever they are that end up paying the highest price."

Students in Paris began to protest late last month against what they deemed as overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, long school days and deteriorating conditions, blaming the government for not investing enough in education.

REPUBLICAN GLEE ERUPTS AS WHITE HOUSE BOASTS SHARP DECLINE IN IMMIGRATION FROM MUSLIM-MAJORITY NATIONS

The demonstrations started peacefully in Paris’ poorer suburbs but quickly spread to Paris itself, then went nationwide in cities like Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours, Nantes, Toulouse ​and Lille, becoming increasingly violent as they expanded.

The protests were also fueled by the government’s 2027 budget unveiling on Thursday, which showed education spending would rise by only 1.7%, excluding teacher pensions, an increase which is below the rate of inflation, Reuters reported.

Rioters have committed arson, vandalism, thrown objects at police and even assaulted people in some cases, prompting authorities to respond with tear gas and rubber bullets.

TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS

More than 5,000 protesters were arrested this week across the country, according to Reuters, and more than 400 schools remained closed as of Friday.

Euronews reported Friday that at least 65 school staff members, including 40 principals, have been injured since the unrest began, along with roughly 170 students.

More than 100 high schools have suffered what Education Minister Édouard Geffray described as "severe damage."

French intelligence agencies told a government crisis meeting Thursday that the protest movement had been initiated by politicians from the hard-left France Unbowed Party, known as LFI, Reuters reported Friday.

LIZ PEEK: ANGRY, AFFLUENT AND ADRIFT — WHAT'S DRIVING SOME YOUNG AMERICANS TO VIOLENCE

LFI has denied the allegations and accused President Emmanuel Macron's government of politicizing the protests ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.

Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the unrest began with legitimate concerns but has since evolved into something far more serious.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The students’ grievances about missing teachers and deteriorating schools were real at first," Rodan-Benzaquen said. "But dousing a principal in gasoline and attacking firefighters are acts of extreme violence. What makes this politically significant is the effort to turn frustration over schools into a much broader confrontation with the government."

Fox News' Efrat Lachter contributed to this report.

World.title: South Carolina football in free fall as Shane Beamer may be out of time with buyout decision looming
World.content:
Another blown lead, another loss for South Carolina. What has ultimately turned into the story of Gamecocks football over the last two years once again caught up with head coach Shane Beamer on Saturday against Kentucky.

Coming off a thrashing against Alabama last week, which came one week after losing to Mississippi State after holding a 16-0 lead, the dam seems to have officially broken in Columbia on different ways to lose a game.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Leading 17-0 against Kentucky at home, South Carolina fans have grown accustomed to never taking a lead for granted. In this case for those wearing Garnett, it was as if the game was tied 0-0 given past instances of being let down by the results.

BIG MONEY, BIGGER DISASTER: MINNESOTA EXPOSES MICHIGAN AS WOLVERINES ARE LATEST EXAMPLE OF WASTED NIL FUNDS

And now, after Kentucky beat South Carolina 35-34 in overtime on a two-point conversion to move to 4-1, the chatter throughout the state will only grow louder for the Gamecocks’ athletic department to make a change at head coach.

This was the Gamecocks eighth straight SEC loss, and also their 12th loss against Power-4 opponents in the past 14 games. If the Gamecocks were to fire Shane Beamer before the end of the year, he would be owed an estimated $22.5 million for his departure.

To be fair to Shane Beamer, the program is not getting a return on investment with the money spent on players like LaNorris Sellers or Dylan Stewart, which reportedly hovers above $5 million combined. If anything, the football team has been robbed blind by Stewart, given his lack of production and antics on the field this season, and we just started the month of October.

In hopes of putting an end to any distractions coming off last week's temper-tantrums along the sidelines in Tuscaloosa, Beamer suspended Dylan Stewart indefinitely this week from the program, with the head coach declaring he was the only one making a decision on when the defensive standout could return.

But, it goes deeper than that.

Those writing the checks are not going to sit with this, and pray for better days

In this era of college athletics, a return on investment for those helping fund these player contracts essentially comes down to whether you make the playoff, or hoist a trophy at season's end. And no, I don't mean the Outback or Gator Bowl trophies.

After a memorable 2024 season that saw the Gamecocks miss out on the college football playoff by just a few spots on the final weekend, the fans have witnessed a program going in the wrong direction.

Finishing 4-8 in 2025, Shane Beamer declared that the national media, and those covering the program on a daily basis, would be changing their tune on the South Carolina program after they put together a 2026 season that would see them competing for both a conference and national title.

"I can one billion percent promise you this... because of the success we're gonna have next season... we're gonna look back at this season and say, 'It sucked going through it, but because of what we went through in '25 it led us to what we just did in '26,'" Beamer said last year.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

And, even though we all understood what he was implying this past week, it obviously didn’t sit well with Gamecock fans when he discussed how good of a practice they had following the loss to Alabama.

In reality, Beamer has always been confident that he was the right man to lead South Carolina back to the same statue as they acquired during the 2024 season. But, thanks to injuries, play-calling and some pretty bad luck, the 2026 campaign was crucial for his future.

Different era means enhanced timing on decisions in college football

Now, after the third loss in five games, those who control the payroll and fundraising at South Carolina will have a decision to make on what the future looks like for a program trying not to be forgotten within the SEC.

Obviously, this is going to only create more chaos around the football building, especially when you are out of contention for a conference title before the second weekend of October.

Schools know that they can no longer wait until seasons end to make these decisions, especially when you are trying to sell season tickets for 2027. At the same time, those within the program are already trying to detour players' agents from shopping them to other teams for next year, which has been the case according to multiple sources.

And, it's not just at South Carolina.

Discussions about player retention, the transfer portal, raises and movement are already taking place, and will only increase over the next two months.

So, on the weekend of October 3rd, influential voices around the Gamecocks athletic department are already having to make a decision about 2027.

Like it or not, that's the world we live in now.

For Shane Beamer, his team will face Florida next, before they are due for a much-needed bye week.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

We will soon find out what kind of a timeline the South Carolina administration is working on, if a change is going to happen over the next eight days.

World.title: Phil Collins gets frank on marriage failures and life regrets: 'I regret my marriages falling apart'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Phil Collins is opening up about his biggest regret throughout the course of his career.

During a recent interview on "Piers Morgan Uncensored," the 75-year-old musician reflected on the toll his career took on his relationships with his children and how it affected his three marriages.

"To some extent, I have to say I regret my marriages falling apart," he explained. "Sometimes I jumped. Well, one time I jumped, two times I was pushed. But I wouldn't have written it like that. But on the other hand, I've got five fantastic kids that I wouldn't have if that hadn't happened. So I have to balance it."

The famous drummer was married to his first wife, Andrea Bertorelli, from 1975 to 1980. Collins adopted Bertorelli's daughter, Joely, and the couple welcomed son Simon.

PHIL COLLINS' BRUSH WITH DEATH LEFT HIS CHILDREN PREPARING FOR THE UNTHINKABLE

He also shares daughter Lily with his second wife, Jill Tavelman, whom he was married to from 1984 to 1996, and sons Nicholas and Mathew with his third wife, Orianne Cevey, whom he was married to from 1999 to 2006.

When looking back on his first marriage, Collins admitted it broke down because he wasn't around, as he was touring with his band, Genesis, and couldn't be home.

"Genesis did, in one year, I think, three American tours, two European tours, and a tour of Japan. And when I ended up getting separated from my first wife, the guys in the band said, ‘Well, why didn’t you tell us? We’d have stopped it.’ But that’s easy to say in retrospect," he said. "I was gone, and we grew apart."

Despite his failure to make his relationships with his wives work, Collins said he "always tried to be there for the kids," and that he never planned on getting married three times, noting, "You don't go into life thinking that."

His daughter Lily, who stars in the hit Netflix series, "Emily in Paris," wrote about her relationship with her father in her 2017 memoir, "Unfiltered: No Shame, No Regrets, Just Me."

"I'm learning how to accept your actions and vocalize how they made me feel," she wrote in an excerpt read by Morgan. "I accept and honor the sadness and anger I felt toward the things you did or didn't do, did or didn't give me. I forgive you for not always being there when I needed it, for not being the dad I expected. I forgive the mistakes you made. And although it may seem like it's too late, it's not. There's still so much time to move forward."

The father-daughter duo has managed to put the past behind them, as she shared photos of them celebrating his 75th birthday together in January, writing "Love you to the moon and back again…"

In a birthday message to her father, she expressed feeling "grateful" to be able to celebrate the milestone birthday with him, saying she considers herself "lucky to have hugged you, laughed with you, and reminisced with you on such a monumental day."

Now as a parent, I have a newly found understanding and deeper appreciation for everything you’ve done and continue to do," she wrote. "Tove is lucky to call you Grandpa P."

World.title: Cornell president says university 'must do better' on handling of sexual assault allegations
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said Saturday that the institution "must do better" as it faces questions over its response to sexual assault allegations involving seven former fraternity brothers.

"What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come. My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff said in a video statement to the Cornell community.

Kotlikoff said the case raises questions about sexual assault, campus party culture, alcohol and drug abuse on the Ithaca, New York, campus, as well as the investigation conducted after the allegations were reported.

"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say we don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves. I believe we as an administration, and we as a community must do better," Kotlikoff said.

INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM

Kotlikoff welcomed an independent review by an outside law firm into Cornell's handling of the case and said the university supports Gov. Kathy Hochul's decision to turn the criminal investigation over to New York Attorney General Letitia James.

He said Cornell would not wait for those reviews to conclude before making changes to prevention and education, student support, mental health and substance use resources and investigative processes.

"We will act," Kotlikoff said.



Jane Doe alleges in a lawsuit that seven former Chi Phi fraternity brothers drugged and sexually assaulted her during an October 2024 night at the fraternity house. Doe was a 20-year-old Cornell undergraduate at the time.

CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS PROMPT NY ATTORNEY GENERAL LETITIA JAMES TO OPEN ‘ACTIVE CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION’

The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men.

Doe filed a 101-page lawsuit last month accusing the former fraternity members of sexual assault and rape and naming Cornell and other entities.

The case came under renewed scrutiny after Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office had not received the full transcript of Doe's November 2024 interview with Cornell University Police before prosecutors initially declined to pursue charges.

Van Houten reopened the investigation before Hochul appointed the Office of the Attorney General as special prosecutor. James said Friday that her office was conducting an "active criminal investigation."

CORNELL SEXUAL ASSAULT CASE REVIVES SCRUTINY OF A LITTLE-KNOWN NEW YORK LAW ON INTOXICATED VICTIMS

Kotlikoff also addressed frustration over Cornell's communication about its response to the allegations and said the university would make a greater effort to be transparent.

"There are real legal and privacy limits on what we can say, but we will make a greater effort to explain what we can to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken and to be more transparent," Kotlikoff said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Kotlikoff said Cornell would also reexamine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus and support efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws.

"You have my commitment that this will not be a moment that passes," Kotlikoff said.

Fox News Digital's Michael Dorgan contributed to this report.

World.title: Trump, campaigning in Ohio, says the midterms will bring a ‘big surprise’
World.content:
VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate.

“I think we’re going to have a big surprise, because they don’t know what’s happening,” Trump said while speaking onstage inside a high school gymnasium near Dayton.

“Just get out and vote,” Trump added. “If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big. And we’re going to shove it up their ass.”

The visit, part of what White House officials have told NBC News will be a push through at least 17 states between now and Nov. 3, was aimed at boosting incumbent Sen. Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP nominee for governor.

Trump, who won Ohio three times by comfortable margins, opened his speech with praise for both before moving into broader remarks to promote himself and his administration. He also offered support for local Rep. Mike Turner and for several House candidates in attendance, including Derek Merrin, the Republican running against longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur in northwest Ohio.

Husted’s bid to keep the Senate seat — which he was appointed to after JD Vance was elected vice president — has in particular become a subject of concern among Republicans in Ohio and Washington. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that Husted’s past enthusiasm for building data centers was hurting his campaign. Others have expressed worries that Husted, who has long wanted to be governor, has not put his full heart into the race.

The battle is one of the most expensive and competitive Senate races in the country this fall. Along with a handful of other key contests, the clash between Husted and Brown could determine partisan control of the chamber. This week, Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, poured another $14 million into Ohio to prop up Husted, bringing the group’s investment in the state to $93 million.

“Senator Jon Husted votes to put Ohio first, and he votes all the time,” Trump said before relating conversations he’s had with Thune and others: “They think he’s phenomenal.”

The high school gym where Trump spoke Saturday night was a smaller venue than has been typical for his rallies. The home court of the Butler High School Aviators seats up to 5,000. There were several stretches of empty seats in upper bleachers as Trump took the stage — and many more by the time he finished speaking 93 minutes later.

In Ohio and elsewhere, Republicans are wrestling with how to win at a time when polls show Trump and the war in Iran are highly unpopular and when voters most loyal to Trump might stay home because he’s not on the ballot.

“As a lifelong Republican who’s voted in every election since I was 18 and in every primary election as a Republican, I have real concerns that we’re going to be able to turn out the every-four-year Trump voter,” Nick Owens, a former GOP chair in Ohio’s Brown County and former member of the state Board of Education, told NBC News last month. “I have real concerns that those voters just will not come to the polls.”

Trump acknowledged that dynamic explicitly Saturday and repeated an argument he’s been making on the campaign trail this fall.

“When I run, we win,” Trump said. “But for some reason, when I don’t run, they draw 44% less people. So what I’m going to do is ask you to just pretend that I’m running, because if we do, and if you draw the people, you’re going to win, and we’re going to win big.”

Husted, speaking to reporters before the rally, described Trump as a unique asset in his race.

“Well, he won Ohio by 11 points in the last election, and if we get those same voters to turn out in this election, we’ll win,” Husted said.

Alex Triantafilou, the Ohio GOP chair, told NBC News that the rally was “hugely important” in the effort to motivate those low-propensity, Trump-loyal voters.

“We know in Ohio that if we turn out the same electorate that we turned out in 2024, that we’ll win every race,” Triantafilou said in an interview. “Nobody speaks to that crowd better than President Trump.”

The Saturday rally included a cameo from Jon Gruden, the former NFL coach who years ago was a teammate of Husted’s on the University of Dayton football team.

“Jon Husted is a lot more than my friend,” an animated Gruden told the audience. “He was a great player. … He will never quit on you or anybody.”

Trump marveled about Husted’s football-playing days, of which he said he was unaware until hearing about them from Gruden.

“Nobody told me you were a great athlete,” Trump said, before taking a jab at his Democratic rival: “And Brown was not — he was not an athlete. That guy can’t tie his shoes.”

For its part Saturday, the Brown team sent a mobile billboard linking Husted’s support for the war in Iran to higher gas prices through Dayton and on the streets near the rally.

“Jon Husted has turned his back on working families — he’s only looking out for his billionaire buddies and special interests,” Brown said in a statement from his campaign.

Ohio also is home to what polls show is a close race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. Ramaswamy faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician who served as the state’s health director under DeWine. Ohioans have not elected a Democrat as governor in 20 years, but at a time when high prices rate as a top-of-mind concern for voters, there are questions about the billionaire Ramaswamy’s appeal, especially in the rural parts of the state.

Ramaswamy, like Husted, addressed the crowd early during the rally, and Trump invited both to return to the stage during his speech for additional remarks. Trump introduced Ramaswamy by noting how he had briefly run against him for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination.

“He was a nasty guy,” Trump said of Ramaswamy. “But you know what? He was smart. He loves the state. He’s actually got a great heart.”

Compared with Husted, Ramaswamy was otherwise less of a focus of Trump’s remarks. Trump, for example, criticized Senate Democrats who this week blocked Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to rein in higher utility costs associated with power-hungry data centers.

Republicans, Trump said, are “taking historic action to ensure that Big Tech data centers benefit local communities.”

Trump then made the argument for data centers, despite the fears it could be a losing issue for Husted.

“We want them,” Trump said. “Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China.”

Trump also recited the lyrics to the 1968 Al Wilson song “The Snake” — a recurring, crowd-pleasing bit in his rally speeches — with a new, localized twist. Trump dedicated the song, which he uses as an allegory to trusting communities that welcome immigrants, to nearby Springfield, Ohio.

The city became a flashpoint in the 2024 presidential election after Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating dogs and pets.

At another point, the crowd broke into chants of “four more years” for the term-limited president.

“I’d love to do the four-more-year thing,” Trump responded in a teasing tone before suggesting that the press would overplay his remarks.

“We’re driving them totally crazy,” Trump said, referring to the media. “But I love doing it. I love being with you. I really do.”

World.title: Ken Paxton’s estranged wife urges voters to back him, yet avoids mentioning him by name
World.content:
The estranged wife of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton urged voters to stand behind the entire Republican midterm ticket in an ad released Saturday, though she neglected to name Paxton directly.

Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton, who filed for divorce from Paxton last year citing “biblical grounds,” appeared in an ad telling Texans that she is “voting for the Republican ticket on Nov. 3,” but did not cite Paxton’s Senate bid by name.

She did, however, invite voters to “talk about the elephant in the room.”

“In a general election, it’s not as much about the individual players on the team; it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line,” Paxton said in the ad. “Either we hold every Republican seat, or we hand the future of Texas to the other team.”

Ken Paxton and his wife, Angela, outside the Supreme Court in Washington, in 2021. Bill Clark / CQ Roll Call via Getty

Angela Paxton’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether she plans to vote for her estranged husband herself.

Ken Paxton’s tenure as attorney general has been beset by allegations of abuse of office and bribery. Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives in 2023, but the state Senate later acquitted him. The Senate trial, however, touched on allegations of infidelity. Paxton has denied any wrongdoing.

The ad comes as Paxton’s daughter, Mattie Hayworth, recently appeared in an ad for her father alongside her husband and children.

Hayworth criticized “liberal politicians” as a graphic showing Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., alongside Paxton’s Democratic opponent, James Talarico, came over the screen.

“When they come after you, my dad goes after them to bring down prices and stand up for families,” Hayworth said.

As Election Day nears, Talarico holds a slight edge over Paxton, defying the deep-red profile of Texas, where Republicans haven’t lost a statewide race since 1994 and Democrats haven’t won a U.S. Senate seat since 1988.

According to an NBC5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll in late September, Talarico was at 46% and Paxton at 43%, within the survey’s margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The poll acknowledges another 8% of potential voters who are still undecided in the race. NBC News currently defines the race as a toss-up.

The ad featuring Angela Paxton, which was funded by Texas PAC, a political action committee affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, comes as the Texas Senate race has become one of the most expensive in the current cycle.

President Donald Trump, who endorsed Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary, has urged voters to get behind the state attorney general. His super PAC, MAGA Inc., has also put millions into Paxton’s race.

The president has visited Texas twice in the last month — first for the GOP midterm convention in Dallas and then again this week for a rally in Denton, which comes as part of Trump’s 17-state campaign blitz.

In a separate campaign appearance Friday night in Alabama, Trump reiterated the high stakes associated with Texas’ race.

“Last night, I went to Texas, where we won by a lot, and then I went to Oklahoma, and they said, ‘Why is he going to Texas?’” Trump said. “Because we have to win that race. Ken Paxton has to win.”

World.title: New revelations in Cornell rape investigation
World.content: We’re seeing dramatic video of a confrontation with one of the men accused in the Cornell sexual assault case. This as questions grow over how the alleged 2024 incident was handled. NBC News’ Valerie Castro reports.Oct. 3, 2026

World.title: ‘It’s not enough to not rape somebody’: How parents are talking to kids about Cornell
World.content:
For parents following the case of a former Cornell student who alleges she was gang-raped at the Chi Phi house in October 2024, one question has been top of mind: Why did no one in the fraternity intervene?

In a lawsuit filed last month, a woman identified as Jane Doe said she was sexually assaulted by Chi Phi members while she was under the influence of several substances. A screenshot of a group Snapchat between members, which was included in the lawsuit, showed one fraternity member saying there was “free p----” available upstairs where Jane Doe was.

01:24 Cornell agrees to outside investigation in assault case 00:00 00:00

The fraternity chapter was subsequently barred from campus, but no one was criminally charged. Prosecutors have reopened a criminal investigation into the allegations.

As the case continues to draw national attention, parents online are sharing how they’re teaching their children to challenge the culture that allows sexual violence to persist. Some have offered advice, suggesting parents pose questions to their kids like, “What have you heard about this story?” and “What questions do you have?” Others have posted candid conversations they’ve had with their kids about the case to help inspire others to do the same.

“I’m parenting to help them become the kind of man who stops this from happening,” Brian Recker, a former pastor with over 450,000 followers on Instagram, said in a video earlier this week.

“It’s not enough to not rape somebody. Because what that girl could’ve really used that night and what she didn’t find was one good man,” Recker added. “One good man in that group chat who would have been willing to risk some social shame from his frat bros, who was willing to put her safety above the approval of men who would hurt her.”

Recker told NBC News that he approaches the subject differently with his 9-year-old twins and his 11-year-old son. With his younger sons, he focuses on their own safety. But as his oldest enters middle school, Recker has asked him to consider what he would do if messages like those described in the Cornell case appeared in one of his group chats.

He views these types of conversations with his sons as a way to “plant seeds” that shape their approach to the world as they grow up.

“It is so easy to just be silent and not want to rock the boat, especially if you think that that’s going to cause other boys, other men to look down on you,” he said. “But I do believe, especially in the early years, we have the opportunity to shape reality for them in some really important ways, and to let them know what kind of world they’re entering, and to prepare them.”

But sexual assault can be an especially difficult topic to tackle with kids, particularly for parents who have their own trauma history, said Sumi Raghavan, a psychologist who was also among those sharing how they spoke to their kids about the Cornell case.

Raghavan said she urges fellow parents to feel empowered to discuss tough topics, noting that some level of discomfort is normal when it comes to these conversations.

Research links open parent-child communication with healthier relationships and safer decision-making. Raghavan said that means that even as kids and teens begin to care more about their peers’ opinions than their parents’, they’re still likely to view their parents as anchors for major decisions.

“One of the most powerful messages you’re sending when you’re willing to have these conversations is that you are a person who they can talk to, and you are demonstrating that you are unafraid of these topics,” she said.

Psychologist Becky Kennedy, the founder of parenting advice service Good Inside, had similar guidance — though she cautioned that parents should also be careful to not treat conversations with their kids as “checking off a box.”

Kids build emotional skills from the patterns they experience growing up. For example, learning to want something and be OK with not getting it, Kennedy said. Often, parents want to say “no” to a child’s request but convince themselves to say “yes” due to fear of the child’s reaction.

“These are things that will play out for the rest of a boy’s life, and eventually, maybe in sexual situations,” she said. “But those patterns are established over and over in everyday interactions.”

Parents should also listen and try to understand when their child wants to say “no,” Kennedy said, rather than forging forward with a decision without considering why the child might be unwilling or uncomfortable. By doing the latter, she said, parents are unwittingly reinforcing the culture that makes it harder for kids to resist group pressure later in life.

Parents are bound to make mistakes, Kennedy said. But that shouldn’t keep them from trying to do things differently once they realize they want to change a pattern.

“It’s actually the whole thought that ‘it’s too late’ that stops us from acting differently in all of those situations,” Kennedy said. “The best way to not repeat a pattern is to actually bring new information to your kid and say, ‘You know what? In my parenting, I feel like I’ve been doing something that I’m not proud of. I learned something new. Here’s what I want to do differently the next time.’”

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at https://www.rainn.org/get-help.

World.title: 12-year-old girl killed in Baltimore shooting sparked by apparent parking dispute
World.content:
A 12-year-old girl was killed and three others were injured when gunfire erupted amid an apparent dispute over parking at a Baltimore park Saturday, officials said.

Police Commissioner Richard Worley said two gunmen were being sought, and two different gun cartridges were found at the scene after the shooting near Leon Day Park.

“What we know is that there was some type of argument between two cowards, and of course they both opened fire on each other,” the commissioner said at a Saturday night news conference. “In the crossfire, a 12-year-old little girl, who was probably down there watching football, was shot and killed.”

Baltimore police said in a statement that a 25-year-old woman and two men, ages 23 and 28, were also struck. The woman was with the girl, Worley said.

Worley said the adult victims had non-life-threatening injuries.

The commissioner said, “The dispute most likely occurred from a stupid parking spot.”

Baltimore Police Commissioner Richard Worley said the shooting likely started with a dispute over a parking spot. WBAL

The mayor of Baltimore, Brandon M. Scott, expressed disgust at the situation and likened the gunmen to cowards, during the evening news conference.

“Two men, or so-called men, got into a argument, and now this baby is gone,” he said.

Coach Mark Brown of the Charm City Buccaneers youth football league said the gunfire broke out mid-game.

“Some miscellaneous outsiders caused this situation,” he told NBC affiliate WBAL-TV at the scene. “It wasn’t us.”

He said the youth league has operated for 29 years without something like this happening. “We strive to give back to the youth,” he said.

He added, “This happened over a parking spot. It was avoidable.”

World.title: Debris found of medical plane that went missing near Nantucket with 6 on board
World.content:
Debris has been found of a medical jet carrying six people that went missing near Nantucket, Massachusetts, while flying from Bermuda to Boston early Saturday, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.

A debris field that was confirmed to belong to the missing aircraft was found Saturday night, the Coast Guard said in a statement. The search for the missing passengers was still ongoing and would continue overnight.

The plane was carrying four Canadian and two Bermudian nationals, the Coast Guard disclosed.

The Federal Aviation Administration had lost contact with the plane around 1 a.m. local time Saturday and issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice for the Gulfstream G-100.

The jet was registered to Canada-based Latitude Air Ambulance, according to the tail number provided by the Coast Guard.

The plane took off at about 11:40 p.m. ET on Friday, according to data from FlightAware.

The U.S. Coast Guard searches for a missing medical transport aircraft in the Atlantic Ocean off the island of Nantucket, Massachusetts, on Oct. 3, 2026. U.S. Coast Guard/PA3 Kiera Shantry

Bermuda airport's operator, Skyport, said in a statement to The Associated Press that the plane departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts. The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard.

"My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time," Steve MacKinnon, Canada's minister of transport, said in a statement. "We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue."

The government of Bermuda said on X that it has been in contact with the families of those on board.

"We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts," Premier David Burt said.

The plane went missing after about 1 hour and 45 minutes in the air. FlightAware data show it quickly dropped from about 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet before losing contact. It had been set to land at Boston's Logan International Airport at about 1:30 a.m. local time.

The search was being conducted off the coast of Nantucket, according to the Coast Guard's Northeast District. The Coast Guard outlined the extensive assets involved in the search, including an HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane, HC-130 Hercules airplane, MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter, a 47-foot Motor Lifeboat and the FRC William Sparling, a Sentinel-class fast response cutter.

Search crews covered a 1,644-square-mile area over the course of 27 hours, the Coast Guard said.

World.title: Cornell president says school "must do better" amid criticism of its investigation
World.content:
Cornell University President Michael I. Kotlikoff said Saturday his school's administration "must do better" amid the criticism and fallout of its investigation into allegations made by a former student that she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024.

"I believe we as an administration and we as a community must do better," Kotlikoff said in a video message posted online Saturday. "We must do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe and everyone before her and anyone after her from ever happening again."

The former student, identified only as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit last month against the university and seven men, alleging she was drugged and raped in October 2024 at the university's Chi Phi fraternity chapter when she was 20 years old.

"This has been one of the most difficult weeks in our history, and I know many of you are angry, saddened and struggling," Kotlikoff said.

Back in 2024, the Tompkins County district attorney found that "there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges." No criminal charges have been filed in the case.

However, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said this week that he was never given the full transcript of Jane Doe's two-day interview with campus police that occurred in November 2024, about three weeks after the incident, but was only presented a six-page sworn statement based on that interview.

Cornell University initially said its police department provided the results of the school's Title IX investigation to the DA. However, in an FAQ published on its website regarding the allegations, the university said in an Oct. 1 update that it "shared the victim's sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."

The Snapchat screenshot refers to a Snapchat group chat that involved members of the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of the alleged rape.

Van Houten said this week he is reopening the investigation, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who has been publicly critical of Van Houten's approach to the case, said she had appointed State Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to lead the investigation.

Kotlikoff revealed that the school would be hiring an outside law firm to conduct an "independent review" of "all aspects of Cornell's handling of the 2024 matter." The school has said that it supports the state's criminal probe, which Kotlikoff reiterated Saturday.

The school president admitted the situation "raises questions around the investigations conducted after the allegations were reported."

Kotlikoff earlier this week disclosed that the school's Title IX investigation resulted in two of the accused being expelled and two being suspended for at least two semesters. One had already graduated before any punishment could be handed down, Kotlikoff said, and two were found not to be responsible for sexual misconduct.

"I also hear the frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough about what the university did after the assault was reported, which has led to distrust," Kotlikoff said in his video. "There are real legal and privacy limits on what we can say, but we will make greater effort to explain what we can, to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken, and to be more transparent."

He noted that in 2025, in the wake of the initial investigation into Jane Doe's allegations, the university established the Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault and endorsed the task force's recommendations.

Kotlikoff said in the coming weeks, the university will create opportunities for community members, including parents of current students, to question and talk to school leadership.

"This is a defining moment in Cornell's history," Kotlikoff said. "We must lead the way. We owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right. And we must keep each other safe."

World.title: Latino Dems urge investment in Hinojosa campaign as Texas governor's race tightens
World.content:
Latino Democratic leaders are renewing calls for the Democratic Governors Association to invest more heavily in Texas after a New York Times/Siena College poll showed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa narrowly leading Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

The poll released Saturday found Hinojosa ahead of Abbott by three points, a result within the poll's margin of error. It comes as Hinojosa continues to face a huge financial disadvantage against the three-term Republican governor. Abbott's reelection campaign and his Republican allies are outspending her by roughly 10-to-1.

More than 70 Latino Democratic leaders from across the country sent a letter this week urging the DGA and its chair, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, to invest $10 million in the Texas governor's race. The New York Times first reported on the letter, which CBS News has confirmed.

Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential contender, has been constrained by the DGA's commitments to first protect incumbent Democratic governors seeking reelection, though some of those incumbents are currently in strong positions.

Julián Castro, who served as secretary of housing and urban development in the Obama administration, renewed the push Saturday following the release of the New York Times poll. Castro, the former mayor of San Antonio and a 2020 presidential contender, took to social media to call for the DGA and Beshear to support Hinojosa "in a real way."

"How much more evidence" of Hinojosa's "strength in Texas" will Beshear and the DGA "have to see before they support her in a real way?" Castro wrote. "She can win!"

The renewed pressure comes as Democrats increasingly see the Lone Star state as competitive in the closing weeks of the campaign, even as Hinojosa continues to face a substantial spending disadvantage --- what some Republicans are describing as a "firewall" --- in a state that President Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024.
