World.title: Peru Votes Sunday in Regional and Lima Elections
World.content:
ANALYSIS · PERU ELECTIONS 2026

Key Facts — The vote Peru elects regional and local officials on Sunday 4 October 2026. Polls are open 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Lima: 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern Time, 1 p.m. to 11 p.m. in Lisbon.

— What is chosen 13,148 posts, including 25 regional governors, 196 provincial mayors and 1,696 district mayors, for terms from 2027 to 2030 (ONPE). Nobody elects a president or Congress.

— Who votes 26,314,648 Peruvian voters, plus 76 foreign residents who may vote only in municipal races (ONPE).

— Lima Former mayor Rafael López Aliaga leads every final poll, with 20% to 30% depending on the pollster. The electoral jury has not said whether he could take office if his list wins.

— The markets Prediction markets put López Aliaga’s chance of becoming mayor at about 90% (Polymarket and Kalshi, Saturday evening).

— The count ONPE says its results site opens at 6 p.m. ET and fills as tally sheets arrive. A governor needs 30% of valid votes to avoid a runoff, set for Sunday 29 November.

— Why Americans care Peru mined about 2.7 million tonnes of copper in 2025 (USGS estimate). Southern Copper, Freeport-McMoRan and Buenaventura trade in New York, and mining regions vote on Sunday.

Peru, a copper powerhouse in the Andes, holds regional and municipal elections on Sunday. Polls open at 8 a.m. Eastern Time and close at 6 p.m. (7 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Lima). The national electoral office, ONPE, says its results website starts showing counted tally sheets from 6 p.m. ET.

The vote does not change who runs the country. President Keiko Fujimori, who took office on 28 July, stays in place. But the races decide who governs 25 regions and the capital, and several of them sit on top of the world’s big copper deposits.

For US readers, the stakes are mining, security and politics. This guide explains the Lima race, the regions to watch, the violence that has marked the campaign and the timetable of the count. Official results can take weeks, so Sunday night will give a first picture, not a final one.





Peru votes · Regional and municipal elections · Sunday, October 4 Peru Election 2026: Live Map of the Regions and Lima Polls are open 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Lima (8 a.m. to 6 p.m. ET, 13:00 to 23:00 Lisbon). The electoral office ONPE publishes official results from 6 p.m. ET; this page carries them with the time of each update. 0% of tally sheets counted (ONPE) Count starts at 6 p.m. ET Lima: who becomes mayor What the betting markets say Who is who: the parties, explained Two kinds of organisations compete on Sunday: 55 national parties, which can run anywhere, and 95 regional movements, which are registered in one region and run only there (JNE). Many Peruvian parties are built around one leader rather than a fixed ideology. Show all parties Key numbers 26.3 million registered voters (ONPE) 13,148 posts on the ballot 25 regional governors 30% of valid votes a governor needs to avoid a runoff Election night and what comes next Sunday, 8 a.m. ET Polls open (7 a.m. Lima, 13:00 Lisbon).

Sunday, 6 p.m. ET Polls close (5 p.m. Lima, 23:00 Lisbon). ONPE's results site starts showing counted tally sheets.

About two weeks ONPE's acting head says a full count of the regional races takes about two weeks; the JNE resolves disputed sheets.

Sunday, November 29 Runoff for regional governor wherever no candidate reached 30% of valid votes. Mayors have no runoff.

January 1, 2027 New governors and mayors take office. What is on the ballot Regional governors (each with a vice-governor) 25

Regional councillors 364

Provincial mayors 196

District mayors 1,696 Nobody elects a president or Congress on Sunday. Voting is compulsory for Peruvians; foreign residents may vote in municipal races only. The regions: tap a region 2026 count Macro-regions Voters Mining regions Choose a region Tap any region on the map, or a row below, for its capital, people and voters, its economy, the 2022 result and, from Sunday night, the official count. Region by region Show all 26 Lima Metropolitana elects a mayor and no governor. Region facts were researched twice independently; a value appears only where both agreed. The final Lima polls Publishing polls has been banned since September 28, so these are the last public numbers. Rafael López Aliaga ran Lima from 2023 to 2025 and is on the ballot as first councillor, not as mayoral candidate; the electoral jury (JNE) has not said whether he could take the mayor's credential if his list wins. Sources: ONPE (official results, posts on the ballot, registered voters); JNE (lists, runoff date); INEI (population); Ipsos, Datum, CPI and IEP as published until September 28; Polymarket and Kalshi (market prices, public data); region facts from INEI, JNE, ONPE, BCRP and Peruvian media where two independent checks agreed. Map: geoBoundaries (public domain). The Rio Times does not call races; a winner or a runoff is shown once ONPE or the JNE declares it.

What Peruvians are voting for

Peru has three layers of local government. Sunday’s ballot fills all of them at once. ONPE lists 13,148 posts in total.

Post Seats on the ballot How a winner is decided Regional governors 25 (plus 25 vice-governors) At least 30% of valid votes, or a runoff on 29 November Regional councillors 364 Seats allocated by party list Provincial mayors 196 (plus 1,724 councillors) Most votes wins, no runoff District mayors 1,696 (plus 9,118 councillors) Most votes wins, no runoff

Voting is compulsory for Peruvians. Voters can use expired identity cards, the electoral jury says. Foreign residents can vote only for mayors and councillors.

Two kinds of organisations compete: 55 national parties, which can run anywhere in Peru, and 95 regional movements, which are registered in a single region and run only there (JNE). In 2022, governors from regional movements won in Puno, Áncash, Junín, Ucayali and Tacna, among others. Many national parties are built around one leader rather than a fixed ideology. Our party guide in the election center above explains each one.

Voters gather outside classrooms used as polling stations at a school in Callao. More than 10,000 schools serve as voting sites on Sunday. (File photo)

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The race for Lima

Lima is the prize. It is Peru’s capital and by far its largest city, and its mayor runs local transport, streets and municipal services. Publishing polls has been banned since 28 September, so the numbers below are the last public ones.

The three front-runners: Rafael López Aliaga of Renovación Popular, a conservative party he leads; Carlos Bruce of Somos Perú, a centre-right party; and Francis Allison of Avanza País, a pro-market party of the right.

Pollster and dates López Aliaga Bruce Allison Datum, 23–25 Sept (simulated valid votes) 29.6% 17.2% 13% Ipsos, 24–25 Sept (valid-vote simulation) 30% 15.6% 15.1% CPI, late Sept (valid-vote simulation) 27.2% 15.2% 10.4% IEP, 4–10 Sept (voting intention) 20.1% 17.1% 4.7%

Ipsos’ direct question, a different measure, gave López Aliaga 25%, Bruce 14% and Allison 13%. Daniel Urresti of Podemos Perú, a populist party, had 8%, and Samuel Daza of Fuerza Popular, President Fujimori’s conservative party, 6%. All four polls point the same way, but the gap to the runner-up ranges from 3 to 14 points.

There is one legal catch. López Aliaga ran Lima from 2023 to 2025 and is on the ballot as first councillor, not as mayoral candidate, because of rules on immediate re-election. If his list wins, it is unclear whether the electoral jury (JNE) would give him the mayor’s credential. JNE president Roberto Burneo said on 28 September that the full court will decide, and no date has been announced. See our Lima poll report.

What the prediction markets say

Prediction markets treat the Lima race as nearly settled. On these sites traders buy contracts that pay US$1 if an outcome happens, so the price reads as a probability. On Saturday evening a López Aliaga contract cost about 92 cents on Polymarket and 90 cents on Kalshi, a chance of about 90%. Francis Allison traded at 4% to 5% and Carlos Bruce at about 2%. Polymarket’s Lima market had drawn about US$344,000 in trades.

The two platforms ask slightly different questions. Polymarket pays out on who actually becomes mayor, so its price also reflects the open question over López Aliaga’s credential. Kalshi pays out on who wins the election.

Polymarket also runs much smaller markets, with about US$23,000 to US$37,000 traded each, on the mayoral races in seven other provincial capitals: Arequipa, Cusco, Piura, Trujillo, Chiclayo, Huancayo and Maynas, the province of Iquitos. None had a favourite above 60% on Saturday evening. In Arequipa, Manuel Vera Paredes of the regional movement Fuerza Arequipeña led at about 46%. In Trujillo the two leading candidates were neck and neck.

Markets are bets, not polls, and a single large trade can move a small one. The Rio Times takes no position on them. Live prices for every market are in the election center at the top of this page, updated every 20 minutes.

The regions to watch

Regional polling is thin. Ipsos published a scientific survey for Arequipa and Datum one for Callao. For most other regions we found only candidate lists and online straw polls, which are not representative, so we do not rank them.

Region Why it matters Latest public signal Arequipa Peru’s second city; home to the Cerro Verde copper mine and the Tía María project Ipsos, 23–25 Sept (405 interviews, margin ±4.9 points): Elmer Cáceres of Alianza para el Progreso (APP, centre-right) 12%, Florentino Zegarra of Fuerza Arequipeña, a regional movement, 12%, Benigno Cornejo 10% Áncash Hosts the Antamina copper and zinc mine; candidate Susy Aponte Polo was shot dead on 19 September Eleven slates remain. No scientific poll found Callao Peru’s main port, next to Lima Datum (6–21 Sept, 1,700 interviews) has Pedro Spadaro ahead in the race for regional governor La Libertad Home to the Pataz gold district; eight slates No scientific poll found Cusco, Puno, Cajamarca, Piura Mining and energy interests across the Andes and the north No scientific poll found; Cajamarca has nine slates Moquegua and Apurímac Core copper regions No scientific poll found

With fragmented fields, a 30% winner is not guaranteed. Runoffs are likely wherever the vote splits many ways.

Mining, informal miners and the vote

Peru mined about 2.7 million tonnes of copper in 2025, the USGS estimates. Mining taxes and royalties flow to regional and local budgets, so governors and mayors in mining regions control real money.

An open-pit mine in the Peruvian Andes. Antamina, in Áncash, is one of the country’s largest copper and zinc mines. (File photo)

Mining licences and environmental approvals are national decisions. Regional and local governments still shape the climate around a project: they spend part of the revenue, mediate protests and decide how hard to push on informal mining.

That last issue is on the ballot. A database compiled by Territorio Tomado and reported by the trade outlet Todominería lists 735 candidates for governor, councillor and mayor registered in REINFO, the formalisation register for small and artisanal miners, whether current or suspended. Of them, 43 run for regional governments in 15 departments. Parties with the most REINFO candidates include Ahora Nación, APP, Perú Primero, Podemos Perú, Progresemos, Somos Perú and Acción Popular. The party guide above explains who they are.

Security and violence

The campaign has been marked by the killing of Susy Aponte Polo, a journalist and candidate for governor of Áncash. She was shot dead at a market in Caraz on Saturday 19 September. Prosecutors treat it as a contract killing with a possible political motive. Press reports say the 15-day preliminary detention of two suspects runs out around election day. Our Caraz case report follows the investigation.

The state has answered with force. The National Police and the Interior Ministry will deploy 57,738 officers, about 46,000 at polling sites and 11,000 escorting election material. More than 41,000 soldiers also deploy, La República reported. See our security plan report. Prosecutors say they will have more than 6,800 staff on duty.

A dry law bans alcohol sales from 8 a.m. on Saturday 3 October to 8 a.m. on Monday 5 October, and rallies are banned. For travellers, expect closed bars, police at schools and slower transport. Details are in our dry-law explainer.

How the count works, and when to expect results

Event Lima Eastern Time Lisbon Polls open 7 a.m. 8 a.m. 1 p.m. Polls close; ONPE results site opens 5 p.m. 6 p.m. 11 p.m.

Results appear on ONPE’s official site. Exit polls and private quick counts are estimates, not official figures. ONPE’s acting head, Bernardo Pachas, said a full count in regional races takes about two weeks. The JNE resolves disputed tally sheets and proclaims the winners. Close races may stay open for weeks while disputed sheets are reviewed.

What is at stake

Nationally, this is the first test for President Fujimori, who beat Roberto Sánchez in the June runoff by 50.135% to 49.865% on ONPE’s final count. Her party’s Lima candidate polls only 6%, so the vote will show how much local ground Fuerza Popular holds.

For investors, nothing on Sunday’s ballot changes national mining or tax law. The risks are local: protest, informal mining and the safety of candidates. The US-listed names with Peruvian exposure include Southern Copper, Freeport-McMoRan, which holds a stake in Cerro Verde, and Buenaventura. A governor who backs or blocks a project can matter more than a national headline.

The wider picture is in our guide to Peru’s role in Latin America.

The runoff on 29 November

Where no governor reaches 30% of valid votes, the top two meet on Sunday 29 November. The JNE set the date on 30 September and will ask the president to formally call it. New officials take office on 1 January 2027. Mayors have no runoff. Read more in our runoff-date report.

What it means for you

Investors: expect a slow, noisy count. Do not read Sunday’s early numbers as final, and watch mining regions for governors who take a firm line on protests or informal mining. The EODHD calendar lists a central-bank rate decision on 7 October, with the policy rate previously at 4.25%.

Expats and residents: Peruvians must vote. Foreign residents can vote only in municipal races. Carry your documents, and avoid buying alcohol on Saturday and Sunday.

Travellers: bars and shops stop alcohol sales until Monday morning. Police and soldiers will be at schools. Avoid large political gatherings and follow instructions at polling sites.

What is not known

Four things remain open. First, whether López Aliaga could take the mayor’s office if his list wins. Second, how many regions need a runoff. Third, how quickly ONPE can count in close races. Fourth, whether the Caraz suspects’ detention is extended after Sunday. We found no verified regional polls for most regions.

Background: Brazil Election Results 2026: Live Updates, Vote Count and Runoff Scenarios.

What time does Peru vote on Sunday, and when are results published?

Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Lima on Sunday 4 October. That is 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern Time. ONPE says its results site opens at 6 p.m. ET and fills as tally sheets are processed.

What is Peru voting for on 4 October?

Voters choose 25 regional governors, 196 provincial mayors, 1,696 district mayors and councillors, 13,148 posts in all. They do not choose a president or Congress.

Who leads the race for mayor of Lima?

Rafael López Aliaga leads the last public polls, with 20.1% to 30% depending on the pollster and measure. Carlos Bruce is second in all of them. The JNE has not said whether López Aliaga could take office if his list wins. Prediction markets on Polymarket and Kalshi put his chance of becoming mayor at about 90%.

Will there be a runoff?

Only for regional governors. If no candidate wins 30% of valid votes, the top two meet on Sunday 29 November. Mayoral races have no runoff.

Why does the vote matter for US investors?

Peru mined about 2.7 million tonnes of copper in 2025, and mining regions elect governors on Sunday. Nothing on the ballot changes national mining law, but local governments shape protests, revenue use and informal mining.

How long will the final results take?

ONPE’s acting head says a full count in regional races takes about two weeks, and disputed tally sheets must be reviewed by the JNE. Close races may take longer.

POLITICS · TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO

Key Facts — The country Trinidad and Tobago, a twin-island Caribbean republic governed by Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar’s United National Congress (UNC) since 2025.

— What happened A cabinet realignment took effect on 30 September 2026. It was set out in Gazette No. 166, published on Friday 2 October, CNC3 reported.

— Who is involved Eight ministers gain duties; nine office-holders, including the Prime Minister, give some up. Land and Legal Affairs Minister Saddam Hosein gains 11 items, by the Rio Times count of the published list.

— What it means for you Self-help housing schemes, the farm lender and disaster management now answer to different ministers. Applicants and borrowers keep dealing with the same agencies.

— Still open No official reason has been given. It is unclear whether staff and budgets follow the moved programmes.

Trinidad and Tobago’s Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has carried out a cabinet realignment, moving programmes and state companies between her ministers. The changes took effect on 30 September.

They are set out in Gazette No. 166, published on Friday 2 October, CNC3 and the Trinidad Guardian reported on 3 October. No minister has been reported moved to a new ministry or dropped from the Cabinet.

Housing and sugar-era firms go to Hosein

The largest single shift goes to Land and Legal Affairs Minister Saddam Hosein. He takes over the Government Aided Self-Help Housing Programme (GASHHP) and the Housing and Village Improvement Programme (HVIP).

He also gains Hydrographic Surveys and a cluster of state companies. They include Caroni (1975) Limited, the former state sugar company, plus Rincon Development, Taurus Services and TRINTOC Services.

Items newly assigned per minister in the cabinet realignment effective 30 September 2026; Hosein gains 11 of 22, and the Prime Minister sheds six. Source: Trinidad and Tobago Gazette No. 166, as reported by CNC3, 3 Oct 2026.

Housing Minister David Lee picks up the Home Improvement Policy and the Oropune Project. Social Development Minister Vandana Mohit takes the National Commission for Self-Help Limited.

The Prime Minister herself gives up six items, including both self-help housing schemes and the Oropune Project. Those duties now sit with Hosein, Lee and Mohit.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Trinidad and Tobago Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Disaster management moves to Defence

Defence Minister Wayne Sturge takes national emergency and disaster management, including the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Management (ODPM). He also gains the National Emblems Committee and the National Mentorship Programme.

Homeland Security Minister Roger Alexander gives those up. In exchange he takes over the management of illegal immigrants and deportees, previously with Sturge.

Finance Minister Davendranath Tancoo gains the Agricultural Development Bank, the state farm lender, from Agriculture Minister Ravi Ratiram. Health Minister Lackram Bodoe hands insect vector control to Local Government Minister Khadijah Ameen. Public Utilities Minister Barry Padarath takes On-the-Job Training from Tertiary Education Minister Prakash Persad.

A realignment, not a reshuffle

The cabinet realignment follows weeks of speculation. Guardian Media reported on 17 September that a list naming Hosein as Attorney General had circulated online.

Persad-Bissessar rejected that list. “So there will be no reshuffle at this time,” she told Guardian Media, adding there was “always room for improvement.”

The reported changes move duties rather than ministers, which fits that line. Because they are gazetted, there is a public record of who answers for what.

Mickela Panday, leader of the opposition Patriotic Front, questioned the logic on social media. She asked whether “experience, expertise, performance” decided the moves, CNC3 reported.

The shift comes as Parliament pushes through major bills, including the Trinidad Procurement Bill Curbing Contracts Watchdog Passes by One Vote. Background on the two-island state is in Trinidad and Tobago Explained: Gas, Politics, the Two Islands and What to Watch.

What Is Not Yet Known

The government has not published a reason for the cabinet realignment, and no statement from the Office of the Prime Minister was reported. The Rio Times has not seen the Gazette itself.

It is not yet clear whether staff, offices and budget lines move with the programmes. Nor is it known whether a fuller reshuffle remains on the table.

Sources: CNC3, “PM realigns Cabinet portfolios”, 3 October 2026; CNC3, “Panday questions Cabinet realignment”, 3 October 2026; Trinidad Guardian, “PM realigns Cabinet portfolios”, 3 October 2026; Trinidad Guardian, “PM shuts down Cabinet reshuffle rumours”, 17 September 2026. The 3 October reports cite Trinidad and Tobago Gazette No. 166.

World.title: BREAKING: Jahrule Gibson shot dead off bicycle in Sandhill
World.content:
BREAKING: Jahrule Gibson shot dead off bicycle in Sandhill

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the Friday night murder of a man in Sandhill Village, Belize District, who has been identified as Jahrrule Gibson.

According to preliminary information, police responded to a report of a shooting in Sandhill at approximately 10:53 p.m. on Friday, October 2, 2026. Upon arriving at the scene, officers found Gibson motionless with a gunshot wound.

Initial investigations indicate that Gibson had been riding a bicycle at around 10:33 p.m. when he was approached by a male person who fired several shots at him, causing fatal injuries.

Information reaching BBN suggests that persons familiar with Gibson believe the shooter may have come from the Ladyville area specifically to target him. That information, however, remains unconfirmed, and police have not publicly identified a suspect or disclosed a motive for the killing.

The murder comes less than a week after another serious armed incident in the Sandhill area. On September 26, a businessman was reportedly pursued along the Philip Goldson Highway, shot at and carjacked by two armed men near Sandhill. Police later recovered both the stolen Honda Civic and the vehicle allegedly used by the attackers in Maxboro. No connection between that incident and Gibson’s murder has been established.

Police investigations into Gibson’s killing continue.

World.title: People’s United Party celebrates 76th anniversary of founding; introduces municipal candidates
World.content:
People’s United Party celebrates 76th anniversary of founding; introduces municipal candidates

By Zoila Palma: Today in Belize City, the People’s United Party (PUP) held its National Party Council in celebration of the 76th anniversary of its founding.

In addition, the PUP introduced their 67 candidates for the upcoming municipal elections—9 Mayoral Candidates and 58 Councillor Candidates from across Belize.

PUP Mayoral Councilor Candidate Aaron Mai said that the PUP’s celebration was one of unity and renewed commitment.

“Most importantly, it was good to be together with family as we continue this journey of serving our communities and our beloved Belize.

76 years of history. One family. One Belize,” Mai said.

World.title: Belize @45 Research Conference concludes with focus on Belize’s past, present and future
World.content:
Belize @45 Research Conference concludes with focus on Belize’s past, present and future

By Zoila Palma: The “Keeping Independence Alive: Belize @45” Research Conference concluded on October 1, 2026, at the University of Belize Conference Centre in Belmopan, bringing together researchers, scholars and participants for two days of discussions on Belize’s development as an independent nation.

The conference’s second day featured 11 academic presentations exploring themes including Belize’s relations with the United States, culture and identity, national security, and community and development.

The discussions encouraged participants to reflect on Belize’s history while examining issues shaping the country’s present and future.

Day Two also saw the launch of “Enduring Diplomacy: Belize 1971–2026,” authored by Assad Shoman and Alexis Rosado and published by the Belize Policy Research Institute (BELPRI). The book is available for purchase at the BELPRI office in Belize City and the University of Belize in Belmopan.

The Institute for Social and Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) expressed appreciation to the presenters, researchers, scholars and participants who contributed to the conference.

World.title: International News: Caribbean Airlines to resume flights between Trinidad and Venezuela
World.content:
International News: Caribbean Airlines to resume flights between Trinidad and Venezuela

By Zoila Palma: Caribbean Airlines (CAL) has announced the resumption of commercial passenger flights between Trinidad and Tobago and Caracas, Venezuela, as part of an expansion of its network aimed at strengthening regional and international connectivity.

The airline said the new and resumed services will provide travelers with more options for leisure, business and family travel while supporting tourism and trade.

Beginning October 25, 2026, CAL will also introduce a weekly non-stop service between Tobago and Toronto, operating on Sundays. The airline said the new route will provide a direct connection between Tobago and one of its key international markets.

From October 31, 2026, Caribbean Airlines will resume commercial passenger service between Trinidad and Caracas. The airline said restoring the direct connection between the neighboring countries will facilitate business travel and tourism.

World.title: International News: Did Mexican TikTok influencer murder her partner and 3 children in Nuevo Leon, Mexico?
World.content:
International News: Did Mexican TikTok influencer murder her partner and 3 children in Nuevo Leon, Mexico?

By Zoila Palma: Mexican TikTok content creator Cinthia Abigail Tamez Rivera, known online as Cindy Tamez, her partner and three children were reportedly found dead on September 30 in Montemorelos, Nuevo León, Mexico, in a case authorities are investigating as a suspected murder-suicide.

Tamez, 34, had more than 71,000 followers on TikTok, where she shared fashion content and aspects of her life.

According to Mexican media outlets including Reforma, Milenio, Meganoticias and El Financiero, Tamez and her 2-year-old son, Gustavo, were found inside a Jeep at around 9:40 a.m.

Her two other children, Christian, 12, and Bruno, 11, were reportedly found at the family’s home, located about three blocks away, along with Tamez’s partner, Leodegario Moya.

The Attorney General’s Office of Nuevo León reportedly believes Tamez killed her three children and her partner before taking her own life.

Investigators are continuing to collect and analyze evidence, including a firearm recovered at the scene and security camera footage, as the investigation remains ongoing.

Tamez’s final social media post was reportedly published on September 30, the same day she was found dead.

The post contained a message in Spanish over a video showing a car dashboard.

“Not everyone knows my s—- side,” she wrote in Spanish, “I am capable of burning down my house just to see the neighbor’s burning, even knowing that I’ll get f—ed too.”

World.title: Male birth control could be 1 step closer to reality
World.content:
Male birth control could be 1 step closer to reality

By Zoila Palma: The World Health Organization (WHO) is calling for expanded access to safe and effective contraceptive options, including emergency contraception, longer-lasting implants and new methods being developed for men.

WHO says broader contraceptive choices can help people select methods that best suit their needs, while an estimated 164 million women who want to delay or avoid pregnancy are currently not using contraception.

Under its new guidelines on expanding contraceptive options, WHO recommends alternative ways of using several existing methods. Combined oral contraceptive pills can be taken for extended periods of up to six months or continuously for up to one year, while contraceptive implants can be used for up to five years, potentially reducing replacement procedures, clinic visits and related costs.

WHO is also recommending mifepristone as an additional emergency contraception option, to be taken as soon as possible and within five days after unprotected sex.

According to WHO, available evidence indicates that mifepristone at doses of 10 to 50 milligrams is likely to be as safe and effective as other emergency contraceptive methods.

While expanding existing options, WHO is also looking toward the development of new contraceptive methods for men.

Men currently have relatively few methods under their control, mainly condoms, withdrawal and vasectomy, although around 30% of couples rely on a male method. WHO research found that more than 75% of surveyed couples would be willing to use a new male contraceptive, while more than 85% of women surveyed said they would trust their male partners to take responsibility for contraception.

WHO has developed its first Target Product Profile for male contraceptive methods, outlining characteristics future products should meet, including safety, effectiveness, acceptability and affordability. Several hormonal and non-hormonal male contraceptives are currently being researched, with some promising candidates in advanced clinical trials.

WHO says this development could mean new reversible male contraceptives may reach the market within the next five to 10 years, potentially giving men more options to participate directly in family planning.

World.title: International News: Human Rights groups urge UN to challenge ICE policy hiding detainee locations
World.content:
International News: Human Rights groups urge UN to challenge ICE policy hiding detainee locations

By Zoila Palma: Human rights organizations are asking a United Nations panel to intervene over a new U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) practice that withholds the locations of thousands of detainees facing deportation from their families and lawyers.

ICE removed the names of detainees with final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System on September 15, a change that reportedly affects more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 people in ICE custody, AP reports.

Immigration advocates say the policy is making it more difficult for detainees to access legal representation and challenge their deportations, while leaving families unable to locate their relatives.

A coalition of more than 30 organizations petitioned the U.N. Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances, asking it to declare the practice a violation of international law and urge ICE to reverse it. More than 45 House Democrats have also called on ICE to restore the detainees’ names to the online system.

The Department of Homeland Security rejected claims that the policy amounts to making detainees disappear, saying detainees have opportunities to communicate with family members and attorneys and that the department’s procedures comply with due process.

However, the human rights coalition said the policy has obstructed lawyers from locating their clients and intervening in cases involving immigration relief, detention challenges and deportation orders.

World.title: International News: Empty nets as El Niño drives fish into cooler waters across Latin America
World.content:
International News: Empty nets as El Niño drives fish into cooler waters across Latin America

By Zoila Palma: Fishermen along Latin America’s Pacific coast are struggling with sharply reduced catches as unusually warm ocean temperatures, intensified by El Niño, push tuna, anchovies and other fish species toward cooler waters.

From Ecuador and Peru to Panama and Guatemala, some small-scale fishermen have stopped going to sea altogether as catches decline close to shore, with ocean temperatures in some areas reaching as much as six degrees Celsius above normal.

In Ecuador’s southwestern fishing port of Santa Rosa, fisherman Juan Ollague said that after spending a night at sea, he returned with just six small tuna, AFP reports.

Fellow fisherman Darwin Zambrano said catches of larger tuna such as albacore and bonito have declined significantly in recent weeks. Oceanographer Jonathan Cedeno said sea surface temperatures off Ecuador have increased by 2.5 to 3 degrees Celsius, while temperatures at a depth of 40 meters have risen by as much as six degrees over the past 10 weeks.

The effects are also being felt across Central America. In Panama, fishermen say they are traveling farther from shore, increasing expenses for fuel, food and ice needed to preserve their catch. Some have decided to remain in port because they can no longer cover their operating costs.

In Guatemala, fisherman Eliseo Ovando said it now takes three days to catch what he previously caught in one day, while in Peru, some fishermen who depend on anchovies have reportedly turned to construction work to support their families.

The decline in catches is also creating economic ripple effects in fishing communities and markets. Vendors in Panama report receiving smaller quantities of fish, while in Ecuador, prices for mahi-mahi and swordfish have reportedly doubled amid shortages.

World.title: East scores brace as Reggae Boyz beat 10-man El Salvador
World.content:
Jamaica's forward #12 Javon East celebrates scoring his team's second goal during the Concacaf Nations League Cup football match between El Salvador and Jamaica at the Cuscatlan Stadium in San Salvador on October 2, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica returned to winning ways in the Concacaf Nations League on Friday as Javon East scored both goals in the Reggae Boyz’ 2-0 victory over host El Salvador.

El Salvador were reduced to 10 men in the 20th minute after Rudy Clavel was shown a straight red card for a challenge on East.

From that point onwards, the Boyz piled on the pressure on the Central Americans and were rewarded in the 39th minute when East volleyed home from an excellent cross by Miguel Freckleton.

East added to his tally in the 64th minute with a brilliant one-time shot after being found by substitute Jahmarie Nolan.

With the win, Jamaica sit at second place in Group B with six points, just a point behind leaders Suriname.

World.title: Strike could not have come at a worse time, says Annotto Bay Hospital CEO
World.content:
Annotto Bay Hospital via its Facebook page.

ANNOTTO BAY, St Mary – With the hospital already grappling with a shortage of doctors, the management of Annotto Bay Hospital on Friday said they were operating in emergency mode as many junior doctors across the country withdrew their services.

Chief executive officer Dale Brown told the Jamaica Observer that while the hospital had activated its contingency plan, deploying consultants and senior medical officers to critical areas, the strain was beginning to show.

“We have the MO4s [senior doctors] out manning the areas to ensure that we do not have any deaths. A few junior doctors turned up, so the amount of persons that turned up we have to utilise them to man areas in case of an emergency,” Brown explained.

He noted that routine clinics were scaled back, with only critical cases being seen. Other appointments were rescheduled. The CEO said the industrial action could not have come at a worse time as the Type C hospital was already understaffed. Annotto Bay Hospital is the main referral medical facility for the eastern parishes of St Mary, Portland and St Ann. Staff say they are bracing for an influx of emergencies while running on a skeleton crew.

The strike is expected to last one day as, in a press release on Friday, Jamaica Medical Doctors Association (JMDA) President Dr Jubilee Brown said the body “cannot guarantee normalcy from 8 am on Friday, October 2, 2026 to 8 am on Saturday, October 3, 2026.

Brown warned that if it goes beyond that, Annotto Bay Hospital’s ability to cope will be severely tested.

“It will have a negative impact on the hospital. However, we will still be able to manage emergencies. The amount of people we have will also have burnout and will require at least some time to pause. Basically, the emergency mode persons are in overdrive,” he said.

“You have to plan just in case it would be prolonged. We will be able to man the emergencies but we do not know how long we can hold out in doing such,” Brown added.

— Ingrid Henry

World.title: Hospitals hobbled
World.content:
The Health and Wellness Ministry says there were no adverse events at the island’s public health facilities Friday after junior doctors stayed away in protest over a long-running dispute with the Government relating to overtime pay.

However, checks by Jamaica Observer journalists in rural areas found long wait times at some facilities, while others showed no evidence of outpatient activity.

World.title: Underhanded insurance companies
World.content:
Government Senator Charles Sinclair his contribution to the debate on the Jamaica Consumer and Competition Authority Bill, 2026 in the Senate on Friday. (Photo: Karl McLarty)

Government Senator Charles Sinclair has ripped into what he has described as “underhanded insurance companies”, which he said only respond to third party claims when court action is initiated.

Sinclair, a veteran attorney- at-law, made the accusation in the Senate on Friday during his contribution to the debate on the Jamaica Consumer and Competition Authority Bill, 2026.

The authority will in effect be a merger of the Consumer Affairs Commission and the Fair Trading Commission. Sinclair described third parties (the victims) as being “on the other side of the coin to policyholders of motor vehicle insurance”. “Many of these third parties are not motor vehicle owners but are pedestrians or cyclists. Many are innocent passengers in a vehicle trying to get from one place to another to earn a living or just get on with their lives.

Unfortunately, an accident arises; they suffer loss or damage, leaving them challenged in many respects and in need of compensation,” Sinclair said. “The policyholder has acted properly in reporting to the insurance carrier with facts which clearly and indisputably establish negligence on his part.

He expects his policy to protect him from a court action,” Sinclair added. However, he lamented that in many instances when a claim is submitted, even in cases when attorneys are engaged, the claimant is met with total silence. He said such silence includes correspondence not responded to for months; telephone calls being screened; calls not returned; and the telephone ringing without answer until the call is disconnected. “Many of the insurance companies move to settlement when court action is brought. That is the only time you see them moving,” Sinclair charged.

He said it was the delay tactics on the part of insurance carriers that force court action to be filed, further placing burden on an overburdened court system. “They know the delay in the Supreme Court, and they know the limit on the monetary jurisdiction in the Parish Court. They know Jamaicans are not generally litigious. Many give up and suffer in silence. Many abandon parts of genuine claims just to get a little compensation,” Sinclair told his colleagues.

“Those practices are blatantly underhanded. The public needs real protection from the bodies that can correct these shortcomings,” he insisted. Sinclair reasoned that these practices, which hurt the victims of accidents, are more egregious when one takes account of the fact that insurance coverage provided by private enterprise is mandated by law under the Motor Vehicle (Third Party Risks) Act and enforced by the Jamaica Constabulary Force.

“The insurance carrier is the only business that has the Government working on its enforcement,” he said. A former mayor of Montego Bay who still sits in the St James Municipal Corporation as a councillor, Sinclair repeated a call for the minister of justice to increase the monetary jurisdiction of the parish court from $1 million to $5 million. He said this was necessary since many of the insurance carriers move to settlement when court action is filed.

“The parish court is the court which gives the small man greater access to justice, and it’s high time we make the adjustment to allow them to recover their full claim without having to abandon any part of their claim,” Sinclair argued. He noted that in other jurisdictions, legislation has been created over the past 10 years to ensure prompt settlement of claims by the creation of timelines and standards.

“We should look at what can be adopted to better fit our circumstances,” he said, while noting that the trust factor is so low between insurers and the insured that Jamaicans were referring to the entire industry as a sham, and deeming those in charge to be scammers.

World.title: Pain and agony at Mandeville Regional
World.content:
A 75-year-old outpatient showing his swollen knee while waiting without knowing whether he will be seen by a doctor on Friday at Mandeville Regional Hospital.

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — A 75-year-old outpatient was among scores of people who either left Mandeville Regional Hospital or waited in pain as most junior doctors withdrew their services on Friday.

“This is not what I am accustomed to, and a lot of the people who were here waiting along with me, they left. I even left too and returned, yet I am still sitting and waiting. I am suffering from pain right now.

I don’t know what cause it and there is nobody to tell me what it is,” the senior citizen who had a swollen left knee told the Jamaica Observer on Friday.

The doctors were protesting the delay by the Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) in handing down a ruling as it relates to overtime payments. Senior medical officer at Mandeville Regional Hospital Dr Everton McIntosh told the Observer that he was “hoping and praying that normalcy” would resume by late Friday or early Saturday.

“If this goes into the weekend then it becomes a lot more stressful, because the few doctors who we have won’t be able to continue indefinitely,” said McIntosh.

He warned the public of the significant delays to access health care at the already overcrowded facility manned by 24 consultants up to mid-afternoon on Friday. “If your condition is not serious, if you are not very sick, perhaps you should consider not coming to the hospital today [Friday]. Our present patient count is 315…

We still have a significant number of patients. A big part of the problem is that over the past several months, since Hurricane Melissa, we have been inundated with patients coming for admissions — particularly medical patients with complications of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, stroke, cancers, and those kinds of things. “In any hospital, the majority of the staff would be the junior [doctors], and then there are the consultants who would lead them.

We should have had a total of 133 doctors on duty but just the consultants are here, which is about 24, who are actually working,” added McIntosh. He said all departments and wards were left without adequate staff on Friday. “We can see the discrepancy there out of a total of 133.

That has grave implications for the ability for us to cover all of the areas adequately in terms of the wards, the emergency departments, the outpatients and the clinics, so it is not physically possible for the few consultants to carry that workload,” McIntosh said while pointing to a drastic scaling down of routine procedures.

“For example, our outpatient clinics where you see patients who are walk-in patients, those services have basically been suspended for the day [Friday],” added McIntosh. He said people who turned up at the hospital were given a rescheduled appointment date and/or prescriptions. “Similarly, elective surgeries [that were] planned maybe weeks or months before to do a particular surgery, those have had to be postponed as well.

We are only focusing on emergency care, serious emergencies,” said McIntosh. “The whole idea is to ensure that we have adequate coverage for persons who are very ill so that nobody will die or suffer serious complications due to lack of care. All those persons who are well enough who can wait will be asked to wait.

“Even at the wards, what we have done also to reduce the workload is to discharge those persons who are stable, and do not require high-level care, and can survive if they go home with some instructions and with medication. Some of them will be asked to come back early to the clinic to be assessed, just to ensure that they are maintaining good health,” added McIntosh.

World.title: Western health centres see fewer patients
World.content:
MONTEGO BAY, St James — There were fewer people than usual seeking medical care at State-run medical facilities in western Jamaica on Friday as members of the public appeared to heed warnings to only seek help if they had no other choice because junior doctors withdrew their services.

“Last night I told them not to come unless it is urgent or an emergency,” clinical coordinator for the Western Regional Health Authority (WRHA) Dr Delroy Fray told the Jamaica Observer Friday afternoon. While he did not have supporting data to share at the time, Fray said there were fewer than usual admissions to accident and emergency (A&E) departments across St James, Hanover, Westmoreland, and Trelawny.

“We kind of control it, because we did not want the patient who needs care to suffer because of [the strike],” Dr Fray explained. At 8:00 am on Friday, junior doctors across Jamaica went on strike to protest the delay by the Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) in handing down a ruling related to years of wrangling over retroactive overtime payments.

To fill the gap, senior doctors, many of them consultants, had to step up and shoulder the additional workload, particularly in A&E departments. “We assigned all the doctors from yesterday; everybody knows what they were supposed to do and they have fulfilled it,” Dr Fray stated. At Noel Holmes Hospital in Lucea, one nurse confirmed that patients stayed away. “Things are slow. [I] don’t even think the doctors see 10 people from morning,” she told the Observer.

Of the three shifts scheduled for the day, the first shift — which ended at 3:00 pm — was staffed by five of its six doctors, comprising senior and Cuban physicians. However, all 14 junior doctors assigned to the parish’s six curative clinics stayed away, according to medical officer of health for the Hanover Health Department Dr Kaushal Singh.

“Due to that, we had to reorganise services. We were supposed to have six curative clinics — meaning the six clinics where doctors are supposed to go, [and] we had to reappoint four clinics [where patients were provided with new dates within two weeks],” Singh told the Observer.

“Two clinics were operated by the senior medical officers — Lucea in the western end of the parish and Mount Peto in the eastern section. Anybody who needs a repeat prescription should go to these clinics and get their prescription filled,” Singh advised. Despite the challenges, Singh confirmed that all 18 health centres in Hanover remained open on Friday, with maternal and child health, family planning, nutrition, and oral health services running smoothly. The Observer spoke with two patients at the Lucea clinic who expressed support for the doctors.

One woman, who identified herself only as McPherson, said she understood the situation and was willing to be patient. “It not easy, but you know we always have the doctors them move fast enough with us here. If they have a delay now we just have to cope with them,” said McPherson. Another patient shared a similar sentiment, highlighting the personal toll the profession takes. “Them have family to support, them have children, and every day them have to be in the hospital.

Them can’t sleep in them bed in peace; every minute them get call,” said the patient as he recalled experiences waiting hours at the hospital due to emergency cases taking precedence. Meanwhile, a visit to Falmouth Public General Hospital in Trelawny found the usually bustling A&E Department almost empty.

“You see, them can do better. But [usually], even if them eyelash a hurt them, them come,” one member of staff said. However, at the A&E at Cornwall Regional Hospital in St James one woman, who was outside with her ailing male relative, said they were inconvenienced by the doctors’ strike.

“We have to go to Type 5 because they are on strike. We’ve been here like two hours but now we are waiting on the drive to go down there,” said the woman who did not give her name. Type 5 is the informal name for Montego Bay Comprehensive Health Centre, and indications are things went smoothly there throughout the day.

“The turnout was the [usual] amounts, nothing really different, because patients wouldn’t know who is on strike,” St James Health Services Parish Manager Lennox Wallace told the Observer. He said in preparation for the strike they had made adjustments to the opening hours on Friday. “We were not going to take the risk, even though [most of] the doctors came out on Friday.

We had to play it by ear so I had given instructions that the clinic be closed at 4:00 pm on Friday and not 10:00 pm — because we have to gauge the risk,” Wallace explained. He said they attended to all patients who turned up Friday, even if some were rescheduled for other dates.

“No patient that came here, as much as you can see that it is empty, not even one was turned away — not even one,” Wallace stressed. He said while fewer doctors showed up for work, each of the 22 health centres in the parish had a doctor present throughout the day. “We would have had like 10 doctors normally.

We had six today but we should have the full complement Saturday and Sunday,” said Wallace.

World.title: STICK OR MOVE!
World.content:
West Indies cricketer Rovman Powell

Jamaican cricketers Rovman Powell, Vitel Lawes and John Campbell are among West Indies players who have two weeks to decide whether to accept reduced contracts offered by Cricket West Indies (CWI).

Last week, the regional governing body announced that international retainer contracts would see fees cut by 25 per cent as part of a series of measures to address CWI’s current financial challenges.

CWI CEO, Jamaica’s Chris Dehring, told ESPN Cricinfo on Thursday, that the West Indies Players Association (WIPA) agreed to the changes following “multiple discussions” which started from 2025.

Dehring revealed that the international players were directly addressed at a meeting last Wednesday. “We held a Zoom call involving CWI, WIPA and both male and female players.

There were over 96 participants in that video conference, where we outlined the plans, explained the situation, and answered questions. The CWI president [Kishore Shallow], the director of cricket [Miles Bascombe] and I were on that call along with the WIPA president [Wavell Hinds] and secretary [Wayne Lewis],” he said.

Although the list hasn’t been made public, it’s understood former T20 Captain Powell, spinner Lawes and opening batsmen Campbell, who are currently part of the Windies squad for the ongoing tour of India, have all been offered retainer contracts along with Windies red ball captain Roston Chase, white ball captain Shai Hope and pacers Shamar Joseph and Alzarri Joseph.

However, Dehring admits there is no guarantee the players will accept the offer, with the option of franchise cricket on the table. “WIPA has agreed with us on the domestic side, and we informed them what we’re able to afford on the international side. So really that is now up to individual players to determine whether or not they would like to sign international contracts that have been offered to them,” he said.

“With regard to them being able to earn outside of West Indies cricket in other lucrative leagues around the world, we have always been very understanding, allowing players leeway where we can. WIPA and ourselves have also discussed various options to seek amicable compromise before coming to an agreement.”

“Of course, we would prefer them to play for the West Indies at all times as a priority, but we also understand that there are opportunities around the world for them to apply their trade.

At the same time, we believe there should be some level of obligation to give back to the institution that is West Indies cricket, which facilitated the opportunity for them to earn from cricket. We believe, by and large, the players understand that obligation.” With the India tour wrapping up on October 17, Dehring believes the players have ample time to weigh their options.

“We don’t want players to feel there is the proverbial gun to their head to sign contracts that have been offered. It’s an important and considered decision for them to make, discuss it with their agents, their lawyers, so we have given them two weeks to review and they can decide whether or not they choose to be internationally contracted players,” he said.

“That would not preclude them from being selected to represent West Indies, or making themselves available to West Indies. So, we will wait to hear from those players that have been offered international contracts as to whether they are accepting or not. And then, we will get them approved at CWI board level and announce those players.”

The Windies Women, who are currently touring Zimbabwe, will also face a 25 per cent pay cut including Jamaicans Stafanie Taylor and Chinelle Henry. — Daniel Blake

World.title: Sandals Foundation Island Challenge off to strong start in Jamaica
World.content:
Men’s Health magazine writer Andrew Tracey competes in Sandals Foundation’s Island Challenge Jamaica on Friday.

OCHO RIOS, St Ann — Sandals Foundation’s Island Challenge Jamaica got off to a strong start on Friday, with approximately 30 participants from the United Kingdom testing their endurance along Jamaica’s north coast.

The event forms part of a four-day fundraising effort aimed at strengthening neonatal and paediatric healthcare.

The opening day saw participants complete a 10-kilometre run from Rio Nuevo Fishing Beach in St Mary to Sandals Ochi Beach Club, before taking to the water for a five-kilometre kayak along the White River Fish Sanctuary.

The challenge, which runs from October 2 to 5, has brought together athletes, travel industry figures and community supporters, with a target of raising £100,000 to purchase essential medical equipment and strengthen paediatric and neonatal services at Falmouth Public General Hospital in Trelawny.

Sandals Foundation Executive Director Heidi Clarke sounded the horn to officially start Friday’s competition, sending participants off on the first leg of what is expected to become an increasingly demanding journey over the next three days.

For Clarke, however, the physical test is secondary to the lives the initiative is intended to impact. “It’s really all about raising money to buy equipment for our hospitals here in the Caribbean,” she said. “For this one, the Falmouth General Hospital is going to benefit. “We’re really thrilled to be able to support the doctors and nurses working there who are working in conditions that have not been ideal since Hurricane Melissa.”

The intensity off the challenge is expected to increase on Saturday when participants climb the world-famous Dunn’s River Falls before embarking on a 10-kilometre rainforest trek and tree-planting exercise in the Bogue 11 Forest. “This challenge is everything from running to kayaking to hiking… to Trelawny up to Blue Hope then into the Blue Mountains for a hike and sampling some great Blue Mountain coffee on Monday,” Clarke said.

On Sunday, the group will be joined by 13 local participants for a 21-kilometre half-marathon through Falmouth. The route will take them past Falmouth Public General Hospital before continuing through the historic town, Hague and on to Good Hope.

The challenge culminates on Monday in St Andrew, where participants will face a military-style endurance test in Newcastle before taking on a partial hike of the Blue Mountains, reaching approximately 4,500 feet above sea level. Among those taking on the challenge is Men’s Health magazine writer Andrew Tracey, who is participating for the second consecutive year after completing the 2025 staging in Saint Lucia.

Tracey said Friday’s opening leg provided an early indication of just how demanding the Jamaican edition could be, particularly because of the humid conditions. “It was tough, it was really tough. It was so humid,” Tracey said. “The sun came out in Saint Lucia so it was like running up a hill in a spotlight, but we were blessed with a little bit of cloud cover today. It wasn’t easy by any stretch of the imagination, but a little bit more enjoyable.”

This year’s fundraising effort has taken on added significance following the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa at Falmouth Public General Hospital last October. The Category 5 hurricane caused extensive damage to the facility, including the loss of approximately 90 per cent of its roofing.

Extensive flooding also compromised electrical systems as well as diagnostic and clinical equipment. Proceeds from the Island Challenge are expected to help purchase equipment and strengthen the hospital’s capacity to provide care for newborns and children.

Peter Davenport of the Daily Mail in the United Kingdom, who is also participating in the challenge, said this year’s event has taken on even greater meaning because of the hurricane’s impact. “Every year is special in what we do, but this year is even more special because of what happened last year,” Davenport said.

“The fact that there is no paediatric care left there now… all the money we make on this trip will go towards that. That’s what it is about. It’s about saving lives.”

Jamaica is the fourth Caribbean country to host the Sandals Foundation Island Challenge, following stagings in Antigua and Barbuda in 2023, St Vincent and the Grenadines in 2024, and Saint Lucia in 2025.

The previous challenges have collectively raised more than £300,000 and benefited approximately 1,800 babies across the region.

Attention now turns to Saturday’s second day, when participants will tackle Dunn’s River Falls before completing the 10-kilometre rainforest trek and tree-planting exercise.

World.title: Tory conference 2026: What POLITICO reporters are watching for
World.content:
U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom

My biggest question for Badenoch’s speech at 11 a.m. Wednesday will be: can she end Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s honeymoon?

Since July, Labour has jumped to 26% in the polls while the Tories lag behind Reform on 19%. There will simply be fewer lobbyists and hangers-on than at Labour’s jamboree.

Badenoch will spend this week arguing that Burnham, with his crusade against “40 years of neoliberalism,” has ushered in the kind of classic left-right ideological fight that she relishes. Expect her to bang on about cutting welfare to fund defense — two weak points for Labour. And the self-described “badass Kemi” plans to be more abrasive than Burnham, who went out of his way not to attack anyone in his speech.

I reckon two things will decide if she can cut through: her personal brand, and how far she can differentiate the Tories from Labour and Reform (plus, well, her own party from 2024). She will try to paint the Tories as the party of fiscal responsibility but that’s a crowded marketplace. It’s worked for the Conservatives in the past but we aren’t in two-party politics anymore — though admittedly, the five-party split has become less dramatic since the summer.

There will be economic policy announcements but perhaps not on the scale of last year’s pledge to scrap stamp duty. Badenoch has talked about getting rid of inheritance tax but aides appear to be suggesting an announcement isn’t ready.

I can’t wait to see the peacocking by would-be candidates for a general election. Tory aides are shouting from the hills that they are on a “war footing” and candidate selection is ramping up. Some of the high-profile Tories who were rejected for being too centrist are swerving this year’s conference, but former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street will be prominent on the fringe. Critics complain that Badenoch has bulldozed the transepts off her party’s ideological church.

World.title: Two Iranians charged with alleged bomb plot against Britain’s Jewish community
World.content:
Police said the two men received instructions and materials to make a homemade bomb for possible use on Jewish targets.

Two Iranian men have been charged with terror offenses over an alleged plot to bomb Manchester’s Jewish community.

Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, appeared in a British court on Saturday on charges of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.

Police said the two men, who were arrested last month on the eve of the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, had received material and instructions on how to make a bomb, identified targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack on Jewish targets.

World.title: Spaniards protest housing crisis as Sánchez weighs snap vote
World.content:
“The people on the streets once again hold the power,” she said while addressing the demonstration, insisting that their movement would “no longer tolerate inaction.”

The protests were triggered after an investment firm evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment where she had lived since 1956. Sánchez’s government sought to contain the discontent on Tuesday by unveiling two long-delayed bills aimed at curbing speculative practices, extending eviction protections for vulnerable tenants and automatically renewing existing contracts. But conservative lawmakers in parliament rejected both bills on Friday.

Amid the defeat, senior government figures indicated Sánchez — already under pressure over the ongoing migrant crisis in Ceuta and corruption cases involving members of his family and close political allies — was considering calling a snap election in a bid to capitalize on anger over housing.

Protesters hold a banner reading ‘towards the general strike’ along Gran Via street during a demonstration against the housing crisis on October 3, 2026 in Madrid. | Pablo Blazquez Dominguez/Getty Images

Saturday’s protests underscored the risks of that strategy. While demonstrators slammed the conservative opposition for voting down the bills, they also accused Sánchez of failing to tackle the housing crisis since taking office in 2018.

“Eight days of people power have achieved more than eight years of progressive government,” Racu said, adding that protesters would continue pressuring politicians “regardless of who governs this country.”

Calling for a general strike to force the adoption of urgent housing measures, Racu said “the feelings of disaffection, desperation, disillusionment and sadness have been replaced by a new energy on the streets.”

World.title: Sandu slams Russia as attack debris hits Moldova in latest airspace violation
World.content:
Moldova's President Maia Sandu reacts during the Coalition of the Willing meeting, in Kyiv on August 24, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images

Three missile and two drones entered Moldovan airspace and caused collateral damage in the country, local authorities said.

Moldovan President Maia Sandu on Saturday hit out at Moscow after saying debris from five Russian air attack weapons violated the country’s airspace and exploded on the country’s territory.

“I condemn Russia’s attack on Ukraine this morning. Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova,” she wrote on X. “Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our soil.”

In all, three missiles and two drones flew over the country between 7.45 a.m. and 8 a.m., with fragments later found in the country’s eastern districts of Hincesti, Anenii Noi and Causeni. The police were dispatched to secure the debris, which caused a fire to break out but no casualties.

World.title: Russia hits major Kyiv bridge, logistics hub in latest attack
World.content:
Russia’s defense ministry confirmed it had carried out the attack, stating the bridge was being used to transport military cargo. It also separately said it had struck the key Hostomel logistics hub and a cargo ship crossing the Black Sea near the southern port of Odessa.

Separately, the UN-linked International Atomic Energy Agency said four strikes in recent days had threatened safety and security” at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, including reportedly disabling an off-site radiation monitoring station.

Moscow has stepped up its bombing campaign in recent weeks against Ukraine’s civil and critical infrastructure, targeting residential areas, energy facilities, sea terminals and data centers, setting the stage for a dire winter for Kyiv. In the past week alone, Russia has launched more than 190 missiles and drones, mostly targeting energy infrastructure.

The Russian foreign affairs ministry issued a statement on Saturday warning “foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel against remaining in” Kyiv.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered his troops to abandon the rules of war, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT this week.

Meanwhile, Ukraine is grappling with a yawning financial deficit and shortage of critical weapons. Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi this week said the country faces a $27 billion defense funding gap this year, with Kyiv hoping to cover about $7 billion domestically and looking to partners for the rest.

This article was updated.

World.title: Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act on Nigel Farage
World.content:
Britain’s head of counter-terrorism policing Vicki Evans said the force had “been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time,” adding: “The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter-terrorism policing network.”

Kerry is set to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday.

In August, the counter-terrorism force reopened a year-long investigation into an alleged firebomb attack against Farage’s home.

“I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family,” said British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood. “Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.”

A Reform official told the BBC: “This is exactly why Nigel needed £5m to protect his security for life.”

Farage is facing a parliamentary watchdog probe into a £5m gift from a billionaire donor before he became an MP in 2024, previously claiming he needed the money to ensure his security.

World.title: Wie Russland die NATO provoziert. Mit Carlo Masala
World.content:
Eine Drohne mit Sprengstoff an einer ukrainischen Frachtmaschine in Leipzig, Explosionen in Munitionsfabriken und Sabotage auf See. Russland intensiviert seine hybride Kriegsführung mitten in Europa und testet gezielt die roten Linien der NATO. Doch was passiert, wenn ein solcher Anschlag auf deutschem Boden tatsächlich gelingt und den Bündnisfall auslöst? Darüber spricht Gordon Repinski in dieser Folge mit Carlo Masala, Professor für Internationale Politik, Universität der Bundeswehr München.

Das Ziel des Kremls ist es, Panik zu schüren und die westliche Unterstützung für die Ukraine zu brechen. Im Gespräch analysiert Carlo, warum Putin gerade jetzt risikofreudiger wird und weshalb Friedrich Merz in der deutschen Debatte als entscheidender Schutzwall für weitere Hilfen gilt. Ein Wegbrechen dieser Unterstützung hätte fatale finanzielle und militärische Folgen für den gesamten Kontinent.

Gleichzeitig wächst der Druck auf Kiew massiv. Die Episode beleuchtet, wie eine mögliche Rückkehr von Trump ins Weiße Haus die Ukraine zu schmerzhaften Deals zwingen könnte und warum das europäische Superwahljahr 2027 Moskau eine beispiellose Chance bietet, die politische Landschaft endgültig zu seinen Gunsten zu drehen.

World.title: Latvian PM faces bittersweet victory in election backdropped by Russia
World.content:
His center-right partners, New Unity, are struggling to cross the 5% electoral threshold, which would be a floundering performance for a party that has been home to many Latvian prime ministers, including current European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis.

But for the party’s prime ministerial candidate and ex-Finance Minister Arvils Ašeradens, the low polling numbers are simply the “political pendulum which shifts from one way to the other,” he told POLITICO in Riga last month.

During the last election in 2022, New Unity was the major beneficiary of a rally-round-the-flag moment as Russia had just launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But in 2026, voters seem frustrated with Latvia’s high inflation, the ongoing uncertainty surrounding national airline airBaltic and instrumentalized migration orchestrated by Russia and Belarus.

The prime minister may need to open talks with Ainārs Šlesers, a right-wing veteran of Latvian politics. | Robert Hegedus/EPA

Kulbergs’ other coalition partner, the agrarian Union of Greens and Farmers (known as ZZS), is also polling below the threshold. And if neither party manages to scrape by, it might force Kulbergs to work with the controversial businessman Šlesers, who carefully advocated expanding trade with Russia.

Kulbergs has dismissed this possibility — “as it is given now: no,” he told POLITICO in early September — because he does not trust the people Šlesers has surrounded himself with. Just weeks earlier, however, he had been less definitive, telling POLITICO in July: “I have to see what chess pieces I will get … to make a coalition.”

Šlesers has been a central figure in Latvian politics for decades, most notably as a local “oligarch” who, via family holdings, exerts influence over the Port of Riga. The capital’s harbor has seen its largely Russian and Belarusian hinterland slowly carved off by EU sanctions. And after Kulbergs slapped 300% tariffs on transited Russian grain this month , Šlesers told Latvian national TV such transit should be allowed, though he supports Ukraine’s EU accession.

World.title: Scientists uncover how the brain adds new information to an existing memory
World.content:
Imagine, for instance, a building site in your neighbourhood. The human brain is capable of remembering three key stages of that process: the original state before the renovation, the work itself and the final result once everything is finished. But how does it manage not to mix up these three memories?

 

The Institute of Neurosciences, a public research centre run by the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) and Miguel Hernández University, believes it has identified this neurological mechanism in a new study published in the journal "PLOS Biology" (source in Spanish).

The team in its Neural Network Plasticity laboratory argues that the brain uses a region of the hippocampus, the dentate gyrus, which is devoted to generating new memories. There, a specific type of neuron inhibits the activity of other cells to help incorporate new experiences.

To demonstrate this, the team carried out experiments on mice, altering this inhibitory process to a greater or lesser degree. "With lower-than-usual levels, their behaviour was more consistent with better memory retrieval and a more detailed recollection," explains Encarni Marcos, co-lead of the study and head of this line of research at the IN CSIC-UMH.

However, there are no fixed levels of inhibition that are objectively better or worse for preserving the maximum amount of information. The computational model the team used for its experiment showed that, with a lighter memory load, this reduced inhibitory activity is beneficial, but that this is no longer the case when the amount of information increases substantially.

The study suggests that, depending on the type of memory, the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus can either favour the incorporation of new inputs or, conversely, keep the existing memory more firmly in place when faced with new stimuli. That will depend on contextual importance, or what the team describes as task demands. "What we infer from these results is that there is a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the mode of operation by using inhibition," Marcos concludes.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Turkey and Uzbekistan join forces in major military exercise
World.content:
Mass drone attacks, cyberattacks, disinformation and attempts to seize a vessel were among the simulations that Azerbaijan, Turkey and Uzbekistan's troops rehearsed for the first time together in Azerbaijan over the past few days, designating the current threats that the military forces of these countries are facing in the current geopolitical shifts.

 

More than 3,500 troops from the three countries took part in the “Power of Unity-2026” exercise, held for the first time in the Hojavend district of Azerbaijan’s Karabakh region.

Turkish Defence Minister Yaşar Güler highlighted the need for military readiness saying “we will prepare in the best possible way, but we will live in peace,” hailing the success of the exercise “in both its planning and execution”.

Türkiye’s Defence Minister, Yaşar Güler, and Azerbaijan’s Defence Minister, Colonel General Zakir Hasanov Euronews Baku Bureau, October, 2026

The simulated training ranged from drone warfare and electronic attacks to border incidents and operations at sea in a new approach to military preparedness.

In the Qızılqaya military training area troops used more than 130 unmanned vehicles, alongside over 70 armoured vehicles, more than 90 artillery systems and over 20 aviation assets.

Drones featured heavily in the training as a sign of evolving warfare, with troops training to repel drone swarm attacks, strikes on advancing military columns, surveillance and the delivery of ammunition and supplies.

The drills combined unmanned systems with artillery, armoured vehicles, aviation and electronic warfare. Troops also practised breaching defensive positions and anti-tank trenches, clearing minefields and advancing with armoured vehicles.

“Power of Unity – 2026” exercise Euronews Baku Bureau, October, 2026

Beyond the conventional battlefield

The training also focused on the new challenges that have not been part of traditional military scenarios until now.

Troops responded to simulated cyberattacks and online disinformation, carried out operations against "terrorist" positions in mountainous terrain, practised clearing settlements and setting up checkpoints.

Training also involved using drones to detect and stop attempted border crossings.

Azerbaijan’s Defence Minister, Colonel General Zakir Hasanov, said the exercise included land, naval and air operations which help raise the combat readiness of the participating armies.

Uzbekistan’s Defence Minister, Lieutenant General Shukhrat Kholmukhamedov, said the participating personnel had demonstrated “high combat readiness” and the ability to carry out missions together.

Uzbekistan’s Defence Minister, Lieutenant General Shukhrat Kholmukhamedov giving his speech during the “Power of Unity – 2026” exercise Euronews Baku Bureau, October, 2026

From the border to the Caspian Sea

The scenarios extended beyond land operations, into the Caspian Sea, with forces practising freeing a vessel and an offshore facility, rescuing hostages and landing on the ground to neutralise a simulated terrorist base.

This exercise was held at training areas in Baku, the Karabakh region, Nakhchivan and Azerbaijan’s part of the Caspian Sea.

Azerbaijan and Turkey describe their defence relationship as an alliance under the 2021 Shusha Declaration. Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan have also expanded cooperation in military, defence-technology and military education.

Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Serbia, Slovakia, Tajikistan, Georgia, Turkmenistan and the United Arab Emirates, as well as Iran, attended the exercise as observers.

Trilateral meeting of the Defence ministers of Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey Euronews Baku Bureau, October, 2026

From Qızılqaya to Shusha

The military exercise was followed by a trilateral meeting of the defence ministers of Azerbaijan, Turkey and Georgia in Shusha.

Azerbaijan’s Defence Minister Colonel General Zakir Hasanov, Türkiye’s National Defence Minister Yaşar Güler and Georgia’s Vice Prime Minister and Defence Minister Irakli Chikovani took part in the 13th trilateral defence meeting, which focused on military cooperation, regional security and trilateral ties.

Hasanov described Azerbaijan-Georgia-Turkey cooperation as “an important platform for regional stability, security, and development”.
