At first, the explicit material mainly circulated on overseas websites and social media, so the impact was limited. But last October, things escalated. Someone shared a misleading video via (the instant-messaging platform) WeChat that combined one of my sales-promotion posters with footage of a woman with a completely different body shape to me undressing in a hotel room. There were also some demeaning AI-generated videos.

This time, the content spread incredibly fast among my circle. Friends, colleagues, and customers all started asking me what was going on. I felt like my world was collapsing. I again reported the videos to the police.

My phone number was also leaked, and I began receiving harassing calls, sometimes at one or two in the morning. A man in Qingdao called out of the blue to ask me to “come over and spend the night with him.” I recorded the conversation and sent it to the police, who issued the man a warning.

My WeChat was blowing up, too. I didn’t know whether a new friend request was from someone looking to buy a car or for something else. Some people would start by talking about cars and then steer the conversation toward asking me out. Others were more covert, asking me to record a video showing the “backseat legroom.” I knew what they really wanted. One person messaged, “I know it’s not you in those videos, but I fantasize that it is. Can you provide me with services?”

Social media is an important source of customers for me, so I couldn’t just ignore it. I still had to livestream. But when I was on camera introducing cars, I’d always see inappropriate comments pop up, like “I saw that video” or “You’re so hot.”

I even overheard some customers in the showroom talking about me. That hit me hard. I could no longer pretend that this online smear campaign wasn’t affecting me.

By now, the enthusiasm and confidence I used to have with customers was gone. I feared talking with people, paranoid that they must be gossiping about me.

At my lowest point, I briefly considered jumping from a building. I felt there was no point in being alive, that the world had become dark. It seemed everyone looked at me differently.

I told my supervisor that I had reached breaking point and needed time off. I was given three days, so I took my son back to my hometown, Yantai (about a three-hour drive from Qingdao), where we stayed at a beautiful guesthouse. I told myself that I had to keep living for my child and be responsible for my family. I had to clear my name.

When I returned to work, I was so anxious I couldn’t walk straight; my muscles were so tense I unconsciously leaned to one side. I wore a neck brace because even the slightest jolt during a test drive would send sharp pains up my back. I developed insomnia and tinnitus. At one point, I even struggled to speak.

Zero to hero

I started in auto sales in 2013, initially selling Audi and Lincoln cars in Beijing. I joined the Porsche dealership in downtown Qingdao in 2018. At first, my performance was so poor that I nearly lost my job.

Most of the salespeople had years of experience, and I was the youngest. Social media wasn’t the powerful tool it is today; business depended largely on walk-ins and referrals. For the first six months, I barely sold anything. At our 2019 New Year’s meeting, the sales manager asked everyone to share their goals for the year ahead. I said, “I want to survive at Porsche.”

I didn’t know the different models or specifications well enough. If a knowledgeable customer asked me a question, I felt intimidated and out of my depth. I started getting up at 6 a.m. to memorize technical information. I’d stand near colleagues and listen as they explained different cars. I studied the way they talked.

One colleague said I needed to dress better, so I started wearing tailored shirts and paying more attention to the cut and quality of everything I wore. In sales, it’s appearance, not skill, that makes the first impression. When I applied makeup, I felt more confident. Even though I had only four days off a month, I scheduled manicures and eyelash extensions, and sometimes skin booster injections.

I was a core consultant by my second year, became one of the dealership’s top performers in 2020, and was closing 17 deals a month in 2021.

Demand for foreign luxury cars has declined in the past two years, but my sales have continued to increase, largely because of social media. Of my 170 customers in 2023, 15% found me through social media. In 2025, it was 41%.

I also run a Porsche owners’ WeChat group with several hundred members. I organize monthly group events, such as camping trips, yacht outings, and nature walks. If I stop talking to someone as soon as a deal is done, they’ll always be just a customer. But if we spend time together, we can become friends. Referrals are an important part of my sales.

My typical workday runs from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. I’ve hardly taken any annual leave in all these years. If I go on vacation, customers disappear. I’m competitive by nature. I crave deals, performance figures, the feeling of being number one. I’m currently leading Porsche’s global sales rankings for September 2026, but someone could still overtake me.

The hardest word

When selling cars, effort usually pays off. But clearing a damaged reputation? That’s different.

Someone can casually share something about me online, and suddenly I have to spend money, time, and energy to respond. I have to pay lawyers and gather evidence. I filed 31 complaints to Douyin (China’s version of TikTok) alone between October 2025 and April this year about abusive messages, videos that used my image without permission, and people cloning my voice to promote get-rich-quick books.

I hand the most egregious messages directly to the police. One man I reported was initially very cocky. He seemed to think I was bluffing and wouldn’t be able to track him down. The authorities eventually found him, and he sent me an apology.

A 20-something Porsche owner in Qingdao forwarded some offensive material about me in a group chat and was given five days of administrative detention. I later accepted his apology, too, but then his family called my dealership’s customer service line to complain — they couldn’t understand why he still needed to be detained. I had no say in his punishment, but they obviously never stopped to think about how his actions might have affected me.

Even the outcomes of such cases haven’t halted the spread of false allegations; I still encounter vitriol during livestreams and on social media.

In July this year, the police gave me details of a 30-something man in the eastern Fujian province who’d been behind one of the AI-generated videos. I’d never met him. He was given 10 days of administrative detention in last October, but he never contacted me to apologize.

I think receiving punishment is not the same as saying sorry. This man was punished for spreading rumors, but what about the harm he caused? So I decided to file a civil lawsuit against him. All I want is for him to apologize and say explicitly that the woman in that video is not me.

Some friends urged me to press criminal charges, but I don’t want him to bear the consequences for the rest of his life. As a mother, I think about what would happen to his child if he were prosecuted. My lawyer says that if the civil case goes to trial, it could take up to two years. No matter how long it takes, I need to see it through.

Now I’m facing claims that the lawsuit is a publicity stunt, that I’m dredging things up again. In reality, just because the story is no longer in the headlines, it doesn’t mean those negative voices have disappeared from my life.

My son is in kindergarten. He doesn’t have a phone, and he knows nothing about what’s going on. All he knows is that his mom is the top salesperson at Porsche Qingdao. When I asked him what he wanted to do when he grew up, he said he wanted to sell cars. He’s proud of his mom.

What happens when he grows up, gets a phone, and sees what people have said about his mother? What if his classmates use the rumors against him? Who takes responsibility for that? The same goes for my parents. I want to clear my name for my family’s sake.

I still like being number one, but after everything that’s happened, my ambition has waned. I want to focus more on family and my health.

My life used to be a straight line between work and home, but over the past two years, I’ve started leaving more time for myself — meals with colleagues and friends, live music bars, taking my son to the mountains or the beach.

I wonder whether the rumors will disappear once the lawsuit is over. If people keep talking, there might be nothing more I can do. I’ve done everything within my power. If I win the case, that will be the end of it for me.

Women have sent me long messages of support, telling me how brave I am. Many professional women have shared that they have been the targets of similar smear campaigns and felt completely helpless. They ask me what they should do. I don’t know what to tell them.

As told to reporter Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Mu Qianwen at her workplace in Qingdao, Shandong province, August 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019076/Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.title: Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019076/Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.content:
A northern Chinese village has announced it will spend 30 million yuan ($4.5 million) to recruit 100 character performers — known in China as NPCs, or non-playable characters — to interact with tourists. Successful hires will receive a range of salaries, with the highest reportedly reaching 10 million yuan a year.

Situ Town, a scenic spot located in Situ Village in the northern Shanxi province, will finance the recruitment partly through its publicity budget and partly from startup funds, Zhou Xiaoming, the village Party secretary, told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper on Sunday.

Once a coal town, Situ Village’s coal was gradually depleted by the end of the 20th century. To address its lack of resources, in 2009, the village built an agricultural ecological park — an area that combines farming with ecological protection and tourism — on a slag heap, which later grew into a highly rated national attraction. The village is known for its “iron flower” performances — a folk art in which local blacksmiths hurl molten iron into the air.

Zhou announced the NPC recruitment on Sept. 19 in a video posted on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. “No matter what your talent is, as long as you can make the tourists on stage have fun, and the audience below enjoy themselves, we’ll give you a platform — and 1 million, even 10 million (yuan),” he said in the video.

The plan quickly drew suspicion online, with some arguing that the money would be better spent investing in the scenic area itself, such as by adding amusement parks, building affordable guesthouses, improving green spaces, upgrading the “iron flower” show, or supporting local artists.

Previously, the scenic spot had announced a short video contest — also led by Zhou — in August in which 5 million yuan was offered to participants based on likes and views. Winning the top prize of 1 million yuan required 10 million likes and 300 million views.

Official data showed that in 2025, Situ Town received 2.2 million tourist visits, double the year prior, generating a total revenue of 350 million yuan. Meanwhile, tourism-related jobs grew from 500 to more than 1,000, the latter accounting for roughly a third of the village’s labor force.

Zhou noted, however, that the scenic spot has faced steep losses in recent years. “In 2023 we lost 500,000 yuan, in 2024 we lost 500,000 yuan, and in 2025 we lost money, but not much,” he said.

More than 7,000 people have applied for the NPC positions so far, with video interviews planned for over 50, Zhou said, adding that they have not yet set an application deadline. Zhou added that NPC salaries will range from 500,000 to 10 million yuan depending on the traffic they generate, the emotional value they bring to tourists, and tourists’ degree of satisfaction.

Recruiting NPCs is reportedly the scenic spot’s first step, with the goal of eventually cultivating its own homegrown talent. Its employees, Zhou said, are actually the biggest NPCs, but they need a good environment and role models to imitate — and those recruited with the 30 million yuan are meant to set an example.

Zeng Bowei, a professor at the Tourism College of Beijing Union University, told The Paper that the most important value of NPCs is transforming culture into something tourists can see and participate in.

“Although NPCs have been called ‘non-playable characters,’ their true value to scenic areas is precisely making each tourist into a player,” Zeng said, adding that with the right roles, stories, and cultural backing, NPCs can increase traffic in the long term.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: [Two Pronged] A student needs financial help. What should I do?
World.content:
Our letter sender, a teacher, asks for help navigating an issue where her student is in need financially

Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.

Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.

Dear Dr. Holmes and Mr. Baer,

I do not know if anyone has ever been in a situation like mine before. I am pretty sure there have been similar cases, but I have not heard of any among my cohorts and fellow professors.

I am a math teacher to undergraduate students. I have been teaching for over 24 years. This year I had a female student (I, too, am female) who I was, at first, angry at. She was always late and, in fact, did not attend the first few days of class because she had not yet enrolled

I once scolded her in public (in a group chat) and subsequently felt so guilty I apologized, also in public, admitting I had no right to single her out that way.

Soon she opened up about how life was so hard at home, about how she needed to work to fund her studies and in fact lived with her aunt while in Metro Manila. Her real family was in Bicol.

Somehow by confiding in me she opened up something that I had never felt for a student before: a certain ”sympathique,” a desire to walk the talk and not just expound on mathematical theories.

Some weeks later, like a bolt out of the blue, she wrote and said she had a problem, was embarrassed to tell me about it. I, of course, encouraged her to do so.

Bottom line. She needs money. But I do not know what for and how much. This really shocked me. I have never been asked such a thing in my life. I have never known any of my colleagues being asked such a thing before either.

I feel I should help her. I do not want to be one of these teachers who tell their students they are on their side and then when they really need help, the teachers back out.

– Pia

Dear Pia,

Thank you for your email.

Cross-cultural issues involving money can be complex and as a foreigner one comes across new examples, such as this one, every now and again. When to give financial support to people who are not family seems to vary from culture to culture. Indeed, in the UK, apart from instances like collections for birthdays/retirements, workplace loans are I think very unusual.

However, there are other considerations at play here. Firstly there are issues around a teacher’s role; secondly there is a power imbalance.

The role of teacher is primarily to impart knowledge as well as provide guidance and support to their students. This is not an unlimited remit; it should relate to the subject/course that the students are studying. Some teachers interpret their role more broadly and offer support beyond the academic, in effect acting as mentors. This is fine provided they remain within the boundaries laid down institutionally as appropriate for relationships between student and teacher.

Support for students can come in various forms and a plea for money can be met even if there is no exchange of cash. Universities often have emergency funds, scholarships, study/work programs, and student affairs offices to help in these situations and helping a student navigate the options is certainly one way of “walking the walk.”

The power imbalance is a slightly different matter. Were you to acquiesce and lend, the student may later feel resentment at the obligation created, you might feel similarly if the money is not repaid, and you risk accusations of favoritism from other students.

All of this distracts from your main job: teaching.

If, despite the foregoing, you decide to go ahead, make sure the amount involved is something you can afford to write off as a simple gift and protect yourself by reporting it to your department head in the interests of transparency.

All the best,

– JAF Baer

Dear Pia:

Thank you very much for your letter. I feel Mr. Baer has answered all your direct and open questions about what happened, and more than adequately at that.

What I therefore hope to do is touch on some of what I feel are your unasked questions. Why were these questions not asked in the first place?

There are, of course, as many answers as there are people and also as there are interactions of specific students with their specific teachers.

Let us not try and guess your student’s (let’s call her Anna) motives in wanting to borrow money from you. Instead, let us focus on why the student felt it was ok to try and borrow money from you instead of any other teacher? At least any other teacher of the same cohort, experience, training, etc as you.

That is a worthwhile question in my mind, especially if this happens more than once. What signals are you sending so that a student feels it is ok to ask you more than what your remit clearly states? You are her professor, not her banker.

In my opinion, another worthwhile question to ask yourself is: have you changed in any way? Is this a function of aging alone? Or realizing there is more to teaching than following the letter of the law? Or becoming “wiser” and/or now feeling there is more to teaching than feeding facts (or even better, inspiring the students to get their own facts by learning HOW to think?). Have you opened your mind to the realization that to some, teaching is more than the letter of the description, but also its spirit?

I ask you these questions because of certain things you wrote, but specifically: “Somehow by confiding in me she opened up something that I had never felt for a student before: a certain ”sympathique”, a desire to walk the talk and not just expound on mathematical theories”.

Two Pronged does not have ready answers for you, but this column would definitely be willing to discuss this further with you if you want to.

All the very best,

– MG Holmes

– Rappler.com

Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

World.title: Olafur Eliasson’s ‘Your Curious Journey’ helped me bring the little things back in focus
World.content:
As someone who loves going to museums, some of my favorite experiences are those that make me think more deeply, those that put me to a halt and stand in appreciation. I love the moment when a simple visual translates into a story without using words, and shows us a world through the artist’s eyes.

It was that same expectation that I brought with me while visiting Olafur Eliasson’s “Your Curious Journey” exhibit at the Museum of Contemporary Art and Design (MCAD) Manila. Unknowingly, I became part of the art itself as I entered my own curious journey in discovering why Olafur’s works captivated many.

A warm welcome?

As I took my first steps into the exhibit, a strong yellow light washed over every corner of the space. It felt like a warm yet cold welcome from Olafur as the yellow slowly started fading everything I saw into grayscale, which made the space feel strangely cold and suspended in reality.

“Yellow Corridor” was one of the pieces that amazed me, not just because it primed me for all the changes I was about to experience. It was preparing me to step into another world – one that was unknown, uncanny, and strange.

It was the first time I saw the world in grayscale. While it was fun to see the colors gradually fade as you entered the corridor, it was also scary. Seeing colors disappear, this piece made me think about how, like yellow light, too much of a certain idea, perspective, or action can create a new kind of blindness.

Nature

As a nature lover, “Beauty” was one of my favorite pieces in this exhibit. The smell of the water, the sound of the falling mist, and the vibrant colors it projects all tie together into a small waterfall.

This piece made me stand in awe; I could have stood there for hours just watching the installation. It was so simple, yet so effective at evoking a sense of peace, as if nothing else in the world existed. It was a reminder of the beauty of nature encapsulated in a room.

As I moved around the mist, the light turned into a rainbow whose colors changed ever so slightly. Thus, someone standing a few steps away would see something totally different. And to me, it showed how perception can be deceiving and ever-changing for each person.

Personally, this reminds me of a childhood lesson my grade school teacher would say: Put yourself in someone else’s shoes.

A Reflection of You

There were lots of other parts of the exhibit, but let me tell you about one more that really caught my attention. “Your Uncertain Shadow” is an installation that turns your shadow into different colors and sizes.

It made me feel like a kid again, playing and seeing how my shadow would react. Feeling that childlike spark again as an adult was a fun experience. It felt like a look back to who we used to be, and that’s what this piece did for me.

Contrary to the title of the work, I see this piece as perfectly depicting who we are. We bring pieces of our childhood into adulthood, pieces from friends and family into our daily lives, and memories from the past that taught us lessons to the present. Seeing my shadow split into these colors reminded me of these parts of myself that I often overlook and even forgot. Recognizing these shades of my shadow comforts me, knowing that I still bring the different pieces of me, especially the ones I thought I had left behind.

Worth the visit

Olafur’s works made me remember all kinds of lessons that I have overlooked throughout my life. I left with the thought of paying more attention to the little, ordinary things that I usually ignore.

If you’re paying a visit, just remember that “Your Curious Journey” includes installations with flashing lights, colored lighting, darkened spaces, as well as a large wall incorporating moss which may emit a certain scent. MCAD offers free entrance to the exhibit which would only run until November 15.

And if this piece made you curious enough, visit https://www.mcadmanila.org.ph/visit/ for online bookings. – Rappler.com

This piece was written by Rappler intern Sebastian Vincent U. Ngo. Basti is a multimedia creative storyteller who focuses on the everyday details that make ordinary moments feel special. He seeks stories and uses design, words, and motion to help people see the familiar in a new light.

World.title: Ayuda to roads: Where the House wants to add billions in the 2027 budget
World.content:
Rappler tracks which lawmakers proposed a bigger budget for certain agencies and programs

The House of Representatives’ Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee (BARSC) on Thursday, October 1, recommended P116.32 billion in budget realignments, with social assistance programs and infrastructure projects among the biggest proposed beneficiaries.

The recommendations are not yet final. They still have to undergo deliberation and approval by the House plenary before they are included in the 2027 General Appropriations Bill.

Among the biggest proposed increases are allocations for government assistance programs, including the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) and the Medical Assistance for Indigent Patients (MAIFIP).

BARSC recommended an additional P25.81 billion for AICS and P24.97 billion for MAIFIP.

These programs have drawn scrutiny from watchdogs, including the People’s Budget Coalition, over concerns about their use in distributing government assistance through lawmakers and local officials, including through guarantee letters. The proposed increases also come ahead of the 2028 elections.

BARSC also recommended P10 billion for the Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk (PAFF), another social assistance program that was not included in the original 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

See the chart below to see how much funding was recommended by lawmakers:

Infrastructure gets billions more

BARSC also recommended additional funding for infrastructure projects under the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH):

P6.9 billion for national roads

P175.87 million for national bridges

P307.5 million for national buildings

P4.09 billion for convergence and special support programs

The total proposed increase for DPWH is P11.49 billion. Surigao del Sur 1st District Representative Romeo Momo was the proponent of the DPWH realignments.

The Department of Agriculture’s (DA) farm-to-market roads program may also receive an additional P4.96 billion.

BARSC likewise recommended an additional P1.55 billion for the DA’s Health Facilities Enhancement Program.

For education, an additional P952 million was proposed for the Department of Education’s Basic Education Facilities Fund, which covers the construction, repair, and improvement of public school infrastructure.

Confidential funds

BARSC also recommended additional funding for confidential funds for several agencies:

P10 million for the National Police Commission

P30 million for the Department of Justice

P50 million for the National Bureau of Investigation

P50 million for the Office of the Ombudsman

The proposed 2027 NEP contains P4.368 billion in confidential funds and P6.405 billion in intelligence funds

Biggest agency gainers

Among government agencies, the Department of Health received the largest proposed increase from the BARSC, at P28.36 billion.

It was followed by DSWD with P26.86 billion, DA P16.44 billion, and DPWH P11.49 billion.

BARSC also recommended an additional P5 billion funding for the House of Representatives.

See the breakdown of additional funding recommended for other agencies below.

Who proposed the biggest realignments?

Rappler also tracked which lawmakers proposed the budget realignments during the BARSC deliberations.

South Cotabato 2nd District Representative Ferdinand Hernandez proposed the largest total realignment, at P29.23 billion.

His recommendations included P24.97 billion for MAIFIP, P2.1 billion for the Tertiary Education Subsidy, and P1.77 billion for the Tulong Dunong Program.

He was followed by Guimaras Representative JC Nava, who proposed P28.86 billion in additional funding for DSWD. A large portion, P25.86 billion, was for AICS.

House Appropriations Committee chair Mikaela Suansing proposed P11.95 billion in realignments, including the P10 billion allocation for the Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk.

Meanwhile, Momo proposed P11.49 billion in additional funding for DPWH, including the allocations for roads, bridges, buildings, and convergence programs.

See the full breakdown below.

Lack of transparency

The BARSC’s hearing on Thursday was criticized by budget watchdogs over its lack of transparency.

The hearing, which was supposed to start at 1 pm, only started at 5:07 pm.

Unlike regular budget hearings, members of the media are not allowed to cover BARSC meetings in person.

People’s Budget Coalition co-convener and technical adviser AJ Montesa said the coalition had asked the House to allow media and civil society organizations to observe the proceedings in person. But, he said, their request was ignored.

During the hearing, Sunasing apologized to the public over the delay.

Civil society organizations also expressed dismay over the House leadership, saying they were sidelined in the budget process. – with research from Zara Pineda/Rappler.com

Zara Pineda is a Rappler volunteer and third-year AB Literature student majoring in Creative Writing and minoring in Commercial Regulations at De La Salle University. She also serves as editor of The LaSallian.

World.title: In southern Philippines, Tawi-Tawi builds feasts to be shared
World.content:
FEAST. A dulang is arranged with seafood, eggs, native dishes, and other local food during Tawi-Tawi’s Maligay and Dulang Festival in Bongao on September 27, 2026.

Food becomes art, memory, and hospitality in Bongao during the Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi celebrations

BONGAO, Philippines – Marilyn Jimlan was standing beside what looked less like a food display and more like an edible house.

Crabs, prawns, mantis shrimp, rice cakes, eggs, seafood, and native delicacies covered its tiers. Bills were tucked among the food. Darkened chickens sat high on the structure, while pastries hung from its sides. Around us, dozens of similarly elaborate creations filled the hall in Bongao on September 27.

Jimlan, 58, the municipal registrar of Bongao, had helped prepare one of the entries for the Maligay and Dulang displays, part of the Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi celebrations marking the province’s founding anniversary.

She has been cooking for most of her life.

“I started really cooking when I was about 14,” she said, speaking mostly in Filipino. Before that, she had already spent years watching and helping in the kitchen, learning the way many family recipes survive in the Philippines, through mothers, elders, repetition, and taste.

A house-shaped food display rises with seafood, native delicacies, and other local produce, turning Tawi-Tawi’s culinary traditions into edible art. All photos by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

Jimlan eventually taught her own children to cook. That detail explained much of what I was looking at. The festival was not simply about displaying what Tawi-Tawi could produce. It was also about knowledge passed from one generation to another, then placed proudly on a table for everyone to see.

At the center of the tradition are two things that can be confusing to someone seeing them for the first time.

The dulang is the feast platter, traditionally a large serving tray around which food is arranged and shared during gatherings, celebrations, religious occasions, weddings, and the welcoming of guests.

The maligay is the house-like structure built to hold and display food. Decorated with local delicacies and whatever imagination its makers can bring to it, the maligay turns the feast into architecture.

Bongao municipal registrar Marilyn Jimlan explains the dishes and ingredients in a festival spread, many of them recipes and food traditions passed down through families.

During the festival, the distinction becomes obvious. One is the spread. The other rises from it.

Some maligay were almost architectural in scale, built with bamboo, trays, baskets, food, and ornamentation. There were crabs with brilliant orange shells, rock lobsters, mantis shrimp, clams, sea urchins, fish, fruits, root crops, eggs, and sweets.

Panyalam, a deep-fried rice cake, and other rice-based delicacies appeared again and again. Some displays carried cash bills, another expression of prosperity and generosity.

Several were crowned with blackened chickens. The dark color comes from the preparation associated with piyanggang, a Tausug chicken dish flavored with coconut that has been charred before being ground with spices.

Jimlan moved easily through the display, naming food and explaining preparations. She spoke about rice, native chicken, seafood, sweets, and coconut. Cooking, to her, did not sound like a special skill she had decided to acquire. It sounded like part of growing up.

That may be why the displays felt different from the food competitions I had seen elsewhere. Yes, there was artistry, and yes, there was judging. But the food was never meant to remain untouched after the photographs were taken. It would be eaten.

Prawns, crabs, shellfish, eggs, and other ingredients crowd one of the elaborate displays at the Maligay and Dulang Festival in Bongao.

Once the judging was finished, people gathered around the displays. Food that had taken hours to cook and arrange was opened, passed around, and shared. The exhibition disappeared the way a feast is supposed to disappear, one helping at a time.

Jimlan made sure I did not leave empty-handed either. She gave me crab, bread, and okó-okó, the Sama-Bajau delicacy of rice cooked inside a sea urchin shell.

There was no ceremony to it. She simply packed food for me. Very Filipino. Very Mindanao. You visit, therefore you must eat. And chances are, you are not leaving empty-handed.

That gesture captured what the enormous maligay and dulang could easily obscure with their spectacle. Behind every arrangement were people who cleaned the seafood, cooked the rice, fried the pastries, prepared the chicken, tied the decorations, and decided where each piece should go.

Piyanggang chicken and Philippine peso bills crown a maligay display, where food, artistry, and symbols of abundance come together during Tawi-Tawi’s provincial anniversary festivities.

The province’s geography explains much of what appears on the table. Tawi-Tawi is an archipelago, and life here is intimately tied to the sea. Seafood was not an accent in these displays. It was everywhere.

But food tells more than geography. It carries family history, trade, religion, and the relationships among the Sama, Sama Dilaut, Tausug, Jama Mapun, and other communities that have shaped Tawi-Tawi.

By then, I had spent days seeing the province through its festivals, dances, music, islands, and people. The Maligay and Dulang displays were the last major event I attended before leaving. Perhaps, that was why it stayed with me.

There are easier ways to explain culture. You can read its history, photograph its landmarks, watch its dances, and listen to its music. But sit beside its food, ask someone who cooked it where she learned, and watch that food passed from hand to hand, and something else becomes clear.

Culture is also what people decide is worth preparing again.

Marilyn Jimlan began cooking seriously at about 14. Decades later, she still cooks, and her children know how because she made sure the knowledge continued.

Around her stood houses made of food and great platters waiting to be shared. By the end, much of the feast was gone. Which, I realized, was exactly the point. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pete Lacaba for National Artist. My mother would have approved.
World.content:
Jose “Pete” Lacaba will be honored by fellow writers and artists in a tribute on October 10

One of my fond memories of my friend Jose “Pete” Lacaba, who will be honored by fellow writers and artists in an October 10 tribute, featured my late mother, Isabel Impelido Pimentel.

One morning in the ’80s, Pete stopped by our house in Cubao for a work meeting. Mommy invited him for lunch even though she didn’t have time to prepare. Lunch that day meant rice and boiled fish with saluyot (jute mallow) leaves, the type of food Mommy grew up with in Sinait, Ilocos Sur.

Pete sat down to eat with us and he appeared to enjoy the meal. After he left, Mommy told me: “He’s a good man. He ate our food.”

WEDDING. Pete Lacaba (standing, 2nd from right) and Marra Lanot (standing, 3rd from right) at the 50th wedding anniversary of the author’s parents (seated) Isabel and Benjamin Pimentel.

She shouldn’t be surprised, I explained. Pete may be a famous writer, but he is a down-to-earth guy who would enjoy a simple Ilocano meal.

Mommy eventually became a fan of Pete’s poetry. She even read them aloud to me one time — which worried me a little bit.

She thought “Paksiw na Ayungin” (Ayungin fish cooked in vinegar) was wonderful. But as she began reading the first two verses of “Pasyong Mahal ni San Jose” (The Holy Passion of Saint Joseph)…

“Pait, katam at martilyo, (Chisel, plane and hammer)

“Ibubulong ko sa iyo (I will whisper to you)

“Ang masaklap kong sikreto…” (My terrible secret)

…I knew I had to distract her and stop her from reading further ..

“Ah, Mommy, have you heard anything from Auntie Cadie?”

It worked. And I felt relieved. A devout Catholic, and a lay Carmelite, she probably would not have appreciated the rest of Pete’s poem, a meditation on exploitation (divine or otherwise) through the eyes of Saint Joseph.

“Hindi ko pa inaano (I haven’t even touched her)

“Buntis na ang nobya ko.” (And my girlfriend’s already pregnant)

When my parents celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary in 2003, Mommy insisted that we invite Pete. He and Marra Lanot, who passed away recently, celebrated with us that evening.

Literature and film

I was a UP student when I first met Pete in 1982 at the Galian ng Arte at Tula studio in Cubao at the launch of Days of Disquiet, Nights of Rage, his classic account of the First Quarter Storm.

Many of us were so impressed with the book that my friends Bertrand Quesada, then editor of Sinag, the paper of the UP College of Arts and Sciences, and managing editor Gani De Castro (and now a Rappler editor), decided to publish a full-page comic strip version of Days of Disquiet, Nights of Rage.

The next time I saw Pete was in the streets.

We were marching toward Liwasang Bonifacio during one of the countless protests after the assassination of Ninoy Aquino. It started to rain. When some protesters took out umbrellas, the more unruly rallyists started taunting them. “No umbrellas. We march in the rain!”

Pete didn’t appreciate that.

“Hindi problema ang payong (Umbrellas are not the problem),” he told the anti-umbrella marchers.

By then, Pete was a major collaborator with one of our best film directors, Lino Brocka. He wrote some of the best and most memorable Brocka films. Kapit sa Patalim (Clinging to a Knife) and Sister Stella L helped define what was then a vibrant protest culture. We were inspired by them, and even moved to action.

I remember how we marched toward Malacañang and passed a giant movie poster of Sister Stella L showing Vilma Santos with a raised fist. Fellow marchers yelled out the line from the movie: “Katarungan para kay Ka Dencio! (Justice for Ka Dencio!)”

I finally got to work with Pete after the EDSA revolution when I joined Midweek. I had just graduated from UP Diliman and actually had a choice. Work for a mainstream newspaper or TV station. Or join a small magazine few people had heard of, but led by two of the best writers in the country: Pete Lacaba and the late Greg Brillantes.

Choosing the latter was one of the smartest decisions I ever made. Until now, I remember what I learned from Pete and Greg whenever I’m writing.

MIDWEEK. Pete Lacaba (3rd from right) and Greg Brillantes (partly hidden, seated next to him) with Neng Torres Yabut, Vivian de Lima, Melanie Manlogon (2nd from left) and the author.

Working with Pete and Greg wasn’t just about work of course. I will always treasure memories of our inuman (drinking sessions), especially at Davao Inihaw on Tomas Morato Avenue and later, at Pete’s house on Mother Ignacia Avenue in Quezon City.

Greg passed away last year before he was finally named National Artist for Literature, an honor that he should have received decades ago.

It’s Pete’s turn. Many of us believe that. Including the many artists and journalists who will be gathering at My Brother’s Mustache Bar in Quezon City for “Salinawit ni Pete: A Tribute” on Saturday, October 10.

Other important writers should be named with Pete, including great writers who have also passed on, Lualhati Bautista and Rogelio Sikat.

I hope it happens the way it happened for Greg.

ARTISTS. The author with Pete Lacaba and Marra Lanot in 2013.

Jose F. Lacaba, my friend and mentor, poet, journalist, screen writer, translator and editor more than deserves to be our next National Artist for Literature or our next National Artist for Film.

Mommy would have agreed. – Rappler.com

Benjamin Pimentel is the author of ‘U.G. An Underground Tale’ published by Anvil Publishing which just released the 2nd printing of the 3rd edition. He is also a journalist and technology editor based in the San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA. Royalties from ‘U.G.’ are donated to Bantayog ng Mga Bayani.
