World.title: Regional audiences to lose Network 10, as licensee warns of TV's future
World.content:
Viewers in parts of regional South Australia, and parts of the Riverina in New South Wales, will lose access to Network 10's terrestrial channels, after the network and license holder, WIN Network, failed to reach an agreement.

WIN has announced it will stop broadcasting 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, with the final broadcasts to be on Friday, October 9.

The network had flagged its agreement with Network 10 would expire in July, and that the channels would be pulled.

However, local audiences were given a three-month reprieve, with Network 10 saying it would provide its feed "free of charge" to WIN while the parties worked on a deal that has not eventuated.

WIN Network says the decision reflects the economics of regional broadcasting. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

High costs of regional TV

In a statement, a WIN Network spokesperson said providing Network 10 services to the impacted markets was "no longer viable".

"This is a business decision that reflects the realities of regional broadcasting," they said.

"Regional markets carry high transmission and infrastructure costs, while digital disruption continues to erode audiences and advertising revenue.

"These economics will continue to make it challenging to maintain services across regional Australia.

"WIN recognises this will be disappointing for viewers and thanks them for their understanding."

The move follows a similar loss of Seven Network channels to the same markets, after Seven and WIN failed to reach an agreement before Seven's deal expired last year.

The channels were eventually restored after a multi-day shutdown that saw the channels replaced with red screens advising they were "no longer available".

Audiences in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith temporarily lost Seven Network channels last year. (ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert)

Country audiences missing out

A Network 10 spokesperson said audiences could continue to access the network's channels online and via its app.

"WIN holds the broadcast licences in the Riverland, Mount Gambier and Griffith regions and although Network 10 has worked closely with WIN to explore options to maintain local access to its content, WIN has advised that continuing to operate them is no longer commercially viable," they said.

" Network 10 remains committed to serving regional Australian audiences. "

The WIN Network holds the broadcast licenses in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith. (ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert)

It is not the first time a regional market has lost Network 10 channels due to the financial challenges of regional broadcasting.

In 2024, audiences in Mildura, Victoria, lost their Network 10 channels when Mildura Digital Television (MDT), which carried 10's signal to the market, was closed by co-owners Seven and WIN.

The networks said "it did not make commercial sense" to keep MDT going, as it had been unprofitable throughout its existence.

Federal Communications Minister Anika Wells has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Man who allegedly crashed into Newcastle Knights fans refused bail
World.content:
The Sydney teenager who was allegedly behind the wheel of a car that crashed into and injured 10 Newcastle Knights fans has been refused bail.

Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, has been charged with three counts of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, three counts of negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and three counts of cause bodily harm by misconduct.

He appeared in the Newcastle Bail Court today and did not apply for release, before bail was formally refused.

The court heard the most serious offence of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm carries a maximal jail term of seven years.

Thousands of people were lining the streets of Newcastle to farewell their grand final bound Knights on Saturday morning, before a car struck the crowd at a roundabout on Newcastle Link Road, Wallsend.

Mr Samarasinghe was arrested at the scene and shielded by police as members of the crowd allegedly turned on him and his passengers.

Police allege Mr Samarasinghe had been driving erratically in the lead-up to the crash.

Witnesses could be heard screaming in videos taken at the scene.

Ten people were injured after a car crashed near the procession of Knights fans at Wallsend on Saturday morning. (ABC News)

Four released from hospital

A five-year-old girl and 67-year-old man, who were critically injured in the crash, are now listed as being in serious but stable conditions in John Hunter Hospital.

Two other young girls, aged five and two, a 31-year-old woman and 48-year-old man remain stable in hospital.

Four others have been discharged.

Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe has appeared in court. (Source: Facebook)

Judge concerned about mental health

With his head bowed and wearing a red, white and yellow T-shirt, Mr Samarasinghe was told his case would be adjourned until later this month.

Mr Samarasinghe was handcuffed for his brief court appearance, and wore jeans, a T-shirt and joggers.

He looked around the cubicle where he sat as his matter was heard via audio visual link.

The 18-year-old's lawyer was on the audio visual link appearing from Sydney.

At the end of proceedings, the judge said the man's health needed attention.

"I endorse a warrant to say that medical attention is required for the young man with serious offences pending," the judge said.



The judge said a medical team could review his general health and "no doubt that might involve a mental health assessment".

The case returns to court on October 15.

World.title: Treasurer downplays chance of cost-of-living relief amid surging debt
World.content:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has vowed there will be more savings in the mid-year budget update but downplayed the prospect of more cost-of-living relief for Australians.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had indicated this week help was on the way for households, but Mr Chalmers said the government was looking to run a "tight ship" because of sustained pressure on the budget.

He told Insiders a savings package would feature in the budget update, which is due in mid-December.

"One of the primary influencers on the mid-year update will be the need to find more savings," he said.

"There is very, very substantial and intensifying pressure, not just on our budget but on budgets around the world."

The treasurer said the package would be influenced by the inflation challenge and the "helpful and responsible role" the government "intend to play" to see that figure come down over time.

"So we can get real wages growing again and so some of this pressure can come off people," he said.

Labor defends spending amid high inflation Another interest rate rise has turned attention to domestic pressures contributing to inflation.

On Wednesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to a 15-year high.

Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said she would not "play the blame game", but warned inflation "isn't all about the Middle East conflict".

On Sunday, Mr Chalmers said "no serious observer" would disagree the war in the Middle East was putting "very substantial" pressure on the Australian economy.

He said additional government spending had been concentrated in areas such as bulk billing, to ease pressure on family budgets.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has called for Mr Chalmers to resign. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The Coalition had argued the government was spending too much and had contributed to inflation.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson labelled Mr Chalmers a "disastrous treasurer" and called for him to step down.

"He's actively stoked inflation, and he's fundamentally undermined the success of this country," Mr Wilson said.

Mr Chalmers said the government was not actively considering another discount of the fuel excise discount.

Bond spike to add billions to budget bill

The treasurer also warned the cost of servicing government debt would rise by billions of dollars as borrowing costs around the world increased.

US government bonds were heavily sold off last month, in a sign investors were demanding higher returns to lend money.

Bond market screaming economic trouble ahead Bond yields are the highest they've been in 20 years as inflation fears rip through global financial markets.

Bonds are essentially IOUs issued by governments to borrow money and are bought and sold by large investment funds as well as individual investors.

The bond market is generally seen as safer than the share market, but big swings in bond prices can be an early warning sign of financial stress.

Mr Chalmers said the government's trillion-dollar debt burden would balloon as cheaper debt is paid off, and the government is forced to turn to new, more expensive borrowing options.

"This spike in borrowing costs in the major economies will also play out here," he said.

"The pressure will still come to Australia, unfortunately, and you'll see in the billions of dollars the magnitude of pressure, coming from those bond yields which are changing so quickly."

World.title: AFP confirms investigation of flydubai co-pilot's Australian links
World.content:
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) says a counterterrorism team is investigating Australian links to a flydubai pilot who allegedly attacked a colleague in the cockpit.

The pilot, Smit Machcharr, was stabbed by his co-pilot in an alleged attempt to crash the flydubai plane on Wednesday.

The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, according to three people with knowledge of the situation, including diplomats, who spoke to AP on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.

The jet plunged nearly 14,000 feet (4,267 metres) in less than 30 seconds in the incident.

The flight bound for Tel Aviv was carrying 174 people and was forced to divert to Tabuk in north-western Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing.

Investigation by joint counterterrorism team

The investigation is being conducted by the Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team, comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, an AFP spokesperson said.

An AFP spokesperson said an update would be provided "at an appropriate time".

Israel to 'ramp up' security after pilot attack A commercial flight carrying 174 people to Tel Aviv is forced to divert to Saudi Arabia after one pilot stabs the other and tries to crash the plane.

Sources close to the incident have confirmed the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014 and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, whereafter he left the country.

His visa was cancelled in 2019.

The ABC understands his visa was not cancelled on character grounds, but due to his lack of enrolment in a course, rendering him ineligible for a student visa.

The ABC understands the Joint Counter Terrorism Team investigation will examine whether the man was radicalised while in Australia.

Questions raised about flydubai's processes

The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain with an axe and trying to seize the controls was an Omani national who had been barred from flying on his country's airline because of concerns about extremist views, officials said.

The United Arab Emirates, which is leading a separate investigation, said the co-pilot attacked with the cockpit's crash axe and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a "terrorist attack".

'Hero' pilot speaks from hospital Captain Smit Machchhar has been hailed a hero for his actions aboard a flydubai flight after his co-pilot stabbed him and the plane began a steep descent.

His actions nearly crashed the flight before passengers and others rushed in and subdued him.

The new details raised questions about how thoroughly flydubai vets potential employees, and how the co-pilot's presence on a flight filled with Israeli passengers got past Israel's strict security protocols.

Israel has said it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots of nations without diplomatic ties from flying there.

Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.

The UAE government has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.

Trained in Morocco but not employed

In a statement to AP, Royal Air Maroc, Morocco's national carrier, said the co-pilot "completed a three-month theoretical training period with the airline in 2025, as part of the pre-employment process. At the end of this training period, his application was not selected for employment".

Buckinghamshire New University spokesperson Keith Coles told AP that Mr al-Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management there but "did not undertake any pilot training".

Inside the flydubai flight Passengers have described the terrifying plummet that saw the jet descend nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds and the cockpit scrum that helped the flydubai flight land safely.

There were no details on the timing.

Visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University Philip Baum said background check systems differ from country to country and there were limits on what types of information can be shared.

"In terms of aviation security itself, obviously we want to have as robust background checks as possible," he said.

"But there are huge limitations on doing background checks in any case, especially in cross-border checks."

ABC/AP

World.title: 'Unnecessary and cruel': People with MS to lose home care
World.content:
Marlene Robinson has been living with the degenerative neurological condition multiple sclerosis for 30 years, with no movement in her legs and limited use of her arms.

The 80-year-old former City of Bayswater councillor and staffer to former Western Australia Premier Geoff Gallop is wheelchair bound and depends on support workers from MSWA for essential personal care, helping her out of bed to shower and dress.

"I can't do that myself, the arms aren't working too well," Ms Robinson said.

Her husband, former anthropologist Michael Robinson, 86, said they could not do without the care.

"It means that just the basic daily needs can be met," he said.

"Whereas if we were just doing it on our own, we probably couldn't do it."

Marlene Robinson and her husband Michael said they depend on support workers for her personal care. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

But the couple recently received a letter from MSWA informing them and 75 other clients that the non-profit organisation would stop providing the Commonwealth-funded Support at Home services.

The program is meant to help older people stay at home instead of moving into residential aged care.

Fears for future

MSWA explained it could not continue because changes to aged care by the Albanese government last year had excessively increased costs and the administrative burden.

The couple received a letter from MSWA saying they are not continuing the Support at Home program. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

It has left Ms Robinson profoundly concerned for her future as she and the other clients, including 16 in the regions, scramble to find a new but inevitably more expensive provider.

She knows other providers' rates are about double MSWA's and she will be able to afford much less care for her basic needs.

"I don't know what I'll do without it," she said.

" When I think about it, I sort of stop. I can't think about the horrific future. "

MSWA was adamant it was not abandoning its clients and would continue providing specialist neurological services.

Chief executive Melanie Kiely said the federal government last year replaced the Home Care Packages program with Support at Home.

Melanie Kiely said it had become unsustainable for MSWA to continue to provide the program. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

"The Support at Home brings in a lot more administration, a lot more regulation into the way we have to do things," she said.

'We understand the pain of this and that is something we want to work with (clients) to transition. Having said that we've kept our prices down so low for so long and we just cannot do it sustainably any longer."

Doubling of rates

MSWA charges $60 an hour for personal care on weekdays, half the market average of $125 an hour.

That means clients face a doubling of the hourly rate.

Marlene Robinson faces the prospect of going into residential care. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

Ms Robinson estimated she would have to pay $1,000 extra from her own pocket to get the same amount of care as before.

"It's a huge amount for us. I mean, we could do it for a month, but you know, we have to survive," Ms Robinson said.

"It just seems so unnecessary and cruel," her husband added.

The couple is now considering whether Ms Robinson can stay at home or will need to go into residential care.

An industry-wide problem

MSWA is proposing to help clients switch to a partner provider.

But this is an industry-wide problem.

MS is on the rise in Australia. Why? The number of people in Australia living with multiple sclerosis has grown by 30 per cent in recent years.

Catherine Stoddart, chair of Advanced Ageing WA and chief executive of Brightwater care, warned higher costs and extra compliance requirements would drive smaller providers under.

"For every hour of care, 31 minutes are spent on administrative work, so therefore people don't get the amount of care that they're entitled to," she said.

"If you're a small provider or have got a small number of clients, that's just too much of a burden to keep going."

Catherine Stoddart said smaller providers may not survive. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

Aged Care Minister Sam Rae's spokesperson said the government's aged care reforms were delivering "stronger provider accountability and enhanced system oversight to support safe, high-quality care".

"We are closely monitoring the rollout of Support at Home to ensure older Australians can access the care they need, when and where they need it, at prices that are reasonable and transparent," the spokesperson said in a statement.

World.title: Police say ball bearings used to smash windows at government buildings
World.content:
ACT Policing is calling for witnesses to come forward after ball bearings were used to damage windows at two government buildings on Thursday night.

Police said on Friday morning that detectives were investigating after windows were damaged at a building near the Housing ACT Central Access Point at Emu Bank in Belconnen.

Staff inside the building were temporarily locked down and then sent home for the day, while the Housing ACT office was closed on Friday.

On Sunday, police issued a media release asking for information relating to the damage.

Police said ball bearings were used to damage windows at the Housing ACT building in Belconnen. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

ACT Policing said between 7pm and 9:30pm on Thursday, October 1, "two incidents of criminal damage occurred at buildings on Emu Bank and Benjamin Way".

"At both locations, ball bearings are believed to have been used to impact shopfront windows," it said.

"No one was harmed by these incidents."

Anyone who saw any people or vehicles in the vicinity is being asked to come forward.

Anyone who can assist police should provide their contact details to Crime Stoppers via the Crime Stoppers ACT website, quoting 8516326.

World.title: A doctor said Tim was incapable of love. His mum knew otherwise
World.content:
When Judy Sharp was told by doctors that her three-year-old son Tim would be "unfeeling and incapable of love", she refused to accept those limitations.

In the years after his autism diagnosis, Tim began using drawings to communicate with his mum, sharing his feelings, sense of humour and love for her.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

These are Judy and Tim's words.

'What's wrong with your son?'

Judy: When Tim was born in 1988, it was the best day of my life, my heart was ready to burst.

It was the same day the queen was opening the new Parliament House in Canberra, so I thought this is a very special day.

Judy says there were early signs of autism when Tim was just a baby. (Supplied: Judy Sharp)

It wasn't easy after he was born, the first thing I noticed was he didn't sleep.

He was distressed all the time, constant crying and unsettled. As he got older, he had to keep moving, he couldn't stay in the same room as people, and he only ate a few foods.

These were unusual things to me that I didn't understand.

Tim almost looked like he was in pain, you could see the fear in his eyes.

The most common thing that was said to me at the time was, "What's wrong with your son?"

The doctors kept saying, "wait till he's three, to see a specialist".

So, the appointment was made for the day after his third birthday and that was the worst day ever.

Don't tell me that boy doesn't love me

Judy: They sent us to a doctor who was supposed to be the best specialist.

He diagnosed Tim with autism and just wrote him off.

He told me all the things that Tim would never do, that he would be unfeeling and incapable of love.

I had a physical reaction, not only mental and emotional, but it was like someone was sucking the life out of me.

The worst thing anyone can do is take away all your hope and that's what he did.

Judy with Tim and her youngest son Sam (middle). (Supplied: Judy Sharp)

So, by the time I got out of that doctor's office and to the car, I was hysterical.

I'm putting Tim into his little car seat and he's patting me on the back and wiping away my tears.

And I wanted to march back in there and say, "You tell me that boy doesn't love me."

This was perfect love and I knew that little boy loved me.

And I was going to keep on loving him no matter what anyway.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

The birth of Laser Beak Man

Judy: One of the things the specialist said to me was that Tim would not speak.

But when he was five, he started to draw.

So, by accident, we started to draw to communicate between the two of us.

And it turned out that Tim had this natural ability for drawing, we thought, "he's got talent".

So, every day, the house was covered in pens, papers, I never put them away.

Tim's Laser Beak Man character has taken him and his mum across the world. (Supplied: Brisbane festival)

Then he did start speaking. And when he was 11, he started walking around the house saying, "When I grew up, I'm going to be Laser Beak Man" — a superhero he had created.

Tim injected his own personality and his own sense of humour into Laser Beak Man.

He's not a classic superhero; he's one defined by Tim in a different way and he's got a very unique way of looking at life.

And Laser Beak Man has taken us on a journey that no-one ever could have imagined; from New York, London, the Sydney Opera House, TV, theatre, movies, you name it.

We've travelled the world with Laser Beak Man and met so many people and Tim's had so many opportunities and things that we never thought would have been possible in any way, shape or form.

Tim: [Drawing] makes me happy and I relax doing it. I can have fun with it. I can use my big imagination.

[Mum and I] made the Laser Beak Man theatre show come true and went to New York with it. He's a superhero and he's really awesome.

One of Tim's drawings of Laser Beak Man represents love. (Supplied: Tim Sharp)

Love is everything, I feel it in everything

Tim: I love that Mum is a good friend and a good mother to me.

She takes care of me.

She is a kind mum.

She sits with me and we don't even talk sometimes, we like being together.

She likes me just the way I am. She makes me feel peaceful and special.

I tell her I love her all the time. I like to help her and make her happy, I like to buy her some flowers and Maltesers.

Love is everything. I feel it in everything. You can see it and hear it. It makes life better and happy.

Tim says love makes "life better and happy". (Supplied: Judy Sharp)

Judy: Tim and I spend most of our time together and I find that a very, very easy thing to do, to be with him.

He's patient and he's kind.

I love that he thinks another way because it makes me think other ways.

I love his natural ability to want to connect with people.

And it's really inspiring to watch him do that in his own way without trying to be like anyone else.

And he will frequently tell me that he loves me.

At the end of the day, he'll say to me, "I've had a really good day with you, Mum. We're a great team."

You don't even get that in a marriage.

The best thing you can do in life is just follow Tim's example; be brave, be yourself and show the world who you really are.

World.title: On duty just after 6pm, these paramedics' shift is about to go bad
World.content:
Abbey Studley sits in the passenger seat of a kitted-out SUV as her colleague, Dave O'Toole, runs through potential scenarios with the intel they have on their comms screen.

It's a little after 6pm on a Tuesday night and the Alice Springs intensive care paramedics have just begun their shift.

They've received a simple call to assist a person experiencing a medical issue, but a recent spate of violence against frontline workers in the Central Australian town means the St John Ambulance crews never know what they will face when they're called out.

Abbey Studley calls the police after a violent incident in which her colleagues were punched and spat on. (ABC News: Emma Haskin)

Earlier this week, they invited the ABC to ride along with paramedics — and although everything is calm when they pick up their first patient, things change en route to the hospital.

By the time they arrive at the ambulance bay at Alice Springs Hospital, the patient has become aggressive and attacks the paramedics, punching and spitting at them as they try to provide care.

It's the 100th attack on Alice Springs ambulance staff for 2026, according to St John data, with the majority being physical assaults.

With just three 24-hour crews and one intensive care unit staffed by 45 paramedics, there aren't many local St John staff members who haven't experienced violence.

Abbey calls the police and the patient is arrested and taken to the watch house.

"It makes me particularly disappointed and I'm angry that another one of my staff have been victims of violence," Abbey says.

Paramedics in Alice Springs have been subject to 100 assaults so far this year. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

" There's never an excuse for violence … and what we've seen tonight is another example of our staff being victims of violence for no reason. "

NT paramedics assaulted, lacking resources The ABC rode along with St John Ambulance NT paramedics to hear the impact under-resourcing is having on the workforce, including stories of staff being assaulted on the job.

The flow-on effects from occupational violence will mean people will be waiting longer for an ambulance.

"We've now got three staff delivering statements to police currently, and as you can see behind me all three of our Alice Springs resources are currently at hospital handing over patients or providing statements to police," Abbey says.

Abbey is no stranger to violence on the job. Two years ago, she was brutally attacked in the line of duty.

'I thought I was going to die'

The attack occurred shortly before midnight in October 2024, just as Abbey finished her shift, when a man pulled her from her fast-response vehicle.

"I thought I was going to die," she says.

Abbey says she had time to activate a duress alarm before the perpetrator dragged her down the street by her arm.

Abbey Studley suffered a traumatic brain injury and blindness in one eye following an attack while she was at work. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Much of that night is a blur due to the level of violence she experienced.

"I've psychologically blocked a lot of that out and it's hard now for me to recall exactly what transpired," Abbey says.

"I think in the police report, I said I got over 20 punches to the head.

"I have blindness in my right eye and I have limited feeling in my left arm."

She also sustained permanent injuries, including a traumatic brain injury.

As a result, she spent two months in an acquired brain injury unit in Melbourne, and many more months seeking treatment to recover.

Abbey Studley and her colleagues never know what will happen on the job. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"I was told by a number of specialists and doctors that I would never return to this career and that made me really devastated and really sad," she says.

But 16 months later, Abbey returned to the community and the job she loves.

"I feel so lucky and privileged to come to work every day and proud to wear this St John uniform and provide life-saving critical care and really high-level compassionate care to the community," she says.

No one has ever been charged with Abbey's assault.

"I think what's tough is knowing that there's still somebody that could be in the community or in the wider community who could perpetrate that level of violence again," she says.

Abbey Studley with colleagues Benson Chan and Gareth Aescht in the midst of a busy night on the job. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Following the assault on her colleagues on Tuesday, Abbey says her team will take their time to regroup and debrief.

"They'll be given time to stand down and recoup, maybe have a cup of tea or a coffee and a break and a little check-in with each other," she says.

"It's up to them whether or not they would like to keep working and that's obviously very individual.

"Look, they're upset. This is a significant number of assaults now in this region since the start of this year."

Searching for solutions

Body-worn cameras and OC spray have been floated as measures to curb violence against paramedics across the Northern Territory.

Last month, Alice Springs Member for Braitling Joshua Burgoyne revealed the NT government had been discussing the two measures with St John management.

According to St John Ambulance data, police have been called to assist their workers on 43 occasions so far this year. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

St John NT chief executive Abigail Trewin says although body-worn cameras pose some privacy challenges, the service is talking to staff about "who and where and how we would roll something like this out".

She says they will also consult with staff about OC spray, although it came with potential problems.

"We work in effectively a tin box — you're transporting a patient," she says.

"It's not a lot of space, so discharging OC spray in that environment is probably not very sensible."

NT Health Minister Steve Edgington says while no paramedics have approached him requesting OC spray for protection in their workplace, the government will consider it.

"If that's something that St John believes will assist them in delivering their services and protecting and providing evidence of any assaults or threatening behaviour against them again, we will work with St John to look at what their needs are," he says.

"They need to be protected. They need to be supported.

"When they go to work they're there to help people. They shouldn't be threatened."

A community partnership

Last month, St John NT joined forces with Tangentyere Council, which manages Aboriginal town camps in Alice Springs.

Ms Trewin says the partnership aims to create "safer, more positive interactions" between paramedics and Aboriginal patients in the town.

"Providing the best emergency healthcare is more than clinical skills," she says.

"It is also about trust, communication and understanding the communities we serve."

She hopes the partnership will eventually lead to Indigenous liaison officers working with the ambulance service, although that will rely on funding.

Alice Springs paramedics hope a new partnership with Tangentyere Council will help strengthen relationships in the community. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Tangentyere Council chief executive Walter Shaw says he hopes the memorandum of understanding will result in a safer work environment for Alice Springs paramedics.

"We need to ensure that we put out a social safety net for our St John's Ambulance Service and also the residents of town camps in Alice Springs," he says.

NT paramedics could carry pepper spray for safety, minister says The NT government has floated the idea of paramedics carrying pepper spray as they continue to face high rates of assault on the job.

"I'd like to see young Aboriginal paramedics working within St John's itself."

For Abbey, the partnership is some of the best preventative work she's ever seen.

"It's about two-way learning, it's about sharing knowledge and it's about becoming part of the community," she says.

Despite all that she's experienced on the job, she remains steadfast in her love of her work.

"It's a real privilege to wear this uniform and it's a real privilege to serve this community," she says.

"We're really grateful for community members for protecting us and keeping us safe whenever they can."

Karen Cooper and Brad Fairbairn at Accor Stadium. Oscar Colman

World.title: On the market: Your team by team guide to AFL trade period
World.content:
The AFL trade period officially opens on Monday when the list managers from all the clubs gather at Marvel Stadium to get serious about the deals that will shape their teams for 2027. In truth, negotiations have been bubbling along for months for some players. The big questions are: Will Zach Merrett make it to Hawthorn at his second attempt? Will Gold Coast match Hawthorn’s free agency offer for Ben King and thereby force a trade? Where will Melbourne heart and soul player Jack Viney land? We examine every club and which players are on the market. Jesse Hogan, Rowan Marshall, Zach Merrett and Jack Viney are likely to feature in the trade period. Marija Ercegovac/Getty Images Follow our live blog every weekday during the trade period, which closes at 7.30pm on Wednesday, October 14. Adelaide



Draft picks: 13, 32, 33, 41, 54, 90

Key players: Nick Murray, Luke Pedlar The Crows were in the box seat for Zac Bailey, only for Bailey to remain a Lion on an eight-year deal. The Crows are set to lose Pedlar to Port Adelaide, but have a call to make on whether they trade key defender Murray, who has a five-year offer from North Melbourne. Murray, who has managed 78 games in six seasons with the Crows, including 11 this year, is contracted for another two seasons. Fellow tall backman Jordon Butts has already left for the Bulldogs in free agency. The Crows have been linked to Suns defender Charlie Ballard. Bigger picture, they are expected to make a play for St Kilda’s Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera and Hawthorn’s Will Day next year. - Jon Pierik Brisbane Lions Draft picks: 18, 39, 40, 51, 57, 77, 95

Key players: Keidean Coleman, Will McLachlan, Sam Marshall The Lions are likely to lose Marshall, who has requested a trade to St Kilda, while forward McLachlan has been linked with Essendon and Melbourne. Lachie Neale is off to Collingwood as a free agent, but Brisbane received only pick 39 as compensation, which will not help them match a bid on potential top-10 academy selection Caylen Murray. Out-of-favour defender Coleman is open to a fresh start at a different club. - Marc McGowan



Moving on: Star midfielder Lachie Neale has had a week of partying after the AFL grand final, but will soon be on his way to Collingwood. Getty Images Carlton Draft picks: 11, 16, 23, 24, 59, 70, 88 Key players: Hudson O’Keeffe, Flynn Riley The Blues have locked in ex-Swans key forward Joel Amartey through free agency, and their primary draft focus is matching a bid on Cody Walker, the son of former Blue Andrew Walker. Their top two selections in the draft add up to 2396 value index points, and they can also go into draft deficit, meaning they will have enough points to cover a bid up to No.2. Carlton also hope to land Giant Lachie Whitfield, while ex-Magpie Wil Parker will join as a delisted free agent. Ruckman O’Keeffe has requested a trade to the Western Bulldogs, while Riley is keen to move to the Magpies on a three-year deal. - Jon Pierik



Collingwood Draft picks: 9, 28, 66, 68, 75, 86

Key players: Scott Pendlebury, Dan Houston, Jordan De Goey, Harry DeMattia The Magpies are determined to remain in the premiership mix, and have landed three-time Brisbane premiership star Lachie Neale, who proved through a tumultuous 2026 campaign that his on-field output won’t be impacted by off-field headlines. A fourth-round pick will be enough to secure Giants forward Jesse Hogan, while they have met with Richmond’s rebounding defender Jayden Short. List boss Justin Leppitsch confirmed the Magpies were open to trading Jordan De Goey, who has a year left on his contract, but wants a long-term deal. Dan Houston’s future remains a point of interest, although he is contracted until the end of 2030 and his management has declared he is going nowhere. Scott Pendlebury will cross to Gold Coast. - Jon Pierik New colours: Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury will play for the Gold Coast Suns next year. Joe Armao Essendon



Related Article AFL 2026 Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft Draft picks: 1, 19, 60, 78

Key players: Zach Merrett, Jordan Ridley Again, the focus at Bomberland is Merrett, who, for the second-straight season, is seeking a trade to Hawthorn. As reported by this masthead, the Hawks have offered picks 15 and 25 in this year’s draft, along with a future selection – either a second- or third-round draft pick – but the Bombers have rebuffed this. It’s unclear what will satisfy Essendon when it comes to relinquishing their seven-time best-and-fairest, and former skipper. Merrett is contracted for 2027. The Bombers are chasing Melbourne premiership veteran Jack Viney, who could replace Merrett in the midfield. Defender Ridley is on Geelong and North Melbourne’s radar. Out-of-favour Cat Jack Bowes has requested a trade to the Bombers. - Jon Pierik Fremantle Draft picks: 17, 38, 58, 76, 94

Key players: Sean Darcy, Nathan O’Driscoll



Darcy’s future remains a point of debate despite the Dockers insisting the ruckman will remain at the club. He fell out of favour this season with Luke Jackson dominant, while Mason Cox was the preferred second ruck in their finals campaign. Darcy, 28, is contracted until the end of 2030. Wingman O’Driscoll has told the club he is exploring his options, having rejected a three-year contract offer amid interest from the Western Bulldogs. The Dockers say they have not expressed interest in luring ex-Magpie Bobby Hill or Sydney’s Chad Warner home, while their discussions with ex-Tiger Nathan Broad are purely about a coaching role. - Jon Pierik Geelong Draft picks: 14, 34, 55, 73, 91

Key players: Gryan Miers, Jack Bowes The Cats were disappointed to miss out on Zak Butters, but can now use that money to load up on other talent. Giants great Toby Greene officially joined on Friday as a free agent, while they are again haggling with the Saints over a trade for ruckman Rowan Marshall. The Cats have offered pick 32 as the crux of the deal, but St Kilda want Geelong’s top pick. The Cats are also chasing Essendon defender Jordan Ridley, and are open to discussing Nick Blakey, should the Swan be determined to leave the club after the alleged Pullman Hotel incident. Miers has completed a medical at West Coast, but remains keen to stay at Geelong, but Bowes has requested a trade to Essendon. - Jon Pierik Gold Coast



Draft picks: 65, 79, 83

Key players: Charlie Ballard, Ben King (restricted free agent), Jamarra Ugle-Hagan, Matt Rowell King will head to Hawthorn on a seven-year, $9 million deal, but the free agency compensation – pick No.7 – may not satisfy the Suns, who could match the Hawks’ offer and force a trade for the star goal-kicker. Gold Coast have yet to indicate whether they will offer Ugle-Hagan another one-year deal, while Rowell is an intriguing case. The 2025 Brownlow medallist has a year to run on his contract, and is weighing up a return home to Victoria. If a sweetheart deal was put before the Suns now, would they move early? Gold Coast may need to engineer a late trade to secure unrestricted free agent Scott Pendlebury, so any compensation from the AFL for King is not diluted. Ballard is likely to stay at the club despite rival clubs’ interest. - Jon Pierik GWS Draft picks: 7, 26, 29, 48, 84

Key players: Harry Himmelberg, Jesse Hogan, Jake Stringer, Lachie Whitfield The Giants already decided not to offer contracts to Hogan and Kieren Briggs, and were comfortable with Stringer’s decision to move back to Victoria, but were hoping to retain Green, who is off to Geelong. Whitfield is poised to become a Blue after completing a medical after GWS were open to shedding his salary as they prioritise their younger group. A fourth-round pick will seal Hogan’s passage to Collingwood early in the trade period, while Briggs joined Richmond on a four-year deal. GWS may look to add more ruck depth and had explored interest in Bulldogs big man Tim English. - Marc McGowan



Hawthorn Draft picks: 15, 25, 27, 35, 69, 92

Key players: Sam Butler, Finn Maginness, Will McCabe, Noah Mraz, Max Ramsden, Jack Scrimshaw They already had some wins when in-demand duo Bailey Macdonald and Calsher Dear re-signed. Ben King and Zach Merrett will be Hawks by the end of the player movement period, but how those deals look remains to be seen. North’s Josh Goater has also requested a trade to Hawthorn. Gold Coast are publicly threatening to match any Hawks free agency offer for King, which would trigger a trade, but that is to be determined – and could impact what Hawthorn can offer Essendon for Merrett. The Bombers are trying to convince the Hawks to include developing defender Mraz in any Merrett deal, but Hawthorn are adamant that won’t happen. Fringe players Butler (West Coast) and Maginness (Western Bulldogs) have opposition interest. - Marc McGowan Melbourne Draft picks: 6, 10, 47, 87

Key players: Trent Rivers, Jack Viney



The Demons missed out on Hawk Calsher Dear, who decided to stay in brown and gold. However, once-prized Roo Zane Duursma wants to join Steven King’s squad and that deal will require some haggling to determine his current value after being the No.4 pick in 2023. Lion Will McLachlan is another possible addition. Viney played just once this past season due mostly to injury, but Melbourne are going in a different midfield direction and encouraged him to explore his options. West Coast and Essendon are duelling for Viney’s signature, and it is unlikely he will net a strong return as effectively a salary dump. Rivers was once considered a big part of Melbourne’s future, but there have been constant murmurings that he might pursue a fresh start this off-season, which is yet to eventuate. - Marc McGowan Jack Viney in action recently. AFL Photos North Melbourne Draft picks: 5, 45, 64, 72, 82

That deal rests on the Crows’ willingness to let him go, and what North would offer to tempt them to relinquish defensive depth. Powell is a South Australian, so is often raised a potential part of any Murray trade. Duursma wants to join Melbourne, while Goater is keen to be a Hawk, so the Roos can expect to be busy in this year’s trade period. Contracted Bomber Jordan Ridley is a target, but his preference is believed to be Geelong. They were also keen on Cat Jack Bowes, but he nominated Essendon instead. Port Adelaide Draft picks: 4, 22, 30, 44, 46, 63, 81

They will score pick five if they choose not to match the Dogs’ enormous nine-year deal, worth up to $18 million. That scenario remains a likely outcome, even after the AFL blocked their proposed side trade that involved Marshall also heading to the Kennel, Port paying a large chunk of his salary, and scoring two first-round picks in return. However, league rules prohibit a club losing a free agent from paying the salary of another player going to the same club, for integrity reasons. It is still probable that Marshall is in different colours next year, with both parties open to a move. Crow Luke Pedlar wants to join the Power. - Marc McGowan Richmond Draft picks: 2, 20, 42, 61

Briggs inked a four-year deal that positions himself as Richmond’s long-term successor for captain Toby Nankervis. Short is exploring his trade options, including meeting with Collingwood, but this masthead previously confirmed that fellow veteran Nick Vlastuin is not interested in continuing his career elsewhere. The Tigers will bring in another top talent in the draft and may be involved in some peripheral trades across the next 10 days. - Marc McGowan St Kilda Draft picks: 8, 49, 67, 85

The Cats have so far knocked back St Kilda’s interest in Lawson Humphries and Sam De Koning, while they are also reluctant to part with their first-round selection. The Tauru saga is a fascinating one, and could still have another twist, but the likeliest outcome is he remains a Saint. Another of St Kilda’s top-10 picks, Phillipou, who is reportedly on a $1 million-a-year salary, was raised in trade dispatches, but club football boss Lenny Hayes denied he was up for grabs. However, Marshall could still find his way to Luke Beveridge’s club – just not in that exact fashion. Out-of-favour Hawk Finn Maginness, who is contracted for 2027, is on the Bulldogs’ radar, while Docker Nathan O’Driscoll could be a name to follow. Ruckman English is expected to remain at the club for next season, while St Kilda have indicated any deal for Lobb was unlikely. - Marc McGowan Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: America’s billionaires are turning their backs on Trump
World.content:
Analysis BusinessBanking & financeUS midterm elections America’s billionaires are turning their backs on Trump Jeremy Warner October 4, 2026 — 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Among the titans of global finance, none are more powerful and influential than Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JPMorgan Chase. So when he turns against Donald Trump and criticises the 47th US president’s repudiation of the old, multilateral, rules-based order, we should sit up and take notice. The more so in that Dimon’s intervention comes just a month before the congressional midterms, where the Republicans are expected to receive a hammering. US President Donald Trump’s popularity has continued to decline as the midterm elections draw closer. Bloomberg A lifelong Democrat, Dimon has admittedly never been part of Trump’s inner circle and in the past year, relations between the two have deteriorated precipitously. He played no part in the undignified and fawning scramble for presidential favours after Trump’s election two years ago. According to accounts, he wisely rebuffed soundings on serving in Trump’s second administration as Treasury secretary.



In January, moreover, Trump launched a $5bn lawsuit against Dimon and JPMorgan for allegedly de-banking him. The bank says the president’s suit “has no merit”. JPMorgan boss Jamie Dimon’s criticism of the Trump administration has become sharper off late. Bloomberg For his part, Dimon has been highly critical of Trump’s mooted plan to cap credit card interest rates at 10 per cent and he has refused to help fund Trump’s White House ballroom. But he’s also been careful not to overstep the mark and to give credit where he thinks it is due. “Take a step back, be honest,” Dimon said in the run-up to Trump’s second stab at the presidency. He “was kind of right about NATO, kind of right on immigration. He grew the economy quite well. Tax reform worked. He was right about some of China. He wasn’t wrong about some of these critical issues”.



Dimon’s remarks played a key role in rehabilitating Trump among the general run of US business leaders after the ignominy of the Capitol Hill riots. If someone as worldly, wise and seasoned as Dimon thinks Trump is basically right, then it sanitises and promotes what he stands for. Be that as it may, judging by an op-ed he wrote in the Wall Street Journal last week, he now seems to have changed his mind. While never truly an insider, Jamie Dimon has mostly maintained a cordial relation with Donald Trump. Andrew Harrer “A strong America with robust military and economic alliances is the foundation for a prosperous and peaceful world,” he wrote in an apparent rebuff of Trump’s MAGA-driven approach to allies, trade and international relations. Nor is he the only critic among those who have hitherto been relatively supportive.



In a recent interview, Peter Thiel, a long-standing Trump backer and a Republican mega donor, said he wished the president had chosen more competent people for his administration. In an interview with Mathias Dopfner, chief executive of The Telegraph’s new owner Axel Springer, the Palantir co-founder accused Trump of “over-correcting for the mistakes of the first term with all these loyalty tests. You got sort of an administration staffed by not very smart but very loyal people”. This is potentially dangerous territory for Thiel. Palantir is still highly dependent on US government contracts. But in another sign that the tide is turning against Trump-style politics, he said it anyway. Peter Thiel, a long-standing Trump backer and Republican mega donor, has also voiced concerns about the Trump administration. AP Not his words, but the sycophancy of Trump’s cabinet is worthy of a banana republic.



Dimon’s suggestion is that a grand alliance be struck with European and other like-minded democracies such as Canada, Japan, Korea, Australia and Mexico. In return for free trade with the US, Europe would agree to full implementation of proposals by former European Central Bank president Mario Draghi for countering loss of economic competitiveness, turbocharging a virtuous circle of rising prosperity for both jurisdictions. If this sounds very much like the old, post-war, pre-Trump contract, that’s because it is. It would be the Western alliance reborn and a very welcome development all round. Yet it would be unwise to count on this happening in practice: political opposition in Europe to some of Draghi’s key recommendations remains strong. But Dimon’s suggestion shows that the US is not yet entirely lost to the cause of multilateral solutions.



Related Article Opinion

Trump diplomacy How Trump’s grovelling emboldens China and imperils the Asia Pacific Peter Hartcher Political and international editor It’s similar to what Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has been suggesting, only with the US at its centre, not as a potentially hostile force kicking in the other direction. Does Trump’s presidency mark a permanent change in the geopolitical and economic weather, or is he a temporary aberration? From the very start of his second term, that’s been the big question. Dimon’s musings suggest the latter. So do the polls before next month’s midterms. The US economy is in many respects booming, but it is not an electorally friendly form of growth. The leaders in this boom, the hyperscalers of the AI arms race, are generally unpopular with voters and though their investment spending binge generates plenty of jobs, it disguises a great hinterland of economic grievance and frustration. Much higher petrol, diesel and mortgage costs are wreaking havoc with the Republican vote, and it’s Trump who is getting the blame.



Ridiculously, Trump gives himself an A+ for everything that’s happened in his second term. Sadly for him, voters do not appear inclined to agree. The president promised no more wars but then promptly started one. No matter, the Iranians would be crushed, and it would be over in weeks. Seven months later, it is still going and there is little sign of a lasting resolution. Related Article US election With a month to go, Republicans’ midterm prospects are ‘catastrophically bad’ The president promised lower interest rates and lower gas prices but all he has managed so far is the reverse. It’s true that Gulf producers have found lots of workarounds for the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Exports of crude from the region are now said to be back to virtually pre-war levels. But in all likelihood, it has come too late to save the Republican vote in the midterms.



There is still a month to go, admittedly, but scarcely anyone thinks this is time enough to reverse either current cost-of-living pressures or the electoral fortunes of the Republican Party. A cynic might say that all Dimon is doing by aligning himself with the Carney view of the world is recognising this change in the political weather. A year ago, it looked as if Trump might be one of the most consequential presidents in US history. As the months pass, that judgment looks ever more doubtful. Business leaders tend to bend with the wind. If they sense that things are going against the political incumbent, they nuance their position to fit. But Dimon, a philosophical as well as a practising globalist, has never bought into Trump’s “America first” nationalism. Trump’s loss of political momentum has given him cover to start talking his mind.



Even if he does lose both houses, Trump will presumably still attempt to govern as before through use of executive order. All the same, he’ll be tied up in legal knots for the remainder of his term and his room for manoeuvre fiscally will be tightly restricted. This should at least begin to reduce the upward pressure on interest rates. A year ago, it looked as if Trump might be one of the most consequential presidents in US history. As the months pass, that judgment looks ever more doubtful. To succeed, the West must pull and act together. Tearing it apart was never the right path. UK Telegraph, London

World.title: Why Iran could choose to escalate the war
World.content:
October 4, 2026 — 1:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In early March, nine days after starting his war with Iran, President Donald Trump held a news conference to crow about his “military success, the likes of which people haven’t seen”. “We’re winning very decisively,” he claimed, and “the result will be lower oil prices”. Instead, Trump’s Iran war should be taught for decades as a model of how not to conduct either war or foreign policy. It’s an example of how hubris can swamp a presidency and lead it to military solutions for difficult global problems – and, in the process, make everything worse. Motorcyclists in Tehran ride past a billboard showing US President Donald Trump. AP “The unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over,” Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group writes in a Foreign Affairs essay titled The New Forever War.



Still, the Trumpian myopia persists, with the administration continuing to claim that its pressure on Iran is a smashing success. “The blockade is working; it’s working like nothing we’ve ever seen,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News in September. Hmm. Diesel prices at a few places in California have hit $US9.99 ($14.40) a gallon, the maximum price those pumps can display. The United States has already spent more than $43 billion on the war, by a lowball Pentagon estimate. Higher prices caused by the war have cost the typical American family about $US1000, according to economist Mark Zandi. More broadly, the US has depleted its arsenal, cost American and Iranian lives, possibly committed war crimes, exposed American vulnerabilities, effectively lost access to some bases and weakened US military credibility as far away as East Asia. Against that, the Trump administration believes it has the upper hand because of the economic pressure the blockade is creating for Iran. Well, maybe. It’s true that the Iranian economy is a catastrophe and that ordinary Iranians – the people we are supposed to be helping – are suffering greatly. The exchange rate is now more than 2.5 million rials to the US dollar, one-tenth of the rial’s value in 2021. Yet Washington doesn’t seem to understand that instead of surrendering, Iran may choose to escalate. “They’ve come to the conclusion that the only way they survive is to shoot their way out,” said Vali Nasr, an Iran expert at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies. He suggested that Iran could increase attacks on shipping and, especially if it is attacked, strike oil infrastructure around the Persian Gulf.



I fear that Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, an Iran watcher at a British think tank, is right when he says: “Iran did not wage a scorched-earth campaign – but it may yet do so if the current situation persists for too long. That is what everyone who actually follows this region and its dynamics is worried about.” It’s difficult to see a deal being reached, partly because both Trump and Iran have a history of overreaching. It doesn’t help that Trump’s chief negotiators, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, are real estate investors chosen for their closeness to Trump rather than for, er, their diplomatic savvy. Related Article Middle East at war G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil to combat soaring fuel prices Iranian leaders also seem cocky. Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, boasted in August that Iran had brought the US “to its knees.” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC’s Meet the Press that Iran was fully prepared for a new round of fighting, “even if it comes to a doomsday war”. One rare issue on which I agree with Trump is the paramount importance of preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. In Trump’s speech to the United Nations – the one in which he mused about whether he should “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly” – he insisted that “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon”.



That’s easy to say. But Trump’s war may have actually increased the likelihood of Iran’s making a drive towards a nuclear weapon. Trump’s war began by killing the previous supreme leader, who had issued a fatwa saying that Iran would not develop nuclear weapons. The new supreme leader, his son, does not inherit that fatwa and has not issued his own, so now “there’s a serious conversation in Iran” about pursuing nuclear weapons, Nasr said. A new measure before the Iranian parliament proposes withdrawing from the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, and 32 Iranian figures have called on the country to do so. That would be a cataclysm. “Any other country but Iran would have pulled out of the NPT if treated the same way,” Araghchi told reporters. We should take these warnings seriously.



One reason professors will teach Trump’s war as an example of military malpractice is that it fits neatly into a larger pattern of counterproductive American policies towards Iran. I deplore the brutality, corruption and economic incompetence of Iran’s rulers – so it’s infuriating that America has repeatedly empowered Iranian extremists. First, the US helped topple a democratically elected prime minister in 1953, energising nationalists and souring Iranians on the West. Then in the 1960s and ’70s, the US gave Iran a nuclear reactor, backed an increasingly autocratic shah and overstepped in ways that helped allow Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini to become a national force by denouncing American imperialism. Related Article Opinion

United Nations Yes, the UN is terrible – but right now, we need it desperately Nicholas Kristof Columnist President George W. Bush’s 2003 Iraq War toppled Saddam Hussein, an enemy of Iran, and empowered Shiite militias that support Iran. In 2018, Trump announced his withdrawal from the Obama nuclear pact with Iran. The capstone in this “march of folly,” to borrow a phrase from historian Barbara Tuchman, was Trump’s war on Iran this year, which has bolstered military hard-liners in Tehran and enabled them to project greater power over the Persian Gulf and global oil markets. That’s what I find particularly worth studying: How is it that for three-quarters of a century, Americans have so bungled our foreign policy that we have systematically empowered Iranian extremists? They call us the “Great Satan,” but in truth our ineptitude has made us their benefactors.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: The mission to quadruple the number of people living in Sydney Olympic Park
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The mission to quadruple the number of people living in Sydney Olympic Park Anthony Segaert October 4, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s a place millions have been to but only 5000 call home. Sydney Olympic Park, the precinct that put its namesake city on the world map at the turn of the century, has for the most part of its two-decade history been defined by transience: just like during the Olympic Games, people leave the precinct as quickly as they arrive. But as the state government attempts to build housing in a model described by the top planning secretary as “everything, everywhere, all at once”, the authority leading Sydney Olympic Park is pushing to transform the suburb from an event destination to a living, breathing home to five times as many people as it currently holds. The plan aims to balance new homes “with the open spaces and walkable spaces”. Janie Barrett In one of the few Sydney suburbs where mangroves, a river, and vast parklands all rub up next to huge stadiums and large apartment blocks, can Sydney Olympic Park really become something new? The Sydney Olympic Park Authority’s masterplan, released earlier this year, aims to balance new homes “with the open spaces and walkable spaces”, said the body’s acting chief executive Chris Martin, who usually acts as the Department of Planning’s chief financial officer.



He says the suburb is essentially a “dormitory suburb” at present: if you live here, you’re likely to come home to sleep and then get out – but he said more housing would bring more jobs and more activities. The Brick Pit ring walk is an 18-metre high walk over the top of the old brick site, which supplied bricks for many Sydney homes. Janie Barrett An artist’s impression of the edge of the Brick Pit in the masterplan. Sydney Olympic Park Masterplan “[The goal is] to really make it that vibrant precinct that has more of a nighttime vibe, has more of a daytime vibe, and people are living and working and then relaxing and playing here as well,” he said, describing the park as an oasis. The key to making the area vibrant is to have more people living there, Planning Minister Paul Scully said.



“I think probably the big change will be the number [of] homes and jobs that were always envisaged for there, but never really took off because there hadn’t been a push,” he told a conference on Wednesday. He said he wanted the area to be recognised as an “everyday space to live, to work, and to go out and have some fun”. Chris Martin, the acting chief executive of Sydney Olympic Park Authority, on the Brick Pit Ring Walk. Janie Barrett The masterplan envisages up to 15,000 homes in the area over multiple high-rise apartments, bringing the total population to about 25,000 by 2050. But the suburb will also get two new schools and at least seven new playgrounds or parks. The government says about 26,000 jobs will be created in the area with new commercial buildings, too – a decrease from the 32,000 it promised in 2024. Grand visions of Sydney Olympic Park’s future have always been thwarted by one thing: its infrastructure. A train line does connect visitors to Lidcombe station but it runs infrequently. An extension of the second stage of the Parramatta light rail service, which the NSW Labor government promised to build, was earlier this year broken into two parts with no timeline for its arrival into the suburb. When the Metro West line opens in 2032, 25,000 passengers every hour will be able to travel between the precinct and the Sydney CBD in about 15 minutes.



Related Article City life Endure the traffic nightmare or risk a broken-down train? The great Sydney Olympic Park debate “This is project will support a vibrant community [and] match housing growth with transport and infrastructure capacity, so that people can live, work, and play close to home in a community they choose,” Scully said. Until then, Martin has some advice for people dropping by for a game or a concert: “Find a shady spot, you can throw a Frisbee. You can frolic,” he said. “Don’t just surgical strike your visit, but do your [event], then go for a wander.”

World.title: Why the Wallabies should rest their best player for opening Bledisloe at Eden Park
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Why the Wallabies should rest their best player for opening Bledisloe at Eden Park Paul Cully October 4, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1. A drawn Bledisloe series would fuel Wallabies’ belief: There is a booby prize awaiting the winner of the Wallabies-All Blacks pool stage clash at the Rugby World Cup next year - a likely quarterfinal against the Springboks. So, beating the All Blacks might not actually serve the Wallabies well at the home tournament in 2027. That said, the momentum starting to build under Kiss would be maintained if the Wallabies can go 1-1 with the All Blacks in the next two weeks. Len Ikitau is carrying an ankle injury sustained in the Wallabies’ win over South Africa. Getty Images As tempting as it must be to rush Len Ikitau back from his ankle injury, holding him back until the Sydney test might be the smarter play. A win by the Wallabies at Eden Park would be an extraordinary achievement, but a loss isn’t the end of the world if they can reverse it in Sydney. With two out of the three Bledisloe Tests set to be in Australia next year, including the Anzac Day fixture in Brisbane, winning back the famous trophy won’t be an unrealistic goal if they get one win across the line in Sydney in a fortnight.



2 Fitzy’s chat with Kiss chat taps into something valuable: Colleague Peter FitzSimons’ piece with Wallabies coach Les Kiss made me want to drape myself in an Australian flag and belt out Waltzing Matilda, even though I’m not Australian. It was stirring stuff, full of promises to play the Wallaby way and references to “the backyard spirit”. If this is not authentic it could come across as glib marketing drivel, but the Wallabies’ performances over the past five Tests suggest it is a genuine motivational tool. Les Kiss poses with the Wallabies team in Mendoza. Getty Images Kiss is obviously a technical coach as well, but in Test rugby a sense of national purpose is vital even if it gives the team an extra few per cent in performance. Can anyone other than an Australian coach deliver this messaging? Arguably not. Looking from the outside, it appears this Wallabies squad can almost feel the home Rugby World Cup next year - it has given them something tangible to aim towards, and everyone saw how the British and Lions tour lifted the players.



3 How the All Blacks could line up: Does item 2 mean a famous win at Eden Park next Saturday is on the cards? It’s not that simple, especially with the unavailable Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper representing huge losses for the Wallabies. Dave Rennie coaching the All Blacks at Eden Park in July. Phil Walter All Blacks coach Dave Rennie gave a radio interview at the weekend and was still frustrated with the tour of South Africa - both the All Blacks’ own mistakes and some of the officiating at the scrums. After three straight Test losses the All Blacks will likely attack the first Bledisloe Test with some purpose of their own. They are down a few troops with injury - notably captain Ardie Savea - but this starting XV won’t be too far from what Rennie reveals on Thursday: Damian McKenzie, Will Jordan, Quinn Tupaea, Jordie Barrett, Josh Moorby, Richie Mo’unga, Cam Roigard, Peter Lakai, Anton Segner, Tupou Vaa’i, Fabian Holland, Josh Lord, Tyrel Lomax, Codie Taylor, Ethan de Groot.



4 Waratahs cop an old-fashioned hiding: The Western Force were crowned Super Rugby AUS champions with a 53-26 win over the Waratahs, and in perfect Perth conditions they again showed what a well-run rugby team they are. New recruit Harry McLaughlin-Phillips played as if he had been in the Force system for about a decade, former Waratah Will Harris has used the competition to reinvent himself as a hard-nosed option in the second row, and midfielder Boston Fakafanua is one to watch. Fakafanua, out of the King’s School, is built low to the ground and played in the No 13 jersey on Saturday, although his long-term position could be at No 12. The Waratahs were never at the races against the Force and it was a reminder of the size of the job facing Michael Cheika, especially with NSW losing so many good players across to Perth. 5 Suaalii’s versatility could be his trump card: Cross-code star Mark Nawaqanitawase has conquered the NRL over the past few years, but there is a real logjam building in the Wallabies’ back three.



Related Article Wallabies Marky Mark has set the NRL alight. But he’ll still have to earn Wallabies spot Dylan Pietsch was the headline act in the Force’s big win over the Waratahs in the Super Rugby Aus decider after his return from injury, and it is easy to forget that he was arguably the form winger in the country before his layoff. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii also enjoyed his best Test in ages against the Springboks last week, and as remarkable as it sounds Nawaqanitawase doesn’t just walk back into the Wallabies’ best 15. Tom Wright and Max Jorgensen are banks, so in effect there is only one place up for grabs, pitting Nawaqanitawase against Suaalii, Pietsch and Harry Potter. That’s a good problem, of course, but it is still an interesting situation given the Wallabies now have two blokes with star billing who could be the face of the Rugby World Cup. In that respect, Suaalii’s ability to cover the midfield is a big advantage.

World.content:
Review Eating outSt Kilda Get proper British pies at a new bayside bakery (plus three more great pie shops to try) Honouring his navy chef grandfather’s knack for baking shepherd and cottage pies, Norman’s Proppa Pies co-owner Dave Pannell has added a good ol’ fashioned pie shop to his St Kilda stable.
