1 / 11 Slow-braised beef brisket pie. Pete Dillon 2 / 11 Owners Brad Balbi (left) and Dave Pannell. Pete Dillon 3 / 11 Norman’s Proppa Pies. Pete Dillon 4 / 11 Pies are best eaten at home, with cutlery. Pete Dillon 5 / 11 Add mushy peas and gravy to your pie for a proper British feed. Pete Dillon 6 / 11 Located on Barkly Street in St Kilda. Pete Dillon 7 / 11 Beef brisket is mixed with fresh jalapenos and Stilton to make a funky, spicy blue cheese and chilli pie. Pete Dillon 8 / 11 Rhubarb and strawberry pie. Pete Dillon 9 / 11 Choose your fighter. Pete Dillon 10 / 11 Two types of sausage rolls are also on the menu. Pete Dillon 11 / 11 Inside the hole-in-the-wall pie shop. Pete Dillon Previous Slide Next Slide Norman’s Proppa Pies Bakery$$$$ Take one idyllic upbringing. Add butter. Lovingly spoon in secret ingredients. Bake until done. Open the doors and serve some of the best pies in town. That’s the basic backstory behind Norman’s Proppa Pies, a new bayside bakery owned by Dave Pannell and Brad Balbi, the pair behind St Kilda coffee-to-spritz-to-nightcap institution Sorsi e Morsi, just around the corner. It’s Pannell’s childhood being channelled. When he was a kid in the English Midlands, young Dave’s best friend was his grandfather, Norman. A navy chef who would make pies for weekend caravanning trips, Norman’s shepherd’s pies (with lamb mince) and cottage pies (with beef) were specialties, both topped with mashed potato, and often inscribed with sentimental messages. For his part, Balbi grew up in bakeries in Far North Queensland, and was roped into pie duties on weekends. When the pair started thinking about a second St Kilda operation, a pie shop seemed perfect, especially because there’s nothing similar nearby. Related Article Join the queue: 13 Melbourne cafes and bakeries worth getting in line for



Their pies are a perfect amalgam of pastry and filling, comforting but interesting, sophisticated yet hearty. Everything is house-made, including two types of pastry. The shortcrust for the base starts with boiling water, butter and vinegar, then the liquid is worked into the flour, making for a smooth, sturdy dough. The puff pastry tops are extravagantly layered and buttery rich, the pastry crisp to the bite but without shattering so dramatically that you wear more than you eat. Inside the hole-in-the-wall pie shop. Pete Dillon Beef is the bedrock, with brisket slow-braised in beef stock with 13 herbs and spices, including a secret ingredient I guessed but will refrain from sharing so I live to pie another day. The tender, lively stew is slurried with flour and tumbled into bases, ready for joy. The beefy base is also mixed with fresh jalapenos and Stilton to make a funky, spicy blue cheese and chilli pie, and a pub-style creamy green peppercorn sauce amps up another beef option. Cue pie rapture. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up There’s also an excellent butter chicken number, made with whole roast chickens (the bones go into the beef stock) plus a vegetarian cauliflower pie with three-cheese sauce. Sausage rolls are serious business so it’s good there are two: a pork version that leans British, and an Aussie-style beef one. Each is a terrific balance of fat and fab. Norman took his shepherd’s pie recipe to the grave but surely he’d be proud of this one: Lamb mince is cooked for hours with mushrooms, rosemary and bay leaves, spooned into its pastry casing, and topped with a swirl of buttery mash. To be traditional, add mushy peas and gravy. The sweet range includes a rhubarb and strawberry pie, and chocolate cream pie, an English indulgence which features custard mixed with melted chocolate to form a silky filling.



Two types of sausage rolls are also on the menu. Pete Dillon We now know about Norman but what about “proppa”? The Northern English rehash of “proper” is Geordie slang for “brilliant”. To lean even more to Blighty, Pannell and Balbi are planning to open select nights to serve the “pie and pea supper”, an alternative to the post-pub spice bag. A couple of caveats: One time I came for a potato-topped pie and it had dried out considerably in the warmer. Ask for a freshie. You also need to consider how well-placed you are to enjoy a pie with gravy, and especially with mushy peas. This is not a one-hand car situation, it’s a full-on dining project. Until bench seats are installed here, a home dining table with cutlery is ideal. Maybe that’s how it should be, anyway. So much work goes into these pies, it’s only proper they’re eaten with a little ceremony. Three more great pie shops to try Rolling Pin Pies This consistent award-winner has outlets around Geelong and the Bellarine. It just cleaned up in the gourmet categories of the Great Aussie Pie Comp with their kangaroo rendang number, the “Bombay beef” and masala mash, and a barbecued brisket, jalapeno and cheese pie. 2/3 Wyndham Street, Drysdale, rollingpin.com.au Hope Bakery It’s easier than you think to strike gold at Sovereign Hill – just head to the pie shop. A traditional wood-fired Scotch oven is used to bake Cornish pasties with apple, various steak pies and renowned sausage rolls. You’ll probably need a Banbury tart (with currants) and some miner’s biscuits, too. Bradshaw Street, Ballarat, sovereignhill.com.au Gum Tree Pies A good option, whether you’re roadtripping through Yack, where the Gum Tree production kitchen is, or swinging by outposts in Wodonga or Bright. As well as classic steak pies, there’s one with Guinness and a Sunday roast-adjacent lamb and mint pie. Vegetarians have good options, such as the Penang pumpkin and creamy cauliflower. 10 High Street, Yackandandah, gumtreepies.com.au Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.title: Cornell case revives anger about handling of campus sexual assault cases
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCourts Cornell case revives anger about handling of campus sexual assault cases Stephanie Saul and Emma Goldberg October 4, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: A lawsuit alleging rape at a Cornell University fraternity house has set off a wave of anger among women on college campuses and beyond. Campus sexual assault survivors and their supporters have published essays in school newspapers and inundated social media in solidarity with the complainant, known in court records only as Jane Doe. Some are using the familiar #MeToo hashtag of an earlier movement to combat sexual abuse and harassment. Others have adopted a new one: #IAmJaneDoe. A survey by Cornell University found that about one-third of undergraduate women said they had had unwanted sexual experiences. AP Photo/Matt Rourke In one opinion article in the University of Pennsylvania campus newspaper, students wrote that “sexual violence happens far too often on college campuses everywhere”.



“It’s time to face the fact that the ‘Cornell incident’ isn’t just born of Cornell problems, or limited to a Cornell issue,” the students wrote. Related Article Crime ‘Heinous’: Frat house gang-rape lawsuit triggers reopening of criminal investigation The outrage flooding social media and rising up on campuses follows similar waves of disgust about campus sexual violence that emerged more than a decade ago and then reignited after the broader #MeToo reckoning that began with Hollywood sexual assault revelations. Driving the campaign in support of Doe is a feeling that not enough changed after similar movements. The Penn students wrote, for example, that past responses have been bureaucratic, and that universities “prioritise bolstering their own image” instead of making deeper changes that protect women from assault. Celebrities have also joined the outcry. Mariska Hargitay and her Joyful Heart Foundation, which supports domestic violence survivors, posted: “Survivors deserve to be believed and kept informed. Silence protects no one. To her: we support you.”



During an appearance in Ithaca, New York, Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called the 2024 episode at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house part of a “culture of rape” on college campuses. In the lawsuit, the young woman says she was assaulted at the Chi Phi house on Cornell’s campus, names seven men who were allegedly involved and says the university and law enforcement agencies did not do enough to punish or pursue prosecution of the men. New York Governor Kathy Hochul, left, has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to take over investigating the case. Bloomberg The men involved have denied the allegations, while the university, the fraternity and prosecutors have said they had responded appropriately given the information they had at the time. Lawyers point out the difficulty of prosecuting such cases in court, particularly when many complainants, including Doe, change their accounts over time. Records obtained by The New York Times present a murky picture of what took place. The woman indicated in one text message to one of the men that “nothing illegal” had happened. But she also told police investigators that “I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped”.



The widespread condemnation of accused men could create an unfair dynamic, according to Andrew T. Miltenberg, a lawyer for one of the Cornell men, Gillio Lopes. He said the “danger in a case like this is that an accusation, amplified often enough, can harden into a verdict before the evidence is ever tested”. Related Article Crime Unsealed documents detail Cornell investigation into alleged rape at fraternity house Miltenberg, known for representing students against sexual misconduct claims, said the attention had been compounded by statements of public officials that seemed to side with Doe. On September 28, New York Attorney-General Letitia James posted on the social platform X: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and prayers.” Several days later, New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed James to take over investigating the case.



Lopes unequivocally denied the allegations, Miltenberg said. The online outpouring in support of Doe has also led to a backlash. Some right-wing commentators condemn her and others are trying to reveal her identity. ‘It’s time to face the fact that the ‘Cornell incident’ isn’t just born of Cornell problems, or limited to a Cornell issue.’ University of Pennsylvania students Federal data shows that nationally, there were 6000 to 6200 reports of rapes on campus a year from 2014 to 2019, or about eight to 11 per 10,000 on-campus students. But reports declined drastically during the pandemic years, when many students took classes remotely. Since then, they have begun to rise again. The data does not show how many reports resulted in action or were substantiated.



But the available data suggests the problem has been widespread. Over a quarter of undergraduate women reported some form of non-consensual sexual contact by physical force, or because they were unable to consent, according to a large survey of students conducted by the Association of American Universities in 2019. That survey also found evidence of a growing awareness about rules and resources, as universities built out new policies and training. The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University. AP At Cornell, a survey conducted by the university found that about one-third of undergraduate women said they had had unwanted sexual experiences. Reading Doe’s claims of assault has prompted some current Cornell students and recent graduates to share memories of their own experiences of sexual misconduct. Many said the allegations weren’t entirely surprising because of how often they had heard about friends who said they had been assaulted at parties.



“To be honest, there are so many during my time there that it almost feels like it all blurs into one,” said Claire Ting, who graduated from Cornell last year and served in student government, referring to conversations with friends about upsetting sexual experiences. “We would see posts and discussions talking about the sexual assaults that happened,” she said. “The buzz would die down, and then it would happen again.” The response, she said, was “hurdle after hurdle of bureaucracy”. There have been other moments in recent decades when campus sexual assault has dominated the national conversation. When the documentary The Hunting Ground was released in 2015, for example, it galvanised a movement. Lady Gaga sang the film’s theme song at the Oscars, where she was introduced by then-vice president Joe Biden. At the time, statistics showed that one in four women on campus reported being victims of sexual assault. Just months before the film’s release, the launch of a White House campaign to end campus sexual assault – “It’s On Us” – seemed to signal a changing tide.



More than a decade later, though, the allegations at Cornell prompted questions among survivors about whether anything has changed. Kacey Lee, who graduated from Cornell in 2025, said she was “shocked and not shocked” in the autumn of 2024 when she heard about Doe’s reported assault. The Hunting Ground featured a freshman who brought sexual assault claims against Jameis Winston, who is now the starting quarterback of the New York Giants. Winston, who denied misconduct, was not prosecuted in the case. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II “Being around frat culture and knowing how people can be there was a level of – not that I was expecting it, but I was not the most surprised,” Lee said. While federal data shows that Cornell has reported as many as 28 campus rapes in some recent years, its on-campus undergraduate population is the largest of any Ivy League school. When adjusted for its size, Cornell mirrors many of its peer institutions.



Cornell officials have said they disciplined the men after investigating Doe’s allegations but they didn’t provide details. They have defended their response and cautioned against a “false narrative”, which they said could depress reports of sexual assault. In a message on its website, the university said it had strengthened its policies on sexual assault in recent years. “Our goal is not simply to respond appropriately when sexual misconduct is reported,” the school said, “but to build a community in which sexual violence is prevented, people feel safe coming forward, those who do are supported, and individuals found responsible are held accountable.” Social media platforms are where the original #MeToo movement gained steam, a little less than a decade ago, spurred by disturbing disclosures about film producer Harvey Weinstein. Adam Gray/POOL Bloomberg via AP Elise Siemering, who has said she was raped 14 years ago by a fellow student at High Point University in North Carolina, said she found comfort in the social media outpouring. “The women and men who say, ‘I am Jane Doe’, it gives you a glimmer of hope that there are people in our nation who try to shield her as much as they can,” said Siemering, who was among more than 30 people who told their stories in the 2016 book We Believe You.



Annie E. Clark, whose allegations of sexual assault at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill served as the basis for The Hunting Ground, said this past week that the growth of social media had, in some ways, helped women. “With the advent of social media, more people are sharing their stories and know that they are not alone,” said Clark, co-founder of the organisation End Rape on Campus. Indeed, social media platforms are where the original #MeToo movement gained steam, a little less than a decade ago, spurred by disturbing disclosures about film producer Harvey Weinstein. Researchers at the University of Chicago documented the role of #MeToo on social media as a catalyst for social change, noting that the hashtag was used on Twitter, now X, 19 million times in 2017 and 2018, the first year of the movement, and in dozens of different languages. The hashtag became “a sign of empowerment for victims who may have feared they were alone,” the researchers found.



But since then, a series of federal regulatory changes has created instability in the handling of campus sexual assault cases, according to End Rape on Campus chief executive Kenyora Johnson. Referring to the release of The Hunting Ground, she said, “Eleven years later, we’re still talking about survivors struggling to be heard.” Cornell University student Jane Wang (left) told a Cornell student government forum on Thursday that she saw herself reflected in Jane Doe’s experiences. AP The film was released shortly after a highly publicised incident at Florida State University. It featured a first-year student who brought sexual assault claims against Jameis Winston, who is now the starting quarterback of the New York Giants. Before that accusation became public, a second woman had sought counselling after reporting a sexual encounter with Winston, saying that she felt violated by the incident.



Winston, who denied misconduct, was not prosecuted in the case, although a story in the Times raised questions about law enforcement handling of the inquiry. In 2016, Florida State and Winston settled lawsuits filed by his accuser, according to reports at the time. Although many of Cornell’s current students and recent graduates are too young to remember the #MeToo movement, they expressed frustration about the pervasiveness of sexual violence around them. At a Cornell student government forum on Thursday afternoon, junior Jane Wang came forward and said she saw herself reflected in Doe’s experiences. “I cannot speak on behalf of all survivors because the pain, hurts and trauma that each of us carries is our own,” Wang told the student government representatives. Students warned one another about the risks of fraternity parties immediately when they got to Cornell, said Hannah Shvets, a senior who also serves on the Ithaca Common Council. Young women, she suggested, are largely left to fend for themselves.



“From the day we get to campus there’s awareness – be cautious, go in groups,” she said. “Students feel like often fraternities can partake in behaviour that other clubs or organisations would get shut down if they did.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: NRL grand final 2026 LIVE updates: Newcastle Knights look to claim first premiership in 25 years against the Sydney Roosters; Broncos face off against Roosters in NRLW final
World.content:
Brad Fairbairn (formerly known as Red Beard when his beard was a little more red than grey), has been a Roosters’ supporter for more than half a century but has never attended a grand final in person.



He’s at Accor today because of a drunken decision after the Roosters’ 36-20 victory against the Dolphins in the preliminary final at Suncorp Stadium last week.

Karen Cooper and Brad Fairbairn at Accor Stadium. Oscar Colman

“Well I got drunk last Friday night and said ‘I don’t care what it costs, we’re going’,” Fairbairn said.



Although Fairburn spent more than $1600 on two tickets, one for himself and one for partner Karen Cooper, he didn’t wake up hungover and regretful the morning after.

“It’s a bucket list thing,” he said. The pair drove up from Moruya on the south coast of NSW on Saturday morning

“We’re not getting any younger, we won’t be back again.”

World.title: On the market: Your team by team guide to AFL trade period
World.content:
The AFL trade period officially opens on Monday when the list managers from all the clubs gather at Marvel Stadium to get serious about the deals that will shape their teams for 2027. In truth, negotiations have been bubbling along for months for some players. The big questions are: Will Zach Merrett make it to Hawthorn at his second attempt? Will Gold Coast match Hawthorn’s free agency offer for Ben King and thereby force a trade? Where will Melbourne heart and soul player Jack Viney land? We examine every club and which players are on the market. Jesse Hogan, Rowan Marshall, Zach Merrett and Jack Viney are likely to feature in the trade period. Marija Ercegovac/Getty Images Follow our live blog every weekday during the trade period, which closes at 7.30pm on Wednesday, October 14. Adelaide



Draft picks: 13, 32, 33, 41, 54, 90

Key players: Nick Murray, Luke Pedlar The Crows were in the box seat for Zac Bailey, only for Bailey to remain a Lion on an eight-year deal. The Crows are set to lose Pedlar to Port Adelaide, but have a call to make on whether they trade key defender Murray, who has a five-year offer from North Melbourne. Murray, who has managed 78 games in six seasons with the Crows, including 11 this year, is contracted for another two seasons. Fellow tall backman Jordon Butts has already left for the Bulldogs in free agency. The Crows have been linked to Suns defender Charlie Ballard. Bigger picture, they are expected to make a play for St Kilda’s Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera and Hawthorn’s Will Day next year. - Jon Pierik Brisbane Lions Draft picks: 18, 39, 40, 51, 57, 77, 95

Key players: Keidean Coleman, Will McLachlan, Sam Marshall The Lions are likely to lose Marshall, who has requested a trade to St Kilda, while forward McLachlan has been linked with Essendon and Melbourne. Lachie Neale is off to Collingwood as a free agent, but Brisbane received only pick 39 as compensation, which will not help them match a bid on potential top-10 academy selection Caylen Murray. Out-of-favour defender Coleman is open to a fresh start at a different club. - Marc McGowan



Moving on: Star midfielder Lachie Neale has had a week of partying after the AFL grand final, but will soon be on his way to Collingwood. Getty Images Carlton Draft picks: 11, 16, 23, 24, 59, 70, 88 Key players: Hudson O’Keeffe, Flynn Riley The Blues have locked in ex-Swans key forward Joel Amartey through free agency, and their primary draft focus is matching a bid on Cody Walker, the son of former Blue Andrew Walker. Their top two selections in the draft add up to 2396 value index points, and they can also go into draft deficit, meaning they will have enough points to cover a bid up to No.2. Carlton also hope to land Giant Lachie Whitfield, while ex-Magpie Wil Parker will join as a delisted free agent. Ruckman O’Keeffe has requested a trade to the Western Bulldogs, while Riley is keen to move to the Magpies on a three-year deal. - Jon Pierik



Collingwood Draft picks: 9, 28, 66, 68, 75, 86

Key players: Scott Pendlebury, Dan Houston, Jordan De Goey, Harry DeMattia The Magpies are determined to remain in the premiership mix, and have landed three-time Brisbane premiership star Lachie Neale, who proved through a tumultuous 2026 campaign that his on-field output won’t be impacted by off-field headlines. A fourth-round pick will be enough to secure Giants forward Jesse Hogan, while they have met with Richmond’s rebounding defender Jayden Short. List boss Justin Leppitsch confirmed the Magpies were open to trading Jordan De Goey, who has a year left on his contract, but wants a long-term deal. Dan Houston’s future remains a point of interest, although he is contracted until the end of 2030 and his management has declared he is going nowhere. Scott Pendlebury will cross to Gold Coast. - Jon Pierik New colours: Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury will play for the Gold Coast Suns next year. Joe Armao Essendon



Related Article AFL 2026 Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft Draft picks: 1, 19, 60, 78

Key players: Zach Merrett, Jordan Ridley Again, the focus at Bomberland is Merrett, who, for the second-straight season, is seeking a trade to Hawthorn. As reported by this masthead, the Hawks have offered picks 15 and 25 in this year’s draft, along with a future selection – either a second- or third-round draft pick – but the Bombers have rebuffed this. It’s unclear what will satisfy Essendon when it comes to relinquishing their seven-time best-and-fairest, and former skipper. Merrett is contracted for 2027. The Bombers are chasing Melbourne premiership veteran Jack Viney, who could replace Merrett in the midfield. Defender Ridley is on Geelong and North Melbourne’s radar. Out-of-favour Cat Jack Bowes has requested a trade to the Bombers. - Jon Pierik Fremantle Draft picks: 17, 38, 58, 76, 94

Key players: Sean Darcy, Nathan O’Driscoll



Darcy’s future remains a point of debate despite the Dockers insisting the ruckman will remain at the club. He fell out of favour this season with Luke Jackson dominant, while Mason Cox was the preferred second ruck in their finals campaign. Darcy, 28, is contracted until the end of 2030. Wingman O’Driscoll has told the club he is exploring his options, having rejected a three-year contract offer amid interest from the Western Bulldogs. The Dockers say they have not expressed interest in luring ex-Magpie Bobby Hill or Sydney’s Chad Warner home, while their discussions with ex-Tiger Nathan Broad are purely about a coaching role. - Jon Pierik Geelong Draft picks: 14, 34, 55, 73, 91

Key players: Gryan Miers, Jack Bowes The Cats were disappointed to miss out on Zak Butters, but can now use that money to load up on other talent. Giants great Toby Greene officially joined on Friday as a free agent, while they are again haggling with the Saints over a trade for ruckman Rowan Marshall. The Cats have offered pick 32 as the crux of the deal, but St Kilda want Geelong’s top pick. The Cats are also chasing Essendon defender Jordan Ridley, and are open to discussing Nick Blakey, should the Swan be determined to leave the club after the alleged Pullman Hotel incident. Miers has completed a medical at West Coast, but remains keen to stay at Geelong, but Bowes has requested a trade to Essendon. - Jon Pierik Gold Coast



Draft picks: 65, 79, 83

Key players: Charlie Ballard, Ben King (restricted free agent), Jamarra Ugle-Hagan, Matt Rowell King will head to Hawthorn on a seven-year, $9 million deal, but the free agency compensation – pick No.7 – may not satisfy the Suns, who could match the Hawks’ offer and force a trade for the star goal-kicker. Gold Coast have yet to indicate whether they will offer Ugle-Hagan another one-year deal, while Rowell is an intriguing case. The 2025 Brownlow medallist has a year to run on his contract, and is weighing up a return home to Victoria. If a sweetheart deal was put before the Suns now, would they move early? Gold Coast may need to engineer a late trade to secure unrestricted free agent Scott Pendlebury, so any compensation from the AFL for King is not diluted. Ballard is likely to stay at the club despite rival clubs’ interest. - Jon Pierik GWS Draft picks: 7, 26, 29, 48, 84

Key players: Harry Himmelberg, Jesse Hogan, Jake Stringer, Lachie Whitfield The Giants already decided not to offer contracts to Hogan and Kieren Briggs, and were comfortable with Stringer’s decision to move back to Victoria, but were hoping to retain Green, who is off to Geelong. Whitfield is poised to become a Blue after completing a medical after GWS were open to shedding his salary as they prioritise their younger group. A fourth-round pick will seal Hogan’s passage to Collingwood early in the trade period, while Briggs joined Richmond on a four-year deal. GWS may look to add more ruck depth and had explored interest in Bulldogs big man Tim English. - Marc McGowan



Hawthorn Draft picks: 15, 25, 27, 35, 69, 92

Key players: Sam Butler, Finn Maginness, Will McCabe, Noah Mraz, Max Ramsden, Jack Scrimshaw They already had some wins when in-demand duo Bailey Macdonald and Calsher Dear re-signed. Ben King and Zach Merrett will be Hawks by the end of the player movement period, but how those deals look remains to be seen. North’s Josh Goater has also requested a trade to Hawthorn. Gold Coast are publicly threatening to match any Hawks free agency offer for King, which would trigger a trade, but that is to be determined – and could impact what Hawthorn can offer Essendon for Merrett. The Bombers are trying to convince the Hawks to include developing defender Mraz in any Merrett deal, but Hawthorn are adamant that won’t happen. Fringe players Butler (West Coast) and Maginness (Western Bulldogs) have opposition interest. - Marc McGowan Melbourne Draft picks: 6, 10, 47, 87

Key players: Trent Rivers, Jack Viney



The Demons missed out on Hawk Calsher Dear, who decided to stay in brown and gold. However, once-prized Roo Zane Duursma wants to join Steven King’s squad and that deal will require some haggling to determine his current value after being the No.4 pick in 2023. Lion Will McLachlan is another possible addition. Viney played just once this past season due mostly to injury, but Melbourne are going in a different midfield direction and encouraged him to explore his options. West Coast and Essendon are duelling for Viney’s signature, and it is unlikely he will net a strong return as effectively a salary dump. Rivers was once considered a big part of Melbourne’s future, but there have been constant murmurings that he might pursue a fresh start this off-season, which is yet to eventuate. - Marc McGowan Jack Viney in action recently. AFL Photos North Melbourne Draft picks: 5, 45, 64, 72, 82

Key players: Zane Duursma, Josh Goater, Tom Powell The Kangaroos’ No.1 off-season target is contracted Adelaide key defender Nick Murray, who they have presented with a five-year contract. That deal rests on the Crows’ willingness to let him go, and what North would offer to tempt them to relinquish defensive depth. Powell is a South Australian, so is often raised a potential part of any Murray trade. Duursma wants to join Melbourne, while Goater is keen to be a Hawk, so the Roos can expect to be busy in this year’s trade period. Contracted Bomber Jordan Ridley is a target, but his preference is believed to be Geelong. They were also keen on Cat Jack Bowes, but he nominated Essendon instead. Could they pivot to players such as Hawthorn’s Jack Scrimshaw and/or Max Ramsden? - Marc McGowan



Port Adelaide Draft picks: 4, 22, 30, 44, 46, 63, 81

Key players: Tom Anastasopoulos, Zak Butters, Ollie Lord, Todd Marshall Butters is the big one here, and specifically, what the Power will garner from his impending move to the Western Bulldogs. They will score pick five if they choose not to match the Dogs’ enormous nine-year deal, worth up to $18 million. That scenario remains a likely outcome, even after the AFL blocked their proposed side trade that involved Marshall also heading to the Kennel, Port paying a large chunk of his salary, and scoring two first-round picks in return. However, league rules prohibit a club losing a free agent from paying the salary of another player going to the same club, for integrity reasons. It is still probable that Marshall is in different colours next year, with both parties open to a move. Crow Luke Pedlar wants to join the Power. - Marc McGowan Richmond Draft picks: 2, 20, 42, 61

Key players: Jayden Short



The Tigers have already bolstered their ruck division with the free agency addition of ex-Giant Kieren Briggs, after they initially pursued his teammate Nick Madden. Briggs inked a four-year deal that positions himself as Richmond’s long-term successor for captain Toby Nankervis. Short is exploring his trade options, including meeting with Collingwood, but this masthead previously confirmed that fellow veteran Nick Vlastuin is not interested in continuing his career elsewhere. They did attempt to recruit Zak Butters, but were never considered as a genuine frontrunner. The Tigers will bring in another top talent in the draft and may be involved in some peripheral trades across the next 10 days. - Marc McGowan St Kilda Draft picks: 8, 49, 67, 85

Key players: Rowan Marshall, Mattaes Phillipou, Alix Tauru St Kilda’s Alix Tauru is talented but raw. Getty Images Fringe Lion Sam Marshall has requested a trade to the Saints, who continue to add secondary players from other clubs as they try to return to the finals. Marshall wanted to join Geelong last year and is again pursuing that move, which should eventuate this time. The Cats have so far knocked back St Kilda’s interest in Lawson Humphries and Sam De Koning, while they are also reluctant to part with their first-round selection. The Tauru saga is a fascinating one, and could still have another twist, but the likeliest outcome is he remains a Saint. Another of St Kilda’s top-10 picks, Phillipou, who is reportedly on a $1 million-a-year salary, was raised in trade dispatches, but club football boss Lenny Hayes denied he was up for grabs. Hayes also revealed it was unlikely they would broker a trade for Bulldog Rory Lobb. - Marc McGowan



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Focus on ex-Dees skipper heats up as Dons, Eagles fight it out; Dogs land defensive help for flag tilt Sydney Swans Draft picks: 36, 37, 50, 52, 74, 93

Key players: Nick Blakey Key forward Joel Amartey has already left in free agency for Carlton after the Swans traded for ex-Blue Charlie Curnow a year ago. That netted Sydney a second-round pick as compensation. The Blakey situation will remain a talking point until it gets shut down. Blakey, who is contracted for five more seasons on a lot of money, is believed to be open to a move to Geelong, but this is a complex situation and any potential deal would require the Cats giving up something significant. - Marc McGowan West Coast



Draft picks: 3, 21, 43, 56, 62, 71, 80

Key players: N/A The Eagles are actively pursuing talent to hasten their rebuild, with Jack Viney, Gryan Miers and Sam Butler among the opposition players on their wish list. They are in a two-way battle with Essendon for Viney, while they have undertaken medical testing on Miers, but he ideally wants to stay at Geelong. Hawthorn’s Butler has never played more than nine games in a season, so could be keen on a fresh start, but is contracted for one more season.
