World.title: America’s billionaires are turning their backs on Trump
World.content:
Analysis BusinessBanking & financeUS midterm elections America’s billionaires are turning their backs on Trump Jeremy Warner October 4, 2026 — 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Among the titans of global finance, none are more powerful and influential than Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JPMorgan Chase. So when he turns against Donald Trump and criticises the 47th US president’s repudiation of the old, multilateral, rules-based order, we should sit up and take notice. The more so in that Dimon’s intervention comes just a month before the congressional midterms, where the Republicans are expected to receive a hammering. US President Donald Trump’s popularity has continued to decline as the midterm elections draw closer. Bloomberg A lifelong Democrat, Dimon has admittedly never been part of Trump’s inner circle and in the past year, relations between the two have deteriorated precipitously. He played no part in the undignified and fawning scramble for presidential favours after Trump’s election two years ago. According to accounts, he wisely rebuffed soundings on serving in Trump’s second administration as Treasury secretary.



In January, moreover, Trump launched a $5bn lawsuit against Dimon and JPMorgan for allegedly de-banking him. The bank says the president’s suit “has no merit”. JPMorgan boss Jamie Dimon’s criticism of the Trump administration has become sharper off late. Bloomberg For his part, Dimon has been highly critical of Trump’s mooted plan to cap credit card interest rates at 10 per cent and he has refused to help fund Trump’s White House ballroom. But he’s also been careful not to overstep the mark and to give credit where he thinks it is due. “Take a step back, be honest,” Dimon said in the run-up to Trump’s second stab at the presidency. He “was kind of right about NATO, kind of right on immigration. He grew the economy quite well. Tax reform worked. He was right about some of China. He wasn’t wrong about some of these critical issues”.



Dimon’s remarks played a key role in rehabilitating Trump among the general run of US business leaders after the ignominy of the Capitol Hill riots. If someone as worldly, wise and seasoned as Dimon thinks Trump is basically right, then it sanitises and promotes what he stands for. Be that as it may, judging by an op-ed he wrote in the Wall Street Journal last week, he now seems to have changed his mind. While never truly an insider, Jamie Dimon has mostly maintained a cordial relation with Donald Trump. Andrew Harrer “A strong America with robust military and economic alliances is the foundation for a prosperous and peaceful world,” he wrote in an apparent rebuff of Trump’s MAGA-driven approach to allies, trade and international relations. Nor is he the only critic among those who have hitherto been relatively supportive.



In a recent interview, Peter Thiel, a long-standing Trump backer and a Republican mega donor, said he wished the president had chosen more competent people for his administration. In an interview with Mathias Dopfner, chief executive of The Telegraph’s new owner Axel Springer, the Palantir co-founder accused Trump of “over-correcting for the mistakes of the first term with all these loyalty tests. You got sort of an administration staffed by not very smart but very loyal people”. This is potentially dangerous territory for Thiel. Palantir is still highly dependent on US government contracts. But in another sign that the tide is turning against Trump-style politics, he said it anyway. Peter Thiel, a long-standing Trump backer and Republican mega donor, has also voiced concerns about the Trump administration. AP Not his words, but the sycophancy of Trump’s cabinet is worthy of a banana republic.



Dimon’s suggestion is that a grand alliance be struck with European and other like-minded democracies such as Canada, Japan, Korea, Australia and Mexico. In return for free trade with the US, Europe would agree to full implementation of proposals by former European Central Bank president Mario Draghi for countering loss of economic competitiveness, turbocharging a virtuous circle of rising prosperity for both jurisdictions. If this sounds very much like the old, post-war, pre-Trump contract, that’s because it is. It would be the Western alliance reborn and a very welcome development all round. Yet it would be unwise to count on this happening in practice: political opposition in Europe to some of Draghi’s key recommendations remains strong. But Dimon’s suggestion shows that the US is not yet entirely lost to the cause of multilateral solutions.



Related Article Opinion

Trump diplomacy How Trump’s grovelling emboldens China and imperils the Asia Pacific Peter Hartcher Political and international editor It’s similar to what Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has been suggesting, only with the US at its centre, not as a potentially hostile force kicking in the other direction. Does Trump’s presidency mark a permanent change in the geopolitical and economic weather, or is he a temporary aberration? From the very start of his second term, that’s been the big question. Dimon’s musings suggest the latter. So do the polls before next month’s midterms. The US economy is in many respects booming, but it is not an electorally friendly form of growth. The leaders in this boom, the hyperscalers of the AI arms race, are generally unpopular with voters and though their investment spending binge generates plenty of jobs, it disguises a great hinterland of economic grievance and frustration. Much higher petrol, diesel and mortgage costs are wreaking havoc with the Republican vote, and it’s Trump who is getting the blame.



Ridiculously, Trump gives himself an A+ for everything that’s happened in his second term. Sadly for him, voters do not appear inclined to agree. The president promised no more wars but then promptly started one. No matter, the Iranians would be crushed, and it would be over in weeks. Seven months later, it is still going and there is little sign of a lasting resolution. Related Article US election With a month to go, Republicans’ midterm prospects are ‘catastrophically bad’ The president promised lower interest rates and lower gas prices but all he has managed so far is the reverse. It’s true that Gulf producers have found lots of workarounds for the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Exports of crude from the region are now said to be back to virtually pre-war levels. But in all likelihood, it has come too late to save the Republican vote in the midterms.



There is still a month to go, admittedly, but scarcely anyone thinks this is time enough to reverse either current cost-of-living pressures or the electoral fortunes of the Republican Party. A cynic might say that all Dimon is doing by aligning himself with the Carney view of the world is recognising this change in the political weather. A year ago, it looked as if Trump might be one of the most consequential presidents in US history. As the months pass, that judgment looks ever more doubtful. Business leaders tend to bend with the wind. If they sense that things are going against the political incumbent, they nuance their position to fit. But Dimon, a philosophical as well as a practising globalist, has never bought into Trump’s “America first” nationalism. Trump’s loss of political momentum has given him cover to start talking his mind.



Even if he does lose both houses, Trump will presumably still attempt to govern as before through use of executive order. All the same, he’ll be tied up in legal knots for the remainder of his term and his room for manoeuvre fiscally will be tightly restricted. This should at least begin to reduce the upward pressure on interest rates. A year ago, it looked as if Trump might be one of the most consequential presidents in US history. As the months pass, that judgment looks ever more doubtful. To succeed, the West must pull and act together. Tearing it apart was never the right path. UK Telegraph, London

World.title: Why Iran could choose to escalate the war
World.content:
October 4, 2026 — 1:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In early March, nine days after starting his war with Iran, President Donald Trump held a news conference to crow about his “military success, the likes of which people haven’t seen”. “We’re winning very decisively,” he claimed, and “the result will be lower oil prices”. Instead, Trump’s Iran war should be taught for decades as a model of how not to conduct either war or foreign policy. It’s an example of how hubris can swamp a presidency and lead it to military solutions for difficult global problems – and, in the process, make everything worse. Motorcyclists in Tehran ride past a billboard showing US President Donald Trump. AP “The unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over,” Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group writes in a Foreign Affairs essay titled The New Forever War.



Still, the Trumpian myopia persists, with the administration continuing to claim that its pressure on Iran is a smashing success. “The blockade is working; it’s working like nothing we’ve ever seen,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News in September. Hmm. Diesel prices at a few places in California have hit $US9.99 ($14.40) a gallon, the maximum price those pumps can display. The United States has already spent more than $43 billion on the war, by a lowball Pentagon estimate. Higher prices caused by the war have cost the typical American family about $US1000, according to economist Mark Zandi. More broadly, the US has depleted its arsenal, cost American and Iranian lives, possibly committed war crimes, exposed American vulnerabilities, effectively lost access to some bases and weakened US military credibility as far away as East Asia. Against that, the Trump administration believes it has the upper hand because of the economic pressure the blockade is creating for Iran. Well, maybe. It’s true that the Iranian economy is a catastrophe and that ordinary Iranians – the people we are supposed to be helping – are suffering greatly. The exchange rate is now more than 2.5 million rials to the US dollar, one-tenth of the rial’s value in 2021. Yet Washington doesn’t seem to understand that instead of surrendering, Iran may choose to escalate. “They’ve come to the conclusion that the only way they survive is to shoot their way out,” said Vali Nasr, an Iran expert at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies. He suggested that Iran could increase attacks on shipping and, especially if it is attacked, strike oil infrastructure around the Persian Gulf.



I fear that Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, an Iran watcher at a British think tank, is right when he says: “Iran did not wage a scorched-earth campaign – but it may yet do so if the current situation persists for too long. That is what everyone who actually follows this region and its dynamics is worried about.” It’s difficult to see a deal being reached, partly because both Trump and Iran have a history of overreaching. It doesn’t help that Trump’s chief negotiators, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, are real estate investors chosen for their closeness to Trump rather than for, er, their diplomatic savvy. Related Article Middle East at war G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil to combat soaring fuel prices Iranian leaders also seem cocky. Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, boasted in August that Iran had brought the US “to its knees.” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC’s Meet the Press that Iran was fully prepared for a new round of fighting, “even if it comes to a doomsday war”. One rare issue on which I agree with Trump is the paramount importance of preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. In Trump’s speech to the United Nations – the one in which he mused about whether he should “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly” – he insisted that “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon”.



That’s easy to say. But Trump’s war may have actually increased the likelihood of Iran’s making a drive towards a nuclear weapon. Trump’s war began by killing the previous supreme leader, who had issued a fatwa saying that Iran would not develop nuclear weapons. The new supreme leader, his son, does not inherit that fatwa and has not issued his own, so now “there’s a serious conversation in Iran” about pursuing nuclear weapons, Nasr said. A new measure before the Iranian parliament proposes withdrawing from the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, and 32 Iranian figures have called on the country to do so. That would be a cataclysm. “Any other country but Iran would have pulled out of the NPT if treated the same way,” Araghchi told reporters. We should take these warnings seriously.



One reason professors will teach Trump’s war as an example of military malpractice is that it fits neatly into a larger pattern of counterproductive American policies towards Iran. I deplore the brutality, corruption and economic incompetence of Iran’s rulers – so it’s infuriating that America has repeatedly empowered Iranian extremists. First, the US helped topple a democratically elected prime minister in 1953, energising nationalists and souring Iranians on the West. Then in the 1960s and ’70s, the US gave Iran a nuclear reactor, backed an increasingly autocratic shah and overstepped in ways that helped allow Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini to become a national force by denouncing American imperialism. Related Article Opinion

United Nations Yes, the UN is terrible – but right now, we need it desperately Nicholas Kristof Columnist President George W. Bush’s 2003 Iraq War toppled Saddam Hussein, an enemy of Iran, and empowered Shiite militias that support Iran. In 2018, Trump announced his withdrawal from the Obama nuclear pact with Iran. The capstone in this “march of folly,” to borrow a phrase from historian Barbara Tuchman, was Trump’s war on Iran this year, which has bolstered military hard-liners in Tehran and enabled them to project greater power over the Persian Gulf and global oil markets. That’s what I find particularly worth studying: How is it that for three-quarters of a century, Americans have so bungled our foreign policy that we have systematically empowered Iranian extremists? They call us the “Great Satan,” but in truth our ineptitude has made us their benefactors.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: The mission to quadruple the number of people living in Sydney Olympic Park
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The mission to quadruple the number of people living in Sydney Olympic Park Anthony Segaert October 4, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s a place millions have been to but only 5000 call home. Sydney Olympic Park, the precinct that put its namesake city on the world map at the turn of the century, has for the most part of its two-decade history been defined by transience: just like during the Olympic Games, people leave the precinct as quickly as they arrive. But as the state government attempts to build housing in a model described by the top planning secretary as “everything, everywhere, all at once”, the authority leading Sydney Olympic Park is pushing to transform the suburb from an event destination to a living, breathing home to five times as many people as it currently holds. The plan aims to balance new homes “with the open spaces and walkable spaces”. Janie Barrett In one of the few Sydney suburbs where mangroves, a river, and vast parklands all rub up next to huge stadiums and large apartment blocks, can Sydney Olympic Park really become something new? The Sydney Olympic Park Authority’s masterplan, released earlier this year, aims to balance new homes “with the open spaces and walkable spaces”, said the body’s acting chief executive Chris Martin, who usually acts as the Department of Planning’s chief financial officer.



He says the suburb is essentially a “dormitory suburb” at present: if you live here, you’re likely to come home to sleep and then get out – but he said more housing would bring more jobs and more activities. The Brick Pit ring walk is an 18-metre high walk over the top of the old brick site, which supplied bricks for many Sydney homes. Janie Barrett An artist’s impression of the edge of the Brick Pit in the masterplan. Sydney Olympic Park Masterplan “[The goal is] to really make it that vibrant precinct that has more of a nighttime vibe, has more of a daytime vibe, and people are living and working and then relaxing and playing here as well,” he said, describing the park as an oasis. The key to making the area vibrant is to have more people living there, Planning Minister Paul Scully said.



“I think probably the big change will be the number [of] homes and jobs that were always envisaged for there, but never really took off because there hadn’t been a push,” he told a conference on Wednesday. He said he wanted the area to be recognised as an “everyday space to live, to work, and to go out and have some fun”. Chris Martin, the acting chief executive of Sydney Olympic Park Authority, on the Brick Pit Ring Walk. Janie Barrett The masterplan envisages up to 15,000 homes in the area over multiple high-rise apartments, bringing the total population to about 25,000 by 2050. But the suburb will also get two new schools and at least seven new playgrounds or parks. The government says about 26,000 jobs will be created in the area with new commercial buildings, too – a decrease from the 32,000 it promised in 2024. Grand visions of Sydney Olympic Park’s future have always been thwarted by one thing: its infrastructure. A train line does connect visitors to Lidcombe station but it runs infrequently. An extension of the second stage of the Parramatta light rail service, which the NSW Labor government promised to build, was earlier this year broken into two parts with no timeline for its arrival into the suburb. When the Metro West line opens in 2032, 25,000 passengers every hour will be able to travel between the precinct and the Sydney CBD in about 15 minutes.



Related Article City life Endure the traffic nightmare or risk a broken-down train? The great Sydney Olympic Park debate “This is project will support a vibrant community [and] match housing growth with transport and infrastructure capacity, so that people can live, work, and play close to home in a community they choose,” Scully said. Until then, Martin has some advice for people dropping by for a game or a concert: “Find a shady spot, you can throw a Frisbee. You can frolic,” he said. “Don’t just surgical strike your visit, but do your [event], then go for a wander.”

World.title: Why the Wallabies should rest their best player for opening Bledisloe at Eden Park
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Why the Wallabies should rest their best player for opening Bledisloe at Eden Park Paul Cully October 4, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1. A drawn Bledisloe series would fuel Wallabies’ belief: There is a booby prize awaiting the winner of the Wallabies-All Blacks pool stage clash at the Rugby World Cup next year - a likely quarterfinal against the Springboks. So, beating the All Blacks might not actually serve the Wallabies well at the home tournament in 2027. That said, the momentum starting to build under Kiss would be maintained if the Wallabies can go 1-1 with the All Blacks in the next two weeks. Len Ikitau is carrying an ankle injury sustained in the Wallabies’ win over South Africa. Getty Images As tempting as it must be to rush Len Ikitau back from his ankle injury, holding him back until the Sydney test might be the smarter play. A win by the Wallabies at Eden Park would be an extraordinary achievement, but a loss isn’t the end of the world if they can reverse it in Sydney. With two out of the three Bledisloe Tests set to be in Australia next year, including the Anzac Day fixture in Brisbane, winning back the famous trophy won’t be an unrealistic goal if they get one win across the line in Sydney in a fortnight.



2 Fitzy’s chat with Kiss chat taps into something valuable: Colleague Peter FitzSimons’ piece with Wallabies coach Les Kiss made me want to drape myself in an Australian flag and belt out Waltzing Matilda, even though I’m not Australian. It was stirring stuff, full of promises to play the Wallaby way and references to “the backyard spirit”. If this is not authentic it could come across as glib marketing drivel, but the Wallabies’ performances over the past five Tests suggest it is a genuine motivational tool. Les Kiss poses with the Wallabies team in Mendoza. Getty Images Kiss is obviously a technical coach as well, but in Test rugby a sense of national purpose is vital even if it gives the team an extra few per cent in performance. Can anyone other than an Australian coach deliver this messaging? Arguably not. Looking from the outside, it appears this Wallabies squad can almost feel the home Rugby World Cup next year - it has given them something tangible to aim towards, and everyone saw how the British and Lions tour lifted the players.



3 How the All Blacks could line up: Does item 2 mean a famous win at Eden Park next Saturday is on the cards? It’s not that simple, especially with the unavailable Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper representing huge losses for the Wallabies. Dave Rennie coaching the All Blacks at Eden Park in July. Phil Walter All Blacks coach Dave Rennie gave a radio interview at the weekend and was still frustrated with the tour of South Africa - both the All Blacks’ own mistakes and some of the officiating at the scrums. After three straight Test losses the All Blacks will likely attack the first Bledisloe Test with some purpose of their own. They are down a few troops with injury - notably captain Ardie Savea - but this starting XV won’t be too far from what Rennie reveals on Thursday: Damian McKenzie, Will Jordan, Quinn Tupaea, Jordie Barrett, Josh Moorby, Richie Mo’unga, Cam Roigard, Peter Lakai, Anton Segner, Tupou Vaa’i, Fabian Holland, Josh Lord, Tyrel Lomax, Codie Taylor, Ethan de Groot.



4 Waratahs cop an old-fashioned hiding: The Western Force were crowned Super Rugby AUS champions with a 53-26 win over the Waratahs, and in perfect Perth conditions they again showed what a well-run rugby team they are. New recruit Harry McLaughlin-Phillips played as if he had been in the Force system for about a decade, former Waratah Will Harris has used the competition to reinvent himself as a hard-nosed option in the second row, and midfielder Boston Fakafanua is one to watch. Fakafanua, out of the King’s School, is built low to the ground and played in the No 13 jersey on Saturday, although his long-term position could be at No 12. The Waratahs were never at the races against the Force and it was a reminder of the size of the job facing Michael Cheika, especially with NSW losing so many good players across to Perth. 5 Suaalii’s versatility could be his trump card: Cross-code star Mark Nawaqanitawase has conquered the NRL over the past few years, but there is a real logjam building in the Wallabies’ back three.



Related Article Wallabies Marky Mark has set the NRL alight. But he’ll still have to earn Wallabies spot Dylan Pietsch was the headline act in the Force’s big win over the Waratahs in the Super Rugby Aus decider after his return from injury, and it is easy to forget that he was arguably the form winger in the country before his layoff. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii also enjoyed his best Test in ages against the Springboks last week, and as remarkable as it sounds Nawaqanitawase doesn’t just walk back into the Wallabies’ best 15. Tom Wright and Max Jorgensen are banks, so in effect there is only one place up for grabs, pitting Nawaqanitawase against Suaalii, Pietsch and Harry Potter. That’s a good problem, of course, but it is still an interesting situation given the Wallabies now have two blokes with star billing who could be the face of the Rugby World Cup. In that respect, Suaalii’s ability to cover the midfield is a big advantage.

World.title: Get proper British pies at a new bayside bakery (plus three more great pie shops to try)
World.content:
Review Eating outSt Kilda Get proper British pies at a new bayside bakery (plus three more great pie shops to try) Honouring his navy chef grandfather’s knack for baking shepherd and cottage pies, Norman’s Proppa Pies co-owner Dave Pannell has added a good ol’ fashioned pie shop to his St Kilda stable. Dani Valent October 4, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1 / 11 Slow-braised beef brisket pie. Pete Dillon 2 / 11 Owners Brad Balbi (left) and Dave Pannell. Pete Dillon 3 / 11 Norman’s Proppa Pies. Pete Dillon 4 / 11 Pies are best eaten at home, with cutlery. Pete Dillon 5 / 11 Add mushy peas and gravy to your pie for a proper British feed. Pete Dillon 6 / 11 Located on Barkly Street in St Kilda. Pete Dillon 7 / 11 Beef brisket is mixed with fresh jalapenos and Stilton to make a funky, spicy blue cheese and chilli pie. Pete Dillon 8 / 11 Rhubarb and strawberry pie. Pete Dillon 9 / 11 Choose your fighter. Pete Dillon 10 / 11 Two types of sausage rolls are also on the menu. Pete Dillon 11 / 11 Inside the hole-in-the-wall pie shop. Pete Dillon Previous Slide Next Slide Norman’s Proppa Pies Bakery$$$$ Take one idyllic upbringing. Add butter. Lovingly spoon in secret ingredients. Bake until done. Open the doors and serve some of the best pies in town. That’s the basic backstory behind Norman’s Proppa Pies, a new bayside bakery owned by Dave Pannell and Brad Balbi, the pair behind St Kilda coffee-to-spritz-to-nightcap institution Sorsi e Morsi, just around the corner. It’s Pannell’s childhood being channelled. When he was a kid in the English Midlands, young Dave’s best friend was his grandfather, Norman. A navy chef who would make pies for weekend caravanning trips, Norman’s shepherd’s pies (with lamb mince) and cottage pies (with beef) were specialties, both topped with mashed potato, and often inscribed with sentimental messages. For his part, Balbi grew up in bakeries in Far North Queensland, and was roped into pie duties on weekends. When the pair started thinking about a second St Kilda operation, a pie shop seemed perfect, especially because there’s nothing similar nearby. Related Article Join the queue: 13 Melbourne cafes and bakeries worth getting in line for



Their pies are a perfect amalgam of pastry and filling, comforting but interesting, sophisticated yet hearty. Everything is house-made, including two types of pastry. The shortcrust for the base starts with boiling water, butter and vinegar, then the liquid is worked into the flour, making for a smooth, sturdy dough. The puff pastry tops are extravagantly layered and buttery rich, the pastry crisp to the bite but without shattering so dramatically that you wear more than you eat. Inside the hole-in-the-wall pie shop. Pete Dillon Beef is the bedrock, with brisket slow-braised in beef stock with 13 herbs and spices, including a secret ingredient I guessed but will refrain from sharing so I live to pie another day. The tender, lively stew is slurried with flour and tumbled into bases, ready for joy. The beefy base is also mixed with fresh jalapenos and Stilton to make a funky, spicy blue cheese and chilli pie, and a pub-style creamy green peppercorn sauce amps up another beef option. Cue pie rapture. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up There’s also an excellent butter chicken number, made with whole roast chickens (the bones go into the beef stock) plus a vegetarian cauliflower pie with three-cheese sauce. Sausage rolls are serious business so it’s good there are two: a pork version that leans British, and an Aussie-style beef one. Each is a terrific balance of fat and fab. Norman took his shepherd’s pie recipe to the grave but surely he’d be proud of this one: Lamb mince is cooked for hours with mushrooms, rosemary and bay leaves, spooned into its pastry casing, and topped with a swirl of buttery mash. To be traditional, add mushy peas and gravy. The sweet range includes a rhubarb and strawberry pie, and chocolate cream pie, an English indulgence which features custard mixed with melted chocolate to form a silky filling.



Two types of sausage rolls are also on the menu. Pete Dillon We now know about Norman but what about “proppa”? The Northern English rehash of “proper” is Geordie slang for “brilliant”. To lean even more to Blighty, Pannell and Balbi are planning to open select nights to serve the “pie and pea supper”, an alternative to the post-pub spice bag. A couple of caveats: One time I came for a potato-topped pie and it had dried out considerably in the warmer. Ask for a freshie. You also need to consider how well-placed you are to enjoy a pie with gravy, and especially with mushy peas. This is not a one-hand car situation, it’s a full-on dining project. Until bench seats are installed here, a home dining table with cutlery is ideal. Maybe that’s how it should be, anyway. So much work goes into these pies, it’s only proper they’re eaten with a little ceremony. Three more great pie shops to try Rolling Pin Pies This consistent award-winner has outlets around Geelong and the Bellarine. It just cleaned up in the gourmet categories of the Great Aussie Pie Comp with their kangaroo rendang number, the “Bombay beef” and masala mash, and a barbecued brisket, jalapeno and cheese pie. 2/3 Wyndham Street, Drysdale, rollingpin.com.au Hope Bakery It’s easier than you think to strike gold at Sovereign Hill – just head to the pie shop. A traditional wood-fired Scotch oven is used to bake Cornish pasties with apple, various steak pies and renowned sausage rolls. You’ll probably need a Banbury tart (with currants) and some miner’s biscuits, too. Bradshaw Street, Ballarat, sovereignhill.com.au Gum Tree Pies A good option, whether you’re roadtripping through Yack, where the Gum Tree production kitchen is, or swinging by outposts in Wodonga or Bright. As well as classic steak pies, there’s one with Guinness and a Sunday roast-adjacent lamb and mint pie. Vegetarians have good options, such as the Penang pumpkin and creamy cauliflower. 10 High Street, Yackandandah, gumtreepies.com.au Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.title: Cornell case revives anger about handling of campus sexual assault cases
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCourts Cornell case revives anger about handling of campus sexual assault cases Stephanie Saul and Emma Goldberg October 4, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: A lawsuit alleging rape at a Cornell University fraternity house has set off a wave of anger among women on college campuses and beyond. Campus sexual assault survivors and their supporters have published essays in school newspapers and inundated social media in solidarity with the complainant, known in court records only as Jane Doe. Some are using the familiar #MeToo hashtag of an earlier movement to combat sexual abuse and harassment. Others have adopted a new one: #IAmJaneDoe. A survey by Cornell University found that about one-third of undergraduate women said they had had unwanted sexual experiences. AP Photo/Matt Rourke In one opinion article in the University of Pennsylvania campus newspaper, students wrote that “sexual violence happens far too often on college campuses everywhere”.



“It’s time to face the fact that the ‘Cornell incident’ isn’t just born of Cornell problems, or limited to a Cornell issue,” the students wrote. Related Article Crime ‘Heinous’: Frat house gang-rape lawsuit triggers reopening of criminal investigation The outrage flooding social media and rising up on campuses follows similar waves of disgust about campus sexual violence that emerged more than a decade ago and then reignited after the broader #MeToo reckoning that began with Hollywood sexual assault revelations. Driving the campaign in support of Doe is a feeling that not enough changed after similar movements. The Penn students wrote, for example, that past responses have been bureaucratic, and that universities “prioritise bolstering their own image” instead of making deeper changes that protect women from assault. Celebrities have also joined the outcry. Mariska Hargitay and her Joyful Heart Foundation, which supports domestic violence survivors, posted: “Survivors deserve to be believed and kept informed. Silence protects no one. To her: we support you.”



During an appearance in Ithaca, New York, Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called the 2024 episode at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house part of a “culture of rape” on college campuses. In the lawsuit, the young woman says she was assaulted at the Chi Phi house on Cornell’s campus, names seven men who were allegedly involved and says the university and law enforcement agencies did not do enough to punish or pursue prosecution of the men. New York Governor Kathy Hochul, left, has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to take over investigating the case. Bloomberg The men involved have denied the allegations, while the university, the fraternity and prosecutors have said they had responded appropriately given the information they had at the time. Lawyers point out the difficulty of prosecuting such cases in court, particularly when many complainants, including Doe, change their accounts over time. Records obtained by The New York Times present a murky picture of what took place. The woman indicated in one text message to one of the men that “nothing illegal” had happened. But she also told police investigators that “I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped”.



The widespread condemnation of accused men could create an unfair dynamic, according to Andrew T. Miltenberg, a lawyer for one of the Cornell men, Gillio Lopes. He said the “danger in a case like this is that an accusation, amplified often enough, can harden into a verdict before the evidence is ever tested”. Related Article Crime Unsealed documents detail Cornell investigation into alleged rape at fraternity house Miltenberg, known for representing students against sexual misconduct claims, said the attention had been compounded by statements of public officials that seemed to side with Doe. On September 28, New York Attorney-General Letitia James posted on the social platform X: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and prayers.” Several days later, New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed James to take over investigating the case.



Lopes unequivocally denied the allegations, Miltenberg said. The online outpouring in support of Doe has also led to a backlash. Some right-wing commentators condemn her and others are trying to reveal her identity. ‘It’s time to face the fact that the ‘Cornell incident’ isn’t just born of Cornell problems, or limited to a Cornell issue.’ University of Pennsylvania students Federal data shows that nationally, there were 6000 to 6200 reports of rapes on campus a year from 2014 to 2019, or about eight to 11 per 10,000 on-campus students. But reports declined drastically during the pandemic years, when many students took classes remotely. Since then, they have begun to rise again. The data does not show how many reports resulted in action or were substantiated.



But the available data suggests the problem has been widespread. Over a quarter of undergraduate women reported some form of non-consensual sexual contact by physical force, or because they were unable to consent, according to a large survey of students conducted by the Association of American Universities in 2019. That survey also found evidence of a growing awareness about rules and resources, as universities built out new policies and training. The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University. AP At Cornell, a survey conducted by the university found that about one-third of undergraduate women said they had had unwanted sexual experiences. Reading Doe’s claims of assault has prompted some current Cornell students and recent graduates to share memories of their own experiences of sexual misconduct. Many said the allegations weren’t entirely surprising because of how often they had heard about friends who said they had been assaulted at parties.



“To be honest, there are so many during my time there that it almost feels like it all blurs into one,” said Claire Ting, who graduated from Cornell last year and served in student government, referring to conversations with friends about upsetting sexual experiences. “We would see posts and discussions talking about the sexual assaults that happened,” she said. “The buzz would die down, and then it would happen again.” The response, she said, was “hurdle after hurdle of bureaucracy”. There have been other moments in recent decades when campus sexual assault has dominated the national conversation. When the documentary The Hunting Ground was released in 2015, for example, it galvanised a movement. Lady Gaga sang the film’s theme song at the Oscars, where she was introduced by then-vice president Joe Biden. At the time, statistics showed that one in four women on campus reported being victims of sexual assault. Just months before the film’s release, the launch of a White House campaign to end campus sexual assault – “It’s On Us” – seemed to signal a changing tide.



More than a decade later, though, the allegations at Cornell prompted questions among survivors about whether anything has changed. Kacey Lee, who graduated from Cornell in 2025, said she was “shocked and not shocked” in the autumn of 2024 when she heard about Doe’s reported assault. The Hunting Ground featured a freshman who brought sexual assault claims against Jameis Winston, who is now the starting quarterback of the New York Giants. Winston, who denied misconduct, was not prosecuted in the case. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II “Being around frat culture and knowing how people can be there was a level of – not that I was expecting it, but I was not the most surprised,” Lee said. While federal data shows that Cornell has reported as many as 28 campus rapes in some recent years, its on-campus undergraduate population is the largest of any Ivy League school. When adjusted for its size, Cornell mirrors many of its peer institutions.



Cornell officials have said they disciplined the men after investigating Doe’s allegations but they didn’t provide details. They have defended their response and cautioned against a “false narrative”, which they said could depress reports of sexual assault. In a message on its website, the university said it had strengthened its policies on sexual assault in recent years. “Our goal is not simply to respond appropriately when sexual misconduct is reported,” the school said, “but to build a community in which sexual violence is prevented, people feel safe coming forward, those who do are supported, and individuals found responsible are held accountable.” Social media platforms are where the original #MeToo movement gained steam, a little less than a decade ago, spurred by disturbing disclosures about film producer Harvey Weinstein. Adam Gray/POOL Bloomberg via AP Elise Siemering, who has said she was raped 14 years ago by a fellow student at High Point University in North Carolina, said she found comfort in the social media outpouring. “The women and men who say, ‘I am Jane Doe’, it gives you a glimmer of hope that there are people in our nation who try to shield her as much as they can,” said Siemering, who was among more than 30 people who told their stories in the 2016 book We Believe You.



Annie E. Clark, whose allegations of sexual assault at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill served as the basis for The Hunting Ground, said this past week that the growth of social media had, in some ways, helped women. “With the advent of social media, more people are sharing their stories and know that they are not alone,” said Clark, co-founder of the organisation End Rape on Campus. Indeed, social media platforms are where the original #MeToo movement gained steam, a little less than a decade ago, spurred by disturbing disclosures about film producer Harvey Weinstein. Researchers at the University of Chicago documented the role of #MeToo on social media as a catalyst for social change, noting that the hashtag was used on Twitter, now X, 19 million times in 2017 and 2018, the first year of the movement, and in dozens of different languages. The hashtag became “a sign of empowerment for victims who may have feared they were alone,” the researchers found.



But since then, a series of federal regulatory changes has created instability in the handling of campus sexual assault cases, according to End Rape on Campus chief executive Kenyora Johnson. Referring to the release of The Hunting Ground, she said, “Eleven years later, we’re still talking about survivors struggling to be heard.” Cornell University student Jane Wang (left) told a Cornell student government forum on Thursday that she saw herself reflected in Jane Doe’s experiences. AP The film was released shortly after a highly publicised incident at Florida State University. It featured a first-year student who brought sexual assault claims against Jameis Winston, who is now the starting quarterback of the New York Giants. Before that accusation became public, a second woman had sought counselling after reporting a sexual encounter with Winston, saying that she felt violated by the incident.



Winston, who denied misconduct, was not prosecuted in the case, although a story in the Times raised questions about law enforcement handling of the inquiry. In 2016, Florida State and Winston settled lawsuits filed by his accuser, according to reports at the time. Although many of Cornell’s current students and recent graduates are too young to remember the #MeToo movement, they expressed frustration about the pervasiveness of sexual violence around them. At a Cornell student government forum on Thursday afternoon, junior Jane Wang came forward and said she saw herself reflected in Doe’s experiences. “I cannot speak on behalf of all survivors because the pain, hurts and trauma that each of us carries is our own,” Wang told the student government representatives. Students warned one another about the risks of fraternity parties immediately when they got to Cornell, said Hannah Shvets, a senior who also serves on the Ithaca Common Council. Young women, she suggested, are largely left to fend for themselves.



“From the day we get to campus there’s awareness – be cautious, go in groups,” she said. “Students feel like often fraternities can partake in behaviour that other clubs or organisations would get shut down if they did.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Labour releases its fiscal plan, promises pay rise for care and social workers
World.content:
Labour has released its long-awaited fiscal plan, saying every promise its made is "fully costed and paid for" - but it hasn't provided a cost for fully re-implementing pay equity legislation.

It does however promise an immediate pay rise to 65,000 care and support workers, costing $2.5 billion over four years, and Labour leader Chris Hipkins says there's "plenty of headroom" within the plan to pay for pay equity overall.

Finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds says Labour will keep operating allowances at the $2.4 billion set by the coalition government in Budget 2026.

The party said it wouldn't rely on a larger operating allowance, stating new investment "must fit within these allowances, alongside cost pressures and other priorities".

"Our announced capital commitments fit comfortably within the $12 billion of future capital allowances," said Edmonds.

"We also have almost $10.5 billion of future operating allowances unallocated. We can deliver what we have promised without increasing those allowances."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406191627112

Edmonds also said Labour would return the books to surplus in 2028/29 and bring net debt down below 20 percent of GDP "over time", maintaining it will use the OBEGAL measure, rather than the government's preferred OBEGALx measure.

"We can do that because we have made better choices about where public money goes and will make every dollar work harder."

Labour said it's announced capital commitments were:

$200 million capital injection for the New Zealand Future Fund

$420 million for the initial student loan write-off

$200 million for hospitals

$400 million for schools

$2.9 billion for Kāinga Ora housing, spread over four years

$7 million for Ratepayer Assistance Scheme (RAS) solar expenditure

On Sunday the party also reconfirmed its plan to restore Pay Equity legislation in its first 100 days.

Leader Chris Hipkins said National promised to grow the economy and get the books in order: "it has done neither."

"171,000 New Zealanders are unemployed, growth is weaker and debt has continued to rise. They have cut jobs and services, and New Zealanders have been left to pay the price."

Hipkins said the choice was clear: "More cuts and decline under National, or a Labour Government that will balance the books without shrinking the economy, get costs under control and back the people and businesses doing the work."

Edmonds reiterated that every election commitment Labour had made was fully costed and fully funded.

"The numbers add up and we have left room to confidently respond to whatever comes next," she added.

World.title: Te Pāti Māori announces 'one-person' party list for 2026 election
World.content:
Te Pāti Māori says it's putting its "money where its mouth is" by announcing a "one-person" party list.

The list announcement for the 2026 General Election came on Sunday morning, with only Lance Norman, General Secretary of Te Pāti Māori, selected "unanimously" as the additional list candidate.

The party said it was "reaffirming its candidate-vote strategy" by selecting just one list candidate outside its candidates for the seven Māori electorate.

"This list proves we are putting our money where our mouth is," Te Pāti Māori Co-Leader Rawiri Waititi said.

"We made a deliberate decision to put collective Māori representation ahead of building a long party list."

"We said this election is bigger than any one party. Our list reflects that commitment," Co-Leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said.

She asked supporters to cast their candidate vote for Te Pāti Māori and party vote for Green or Labour.

"We are backing our seven candidates to win the Māori electorates and standing by the strategy we announced to our people."

In August, the party urged supporters to give their candidate vote to TPM, and their party vote to the left bloc.

At the time, Waititi suggested the party's strategy could see up to 13 Māori MPs get into power.

The strategy could lead to the creation of an overhang, where there are more seats in Parliament.

Earlier this year, Labour's Māori campaign chair Willie Jackson criticsed the approach, saying it threatened a backlash against the Māori seats that could lead to their abolition "when you start working the system like that".

World.title: ACT pledges removing tax on KiwiSaver earnings
World.content:
The ACT Party has promised to remove tax on KiwiSaver earnings.

Leader David Seymour has unveiled the policy during ACT's campaign launch in Auckland on Sunday.

He said it would allow people's returns to stay invested and generate savings for generations.

"Other parties want to force your money into KiwiSaver, then tax you," he said.

"ACT says it should be your choice, but if you save for the future we will let you get the full benefit of compounding returns instead of taxing you every step of the way."

Seymour said long-term investments benefit from the "magic" of compound interest.

"Interest on interest, year after year, grows your KiwiSaver balance exponentially," he said.

"Every time you get taxed on your earnings you don't just lose that money, but all the future savings that would be compounded from it."

Seymour used the example of a 20-year-old builder earning $60,000 salary, who would save an extra $209,486 by the time they turned 65 under the policy.

ACT would also end the KiwiSaver government contribution for members who receive employer contributions, and replace it with the new tax relief.

The whole plan would cost about $2.4b over four years (including the benefits gained from ending the government contribution).

ACT's fully costed fiscal plan will be released later in the election campaign, its policy document said.

World.title: Greens eye free, fast and reliable public transport with election promises
World.content:
The Green Party has pledged to make public transport free for eligible groups and cap bus and train fares at $2 for everyone else.

It says its transport plan offers fast, frequent and affordable services.

Under the Greens' policy, public transport would be free for children, students, apprentices, Community Service Card holders and Total Mobility users, while everyone else would pay a maximum fare of $2.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406186515112

It would also build mass rapid bus and light rail services in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, offer more frequent inter-regional bus services, strengthen rural bus services and allow councils to pedestrianise more inner-city areas and increase safe walking and biking spaces.

The party has also promised overnight passenger trains from Auckland to Wellington, as well as bringing back the Southerner between Christchurch and Dunedin and extending Te Huia to Tauranga.

"In the middle of a fossil fuel crisis, these common sense investments will save New Zealanders money, stress and time," said co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick.

"It'll cut emissions and improve quality of life."

Swarbrick and transport spokesperson Julie-Anne Genter addressed media in Auckland on Sunday from outside Maungawhau City Rail Link station.

Swarbrick referred to the more than a million trips that have been taken on the CRL since it opened last month.

"What that tells us and shows us so clearly is that when we build transport infrastructure that makes it easy, affordable, and even fun to get around, people will use it.

"But right now, too many New Zealanders are driving around with the fuel light on, hoping and praying that petrol prices will drop," she said.

Swarbrick said the government could not control oil shocks like that caused by the Middle East war - but it could make investments that reduce the cost of living and reduce dependence on fossil fuels.

She described the party's plan as "straight up common sense".

Swarbrick said meaningful change could be made immediately, but some parts of the plan like light rail networks could take a decade or so.

The major investments would go through the Infrastructure Commission's assurance process, she said.

The entire plan would cost around $23.9b: $21b for mass rapid transit and rail investments, $1.3b for capped and free fares, $75m for electric buses, $290m for councils to expand walking and biking spaces, $824m for public transport improvements and $406m for inter-regional buses.

"What we are proposing today is to meet the needs not only of our immediate cost of living crisis, but also our medium and longer term needs to build infrastructure that is fit for purpose for the future. Yes, that will cost money," Swarbrick said.

She cited the Greens' wealth tax as a way of paying for some of it, but said the party's full fiscal plan would be laid out in the next few weeks.

World.title: National promises $1.75b to build Mill Road as part of  Roads of National Significance
World.content:
National is promising to start construction on Mill Road, one of its Roads of National Significance, if it leads the next government.

It will allocate $1.75 billion in Budget 2028 so construction can begin in late 2028, and look to progress route protection on Stages Two and Three by allocating $100 million.

The Mill Road highway has been dogged in controversy for nearly two decades with political flip-flopping about building it, legal battles launched by climate advocacy groups and nearly 300 property owners left in uncertainty.

National's transport spokesperson Chris Bishop said "after years of debate and discussion about Mill Road, National in government is getting on with it".

Mill Road was one of the projects relegated to the slow lane in July as part of a "phased approach" to the Roads of National Significance (RONS) delivery, after questions over cost and implementation saw the government "recalibrate people's expectations".

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406182202112

Making the announcement on Auckland's Redoubt Road alongside the National leader Christopher Luxon on Sunday, Bishop said Mill Road was an important Road of National Significance that was part of the government's Major Transport Projects Pipeline, included in the Auckland City Deal, as well as NZTA's Auckland Strategic Motorway Plan.

Stage One was between Manukau and Alfriston, while Stages Two and Three were between Alfriston and Drury.

Some residents living near the site of the proposed four-lane highway say it can't be built soon enough.

Greg Simmons says traffic congestion is a nightmare at the moment. He says it can take half an hour just to travel three kilometres to State Highway 1.

"In the 24 years that we've been here, we've just seen exponential growth of population and it's the only place they can feed on. There have been times when the motorway has been closed because of an accident and no one can get into town.

"I just think it's just going to help the whole of South Auckland commercially because time is money and even courier drivers spend so much time just sitting in traffic. The whole area just grinds to a halt on a regular basis," Simmons said.

Bishop said South Auckland was one of the fastest growing parts of the country.

"Drury is at the centre of that growth, but the roading network hasn't kept up."

He said people travelling between Drury, Papakura and Manukau are funnelled onto an "already congested Southern Motorway," while roads like Redoubt Road and the existing Mill Road were built for a "semi-rural community, not tens of thousands of new households."

Bishop said Mill Road would "change that", and once completed, would be a new four-lane, 21.5km corridor running alongside State Highway 1 from Manukau to Drury, "crushing congestion, improving safety, and unlocking land for the homes and jobs the region needs."

The New Zealand Transport Agency estimated Stage One of Mill Road would reduce congestion by 30 percent on that corridor, Bishop added, as well as cut journey times by 25 percent and result in the reduction of more 60 percent of deaths and serious injuries.

Bishop said National would allocate $1.75 billion in Budget 2028 so construction can begin "in the late-2028 construction season."

Currently, NZTA was completing the design work and taking the project through the fast-track process to secure the consents it needs, he explained.

"The commitment to Mill Road builds on the strong progress National has made on transport across Auckland over the last three years.

"We're building the transport infrastructure Auckland needs for the future."

Speaking to reporters after the announcement, Bishop was asked whether he expected the costs to blow out, but he said no.

"NZTA is actually getting good sharp pricing on projects at the moment."

He said one of the reasons was the fast-track regime.

"For example, they're now getting a lot greater certainty over when projects can start, and they're now getting much more proportionate consenting conditions."

He said costs blow out because consenting gets so expensive.

Asked when people would actually be able to drive the road, Bishop said "a few years after" construction started in 2028.

"But the point is to get on with it."

Bishop acknowledged the project was on again off again for years, but said it hadn't progressed in the last three years because it wasn't consented and wasn't ready for construction.

He blamed labour for putting "barely half the amount of money required" toward it in 2020.

In terms of funding the rest of the RONS, Bishop said the party would fund and construct those roads "over time".

"We've always talked about it as a long-term pipeline of projects to build the future of this great country.

"They were never all going to start at the same time."

World.title: Two men jump into river after failing to stop for Police
World.content:
Police in the Ōpōtiki area in the Bay of Plenty are appealing for sightings of two men who failed to stop for officers before jumping in a river.

Duty Inspector Phil Edwards said about 3.45am on Sunday a vehicle ran a red light in Wainui.

"Road spikes were successfully deployed about 10km from Ōpōtiki shortly after 4am, before the vehicle came to a stop down Snell Road, by the Otara River," he said.

"The two occupants have then got out of the vehicle and jumped into the water."

A search and rescue operation was launched, with assistance from the Harbourmaster, Coastguard Ōpōtiki, and a rescue helicopter, but the two men have not been found.

"Police Search and Rescue staff are continuing the search this morning, and are appealing to the public for help," Edwards said.

Edwards said a "large-scale" operation was underway and police had searched the river and deployed helicopters and ground crew across farmland to find the men.

"If you are one of these males, you know who they are, or you have any other information which may help us locate them, please get in touch. We're also after information about any suspicious behaviour in the area."

Edwards said the priority at this time was ensuring the men were safe.

Urgent information could be passed on via 111, referencing job number P067829874.

World.title: Healthcare 'roady' seeks first-hand accounts from concerned communities
World.content:
An advocate is concerned local communities are unable to access healthcare due to growing pressure on the public system.

Kaitiaki Hauora - "guardians of health" in te reo Māori - will host the first public meeting in the Save Our Public Healthcare Roady on Sunday.

Malcolm Mulholland and David Galler will travel from Bluff to Cape Reinga between 4 and 17 October.

The tour will begin in Invercargill at 4.30pm on Sunday before heading to Gore, Dunedin, Timaru, Christchurch, Westport, Nelson, Lower Hutt, Masterton, New Plymouth, Whanganui, Palmerston North, Napier, Gisborne, Tauranga, Whakatāne, Taupō, Rotorua, Tokoroa, Hamilton, Thames, Auckland, Dargaville, Whangārei and Kaitaia.

Mulholland told RNZ he hoped to hear from people about their local hospitals and access to healthcare, as well as what was happening to health services in their communities.

"There's been no shortage of concern around what is happening at the moment, and we want to hear first-hand what the experiences have been of different communities around the country," he said.

While Mulholland hoped that politicians would listen to these, and develop policies to address them, ahead of the general election on 7 November, he said that the group was not advocating for any particular outcome.

He wanted to ensure that local voices were heard in the wider national conversation, Mulholland said.

"People are really concerned about the state of the public health system. They're worried about the level of funding and where that funding is being directed. They're worried about the creep of privatisation, and they're also worried about Māori not having a voice, especially when so many of our statistics will tell you that Māori are adversely affected when it comes to health."

Mulholland said up to 300 people had attended a public meeting in the lower North Island after six staff resigned from Pahīatua Medical Centre [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/health/1533862/locals-voice-concerns-about-pahiatua-medical-centre-at-public-meeting

in Tararua], which almost 5000 patients had depended on.

"They're all very concerned about where they're going to go in order to be seen, in order for their health needs to be met."

Around 300 people attended a community meeting regarding challenges at Pahīatua Medical Centre. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

While he was not sure how many would attend the roadshow, Mulholland said he would be happy with "just a few people".

World.title: Up There Cazaly singer vowed to make AFL grand final after horrific fall
World.content:
He is a name synonymous with the AFL grand final.

While teams change, pre-game acts change and even the rules themselves change, Mike Brady's performance of unofficial AFL anthem Up There Cazaly has been a fixture of the big day for decades.

Last weekend's grand final was no different — but that was not always a given.

In January, the 78-year-old suffered a horrific fall during a routine evening walk near his Great Ocean Road home.

Mike Brady performed on ABC's Countdown program in 1979 to promote his Up There Cazaly single. (ABC News)

"I fell and landed on my ample backside," he said, laughing.

But the injury was no laughing matter.

Brady described the horror of having to twist his ankle back into place before dragging himself to a nearby fire station, "leaving a trail of blood and mud".

Brady would later learn he had fractured his leg, ankle and foot in 12 places.

With his doctor telling him not to push himself and that it was unlikely he would be able to walk anytime soon, his grand final call-up nine months later was all but certainly out of the picture.

When the AFL asked if he would still be up to performing, he vowed to be there even if he had to crawl on stage.

"I said, 'Try and stop me,'" he said.

"Because I love it. It's a part of me."

'The place was closing in on me'

Mike Brady performed during the 2022 AFL grand final match between Geelong and Sydney. (Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

A self-described "outdoors person" who relishes being active, Brady is the first to admit that even he doubted he would make it during parts of the nine-month journey that followed.

"I wasn't doing well," he said.

"I was waking up and felt like the place was closing in on me.

" I was put in a palliative care place, and that was tough because I felt like I shouldn't be there. "

After five months in hospital, he was able to return home with the help of a wheelchair.

He slowly transitioned to crutches, and now mostly gets around using a walking stick.

But Brady defied all expectations and ditched the walking stick to walk out on stage on September 26.

Mike Brady was interviewed about his famed football anthem in 2002. (ABC News)

The 100,000-strong crowd gave him the strength not just to walk, he said, but to fly.

"At the beginning of the song, I'm singing it kind of normally, but then I thought, 'I've got this, I'm going to be able to sing it!'

"I sang harder than I've ever sung before.

"One hundred thousand people reacted, and the roar — I've never heard anything like it.

"It was fantastic. I felt absolutely vindicated for pushing myself so hard."

Musician vows to perform for years to come

Mike Brady performed at the 1979 VFL grand final. (Supplied)

Brady says he is not one to dwell on the past and spent much of his recovery writing new poetry and music.

But many hours alone with his thoughts left him to reminisce on a career he never expected.

As an English immigrant, Brady moved to Melbourne at the age of 11.

The musician and jingle-maker had never even been to a full AFL game when he was asked to create a tune to market the Victorian Football League.

"What an honour," he said.

He went on to pen what would become a footy phenomenon.

Recalling the day he first performed Up There Cazaly at the 1979 VFL grand final, introduced by his friend John Farnham, Brady said it was the first time he felt truly at home in the country he had lived in for nearly two decades.

"I really felt like I belonged in Australia," he said.

"I'd never felt that before. But hearing men and women in the crowd shouting, 'Good on ya, Mike', I really felt the warmth."

Mike Brady says the 1979 VFL grand final, which featured Carlton legend Alex Jesaulenko (pictured), was a key moment in his Up Their Cazaly journey. (Getty Images)

Even 48 years later, the feeling remains every time the words "up there cazaly" leave his mouth.

"I often say the smile on my face when I sing it is actually me chuckling at the irony," he said.

"I love the irony of being a Pommy immigrant that was taken to heart by so many Australian people, and if that's not a great honour, I don't know what is."

While the honour of performing the track has been handed to other performers over the years, he wants to perform for the next two years, taking it to the song's 50-year anniversary and his own 80th birthday.

"I just hope the crowd is as kind to me as they have been for all those 48 years," he said.

In fact, Brady was more determined than ever to take to the stage this year, fearing the AFL might not ask him back if he did not.

If the crowd's reaction was anything to go by, it was an unlikely fear.

World.title: Aussie duo and new world number one fall at China Open
World.content:
Australian women's involvement at the China Open is down to just one singles player after Kimberly Birrell and Storm Hunter were both second-round casualties.

World number 41 Birrell suffered a 6-4, 6-4 loss to Czech Marie Bouzkova at the WTA 1000 event in Beijing on Saturday night.

Birrell, 28, who won the Korea Open last Sunday with a win over compatriot Maya Joint in the final, raced out to a 3-1 first-set lead before dropping serve twice to lose it in 42 minutes.

Down 3-0 in the second, Birrell lifted and won the next four games but was broken twice more to see her involvement in the Chinese capital come to a premature end.

For Bouzkova, the 28-year-old 18th seed, a meeting with China's Zheng Qinwen awaits.

The 2024 Olympic champion was leading Anna Kalinskaya 6-7 (4/7), 6-4, 3-0 when the Russian retired.

Earlier, Queensland veteran and former doubles world number one Storm Hunter was beaten 6-2, 6-2 by Maria Sakkari in just 73 minutes.

The 182nd-ranked Hunter failed to join 20-year-old fellow Aussie Taylah Preston in round three, losing serve six times in her latest hardcourt tournament clash in Asia.

Next up for Sakkari, the Greek 25th seed and former world number three, is Elina Svitolina.

The sixth-seeded Ukrainian came from a set down to eliminate Czech Katerina Siniakova, 1-6, 6-4, 6-2.

Shock of the day came with newly crowned world number one Elena Rybakina crashing out ‌3-6, 6-4, 6-3 to unseeded Alina Charaeva in the second round.

It couldn't have been a worse start to her reign as the number one as Rybakina lost in her first match since defeating four-times major winner Aryna Sabalenka to capture the US Open title last month.

Charaeva, a 24-year-old Russian-born Armenian ranked 118th ​in the world, etched her name into the record books by becoming the lowest-ranked competitor since the introduction of the WTA rankings in 1975 to rally from a set down to defeat a world number one.

Elsewhere, there were wins for third seed Coco Gauff, eighth seed Iga Swiatek, 21st seed Ann Li and 24th seed Jelena Ostapenko.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: NRL and NRLW grand final day has arrived. Here's what you need to know
World.content:
The final day of the NRL and NRLW seasons is here. The grand finals for the men and women will be held today.

In the women's decider, the Sydney Roosters and Brisbane Broncos face off in a rematch of last year's grand final.

In the men's grand final, the Sydney Roosters are facing the Newcastle Knights.

Here's everything you need to know about NRL and NRLW grand finals day.

What time are the NRL and NRLW grand finals?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals will be held on Sunday, October 4, the first day of daylight saving time in many states and territories across the country.

Here is when each grand final begins in each state and territory.

NRL grand final

7:30pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

7pm ACDT: South Australia

6:30pm: Queensland

6pm: Northern Territory

4:30pm: Western Australia

NRLW grand final

4pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

3:30pm ACDT: South Australia

3pm: Queensland

2:30pm: Northern Territory

1pm: Western Australia

How can you watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 9 and 9Now, but be aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire NRL season that is exclusive to Channel 9.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

Where are the NRL and NRLW grand finals being played?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals are being played at Stadium Australia in Sydney.

Stadium Australia has hosted every NRL grand final since 1999, with the exception of the 2021 decider which was played at Brisbane's Lang Park during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since the NRLW's inception in 2018, all grand finals have been played at Stadium Australia, again with 2021 being the exception. That decider was played at Dolphin Stadium in Redcliffe.

Who is playing in the NRL grand final?

The Sydney Roosters face the Newcastle Knights for the NRL premiership.

The Roosters finished the season fourth on the ladder, and lost their opening match of the finals before victories over Cronulla and the Dolphins.

The Newcastle Knights finished seventh on the ladder. After defeating Souths in the first week of the finals, the Knights went to Auckland and defeated the Warriors, then beat Penrith while being down to 12 players for all of the second half.
